Evaluated on a decade of southeast Texas rainfall, it produces close counterparts for 4-5% of the most severe 2% of storms, compared with 3% for stochastic storm transposition.
AI.motivation: Historically rare storms are occurring with unprecedented frequency, while infrastructure is designed around short observational records that sparse data cannot adequately represent.
AI.method: A generative machine-learning model transforms an observed storm's initial hours into complete hourly rainfall lifecycles in minutes, with the aim of producing physically plausible scenarios.
AI.result: StormGen produced close counterparts for 4-5% of the most severe 2% of storms, compared with 3% for stochastic storm transposition, and maintained spatial coherence over full 24-hour sequences. From a single hour of initial rainfall it reconstructed the lifecycle, spatial pattern, and extreme catchment totals of Hurricane Harvey, although Harvey is entirely absent from training.
AI.conclusion: Complete generated scenarios give a way to stress-test flood protections against unprecedented extremes, since storm timing alone can more than double peak flows.

title: What We Keep of What We Forget: Replacement Operators and Routing Semantics in Training-Free MoE Expert Pruning
summary: Training-free expert pruning makes two decisions: which experts to remove, and what the layer computes when its router still selects a removed expert. Published methods change both at once. Holding the mask fixed, we compare replacement operators from three families on OLMoE, DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Moonlight, with Granite as a fourth router, using paired, multiplicity-corrected tests. The largest effect is a choice usually left implicit: the survivors' gate scale. On routers trained without top-k renormalization, renormalizing the survivors' gates, a common implementation choice, costs 0.8-8.5 points and reverses whether rerouting beats MoNE's mean-output replacement; on two routers trained with renormalization, the trained scale wins at 50% pruning. We introduce the tilted novice, a closed-form low-rank map of the pruned expert's input whose rank-0 case is MoNE's constant. At 50% pruning it adds 1.2-1.8% parameters and gains 3.45 and 1.37 points over the constant on OLMoE and Moonlight, stable across calibration draws and largely unchanged by 4- and 3-bit quantization. No operator dominates: trained-scale rerouting is best on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and a partial copy of each pruned expert is statistically indistinguishable from the tilted novice on two models. Evaluation can change conclusions: at 25% pruning MoNE's constant keeps 92-97% of dense multiple-choice accuracy but only 5-65% of GSM8K and 0-17% of code scores, and the calibration domain moves the mask 4-9 times more than resampling. We propose a five-item reporting checklist.

AI.tldr: The paper compares replacement operators for training-free mixture-of-experts expert pruning with the mask held fixed, and finds that the survivors' gate scale is the largest effect. It introduces the tilted novice, a closed-form low-rank replacement that adds 1.2-1.8% parameters at 50% pruning and gains 3.45 and 1.37 points over the constant replacement on OLMoE and Moonlight.
AI.motivation: Published training-free expert pruning methods change both which experts are removed and what the layer computes when the router still selects a removed expert, so the two effects are confounded.
AI.method: With the mask fixed, the paper compares replacement operators from three families on OLMoE, DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Moonlight, with Granite as a fourth router, using paired, multiplicity-corrected tests. It introduces the tilted novice, a closed-form low-rank map of the pruned expert's input whose rank-0 case is MoNE's constant.
AI.result: On routers trained without top-k renormalization, renormalizing the survivors' gates costs 0.8-8.5 points and reverses whether rerouting beats MoNE's mean-output replacement; on two routers trained with renormalization, the trained scale wins at 50% pruning. The tilted novice gains 3.45 and 1.37 points over the constant on OLMoE and Moonlight, stable across calibration draws and largely unchanged by 4- and 3-bit quantization. No operator dominates. At 25% pruning, MoNE's constant keeps 92-97% of dense multiple-choice accuracy but only 5-65% of GSM8K and 0-17% of code scores, and the calibration domain moves the mask 4-9 times more than resampling does.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation choices can change conclusions in expert pruning studies, and the paper proposes a five-item reporting checklist.

title: Anomalies as Residuals: Cauchy Displacement Networks
summary: Neighbourhood-based detectors such as KNN, LOF and LUNAR remain among the most accurate methods for tabular anomaly detection, but they compare every query with the stored training set, so their inference cost and memory grow with the data and the data must be kept at deployment. We ask whether the neighbourhood geometry these detectors exploit can be compiled into a small network that scores a query with a single forward pass. We propose the Cauchy Displacement Network (CDN), which regresses each normal point onto the mean of its $k$ nearest training neighbours with a single-hidden-layer network of Cauchy activations and scores a query by the length of its predicted displacement. This displacement is an empirical mean-shift vector, whose fixed-radius population counterpart locally approximates a scaled gradient of the log density. We show that Cauchy units exactly represent the score fields of a structured family of Student-$t$ expert densities, and establish a constructive approximation bound for the corresponding population neighbourhood-mean map using a single-hidden-layer Cauchy network. We further show that the bounded network output guarantees asymptotically linear residual-score growth along every fixed direction. On 46 benchmark datasets against 28 baselines, CDN obtains the best mean rank under both AUC-ROC and AUC-PR, while scoring $10^4$ queries in a few milliseconds on a single CPU thread, up to three orders of magnitude faster than neighbourhood-based detectors, with a model whose size does not depend on the training set.

AI.tldr: The Cauchy Displacement Network (CDN) compiles the neighbourhood geometry of tabular anomaly detectors into a single-hidden-layer network that scores a query in one forward pass, by regressing each normal point onto the mean of its k nearest training neighbours and scoring by the length of the predicted displacement. On 46 benchmark datasets against 28 baselines it obtains the best mean rank under both AUC-ROC and AUC-PR.
AI.motivation: Neighbourhood-based detectors such as KNN, LOF and LUNAR are among the most accurate methods for tabular anomaly detection, but their inference cost and memory grow with the data, which must be kept at deployment.
AI.method: CDN regresses each normal point onto the mean of its k nearest training neighbours with a single-hidden-layer network of Cauchy activations and scores a query by the length of its predicted displacement. Cauchy units exactly represent the score fields of a structured family of Student-t expert densities.
AI.result: On 46 benchmark datasets against 28 baselines, CDN obtains the best mean rank under both AUC-ROC and AUC-PR, and it scores 10^4 queries in a few milliseconds on a single CPU thread, up to three orders of magnitude faster than neighbourhood-based detectors, with a model whose size does not depend on the training set.
AI.conclusion: Neighbourhood geometry can be compiled into a compact network that scores queries without storing the training data at deployment, with a constructive approximation bound supporting the population version.

title: Certifying Retraining Regret through Residual Structure
comment: 46 pages, 5 figures. Code and reproduction materials: this https URL
summary: We certify a fixed ridge predictor's regret against full-feature retraining over every continuous completion of an interval-valued table. Our main theorem gives verifiable original-row residual conditions for a uniform error bound independent of nuisance-feature scale and rank, with an asymptotically sharp leading constant and quantitative leakage stability. Full-rank constructions separate certification dimension from feature dimension, including examples requiring directions beyond the candidate. Observed-row anchors make the conditions computable, while exact row geometry and global search return valid upper bounds and feasible original-table witnesses. A finite-scale contraction and common-domain moment fallback implement the structural result. Four real-world tasks retain all model features and certify twenty rank-three instances to width $10^{-5}$. Their primary median widths improve over centered moments. Joint residual refinement additionally certifies all twenty new response-independent masks to the same precision within 76.21 seconds. For a concrete fixed-point predictor contract, pure energy certifies thirteen of fifteen stopping decisions in ten seconds, versus five for moments. Refinement certifies all fifteen within 91.68 seconds at the same objective threshold.

AI.tldr: The paper certifies the regret of a fixed ridge predictor against full-feature retraining over every continuous completion of an interval-valued table, with a uniform error bound that is independent of nuisance-feature scale and rank. Four real-world tasks certify twenty rank-three instances to a width of 10^-5.
AI.motivation: Whether a fixed predictor remains close to full-feature retraining is hard to decide when table entries are known only as intervals, and the paper addresses this with verifiable certificates.
AI.method: Verifiable original-row residual conditions give a uniform error bound with an asymptotically sharp leading constant and quantitative leakage stability. Observed-row anchors make the conditions computable, while exact row geometry and global search return valid upper bounds and feasible original-table witnesses. A finite-scale contraction and a common-domain moment fallback implement the structural result.
AI.result: Four real-world tasks retain all model features and certify twenty rank-three instances to width 10^-5, with primary median widths improving over centered moments. Joint residual refinement certifies all twenty new response-independent masks to the same precision within 76.21 seconds. For a fixed-point predictor contract, pure energy certifies thirteen of fifteen stopping decisions in ten seconds versus five for moments, and refinement certifies all fifteen within 91.68 seconds at the same objective threshold.
AI.conclusion: Residual-structure certificates are practical and tighter than the moment baseline, and joint refinement certifies all cases at the target precision.

title: SparseGDN: Chunk Sparse in Linear Attention
summary: Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) offer linear-time sequence modeling, yet long-context prefill remains costly due to dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate state storage. We introduce SparseGDN, a hardware-aware framework that combines structured intra-chunk approximation with input-dependent recurrent-event selection while producing outputs for every token. A block-adjacent solver reduces local Delta-solve computation, while a dynamic selector allocates recurrent-update budgets across head pairs. The GPU implementation materializes updates only for selected events and reconstructs token outputs using compact state snapshots and group-local interactions, reducing computation and memory traffic. We evaluate SparseGDN on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B across RULER tasks and context lengths from 4K to 128K. Retaining approximately 29% of recurrent events on average, SparseGDN achieves 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including online selection overhead.

AI.tldr: SparseGDN is a hardware-aware framework for long-context prefill of Gated Delta Networks that combines a structured intra-chunk approximation with input-dependent selection of recurrent-state updates. Retaining about 29% of recurrent events on average, it achieves 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B.
AI.motivation: Gated Delta Networks offer linear-time sequence modelling, yet long-context prefill remains costly because of dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate state storage.
AI.method: A block-adjacent solver reduces local Delta-solve computation, and a dynamic selector allocates recurrent-update budgets across head pairs. The GPU implementation materializes updates only for selected events and reconstructs token outputs using compact state snapshots and group-local interactions.
AI.result: Evaluated on RULER tasks at context lengths from 4K to 128K on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B, retaining about 29% of recurrent events on average, SparseGDN achieves 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including online selection overhead.
AI.conclusion: Selective recurrent updates and compact state handling reduce both computation and memory traffic in GDN prefill while still producing outputs for every token.

title: A Unified XAI-NSAI Analytical Framework for Trustworthy IoT Anomaly Detection
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the IEEE Annual Congress on Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT), 2026
summary: The widespread deployment of Internet of Things (IoT) devices in critical environments makes anomaly detection essential for identifying abnormal behaviors and supporting timely investigation and response. However, accurate detection alone is insufficient. Practical IoT deployments must also provide explanations, incorporate domain knowledge and reasoning, operate under IoT constraints, and support human decision making. Although recently proposed approaches increasingly incorporate Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) or Neuro-Symbolic Artificial Intelligence (NSAI), XAI and NSAI methods are often considered independently. We argue that they should be considered together to better understand their complementary roles in supporting trustworthy IoT anomaly detection. To address this gap, we propose a unified analytical framework organized around five complementary dimensions. The framework provides a structured basis for characterizing existing approaches, identifying capability gaps and design trade-offs, and guiding the design of new anomaly detection systems for different IoT applications. We demonstrate the framework's analytical utility by applying it to three representative studies and illustrate its design utility through its application to a Medical IoT anomaly detection system.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified analytical framework that treats explainable AI (XAI) and neuro-symbolic AI (NSAI) together for trustworthy IoT anomaly detection, organized around five complementary dimensions. It is applied to three representative studies and to the design of a Medical IoT anomaly detection system.
AI.motivation: XAI and NSAI are often considered independently, although practical IoT anomaly detection must also provide explanations, incorporate domain knowledge, operate under IoT constraints, and support human decision making.
AI.method: A unified analytical framework organized around five complementary dimensions, used to characterize existing approaches, identify capability gaps and design trade-offs, and guide the design of new anomaly detection systems.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results. The framework's analytical utility is shown by applying it to three representative studies, and its design utility by applying it to a Medical IoT anomaly detection system.
AI.conclusion: Considering XAI and NSAI together clarifies their complementary roles in supporting trustworthy IoT anomaly detection.

title: From Representation to Readout: Mechanistic Analysis of Membership Signals in Language Models
summary: Membership inference aims to determine whether a particular example was included in a model's training data. Such membership signals are often broadly described as memorization, while the underlying mechanisms can involve both how information is represented internally and how it is accessed by the model to produce behaviors. We therefore present a mechanistic study of membership signals in large language models (LLMs). We introduce Decodable Information Score, Used Information Score, and Readout Accessibility Gap (DUG), a set of complementary measures that separately quantify membership information decodable from internal representations and the extent to which it is exposed through the model's readout. Across supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL)-based membership inference methods, membership-specific effects appear in both the amount of decodable information and readout under SFT, while under RL-based membership inference methods they appear primarily in readout. Activation patching further localizes this membership-specific effect to intermediate layers. To examine whether these findings extend to a more general RL setting, we further study reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) contamination, where the training reward is independent of the reference solution. In this setting, we find that behavioral changes can emerge without a corresponding increase in likelihood-based membership inference signals.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DUG, three complementary measures (Decodable Information Score, Used Information Score, and Readout Accessibility Gap) that separately quantify membership information decodable from internal representations and how much of it the model's readout exposes. Membership effects appear in both decodable information and readout under SFT, but primarily in readout under RL-based membership inference.
AI.motivation: Membership signals are often broadly described as memorization, yet their mechanisms involve both how information is represented internally and how the model accesses it to produce behavior, and these two parts have not been separated.
AI.method: The paper introduces DUG and uses it in a mechanistic study of membership signals across supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL)-based membership inference methods. Activation patching localizes the membership-specific effect, and the study extends to RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) contamination, where the training reward is independent of the reference solution.
AI.result: Under SFT, membership-specific effects appear in both the amount of decodable information and readout; under RL-based methods they appear primarily in readout. Activation patching localizes the effect to intermediate layers. In the RLVR contamination setting, behavioral changes can emerge without a corresponding increase in likelihood-based membership inference signals.
AI.conclusion: Membership signals have representation and readout components whose relative weight depends on the training method, and behavior can change without a detectable likelihood-based membership signal.

title: When Everyone Can Build a Model: Mechanistic Inference in the Age of AI
summary: Modern deep learning and AI-assisted code generation are lowering the technical barrier to building mathematical models of biological systems that reproduce complex observations. This lets researchers with domain expertise build semi-mechanistic, hybrid models constrained by prior knowledge and augmented with learned structure without extensive training in modelling. However, easier construction does not make interpretation easier: predictive success of such so-called grey-box models does not establish that an inferred mechanism corresponds to the one that generated the data, and the learned component can absorb errors in the mechanistic part. Many biological modelling problems are underdetermined, so several, possibly infinitely many, models may reproduce the same data equally well. This ambiguity enters at two modelling choices: which variables can affect others, and which response function describes the underlying mechanism. For the first choice, causal inference provides a formal framework stating which causal relationships and intervention effects are identifiable from the data and available knowledge. For the second, ensemble analyses quantify the uncertainty and the range of behaviours still allowed by models that fit equally well. Together, they turn a single good fit into an explicit account of what is supported, what remains open, and which experiment would decide.

AI.tldr: Argues that AI-assisted construction of grey-box biological models makes a good fit an unreliable guide to the true mechanism, and proposes causal inference and ensemble analysis to show what a fitted model supports, what stays open, and which experiment would decide.
AI.motivation: Easier model building lets domain experts construct hybrid models, but predictive success does not establish that the inferred mechanism is the true one, because the learned component can absorb errors and many underdetermined models fit the same data equally well.
AI.method: Identifies two sources of ambiguity: which variables can affect others, addressed with causal inference to determine identifiable relationships and intervention effects, and which response function describes the mechanism, addressed with ensemble analyses of the range of behaviours among equally good fits.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experiments or numerical results; it is a perspective on how the two frameworks together turn a single good fit into an explicit account of what is supported, what remains open, and which experiment would decide.
AI.conclusion: Interpreting grey-box models requires explicit identifiability and ensemble uncertainty analysis rather than predictive accuracy alone, so modellers can state what the data support and which experiment would resolve the remaining ambiguity.

title: Improving the Optimization Landscape of Matrix Completion with $ε$-close Surrogates
summary: Non-convex optimization is central to machine learning and AI, yet unlike its convex counterpart, it still lacks a general and principled framework. In this work, we try to highlight the importance of combining noisy perturbations with over-parametrization mathematically under the classic setting of matrix completion (MC). Matrix completion is an important non-convex recovery problem in which only a subset of a matrix's entries is observed, and the remaining entries must be recovered using low-rank constraints. This problem is notoriously difficult because observations are limited. However, we show that by injecting $\epsilon$-level perturbations into the nullspace of the observation mask, we can construct noisy matrix sensing surrogates whose solutions remain $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)$-close to the ground truth with valid restricted isometry property (RIP) constants. The existence of RIP further enables powerful tensor frameworks to be applied with theoretical guarantees. This approach reflects a broader empirical trend in which stochasticity or noise improves the curvature of the optimization landscape, allowing over-parameterized (a.k.a large) models to better separate signal from noise. Assuming each matrix entry is observed independently, we establish quantitative recovery guarantees without explicit requirements on sampling rate or incoherence, and discuss how such assumptions can further strengthen our results.

AI.tldr: Shows that injecting epsilon-level noise into the nullspace of the observation mask yields noisy matrix sensing surrogates whose solutions stay O(epsilon)-close to the ground truth, giving matrix completion recovery guarantees without sampling-rate or incoherence requirements.
AI.motivation: Matrix completion is notoriously hard from limited observations, and non-convex optimization lacks a general principled framework; existing recovery guarantees typically depend on sampling-rate or incoherence conditions.
AI.method: Adds epsilon-level perturbations to the nullspace of the observation mask to build noisy matrix sensing surrogates with valid restricted isometry property constants, so that tensor frameworks with theoretical guarantees can be applied; assumes each matrix entry is observed independently.
AI.result: The surrogate solutions remain O(epsilon)-close to the ground truth and have valid RIP constants. The analysis yields quantitative recovery guarantees with no explicit sampling-rate or incoherence requirement. The abstract describes no numerical experiments.
AI.conclusion: Noise combined with over-parameterization can improve the optimization landscape and help separate signal from noise, offering a principled route to guaranteed non-convex recovery.

title: NormDetect: Anchored Calibration for Low-False-Positive Detection of Machine-Generated Web Text
summary: Web platforms screen posts for text written by large language models, and every false flag hits a human writer. Detectors must therefore run at a very low false positive rate (FPR). Zero-shot detectors such as Binoculars score text with frozen language models, but invisible edits such as homoglyphs shatter tokenization and push machine text into the human range. Unicode normalization undoes these edits, yet the normalized score still misses half of the machine text at a strict FPR, under attacks that leave nothing to clean. We find that with the Falcon-7B scoring pair, heads on token statistics recall less than the normalized score at this FPR, and several flag too many human posts in some sections. We propose NormDetect, which anchors a learned per-section head to the normalized zero-shot score. A blend weight chosen on training folds under a human FPR cap combines the two scores, and one threshold is calibrated on human text only. On eight sections of the RAID benchmark with eleven attacks, NormDetect raises recall at a 0.1% calibrated FPR by 5.0 points over normalized Binoculars. Its human FPR bound stays at most 1% in every section, and no other detector within this bound recalls as much.

AI.tldr: Proposes NormDetect, which combines a learned per-section head anchored to a normalized Binoculars score under one calibrated threshold, to detect machine-generated web text at a very low false positive rate.
AI.motivation: Each false flag hits a human writer, so detectors must run at very low FPR; yet normalized Binoculars still misses half the machine text at a strict FPR under attacks, and token-statistics heads flag too many human posts in some sections.
AI.method: Anchors a learned per-section head to the normalized zero-shot score using the Falcon-7B scoring pair; a blend weight is chosen on training folds under a human FPR cap, and a single threshold is calibrated on human text only.
AI.result: On eight sections of the RAID benchmark with eleven attacks, NormDetect raises recall at a 0.1% calibrated FPR by 5.0 points over normalized Binoculars, keeps its human FPR bound at most 1% in every section, and no other detector within this bound recalls more.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring a learned detector to a zero-shot score and calibrating on human text only gives a practical low-FPR detector for web platforms facing invisible-edit attacks.

title: RetryRoute: Retry-Aware Model Routing for Agentic Image Editing Services
summary: Web agents increasingly edit images by calling open editing models in a critique-and-retry loop, and these models differ in cost by more than an order of magnitude. After every rejected edit, a service must decide whether to retry the same model, escalate to another or give up. Existing routers pick one model per request, and cascades escalate in a fixed order. However, both treat a retry as an independent draw. We identify sticky failures, meaning that a retry after a failure succeeds only 17-53% as often as a first try across six open models, three benchmarks and two judges. Based on this finding, we propose RetryRoute, a retry-aware router that estimates each model's chance of success given the request's failure history. It plans retries, escalations and abandonment over failure states and adds live queue waits to the cost, so the same plan becomes load-aware dispatch. At the main budget, RetryRoute's success under the in-loop judge exceeds the strongest of eleven prior baselines by 2.8 points on average over eight groups. On a GPU serving testbed it raises the share of edits delivered within the service-level objective by 5.0-6.3 points over the best prior baseline at every load.

AI.tldr: Proposes RetryRoute, a router that accounts for sticky failures, where a retry after a failed edit succeeds far less often than a first try, to plan retries, escalations and abandonment for agentic image editing.
AI.motivation: Existing routers pick one model per request and cascades escalate in a fixed order, and both treat each retry as an independent draw, although the models differ in cost by more than an order of magnitude.
AI.method: Estimates each model's chance of success given the request's failure history and plans retries, escalations and abandonment over failure states, adding live queue waits to the cost so that the same plan becomes load-aware dispatch.
AI.result: A retry after a failure succeeds only 17-53% as often as a first try across six open models, three benchmarks and two judges. At the main budget, RetryRoute's success under the in-loop judge exceeds the strongest of eleven prior baselines by 2.8 points on average over eight groups; on a GPU serving testbed it raises the share of edits within the service-level objective by 5.0-6.3 points over the best prior baseline at every load.
AI.conclusion: Modelling retry dependence on failure history, together with queueing, improves both success and latency-constrained delivery for editing services that use critique-and-retry loops.

title: When Links Mislead: Label-Free Structural Polarity for Zero-Shot Classification of Web Pages
summary: Web platforms such as digital libraries, online stores and university sites must classify new pages before anyone labels them. Large language models (LLMs) can label each page from its text, but these labels are noisy, and links could correct them only where linked pages share classes. Existing zero-shot methods ignore the links, or pull a page toward its neighbours as label propagation and graph neural networks (GNNs) do, which hurts where linked pages differ in class. Others weight propagation by an LLM-estimated homophily that costs extra calls and drifts across LLMs. We find that the sign with which links should enter a prediction, which we call structural polarity, is readable without true labels. It is the excess agreement of LLM labels and text-prototype predictions along links. We thus propose ZeroPolar, which gates one signed propagation step by this statistic. Training-free ZeroPolar mixes prototype scores with any number of LLM labels, and ZeroPolar-T denoises the labels with a text classifier once half of the pages carry one. With one GPT-4o label per page, ZeroPolar-T reaches the highest mean accuracy on eleven graphs (73.99%), 6.01 points above LLM-BP and significantly above all eighteen baselines we compare. With LLM labels on only 5% of the pages, training-free ZeroPolar leads a GNN trained on these labels by 10.80 points.

AI.tldr: Proposes ZeroPolar, a training-free zero-shot web page classifier that uses links only where a label-free statistic shows they agree in class, and ZeroPolar-T, which adds a text classifier once half the pages carry labels.
AI.motivation: LLM labels are noisy and links could correct them, but existing methods either ignore links or propagate labels along all of them, which hurts where linked pages differ in class, while LLM-estimated homophily costs extra calls and drifts across LLMs.
AI.method: Defines structural polarity as the excess agreement of LLM labels and text-prototype predictions along links, and uses it to gate one signed propagation step; training-free ZeroPolar mixes prototype scores with any number of LLM labels, and ZeroPolar-T denoises the labels with a text classifier once half of the pages have one.
AI.result: With one GPT-4o label per page, ZeroPolar-T reaches the highest mean accuracy on eleven graphs (73.99%), 6.01 points above LLM-BP and significantly above all eighteen baselines compared. With LLM labels on only 5% of pages, training-free ZeroPolar leads a GNN trained on those labels by 10.80 points.
AI.conclusion: The sign with which links should enter a prediction can be estimated without true labels, so links can help zero-shot classification without the harm of assuming homophily.

title: Spectral Haar Binarizer: Compact Boolean Contrast Representations for Hyperspectral Classification
summary: Tsetlin Machines offer an interpretable, hardware-friendly alternative to conventional machine learning models, but applying them to continuous hyperspectral measurements requires converting spectral signals into Boolean representations. Standard binarisation methods typically discretise each spectral band independently, potentially discarding important relationships between neighbouring wavelengths. In this paper, we introduce the Spectral Haar Binarizer (SHB), a contrast-based spectral representation method that constructs Boolean predicates from differences between selected spectral intervals. Inspired by Haar-like contrast features, the method uses an AdaBoost-style selection procedure to obtain a compact set of discriminative spectral predicates. We evaluate SHB on five heterogeneous hyperspectral datasets covering forensic blood detection, agricultural and urban remote sensing, and rainforest tree-species classification. Across binary and multiclass tasks, SHB consistently outperforms standard per-band binarisation strategies and provides the strongest or near-strongest results across classifiers. In binary tasks, TM-SHB achieves the best average performance, while RF-SHB is strongest in multiclass settings. Bayesian and rank-based analyses confirm that SHB's advantage is robust across datasets and not driven by isolated cases. The results show that representing continuous hyperspectral measurements is a central processing step for efficient classification. That contrast-based Boolean features provide an effective bridge between information-rich sensor measurements and compact, logic-based processing.

AI.tldr: Introduces the Spectral Haar Binarizer (SHB), which turns hyperspectral spectra into Boolean predicates based on differences between spectral intervals, selected by an AdaBoost-style procedure, for Tsetlin Machines and other classifiers.
AI.motivation: Tsetlin Machines are interpretable and hardware-friendly but need Boolean inputs, and standard per-band binarisation discards relationships between neighbouring wavelengths.
AI.method: Constructs Boolean predicates from differences between selected spectral intervals, inspired by Haar-like contrast features, with an AdaBoost-style selection of a compact set of discriminative predicates.
AI.result: Across five hyperspectral datasets (forensic blood detection, agricultural and urban remote sensing, and rainforest tree species), SHB consistently outperforms standard per-band binarisation and gives the strongest or near-strongest results across classifiers. TM-SHB achieves the best average in binary tasks and RF-SHB is strongest in multiclass settings; Bayesian and rank-based analyses confirm robustness across datasets.
AI.conclusion: Contrast-based Boolean features give a compact and effective bridge between continuous hyperspectral measurements and logic-based classifiers.

title: PCD: Predictive Coding Dynamics for Irregularly Sampled Time Series
comment: 15 pages. Supplementary material (2 pages) available as an ancillary file
summary: Dynamic systems evolve continuously over time, whereas observations in real scenarios are often sparse, irregular, and asynchronous. Accurate prediction therefore requires inferring latent state evolution between observations, as future values depend on partially observed trajectories. We propose Predictive Coding Dynamics (PCD), a residual feedback mechanism for irregular continuous dynamic models. PCD maintains previous reconstructions, predicts observed entries from them, and incorporates masked signed residuals into state recognition through an energy penalty. The mechanism is implemented with ODE-RNN and Latent ODE, supporting event-based hidden updates and latent state recognition. Experiments on forecasting and trajectory recovery tasks show that PCD improves continuous dynamic backbones under sparse and irregular sampling. The results further indicate that predictive error feedback improves latent state estimation when observations constrain the current trajectory. These results suggest that PCD provides a residual feedback framework that jointly supports trajectory generation, observation consistency checking, and state refinement in continuous-time series modeling. The source code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes Predictive Coding Dynamics (PCD), a residual feedback mechanism that adds prediction-error feedback to ODE-RNN and Latent ODE models for irregularly sampled time series.
AI.motivation: Real observations are sparse, irregular and asynchronous, so forecasting requires inferring latent state evolution between observations, which continuous dynamic backbones handle imperfectly.
AI.method: PCD keeps previous reconstructions, predicts observed entries from them, and feeds masked signed residuals into state recognition through an energy penalty, supporting event-based hidden updates and latent state recognition.
AI.result: Experiments on forecasting and trajectory recovery tasks show that PCD improves continuous dynamic backbones under sparse and irregular sampling, and that predictive error feedback improves latent state estimation when observations constrain the current trajectory.
AI.conclusion: Predictive error feedback provides a single residual framework that jointly supports trajectory generation, observation consistency checking and state refinement in continuous-time modelling.

title: Infinite ResNets are Gaussian Mean ODEs
summary: Understanding the training dynamics of deep neural networks in large-scale limits is a question both of foundational and of practical importance. Prior works have obtained such descriptions through dynamical mean field theory (DMFT), yielding a system of non-Markovian dynamics that are challenging to analyze and that obscure the optimization structure of the original dynamics. In this paper, we obtain instead a simple description of the large-scale limit training dynamics for ResNets in standard shape scalings and in the $1/\text{depth}$ branch scaling that allows maximal (local) feature updates. For a model trained with gradient descent (GD) from a random initialization, the limit dynamics is simply GD on a Neural Mean ODE with Gaussian initial weights. Our analysis covers population or empirical risk GD in the joint limit of large width, depth and embedding, input, and output dimensions. We obtain approximation scaling laws that depend on the shape of the ResNet and the covariance spectrum of the data. We also illustrate the flexibility of our approach by discussing Mixture of Expert models, where likewise the limit admits an intuitive (nested) Mean ODE description.

AI.tldr: Shows that in standard large-scale limits, gradient descent training of a ResNet reduces to gradient descent on a Neural Mean ODE with Gaussian initial weights, a simpler description than dynamical mean field theory.
AI.motivation: Prior large-scale descriptions via dynamical mean field theory give non-Markovian dynamics that are hard to analyze and obscure the optimization structure of the original training dynamics.
AI.method: Analyzes ResNets under standard shape scalings and the 1/depth branch scaling that allows maximal local feature updates, in the joint limit of large width, depth and embedding, input and output dimensions, for population or empirical risk gradient descent from random initialization.
AI.result: The limit dynamics is gradient descent on a Neural Mean ODE with Gaussian initial weights. The paper derives approximation scaling laws that depend on the ResNet shape and the covariance spectrum of the data, and extends the description to Mixture of Experts models as a nested Mean ODE.
AI.conclusion: The Neural Mean ODE gives an intuitive and analyzable description of deep ResNet training in large-scale limits, exposing the optimization structure that dynamical mean field theory obscures.

title: Enhancing Sentiment Classification on Small Datasets through Data Augmentation and Transfer Learning
summary: Small-scale sentiment classification often suffers from data scarcity, which limits the generalization ability of the models. This study evaluates and compares the effectiveness of three data augmentation strategies: Easy Data Augmentation (EDA), back-translation, and contextual token substitution (nlpaug-style), with both traditional machine learning classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest) and transformer-based models (BERT). We perform a comprehensive empirical comparison with low-resource sentiment datasets by summarizing the results of recent studies and performing targeted head-to-head experiments. Our findings indicate that all augmentation methods improve performance. Contextual augmentation yields the most consistent gains for BERT models, while EDA and back-translation provide greater benefits for traditional classifiers. These insights help guide the selection of data augmentation techniques tailored to model type and dataset size, filling a critical gap in research on data augmentation for sentiment classification on small datasets.

AI.tldr: Compares Easy Data Augmentation, back-translation and contextual token substitution for small-data sentiment classification with Logistic Regression, Random Forest and BERT, finding that all augmentations help but the best method depends on the model.
AI.motivation: Small sentiment datasets limit generalization, and it is unclear which augmentation strategy suits which model type and dataset size for sentiment classification.
AI.method: Combines a summary of recent studies with targeted head-to-head experiments on low-resource sentiment datasets, comparing three augmentation strategies across traditional classifiers and a transformer model.
AI.result: All augmentation methods improve performance. Contextual augmentation gives the most consistent gains for BERT, while EDA and back-translation give greater benefits for traditional classifiers. The abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Augmentation choice should match model type and dataset size: contextual substitution for transformers, and EDA or back-translation for traditional classifiers.

title: FOCUS: First-Order Control Using Optimal Transport Supervision for Imitation from Observations
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Physical Understanding for Decision-Making
summary: Imitation learning from observations must recover behavior from state-only demonstrations without known temporal correspondence. Differentiable simulators provide pathwise policy gradients, but differentiating through long, contact-rich trajectories can make optimization unstable. We introduce FOCUS, which combines local optimal-transport alignment with short-horizon differentiable actor-critic learning. FOCUS matches agent rollout windows to multiple sampled expert segments using a soft best-of-$K$ objective that emphasizes locally compatible matches. The resulting transport-based costs provide differentiable imitation rewards, while a learned critic bootstraps value beyond the rollout horizon. FOCUS requires neither temporally aligned trajectories nor expert-aligned initialization or teacher forcing. Across contact-rich locomotion tasks in DFlex, including a musculoskeletal humanoid controlled by 152 muscle activations, FOCUS improves sample efficiency and training stability over adversarial imitation-from-observation methods and prior differentiable imitation baselines.

AI.tldr: Proposes FOCUS, which trains imitation-from-observation policies through differentiable simulators by aligning short rollout windows to expert segments with soft optimal transport and a short-horizon actor-critic.
AI.motivation: Learning from state-only demonstrations without known temporal correspondence is hard, and differentiating through long contact-rich trajectories makes pathwise policy gradients unstable.
AI.method: Matches agent rollout windows to multiple sampled expert segments with a soft best-of-K objective that emphasizes locally compatible matches; the transport-based costs give differentiable imitation rewards, and a learned critic bootstraps value beyond the rollout horizon. It needs no temporally aligned trajectories, expert-aligned initialization or teacher forcing.
AI.result: On contact-rich locomotion tasks in DFlex, including a musculoskeletal humanoid controlled by 152 muscle activations, FOCUS improves sample efficiency and training stability over adversarial imitation-from-observation methods and prior differentiable imitation baselines.
AI.conclusion: Local optimal-transport alignment combined with short-horizon differentiable learning offers a stable and sample-efficient route to imitation from observations in contact-rich settings.

title: ORION: An Outcome-Driven LLM Advisor for RL-Based Multi-Domain 6G Slice Placement
summary: Deploying 6G network slices across administrative domains requires an online decision for each arriving request: which domain hosts each virtual network function, how traffic crosses domain boundaries, and whether the slice is admitted. This joint decision problem is NP-hard under continuous arrivals. Experiments on a parametrized family of multi-domain topologies show that no fixed planning strategy dominates across all regimes: the performance ranking reverses between topology classes, and feasible placements exist for most rejected requests but remain undiscovered. These findings identify the plan layer as the decisive performance lever. We introduce ORION, a hierarchical orchestrator in which two LLM agents translate service intents into structured requests and generate abstract placement plans. A cooperative multi-agent RL coordinator selects the cross-domain partition, treating the plan as a persistent soft prior, while per-domain agents place the functions. ORION main contribution lies at the plan layer: an outcome-driven episodic memory that records, for each completed attempt, the network-condition profile, the proposed plan, and its verified feasibility outcome. The memory feeds verified successes and labelled failures back to the planner, thereby closing the adaptation loop using deployment feasibility rather than a scalar reward assigned to the planner's own proposals. To isolate the effect of the plan quality, we evaluate the planner on held-out topology families while keeping the downstream selection and execution mechanisms fixed. Under this controlled setting, the proposed memory improves admission by $4.6$--$11.5$ percentage points over the same planner without memory, while importance-based retention accounts for most of the improvement over a first-in-first-out store.

AI.tldr: Presents ORION, a hierarchical orchestrator for 6G slice placement across domains in which LLM agents produce placement plans and an outcome-driven episodic memory of verified feasibility outcomes improves the planner's admission rate.
AI.motivation: Joint multi-domain slice placement is NP-hard under continuous arrivals, no fixed planning strategy dominates across topology classes, and feasible placements for many rejected requests remain undiscovered.
AI.method: Two LLM agents translate service intents into structured requests and abstract placement plans; a cooperative multi-agent RL coordinator selects the cross-domain partition, treating the plan as a persistent soft prior, and per-domain agents place the functions. The main contribution is an episodic memory that records the network-condition profile, proposed plan and verified feasibility outcome, with importance-based retention, feeding successes and labelled failures back to the planner.
AI.result: On held-out topology families with downstream selection and execution held fixed, the memory improves admission by 4.6 to 11.5 percentage points over the same planner without memory, and importance-based retention accounts for most of the improvement over a first-in-first-out store.
AI.conclusion: Plan quality is the decisive lever, and feedback based on verified deployment feasibility, rather than a scalar reward on the planner's own proposals, can effectively close the adaptation loop.

title: A Constructive Orbit-Based Theory of Learnability
summary: We develop a finite-dimensional orbit framework for constructing data-adapted dictionaries, sparse realizations, and predictive extensions. The method uses wrapped weighted shifts to generate orbit dictionaries and local interpolation maps from independent orbit representatives, turning the learning problem into three explicit tasks: scaffold discovery, sparse realization on the discovered dictionary, and prediction through learned sparse coordinates. We introduce CCDS as the main constructive ingredient: a deviation-controlled sparse realization procedure that recovers MP/OMP-type behavior at the minimal-deviation boundary while allowing feasible interior paths with prescribed residual geometry that is inaccessible to MP/OMP. We prove generic orbit independence, exact block interpolation with norm control, observable bounds on sparse approximation distortion, sparse realization guarantees on selected supports, and fixed-path stability under admissible perturbations of the block interpolants. These results connect sparse approximation, interpolation, and finite-dimensional operator dynamics through the construction and analysis of data-induced orbit dictionaries. Experiments on synthetic geometry, controlled realization tests, and standard classification benchmarks show that selected orbit scaffolds have substantially better matched-rank projection behavior than random orbit or unstructured alternatives, that CCDS attains near-zero realization error at the minimal-deviation boundary, and that predictors trained from the sparse CCDS certificates give competitive performance.

AI.tldr: Develops a finite-dimensional orbit framework for building data-adapted dictionaries and sparse realizations, with a CCDS procedure that matches MP/OMP at the minimal-deviation boundary and also reaches feasible interior paths that MP/OMP cannot.
AI.motivation: Sparse approximation, interpolation and prediction are usually treated separately, and the paper seeks to connect them through data-induced orbit dictionaries.
AI.method: Wrapped weighted shifts generate orbit dictionaries and local interpolation maps from independent orbit representatives, reducing learning to scaffold discovery, sparse realization on the discovered dictionary, and prediction through learned sparse coordinates; CCDS is a deviation-controlled sparse realization procedure.
AI.result: The paper proves generic orbit independence, exact block interpolation with norm control, observable bounds on sparse approximation distortion, realization guarantees on selected supports, and fixed-path stability. Experiments show that selected orbit scaffolds give better matched-rank projection than random or unstructured alternatives, CCDS reaches near-zero realization error at the minimal-deviation boundary, and CCDS-trained predictors are competitive on classification benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Orbit-based dictionaries link sparse approximation, interpolation and finite-dimensional operator dynamics, and the sparse CCDS certificates yield competitive predictors.

title: On the Generation Order in GFlowNets
summary: Sampling from discrete distributions specified by unnormalised probability functions is a classical statistical problem. GFlowNets address this problem by constructing objects sequentially, adding one discrete component at a time in either a predefined or a learned order. The choice of order determines which conditional distributions the neural network must learn, some of which may be easier to learn than others. Yet whether existing GFlowNet algorithms discover interpretable generation orders and make use of them during training remains unexplored. We introduce controlled problems where generation order is experimentally shown to affect convergence and standard GFlowNet training struggles to discover useful orders. To address this difficulty, we develop Learning-Order GFlowNet, a training recipe that learns interpretable generation orders without order annotations and improves convergence on these problems. Finally, we investigate gradient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) as a possible explanation for order emergence: orders associated with faster convergence exhibit higher SNR at comparable validation loss, suggesting both a mechanism favouring their emergence and an SNR-based characterisation of a good generation order.

AI.tldr: Introduces Learning-Order GFlowNet, a training recipe that learns interpretable generation orders without order annotations, and shows that generation order affects GFlowNet convergence and that gradient SNR tracks which orders emerge.
AI.motivation: GFlowNets build objects one component at a time, so the order determines which conditional distributions the network must learn; whether existing algorithms discover interpretable orders and use them during training was unexplored, and standard training struggles to find useful orders.
AI.method: Constructs controlled problems in which generation order is shown to affect convergence, develops Learning-Order GFlowNet to learn orders without annotations, and investigates gradient signal-to-noise ratio as an explanation for order emergence.
AI.result: Learning-Order GFlowNet improves convergence on the controlled problems. Orders associated with faster convergence show higher gradient SNR at comparable validation loss.
AI.conclusion: Generation order matters for GFlowNet training, and gradient SNR offers both a mechanism for order emergence and a characterization of a good generation order.

title: Does Reasoning Make Language Models Agree?
summary: Language models face two opposing concerns: monoculture, in which models err in correlated ways, and multiplicity, in which equally accurate models make conflicting decisions. The rise of reasoning models has complicated this debate: On the one hand, reasoning may increase model agreement if models anchor on the same salient features or follow similar reasoning paths. On the other hand, stochastic reasoning traces may introduce additional branch points leading to more diverse predictions. We resolve this tension by distinguishing reasoning as an intervention from reasoning as an observed behavior. We compare agreement under controlled changes in reasoning effort with agreement across observed reasoning lengths, measuring both against the agreement expected from model accuracy. Across nine models from two developers and three classification tasks, enabling reasoning increases agreement between models evaluated on the same individuals. Yet the individuals who elicit longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models. Both patterns persist after accounting for differences in accuracy. Asking models to reason more thus promotes agreement, while observing them reason longer signals disagreement.

AI.tldr: Finds that enabling reasoning in language models increases agreement between models on the same individuals, while individuals who elicit longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models.
AI.motivation: Monoculture and multiplicity pull in opposite directions, and reasoning may either anchor models on shared features, raising agreement, or add stochastic branch points, lowering it, so the net effect is unclear.
AI.method: Distinguishes reasoning as an intervention (controlled changes in reasoning effort) from reasoning as an observed behaviour (observed reasoning lengths), measuring both against the agreement expected from model accuracy across nine models from two developers and three classification tasks.
AI.result: Enabling reasoning increases cross-model agreement on the same individuals, and individuals who elicit longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models. Both patterns persist after accounting for differences in accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Asking models to reason more promotes agreement, while observing that they reason longer signals disagreement, so the two should be interpreted differently.

title: From WSIs to Bulk, Spatial and Single-Cell Transcriptomics via Multi-Scale Graph Neural Networks
summary: Understanding the spatial distribution of gene expression is key to studying complex diseases like cancer. While Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) and Single-Cell Transcriptomics (scT) provide high-resolution insights, they remain expensive and scarce. In contrast, standard histopathology Whole-Slide Images (WSIs) paired with bulk RNA sequencing are widely available. This work introduces a Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network (GNN) capable of simultaneously predicting bulk, spatial, and single-cell transcriptomics directly from WSIs. By extracting morphological features using a Pathology Foundation Model (PFM) (UNI2-h) and constructing spatial graphs at both patch and cell levels, the model learns the hierarchical relationships within the tissue. The network is trained on a combined dataset of The Cancer Genome Atlas Program (TCGA), Visium, and Xenium samples across lung, kidney, and breast tissues. A hybrid training strategy is employed, leveraging direct supervision alongside weakly supervised consistency losses to ensure predictions align across biological scales. Results show the model accurately predicts gene expression at the slide level and moderately at the patch level (strongest on Xenium), and achieves moderate correlation at the challenging single-cell level. Furthermore, downstream tasks explore the clinical relevance of these predictions, demonstrating their utility in survival analysis, spatial hazard mapping, and tumor classification via molecular signatures.

AI.tldr: Proposes a multi-scale graph neural network that predicts bulk, spatial and single-cell transcriptomics from whole-slide histopathology images using a pathology foundation model, with weakly supervised consistency losses across scales.
AI.motivation: Spatial and single-cell transcriptomics are high-resolution but expensive and scarce, whereas whole-slide images paired with bulk RNA sequencing are widely available.
AI.method: Extracts morphological features with the UNI2-h pathology foundation model, builds spatial graphs at patch and cell levels, and trains on combined TCGA, Visium and Xenium samples from lung, kidney and breast tissues, using direct supervision plus weakly supervised consistency losses that align predictions across scales.
AI.result: Slide-level gene expression is predicted accurately and patch-level moderately, strongest on Xenium, while single-cell correlation is moderate. Downstream tasks show utility for survival analysis, spatial hazard mapping and tumour classification via molecular signatures.
AI.conclusion: Histopathology images can yield multi-scale transcriptomic predictions useful for clinical tasks, although single-cell accuracy remains moderate.

title: From fleet trajectories to single-cell promises: hierarchically weighted conformal prediction for battery SOH monitoring
summary: Interval predictions from conformal prediction are usually read as "90% coverage", but on nested battery data that number promises the fleet average, not the individual cell. We measure the gap on 124 public LFP cells under a preregistered three-tier reporting protocol (fleet, batch, cell): pooled coverage looks healthy (0.875-0.906 across splits) while the worst cell is covered 0.1-2% of the time, with exact binomial tests against the nominal level. We then repair part of the gap with a hierarchically weighted conformal engine whose weights consume only side information frozen at prediction time - signature features, batch labels, cycle indices - and never touch residuals. The preregistered repair criterion passes: 10th-percentile cell coverage moves 0.750 to 0.830 (53% of the gap), the worst cell 0.642 to 0.694, with zero deferrals and a flat sensitivity spectrum. What the engine does not repair is localized rather than left open: under protocol drift the frozen weights harm monotonically on the SOH scale (the absolute scale is reported in full), a structural dead end we report instead of tuning away; and repair capacity is bounded by calibration-pool battery diversity, measured on both datasets. On a cross-chemistry external set the calibrated intervals collapse (0.286), while the within-domain skeleton replicates (pooled 0.933, worst cell 0.686). The deliverable is a reporting protocol - three tiers of promise anchored to measured regimes, worst-cell statistics, deferral share - that makes per-cell interval claims auditable before deployment.

AI.tldr: Shows that pooled conformal coverage for battery state-of-health intervals hides very poor per-cell coverage, and proposes a hierarchically weighted conformal engine that partly repairs the gap using side information frozen at prediction time, under a three-tier reporting protocol.
AI.motivation: A nominal 90% coverage on nested battery data describes the fleet average rather than an individual cell; pooled coverage looks healthy while the worst cell is covered only 0.1-2% of the time.
AI.method: On 124 public LFP cells under a preregistered three-tier protocol (fleet, batch, cell), coverage is measured with exact binomial tests; hierarchical weights built from signature features, batch labels and cycle indices are frozen at prediction time and never touch residuals.
AI.result: Pooled coverage is 0.875-0.906 across splits. The preregistered repair criterion passes: 10th-percentile cell coverage rises from 0.750 to 0.830 (53% of the gap) and worst-cell coverage from 0.642 to 0.694, with zero deferrals. Under protocol drift the frozen weights harm performance monotonically, and repair capacity is bounded by calibration-pool battery diversity. On a cross-chemistry external set the calibrated intervals collapse to 0.286 coverage, while the within-domain skeleton replicates (pooled 0.933, worst cell 0.686).
AI.conclusion: Per-cell interval claims need worst-cell statistics and tiered reporting before deployment; the engine repairs part of the gap but not drift or cross-chemistry transfer, which the paper reports as open limits.

title: Hierarchical Residuals: A Minimalist Decoupling of Residual Width from Compute Width
summary: Residual connections underpin Transformers, but they implicitly tie the residual width carried through depth to the compute width used inside each layer. We introduce Hierarchical Residuals (HiRes), a minimalist architectural change that decouples these dimensions, widening the residual state while keeping per-layer compute width fixed. HiRes groups layers into blocks: standard d-dimensional PreNorm layers operate inside each block, while a wider D-dimensional PostNorm outer residual connects blocks. Learned read/write projections bridge the two spaces at block boundaries, leaving individual Transformer layers unchanged. Across different model sizes and depths, HiRes consistently outperforms vanilla residual addition, with fitted scaling laws indicating a 1.30-fold improvement in FLOPs efficiency. On OLMoE-1B-7B pretraining for 500B tokens, HiRes achieves 0.0208 lower training loss and 1.14-point higher downstream accuracy. HiRes is also competitive with other residual expansion methods such as VWN, mHC and AttnRes with less activation memory and I/O costs. Built from only dense projections and normalizations, it requires neither specialized kernels nor infrastructure-level optimizations. HiRes thus exposes residual width as a practical scaling variable using only standard operators.

AI.tldr: Proposes Hierarchical Residuals (HiRes), which widens the residual stream through a D-dimensional PostNorm outer residual connecting blocks of standard d-dimensional PreNorm layers, decoupling residual width from compute width.
AI.motivation: Residual connections tie the width carried through depth to the width used inside each layer, so the residual width cannot be scaled independently of compute.
AI.method: Groups layers into blocks; standard PreNorm layers operate inside each block, a wider PostNorm outer residual connects the blocks, and learned read/write projections bridge the two spaces at block boundaries, using only dense projections and normalizations.
AI.result: HiRes consistently outperforms vanilla residual addition across model sizes and depths, with fitted scaling laws indicating a 1.30-fold FLOPs efficiency gain. On OLMoE-1B-7B pretraining for 500B tokens it gives 0.0208 lower training loss and 1.14 points higher downstream accuracy, and it is competitive with VWN, mHC and AttnRes with less activation memory and I/O cost.
AI.conclusion: Residual width is a practical scaling variable that can be exploited with standard operators, without specialized kernels or infrastructure-level optimizations.

title: UpLoop: Training Looped Transformers via Upcycling at No Extra Pretraining Compute
summary: Looped language models can strengthen reasoning through repeated computation with shared weights, increasing execution depth without adding independent parameters. However, each additional pass increases training floating-point operations (FLOPs), making these gains more expensive to obtain. To address this cost, we propose UpLoop, a pretraining schedule that uses upcycling to train looped Transformers while exactly matching a standard dense baseline in final parameter count, total training tokens, and training FLOPs. Specifically, UpLoop begins with a shallow Transformer, progressively grows its depth by copying learned layers, and uses the computation saved early to support repeated execution of a shared middle block later in training. Experiments across model scales show improvements in language modeling and downstream performance, with the average score across 22 downstream tasks increasing from 22.99 to 27.52 at 1.3B parameters. These gains also extend to mathematical reasoning after supervised fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: Proposes UpLoop, a pretraining schedule that upcycles a shallow Transformer into a looped model with a shared middle block, matching a standard dense baseline in final parameter count, training tokens and training FLOPs.
AI.motivation: Looped language models gain reasoning depth through repeated shared-weight computation, but each extra pass raises training FLOPs, which makes the gains expensive to obtain.
AI.method: Starts from a shallow Transformer, progressively grows its depth by copying learned layers, and uses the computation saved early to support repeated execution of a shared middle block later in training.
AI.result: Improves language modelling and downstream performance across model scales. The average over 22 downstream tasks rises from 22.99 to 27.52 at 1.3B parameters, and the gains extend to mathematical reasoning after supervised fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Looping can be added to pretraining without extra parameters, tokens or FLOPs by reallocating compute from early depth growth to repeated execution.

title: Leakage-Controlled Structure-Preserving Augmentation and Template-Aware Evaluation for Bangla Symptom-Based Disease Prediction
summary: Bangla symptom-based disease prediction is commonly evaluated on a small, imbalanced structured benchmark containing many profiles that differ by only one or two symptoms. We test whether train-only asymmetric Bernoulli perturbation improves classification using 725 unique profiles spanning 85 diseases and 172 binary symptoms. Experiments use ten repeated real-profile holdouts and parent-grouped inner cross-validation. The 2 x 2 design separates augmentation from hyperparameter tuning, with exact duplication, random oversampling, class weighting, and SMOTEN as balancing controls. For Bernoulli Naive Bayes (BNB), the gain over tuned raw training does not withstand Holm correction, although BNB attains the highest mean accuracy (97.50%). The boosted-tree models benefit substantially: XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost improve by 18.10, 28.45, and 10.09 percentage points, respectively. A Hamming-distance audit places 91.0% of standard held-out profiles within one symptom bit of the training data. Accuracy decreases on a same-disease 1-bit-purged challenge; nevertheless, XGBoost and LightGBM retain large augmentation gains. We also evaluate robustness to missing and spurious symptoms and the faithfulness of BNB explanations. Overall, Bernoulli perturbation is useful for some model families, but benchmark accuracy should be interpreted together with template proximity.

AI.tldr: Evaluates train-only asymmetric Bernoulli perturbation for Bangla symptom-based disease prediction, finding large gains for boosted-tree models, and cautions that benchmark accuracy is inflated by near-duplicate symptom profiles.
AI.motivation: The standard Bangla benchmark is small and imbalanced and contains many profiles that differ by only one or two symptoms, so its accuracy may reflect template proximity rather than generalization.
AI.method: Uses 725 unique profiles across 85 diseases and 172 binary symptoms, with ten repeated real-profile holdouts and parent-grouped inner cross-validation in a 2 x 2 design that separates augmentation from hyperparameter tuning; exact duplication, random oversampling, class weighting and SMOTEN serve as balancing controls, and robustness to missing and spurious symptoms and the faithfulness of BNB explanations are also assessed.
AI.result: The gain over tuned raw training for Bernoulli Naive Bayes does not survive Holm correction, although BNB attains the highest mean accuracy (97.50%). XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost improve by 18.10, 28.45 and 10.09 percentage points. A Hamming-distance audit places 91.0% of standard held-out profiles within one symptom bit of the training data, and accuracy decreases on a same-disease 1-bit-purged challenge, although XGBoost and LightGBM retain large augmentation gains.
AI.conclusion: Bernoulli perturbation is useful for some model families, and benchmark accuracy should be interpreted together with template proximity.

title: Locality-Controlled Out-of-Distribution Guidance for Robust Regulatory DNA Sequence Design
summary: Designing regulatory DNA sequences for targeted gene-expression control is an important challenge. Recent approaches frame this task as property-conditioned generation, where diffusion models trained on natural sequences are guided toward high predicted activity through reward-based fine-tuning or sampling-time guidance. We show that single-reward evaluation can obscure reward-hacking behavior. By decomposing evaluation into property, novelty, and plausibility, we identify an empirically underexplored region of the evaluation space in which all three objectives are satisfied, but no existing baseline succeeds. We postulate that this gap arises because prior methods treat guidance primarily as a matter of magnitude. In regulatory DNA, however, sequence grammar is spatially nonuniform: motif positions are sensitive to perturbation, while background regions allow more exploration. We therefore propose LOCOGEN by reformulating guidance as a problem of locality. LOCOGEN learns an invariant motif mask through sequence-level invariance learning to protect motif positions, while applying OOD damping only to background positions. It operates at sampling time on a frozen diffusion backbone, without retraining the backbone. Across HepG2, K562, and SK-N-SH, LOCOGEN reaches this previously underexplored region of the property-novelty-plausibility space. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes LOCOGEN, which guides a frozen diffusion model for regulatory DNA design by protecting learned motif positions and applying out-of-distribution damping only to background positions, reaching a previously underexplored region of the property-novelty-plausibility space.
AI.motivation: Single-reward evaluation can hide reward hacking, and prior guidance methods treat guidance as a matter of magnitude, although regulatory DNA grammar is spatially nonuniform, with motif positions sensitive to perturbation and background regions allowing more exploration.
AI.method: Learns an invariant motif mask through sequence-level invariance learning to protect motif positions, and applies OOD damping only at background positions; it operates at sampling time on a frozen diffusion backbone without retraining.
AI.result: Across HepG2, K562 and SK-N-SH, LOCOGEN reaches the region of the property-novelty-plausibility space where all three objectives are satisfied, a region no existing baseline reaches. The abstract gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: Reformulating guidance as a problem of locality allows high predicted activity together with novelty and plausibility, and evaluating along all three axes exposes failures that a single reward hides.

title: Task Vectors Can Be Linearly Decomposed into Interpretable and Controllable Components
summary: Task Vectors (TVs) provide a compact way to steer large language models, but they are typically treated as atomized directions merely extracted from hidden states, leaving their internal functional structure poorly understood. Motivated by prior work that decomposes in-context learning into Task Recognition (TR) and Task Learning (TL), we ask whether a single TV can likewise be decomposed into functionally meaningful components. We formulate a TR/TL-based decomposition from candidate-label unembeddings, separating each TV into TR, TL, and residual components, and try to optimize the TR and TL coefficients using Bayesian optimization for more effective intervention. We evaluate this formulation across multiple model families, classification tasks, and both instruction- and demonstration-based TVs. Across these settings, TR/TL-based optimization identifies intervention directions that outperform the original TVs. Although optimization over random directions can also improve performance, TR/TL-based search yields more reliable gains, particularly for instruction-based TVs. Moreover, isolated interventions on the decomposed components produce distinct logit-level effects that are consistent with their intended functional roles. Together, these results suggest that TVs are not monolithic steering directions, but can be decomposed into functionally meaningful components that support both interpretation and control.

AI.tldr: Decomposes a task vector (TV) used to steer LLMs into task recognition (TR), task learning (TL) and residual components built from candidate-label unembeddings, and optimises the TR and TL coefficients with Bayesian optimisation; the resulting interventions outperform the original TVs.
AI.motivation: Task vectors are used to steer LLMs but are treated as atomised directions whose internal functional structure is poorly understood, although in-context learning has been decomposed into task recognition and task learning.
AI.method: A TR/TL-based decomposition separates each TV into TR, TL and residual components using candidate-label unembeddings, and the TR and TL coefficients are tuned with Bayesian optimisation for intervention; evaluated across several model families, classification tasks, and instruction- and demonstration-based TVs.
AI.result: TR/TL-based optimisation yields intervention directions that outperform the original TVs; optimising over random directions also helps, but TR/TL search gives more reliable gains, especially for instruction-based TVs; isolated interventions on the decomposed components produce distinct logit-level effects consistent with their intended functional roles.
AI.conclusion: Task vectors are not monolithic steering directions and can be decomposed into functionally meaningful components that support both interpretation and control.

title: Do LLMs Know When They Are Wrong About Molecules? In-Context Property Prediction with Self-Reported Uncertainty
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are used in many domains, but molecular property prediction with them is still little explored. In this work we evaluate the capability of 7 frontier LLMs to predict molecular properties together with a self-reported uncertainty from in-context examples, and compare them with classical baselines trained on the same molecules. We use 4 datasets and screen each for contamination of the training data of the LLMs: three are clean, and the fourth, ESOL, is memorised by most of the models and serves as a comparison. On the clean datasets every LLM improves with the context, at 30 examples the most accurate one beats every baseline. The requested reasoning effort changes accuracy little. The self-reported uncertainty ranks the prediction errors weakly, with Spearman rank correlations of up to 0.46, about the level reached by the uncertainties of the baselines. Combining uncertainty and prediction, on lipophilicity the most certain half of the best LLM is the most accurate at small context sizes; on BACE and antiviral, and on lipophilicity at large context sizes, the best LLMs are on par with the best baseline. On the contaminated ESOL dataset the LLMs show no improvement with the context size, as expected for a memorised dataset, and their stated uncertainty is smaller on the molecules whose value they recall.

AI.tldr: Evaluates seven frontier LLMs on in-context molecular property prediction with self-reported uncertainty across four datasets, comparing them with classical baselines; on the three clean datasets the best LLM matches or beats the baselines at larger context sizes, but the self-reported uncertainty ranks errors only weakly.
AI.motivation: LLMs are used in many domains, but their use for molecular property prediction is little explored, and it is unknown whether they can indicate reliably when they are wrong.
AI.method: Seven frontier LLMs predict molecular properties from in-context examples (up to 30) together with a self-reported uncertainty, and are compared against classical baselines trained on the same molecules; the four datasets are screened for training-data contamination, with ESOL, which most models have memorised, used as a comparison.
AI.result: On the clean datasets every LLM improves with more context, and at 30 examples the most accurate one beats every baseline; the requested reasoning effort changes accuracy little; self-reported uncertainty has Spearman rank correlations with prediction errors of up to 0.46, about the level of the baseline uncertainties; on lipophilicity the most certain half of the best LLM is the most accurate at small context sizes, while on BACE and antiviral the best LLMs are on par with the best baseline; on the contaminated ESOL dataset there is no improvement with context size.
