Game theory says what a rational outcome of a strategic interaction is; reinforcement learning says how an agent could reach one through experience. The two literatures nevertheless keep separate vocabularies for identical structures, and the treatments that bridge them present the correspondence as analogy rather than theorem. This monograph supplies the theorems. A game is a Markov decision process in three distinct senses, and every table entry is labelled with the one that applies: a definitional identity, an exact reduction carried by a value- and solution-preserving map, or a structural analogy that fails under identifiable conditions. We take every standard class of game, from normal-form through repeated, stochastic, partially observable, extensive-form with imperfect information, Bayesian, graphical, Stackelberg, potential, coalitional, mean-field and evolutionary games, and identify for each the decision-theoretic model that reinforcement learning already studies under another name. The same treatment is applied to solution concepts: Nash equilibrium and the fixed point of the Bellman optimality operator, quantal response equilibrium and the soft Bellman operator, the Shapley value and credit assignment, Blackwell approachability and no-regret learning. We map each model class onto the training procedures sound for it and record the complexity of the associated solution problems. A final part collects the correspondences that do not hold: the non-stationarity that invalidates the independent-learner reduction, the impossibility results that forbid uncoupled convergence to Nash equilibrium, and the gap between the coarse correlated equilibria that no-regret self-play reaches and the correlated equilibria it is credited with.

AI.tldr: A monograph establishing theorems that map game-theoretic models and solution concepts onto reinforcement learning, labelling each correspondence as a definitional identity, an exact reduction, or a structural analogy that fails under identifiable conditions.
AI.motivation: Game theory and RL describe the same strategic objects with separate vocabularies, and existing bridges present the correspondence as analogy rather than theorem.
AI.method: The authors treat each standard class of game, from normal-form through repeated, stochastic, partially observable, imperfect-information extensive-form, Bayesian, graphical, Stackelberg, potential, coalitional, mean-field and evolutionary games, as an MDP in one of three labelled senses. The same treatment is applied to solution concepts, and each model class is mapped to sound training procedures with the complexity of its solution problem.
AI.result: The abstract reports no numerical results. It identifies the RL model that corresponds to each game class and collects the correspondences that do not hold, including non-stationarity that invalidates the independent-learner reduction, impossibility results that forbid uncoupled convergence to Nash equilibrium, and the gap between coarse correlated equilibria reached by no-regret self-play and the correlated equilibria it is credited with.
AI.conclusion: The monograph gives a rigorous account of when a game is an MDP and where that correspondence breaks, clarifying what no-regret self-play can and cannot deliver.

title: A Neural Network Approach towards Real-Time Knot Point Density Estimates for the Nonlinear Quadrotor
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible. This work is presented at IEEE CDC 2026
summary: Spline representations provide a compact way to approximate continuous trajectories using a finite number of parameters. When approximating trajectories generated by dynamical systems, the efficiency of a spline representation depends strongly on the placement of knot points. Uniform knot distributions often lead to inefficient representations, requiring either unnecessary control points or producing poor approximations in regions where the trajectory varies rapidly. In this work we propose a learning-based method for adaptive knot placement in B-spline approximations of trajectories generated by ordinary differential equations. A neural network learns a mapping from the initial condition of the system to quantities that characterize the local variation of the resulting trajectory. These estimates are used to construct nonuniform knot distributions that approximately equidistribute a local error indicator, reducing the number of control points needed to meet a prescribed accuracy.

AI.tldr: Proposes a learning-based method for adaptive knot placement in B-spline approximations of ODE trajectories, where a neural network predicts local variation from the initial condition so that fewer control points are needed for a prescribed accuracy.
AI.motivation: Uniform knot distributions give inefficient spline representations, requiring either unnecessary control points or producing poor approximations where the trajectory varies rapidly.
AI.method: A neural network maps the initial condition of the system to quantities characterizing the local variation of the resulting trajectory. These estimates are used to build non-uniform knot distributions that approximately equidistribute a local error indicator.
AI.result: The abstract does not report quantitative results. It states that the approach reduces the number of control points needed to meet a prescribed accuracy. The title names a nonlinear quadrotor as the application.
AI.conclusion: Learned knot placement from initial conditions offers a way to obtain compact B-spline representations of ODE trajectories.

title: Empirical Evaluation of Quantum Kernel Methods for Classification: A Comparative Study with Classical Kernels
summary: Quantum kernel methods are the most concrete near-term proposal for quantum machine learning on classical data, yet published benchmarks disagree on whether they outperform tuned classical kernels, and the disagreement cannot be resolved from the literature because the comparisons are not protocol-controlled. We argue that the obstacle is one of measurement, not theory: the usual setup fixes the quantum feature map's data scaling while grid-searching the classical kernel's hyperparameters, recomputes nothing per fold, and reports cost in simulator time. We therefore treat the comparison itself as the object of study and impose three controls. The bandwidth is tuned on the same grid budget as the classical $\gamma$, the kernel is recomputed inside every fold from fold-fitted preprocessing, and cost is counted in hardware circuit evaluations. On top of these we run a factorial design of 324 cells in which dimensionality, training size, class separability and data structure are explicit covariates, together with four standard datasets, a shots-versus-gate-noise ablation, and a cost sweep. The dominant effect we measure is not quantum: tuning the feature map's bandwidth is worth 0.120 accuracy on synthetic data and 0.339 on real data, exceeding every quantum-classical difference we observe. Tuned quantum kernels are then statistically indistinguishable from a tuned RBF on all four real datasets. The advantage on synthetic data is confined almost entirely to data generated by the feature map itself, and it shrinks with dimensionality (-0.0045 per qubit) while growing with sample size. Finite sampling costs an order of magnitude more accuracy than gate and readout noise, and a fidelity kernel needs $5\times10^{7}$ circuits at n = 10,000. Protocol variance is thus sufficient to explain the field's contradictory conclusions.

AI.tldr: A protocol-controlled factorial study finds that tuning the feature map's bandwidth matters far more than the quantum-versus-classical choice, and that tuned quantum kernels are statistically indistinguishable from a tuned RBF kernel on four real datasets.
AI.motivation: Published benchmarks disagree on whether quantum kernels beat tuned classical kernels, and the comparisons are not protocol-controlled: quantum bandwidth is fixed while the classical kernel is tuned, preprocessing is not refit per fold, and cost is reported in simulator time.
AI.method: The authors impose three controls: the bandwidth is tuned on the same grid budget as the classical gamma, the kernel is recomputed inside every fold from fold-fitted preprocessing, and cost is counted in hardware circuit evaluations. They run a 324-cell factorial design over dimensionality, training size, class separability and data structure, together with four standard datasets, a shots-versus-gate-noise ablation and a cost sweep.
AI.result: Tuning bandwidth is worth 0.120 accuracy on synthetic data and 0.339 on real data, exceeding every quantum-classical difference observed. Tuned quantum kernels are statistically indistinguishable from a tuned RBF on all four real datasets. The synthetic advantage is confined almost entirely to data generated by the feature map and shrinks by 0.0045 per qubit. Finite sampling costs more accuracy than gate and readout noise, and a fidelity kernel needs 5 x 10^7 circuits at n = 10,000.
AI.conclusion: Protocol variance is sufficient to explain the field's contradictory conclusions about quantum kernel advantage.

title: Learning Clean Generative Processes from Noisy Measurements
summary: We study how to learn a generative model of clean images using only noisy observations. Diffusion processes and their generalizations to non-Gaussian noise require posterior predictions at every noise level. We first show that it is possible to learn these predictions from independent noisy views using Noise2Noise regression, but only at or above the noise level of the training data. To learn the predictions below that level, needed to generate clean images, we impose consistency: a prediction should equal its expectation after continuing the sampling process. We derive conditions under which consistency uniquely determines the continuation to the clean image distribution and verify them for Poisson, binomial, Gamma, and negative-binomial measurements. Experiments on CIFAR-10, photon-counting microscopy, and synthetic aperture radar show that the required posterior predictions can be learned from noisy views alone and that the consistency relation repairs the continuation beyond the noise level of the data, which severely deteriorates without consistency.

AI.tldr: Shows how to learn a generative model of clean images from noisy measurements alone, using Noise2Noise regression above the training noise level plus a consistency condition that extends the learned posterior predictions below it.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-style generative models normally need clean data, and posterior predictions below the training noise level cannot be learned from noisy observations directly.
AI.method: Noise2Noise regression learns posterior predictions from independent noisy views at or above the training noise level. Below that level the method imposes consistency, requiring a prediction to equal its expectation after continuing the sampling process. Conditions are derived under which consistency uniquely determines the continuation to the clean distribution, and they are verified for Poisson, binomial, Gamma and negative-binomial measurements.
AI.result: Experiments on CIFAR-10, photon-counting microscopy and synthetic aperture radar show that the required predictions can be learned from noisy views alone, and that consistency repairs the continuation beyond the noise level of the data, which otherwise deteriorates severely.
AI.conclusion: Clean-image generative models can be learned from noisy data, and consistency is what makes generation below the measurement noise level work.

title: Exact Theory and Optimal Stepsizes for Stochastic Gradient Descent in Smooth Convex Minimization
summary: This work considers the design of stepsize schedules for stochastic gradient descent in smooth convex optimization. Throughout, we assume that gradient noise is conditionally zero-mean with bounded variance. Among problems with dimension $d\geq N+1$, we provide an exact worst-case analysis of the expected suboptimality of stochastic gradient descent's final iterate. Our analysis applies to any (potentially nonconstant) schedule of $N$ stepsizes in $[0,1.5]^N$. Here, exact means that we provide a matching objective function and noise distributions where our guarantee is attained. Whenever the variance bound is at least $\Omega(1/\sqrt{N})$, our theory provides the minimax optimal stepsize schedule for stochastic gradient descent and proves its uniqueness. These optimal stepsizes monotonically decrease, ruling out any accelerations in expected final suboptimality from fixed fractal schedules observed in the deterministic case.

AI.tldr: Gives an exact worst-case analysis of the final-iterate suboptimality of SGD with any schedule of N stepsizes in smooth convex minimization, and shows that when the variance bound is at least order 1/sqrt(N) the minimax optimal schedule is unique and monotonically decreasing.
AI.motivation: Stepsize schedules for SGD in stochastic smooth convex optimization lack an exact worst-case characterization of expected final-iterate suboptimality, and the deterministic case shows fractal schedules that accelerate convergence, whose behaviour under noise was unknown.
AI.method: The analysis covers any schedule of N stepsizes in [0, 1.5]^N under conditionally zero-mean gradient noise with bounded variance, for dimension d at least N+1. It provides a matching objective function and noise distributions under which the guarantee is attained.
AI.result: Whenever the variance bound is at least order 1/sqrt(N), the theory gives the minimax optimal stepsize schedule for SGD and proves its uniqueness. These optimal stepsizes decrease monotonically.
AI.conclusion: Fixed fractal schedules cannot accelerate expected final suboptimality under gradient noise, because the optimal schedule decreases monotonically.

title: RAMA: Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Agent Routing with Episodic Memory for LEO Satellite Networks
summary: Low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks present a challenging routing environment due to rapidly changing topology, traffic, and link conditions. Existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) routing methods typically rely on current observations and information encoded in network weights, limiting their ability to exploit successful past experiences. We propose RAMA, a retrieval-augmented multi-agent DRL framework with Approximate Information State (AIS), in which each satellite combines its local observation, recent routing history, neighboring state information, and retrieved entries from a per-satellite episodic memory. Retrieved experiences are integrated through a Transformer-based decision network trained with AIS-based auxiliary objectives. With weights frozen in a 140-satellite Kepler constellation, RAMA reduces mean end-to-end latency by 13.4% and 99th-percentile latency by 66.7% relative to the state-of-theart double deep Q-network (DDQN) routing method, mainly by avoiding long detours. Updated online, RAMA remains stable while DDQN degrades. On the 1,584-satellite Starlink shell 1, the reduction in mean latency grows to 93.2%, and updating RAMA online lowers its mean latency by a further 25.5%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented memory for scalable decentralized routing in LEO satellite networks.

AI.tldr: Proposes RAMA, a retrieval-augmented multi-agent DRL routing framework for LEO satellite networks in which each satellite retrieves entries from a per-satellite episodic memory, reducing mean latency relative to the DDQN routing baseline.
AI.motivation: Existing DRL routing methods for LEO networks rely on current observations and information encoded in network weights, which limits their ability to exploit successful past experiences in a rapidly changing topology.
AI.method: Each satellite combines its local observation, recent routing history, neighbouring state information and entries retrieved from a per-satellite episodic memory. Retrieved experiences are integrated through a Transformer-based decision network trained with Approximate Information State auxiliary objectives.
AI.result: With weights frozen in a 140-satellite Kepler constellation, RAMA reduces mean end-to-end latency by 13.4% and 99th-percentile latency by 66.7% relative to DDQN, mainly by avoiding long detours. Updated online it remains stable while DDQN degrades. On the 1,584-satellite Starlink shell 1 the mean latency reduction grows to 93.2%, and online updating lowers mean latency by a further 25.5%.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-augmented memory is an effective way to achieve scalable decentralized routing in LEO satellite networks.

title: Hard Constraint Projection in a Physics Informed Neural Network (Burgers)
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, In proceedings of 1st international Symposium on AI and Fluid Mechanics 2025 (Paper No. S11P2)
summary: Physics informed machine learning provides a framework to study and simulate fluid dynamics, potentially at a fraction of the computational cost of traditional numerical methods, with the goal of improving the explainability, accuracy and robustness of purely data driven machine learning methods. In this work, we extend the hard constraint projection (HCP) method developed by Chen et al. [Journal of Computational Physics, 445, 110624, 2021] from a linear partial differential equation (PDE) to a nonlinear PDE: the 1D Burgers' equation. To strictly impose a discrete approximation of the governing equation, the Burgers' equation is first locally discretised (using a finite difference stencil) then decomposed into a constraint matrix and a prediction matrix. Using tools from linear algebra, the constraint matrix is used to construct a projection matrix. A physics informed neural network (PINN) [Raissi et al. Journal of Computational Physics, 378, 686, 2019] is used to predict the velocity, and a final unlearnable layer projects the velocity prediction to the hyperplane of exact solutions to a discretised form of the Burgers' equation. Our initial results indicate that the HCP-PINN initially trains similarly to an equivalent PINN, and as the PINN loss plateaus, the HCP-PINN loss continues to decline. When tested on a previously unseen uniform grid of points covering the domain, the HCP-PINN exhibits higher accuracy, converging to a data error approximately an order of magnitude lower than the comparable PINN. We also observe that the inclusion of the HCP layer results in better observance of the governing PDE. Our findings suggest that the HCP-PINN can be more robust to the selection of physics collocation points, and less dependent on collocation point quantity.

AI.tldr: Extends hard constraint projection to the nonlinear 1D Burgers' equation, enforcing a discrete finite-difference form of the PDE in a PINN, and reports an error roughly an order of magnitude lower than a comparable PINN on an unseen grid.
AI.motivation: Hard constraint projection was developed for linear PDEs, and physics-informed networks can be sensitive to the selection and quantity of collocation points.
AI.method: The Burgers' equation is discretised with a finite-difference stencil and decomposed into a constraint matrix and a prediction matrix, from which a projection matrix is built. A PINN predicts the velocity, and a final unlearnable layer projects that prediction onto the hyperplane of exact solutions of the discretised equation.
AI.result: The HCP-PINN trains similarly to a PINN at first, but its loss keeps declining after the PINN loss plateaus. On an unseen uniform grid it converges to a data error about an order of magnitude lower than the comparable PINN, and it observes the governing PDE better.
AI.conclusion: The HCP-PINN appears more robust to the choice of collocation points and less dependent on their quantity, according to these initial results.

title: Regret-Optimal Wasserstein-Robust Linear Regression
summary: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) minimizes worst-case risk under distributional uncertainty, but its decisions can be suboptimal in terms of their excess risk, or regret. We study this gap for multivariate least-squares regression, assuming that the observed source law and unknown target law differ by an adversarial 2-Wasserstein perturbation of size $\varepsilon$. We first identify the asymptotic complexity of robust decision-making in the $\varepsilon \to 0$ limit, characterized by a problem-specific condition number $\kappa$. Here, a wide spectrum of simple algorithms, including DRO, achieve the instance-optimal rate of $O(\kappa \varepsilon^2)$. For fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, we prove that DRO still achieves the minimax rate if the problem has bounded residual effective rank. On the other hand, we identify significant failure modes where DRO is provably suboptimal by dimension-dependent factors. Fortunately, we prove that two alternative procedures, minimax regret optimization (MRO) and spectral-norm regularization (SNR), attain the minimax rate. We derive an exact convex reformulation of MRO and an accelerated proximal algorithm for SNR, along with high-probability finite-sample guarantees. We support these theoretical results with numerical experiments separating the performance of MRO and SNR from DRO.

AI.tldr: Shows that distributionally robust optimization can be regret-suboptimal for least-squares regression under a 2-Wasserstein shift, and proves that minimax regret optimization and spectral-norm regularization attain the minimax rate where DRO does not.
AI.motivation: DRO minimizes worst-case risk under distributional uncertainty, but its decisions can be suboptimal in excess risk, or regret.
AI.method: For multivariate least squares with an adversarial 2-Wasserstein perturbation of size epsilon, the authors identify the small-epsilon complexity through a problem-specific condition number and study DRO at fixed epsilon through residual effective rank. They derive an exact convex reformulation of minimax regret optimization (MRO) and an accelerated proximal algorithm for spectral-norm regularization (SNR), with high-probability finite-sample guarantees.
AI.result: In the small-epsilon limit a wide range of simple algorithms, including DRO, attain the instance-optimal rate O(kappa epsilon^2). DRO attains the minimax rate under bounded residual effective rank but is provably suboptimal by dimension-dependent factors in identified failure modes, whereas MRO and SNR attain the minimax rate. Numerical experiments separate their performance from DRO.
AI.conclusion: Regret-based robust procedures are needed in regimes where DRO is provably suboptimal by dimension-dependent factors.

title: SATFRONT: Detecting Atmospheric Fronts with Satellite Data using Machine Learning
summary: Atmospheric fronts are associated with much of the high-impact weather in the mid-latitudes, yet their identification and classification remain largely manual and subjective. Existing deep learning approaches rely primarily on gridded reanalysis or forecast data, limiting their applicability to satellite observations available for time-critical applications. We introduce SATFRONT, a machine learning framework for detecting cold, warm, and occluded fronts over Europe from geostationary satellite observations, with reanalysis data as an optional additional input. The model is trained on frontal analyses from five European national meteorological services and evaluated against UK Met Office analyses for 2024. Using satellite observations alone, SATFRONT achieves a Critical Success Index (CSI) of 0.428 at a 150 km tolerance, within the range of agreement between analyses from different meteorological services (0.277-0.501) and higher than that of an operational rule-based front detector that uses satellite data (0.133). Adding ERA5 reanalysis increases the CSI to 0.591. ERA5 substantially improves the placement of individual fronts, although its effect on their annual spatial distribution varies by front type. These results demonstrate that cold, warm, and occluded fronts can be detected directly from geostationary satellite observations, providing a basis for automated frontal analyses at the high temporal frequency required for time-critical applications.

AI.tldr: Presents SATFRONT, a machine learning framework that detects cold, warm and occluded fronts over Europe directly from geostationary satellite observations, with ERA5 reanalysis as an optional input, and outperforms an operational rule-based satellite detector.
AI.motivation: Atmospheric front identification is largely manual and subjective, and existing deep learning approaches rely on gridded reanalysis or forecast data, which limits their use for satellite observations in time-critical applications.
AI.method: The model is trained on frontal analyses from five European national meteorological services, with reanalysis data as an optional additional input, and is evaluated against UK Met Office analyses for 2024.
AI.result: With satellite observations alone SATFRONT reaches a CSI of 0.428 at a 150 km tolerance, within the range of agreement between analyses from different services (0.277 to 0.501) and above an operational rule-based satellite detector (0.133). Adding ERA5 raises the CSI to 0.591 and substantially improves the placement of individual fronts, although its effect on annual spatial distribution varies by front type.
AI.conclusion: Fronts can be detected directly from geostationary satellite observations, providing a basis for automated frontal analysis at the temporal frequency needed for time-critical applications.

title: A Better Critic Matters for Distribution Matching Distillation
comment: 35 pages, 16 figures. Project page and code: this https URL
summary: Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) trains a few-step student using the difference between a teacher's score and an online critic's estimate of the student distribution's score. We investigate what the critic needs, in capacity and in information, to provide a reliable training signal. On the capacity side, controlled experiments across seven SiT model sizes on ImageNet show that increasing teacher size while keeping a small critic fixed can degrade student quality and cause training collapse. Scaling the critic alongside the teacher, a strategy we call joint scaling, prevents collapse in our experiments and allows the student to benefit from larger teachers. On the information side, rather than forcing the critic to model a step-agnostic mixture of student outputs, we introduce a step-aware critic (STAC) that conditions on the student's generation step to estimate step-specific scores. Together, joint scaling and STAC consistently improve few-step distillation across class-conditional ImageNet generation, text-to-image generation with SDXL and FLUX.2, and text-to-video generation with Wan2.1.

AI.tldr: Shows that Distribution Matching Distillation depends on the critic's capacity and information, proposing joint scaling of teacher and critic to prevent collapse and a step-aware critic (STAC) that conditions on the generation step, consistently improving few-step distillation across image and video models.
AI.motivation: In DMD the critic estimates the student distribution's score, and a fixed small critic paired with a larger teacher can degrade student quality and cause training collapse, while a step-agnostic critic must model a mixture of student outputs across steps.
AI.method: Controlled experiments across seven SiT model sizes on ImageNet vary teacher and critic size. Joint scaling grows the critic alongside the teacher, and STAC conditions the critic on the student's generation step to estimate step-specific scores.
AI.result: Joint scaling prevents collapse in the experiments and lets the student benefit from larger teachers. Joint scaling and STAC consistently improve few-step distillation across class-conditional ImageNet generation, text-to-image generation with SDXL and FLUX.2, and text-to-video generation with Wan2.1.
AI.conclusion: Critic capacity and step-aware information both matter for providing a reliable training signal in few-step distribution matching distillation.

title: Latent Reasoning in Continuous Space for Unified Multimodal Models
comment: Published as conference proceeding for NeurIPS 2026. Last two authors advised equally
summary: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) achieve remarkable success on diverse multimodal understanding and generation tasks, yet they still struggle to effectively leverage language-based chain-of-thought reasoning for image generation. As a result, existing reasoning-augmented UMMs often fail to inherit the test-time scaling and fine-grained controllability observed in large language models. We attribute this failure to a fundamental modality mismatch: reasoning is performed in a discrete token space, whereas image generation operates in a continuous space. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Latent Reasoning framework in Continuous space (LARC), which alleviates the token-level bottleneck by reasoning over continuous hidden states. Specifically, the training framework consists of two stages: (i) curriculum supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and (ii) information-gain reinforcement learning (RL). First, the curriculum SFT stage gradually converts token-level reasoning into latent reasoning. Subsequently, the information-gain RL stage self-evolves latent reasoning without ground truth supervision. Experiments across diverse text-to-image generation benchmarks show that LARC consistently improves generation quality, prompt following, and compositional fidelity. Notably, LARC achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval with a 7%p gain over BAGEL and demonstrates clear test-time scaling behavior, outperforming token-based generation under both parallel and sequential test-time scaling strategies.

AI.tldr: LARC performs chain-of-thought reasoning over continuous hidden states instead of discrete tokens to improve text-to-image generation in unified multimodal models, and reports gains in generation quality, prompt following and compositional fidelity, with state-of-the-art GenEval results.
AI.motivation: Reasoning-augmented unified multimodal models do not inherit the test-time scaling and fine-grained controllability of LLMs because language reasoning happens in a discrete token space while image generation operates in a continuous space, a modality mismatch that existing methods do not address.
AI.method: A two-stage training framework: curriculum supervised fine-tuning that gradually converts token-level reasoning into latent reasoning, followed by information-gain reinforcement learning that self-evolves latent reasoning without ground-truth supervision.
AI.result: Consistent improvements across diverse text-to-image benchmarks in generation quality, prompt following and compositional fidelity; state-of-the-art on GenEval with a 7 percentage point gain over BAGEL; clear test-time scaling that outperforms token-based generation under both parallel and sequential scaling strategies.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning over continuous latent states relieves the token-level bottleneck and lets reasoning-augmented unified multimodal models gain test-time scaling and controllability in image generation.

title: More Rules, Longer Lists? Benchmarking Self-Evolving Agents on a Hidden-Rule Curriculum
summary: Self-evolving agents rewrite a persistent state from feedback, but it is largely untested whether this lets them learn a rule nobody told them. An agent can also pass by writing down each correction as an exception, and its list then grows with every new rule. We introduce CLR-Bench, a Curriculum of Latent Rules benchmark. Each chain adds one hidden rule per level on top of the earlier ones. A rule acts on an opaque label that stands for a named grouping published on the Web, such as the founding members of an airline alliance. The task gives one example value, practice feedback reveals one more member and one non-member, and the test checks unseen members and similar non-members. Probes certify that the base model knows the members of each grouping and does not guess it without feedback, and that the evidence identifies the grouping once labels are read as named groupings. An automated pipeline builds chains from a new data domain, and we release 20 chains over 10 domains. We evaluate six recent self-evolution methods. With the certifying model they barely learn. The best gain at most 5 points over a frozen agent and exclude only 6-12% of the unseen members from the count, fewer than the 20% reached by simply keeping the raw practice history. A fixed lesson that states the named-grouping convention lifts the same methods by 14.5 to 16.5 points. Their states hold the revealed member in 75-98% of cases and almost never the class name, and when practice exposes a member the list misses, they add that member to the list. With the stronger GPT-6-Sol, ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet learn from feedback alone. They reach 78% accuracy and solve 59-60% of the single cells, against 53% and 8% with the certifying model, and they surpass the raw history. CLR-Bench therefore measures how well an agent learns, and this ability differs across models.

AI.tldr: CLR-Bench is a benchmark of curricula with hidden latent rules that tests whether self-evolving agents learn a rule from feedback rather than accumulating exceptions. With a certifying base model, six self-evolution methods barely learn, but a fixed lesson stating the named-grouping convention lifts them by 14.5 to 16.5 points.
AI.motivation: It is untested whether self-evolving agents can learn a rule that nobody states, and an agent can pass by writing each correction as an exception, so its persistent state grows with every new rule.
AI.method: Each chain adds one hidden rule per level over opaque labels that stand for named groupings published on the Web. The agent gets one example value, practice feedback reveals one member and one non-member, and the test uses unseen members and similar non-members. Probes certify the base model's knowledge of each grouping; an automated pipeline builds chains from new data domains; 20 chains over 10 domains are released and six recent self-evolution methods are evaluated.
AI.result: With the certifying model the best method gains at most 5 points over a frozen agent and excludes only 6 to 12 percent of unseen members, fewer than the 20 percent reached by keeping the raw practice history. A fixed lesson stating the named-grouping convention lifts the same methods by 14.5 to 16.5 points. With the stronger GPT-6-Sol, ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet reach 78 percent accuracy and solve 59 to 60 percent of single cells, against 53 percent and 8 percent with the certifying model, and surpass the raw history.
AI.conclusion: CLR-Bench measures how well an agent learns from feedback, and this ability differs across models, so it should be assessed separately from base-model knowledge.

title: PathoJev: Efficient Pathology Decisions from Shared Visual Context
summary: Pathology workflows require multiple visual judgments about the same slide, from identifying tumor type to assessing grade and invasion. Generating and parsing a separate textual response for each structured question adds latency between visual evidence and usable decisions. Building on the System One paradigm, we introduce PathoJev, a pathology model that directly predicts answer probabilities for whole-slide and region-level assessment. PathoJev encodes each slide once and evaluates independent question suffixes in batches over the shared visual context. Reusing the hybrid backbone's recurrent states further limits the computation that grows with slide-context length for each additional question. Across three whole-slide benchmarks, the 9B and 27B models achieve mean accuracies of 77.2% and 78.1%, exceeding SlideChat by 5.4 and 6.3 percentage points. Both scales also maintain competitive accuracy on five ROI benchmarks. On WSI-Bench, the 9B model runs 9.1x faster than SlideChat. Shared context accelerates eight-question workloads by 6.9x and 5.9x over separate prefix encoding, rising to 11.2x and 8.9x for 64 questions. These results provide a reusable probabilistic interface for combining multiple visual judgments in whole-slide and local tissue assessment. Code: this https URL.

AI.tldr: PathoJev is a pathology model that encodes a whole slide once and predicts answer probabilities for several independent questions in batches over the shared visual context. It matches or exceeds SlideChat's accuracy while answering multiple questions much faster.
AI.motivation: Pathology workflows need several visual judgments about the same slide, but generating and parsing a separate textual response for each structured question adds latency between visual evidence and usable decisions.
AI.method: Building on the System One paradigm, the model directly predicts answer probabilities instead of generating text. It encodes each slide once, evaluates independent question suffixes in batches over the shared visual context, and reuses the hybrid backbone's recurrent states to limit the computation that grows with slide-context length for each additional question.
AI.result: Mean accuracies of 77.2 percent (9B) and 78.1 percent (27B) across three whole-slide benchmarks, exceeding SlideChat by 5.4 and 6.3 percentage points; competitive accuracy on five ROI benchmarks; the 9B model runs 9.1 times faster than SlideChat on WSI-Bench; shared context speeds up eight-question workloads by 6.9 and 5.9 times over separate prefix encoding, rising to 11.2 and 8.9 times for 64 questions.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a reusable probabilistic interface for combining multiple visual judgments in whole-slide and local tissue assessment.

title: Stochastic Mirror Descent under Dependent Observations
summary: We study the non-asymptotic convergence of Stochastic Mirror Descent (SMD) algorithm when the noisy first-order oracle is driven by dependent observations. Departing from the classical i.i.d. assumption underlying most existing guarantees, we introduce a flexible ``forgetting" condition that accommodates geometrically or polynomially dependent sequences. Under this condition we derive explicit finite-sample accuracy bounds for the averaged SMD iterates, recovering the classical $O(1/T)$ and $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ rates in the large- and small-initial-error regimes. We instantiate the general framework on two applications: high-dimensional linear regression with dependent regressors and nonparametric estimation of the drift function of a functional autoregressive model.

AI.tldr: The paper proves non-asymptotic convergence bounds for averaged Stochastic Mirror Descent when the oracle observations are dependent rather than i.i.d., under a flexible forgetting condition. The classical O(1/T) and O(1/sqrt(T)) rates are recovered in the two initial-error regimes.
AI.motivation: Most existing Stochastic Mirror Descent guarantees assume i.i.d. observations, an assumption that fails for many practical data-generating processes with temporal dependence.
AI.method: A flexible forgetting condition that accommodates geometrically or polynomially dependent sequences, used to derive explicit finite-sample accuracy bounds for the averaged iterates.
AI.result: The classical O(1/T) and O(1/sqrt(T)) rates are recovered in the large- and small-initial-error regimes. The framework is instantiated on high-dimensional linear regression with dependent regressors and on nonparametric estimation of the drift function of a functional autoregressive model.
AI.conclusion: Standard mirror descent rates persist under dependent data that satisfies the forgetting condition, extending the theory to dependent regressors and autoregressive drift estimation.

title: Instrumental Transfer Learning for Solution Operators
summary: Data-driven learning for the solution operator of a differential equation has broad scientific importance, but observations from a target system are often scarce and costly to collect. Related source systems may provide abundant observations under similar physical conditions, whereas even small changes in the governing equation can induce complex changes in the solution operator, making naive data pooling ineffective. We propose a structured transfer learning method that accounts for unknown sparse differences in the governing equations from a known library of candidate terms. Using the resolvent identity and a whitened instrumental variable approach, we construct unbiased source estimating equations for the target operator. Building on these equations, we develop a three-stage estimator that consists of a target-only ridge pilot, source-wise sparse calibration, and a projected refit designed to remove the leading calibration error inherited from the pilot. An iterative recalibration scheme further reduces the remaining error. We establish non-asymptotic prediction bounds showing when transfer achieves the pooled all-source rate, together with minimax lower bounds that characterize both rate optimality and fundamental identifiability limits under common shifts. Simulations and an electronic band-pass filter application demonstrate clear gains over target-only learning, naive pooling and existing transfer methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a transfer learning estimator for the solution operator of a differential equation that uses abundant source-system data while handling sparse, unknown differences in the governing equation. It achieves the pooled all-source rate when transfer is possible and outperforms target-only learning, naive pooling and existing transfer methods in simulations and an electronic band-pass filter application.
AI.motivation: Observations from a target system are scarce and costly, while naive pooling of source data is ineffective because even small changes in the governing equation can alter the solution operator substantially.
AI.method: Using the resolvent identity and a whitened instrumental variable approach to build unbiased source estimating equations, followed by a three-stage estimator: a target-only ridge pilot, source-wise sparse calibration over a known library of candidate terms, and a projected refit that removes the leading calibration error inherited from the pilot, with an iterative recalibration scheme.
AI.result: Non-asymptotic prediction bounds show when transfer achieves the pooled all-source rate. Minimax lower bounds characterize rate optimality and fundamental identifiability limits under common shifts. Simulations and the band-pass filter application show clear gains over target-only learning, naive pooling and existing transfer methods.
AI.conclusion: Structured, sparsity-based transfer is provably beneficial under identifiable conditions, and the minimax bounds mark its fundamental limits.

title: Bethe Hessian Recovery through the Kesten-Stigum Regime
summary: We show that outlier eigenvectors of the Bethe Hessian achieve weak recovery in the stochastic block model down to the Kesten-Stigum threshold, for every fixed common expected degree $d>1$. This extends previous recovery guarantees, which required $d$ to be sufficiently large. This threshold is information-theoretically optimal for the symmetric two-community model and is conjectured to mark the limit of efficient recovery in broader symmetric models. Our result matches the recovery guarantees of non-backtracking spectral methods while using Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices. To do this, we identify recursive formulas for the negative outlier eigenvalues and show that their eigenspaces have nonvanishing overlap with the corresponding planted eigenspaces. The proof constructs approximate eigenvectors from the planted labels on the limiting Poisson tree, with weights given by its Green's function, and transfers these approximations to the finite graph.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that outlier eigenvectors of the Bethe Hessian achieve weak recovery in the stochastic block model for every fixed common expected degree d greater than 1, down to the Kesten-Stigum threshold. This removes the earlier requirement that d be sufficiently large.
AI.motivation: Previous recovery guarantees for the Bethe Hessian required the expected degree to be sufficiently large, leaving the regime near the Kesten-Stigum threshold unresolved.
AI.method: Identifying recursive formulas for the negative outlier eigenvalues and showing that their eigenspaces have nonvanishing overlap with the planted eigenspaces. Approximate eigenvectors are built from the planted labels on the limiting Poisson tree, weighted by its Green's function, and transferred to the finite graph. The method uses Hermitian n by n matrices.
AI.result: Matches the recovery guarantees of non-backtracking spectral methods while using Hermitian n by n matrices. The threshold is information-theoretically optimal for the symmetric two-community model.
AI.conclusion: Bethe Hessian spectral recovery reaches the Kesten-Stigum threshold, giving a Hermitian alternative to non-backtracking methods with the same guarantees.

title: On Statistical-Computational Gaps in Graph Combinatorial Testing Problems
summary: We study high-dimensional graph combinatorial hypothesis testing problems in which a signal is supported on the edge set of an unknown subgraph drawn from a class invariant under vertex relabeling. For Gaussian observations, we characterize sharp statistical and computational thresholds (at polynomial order) for the signal magnitude required for strong detection across various combinatorial graph alternatives. Our analysis is based on bounding the second moments of the full and low-degree likelihood ratios in terms of the overlap of two independent latent structures and comparing the resulting lower bounds with scan, average, and coordinatewise maximum tests. Under an appropriate low-degree conjecture for computational hardness, we obtain planted-clique thresholds matching those known for Gaussian submatrix detection and identify new statistical-computational gaps for multiple planted cliques and hypercliques, thick cycles and thick paths. We also establish a novel transfer principle across natural exponential family observation models: matching the one-coordinate chi-square divergence preserves full likelihood-ratio second moments exactly and makes low-degree second moments equivalent up to constant factors under a degree condition. Under local regularity, we obtain corresponding testing upper bounds in terms of an effective signal strength. When these upper and lower bounds match, they yield universal threshold scales in the local alternative regime. As a consequence, statistical-computational gaps for planted-clique detection in Erdős--Rényi settings can be deduced from the Gaussian model.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes sharp statistical and computational thresholds for detecting a signal on the edges of an unknown structured subgraph under Gaussian observations. It identifies new statistical-computational gaps and gives a transfer principle that carries results across natural exponential family observation models.
AI.motivation: Detecting structured graph signals such as planted cliques, thick cycles and thick paths lacks sharp statistical and computational thresholds, and hardness results for different observation models are not directly comparable.
AI.method: Bounding the second moments of full and low-degree likelihood ratios in terms of the overlap of two independent latent structures, and comparing the resulting lower bounds with scan, average and coordinatewise maximum tests. A transfer principle matches the one-coordinate chi-square divergence across exponential family observation models, and testing upper bounds are derived under local regularity.
AI.result: Under an appropriate low-degree conjecture, the planted-clique thresholds match those known for Gaussian submatrix detection, and new gaps are identified for multiple planted cliques and hypercliques, thick cycles and thick paths. Statistical-computational gaps for planted-clique detection in Erdos-Renyi settings can be deduced from the Gaussian model.
AI.conclusion: When upper and lower bounds match they give universal threshold scales in the local alternative regime, and results from the Gaussian model transfer to other exponential family observation models.

title: Near-Optimal Second-Order Convex Finite-Sum Optimization under Individual Smoothness
summary: We study the stochastic second-order oracle complexity of solving smooth convex finite-sum optimization with $n$ components. Very recently, Tsedenov \& Kovalev (2026) showed that the minimax optimal complexity under averaged smoothness and convexity is $\tilde{\Theta}(n + n^{6/7} \epsilon^{-2/7})$ by establishing nearly matching upper and lower bounds. In this paper, we show that individual smoothness and convexity provably enable further acceleration, where the lower complexity bound is $\Omega(n+ n^{5/7} \epsilon^{-2/7})$ under this stronger assumption. Then, by establishing a novel second-order self-bounding inequality, we design a new Taylor-corrected lazy Newton method, which can lead to a better complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n + n^{5/7} \epsilon^{-2/7})$ by applying the optimal Monteiro-Svaiter acceleration, matching our lower bound up to only logarithmic factors.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that individual smoothness and convexity enable further acceleration for stochastic second-order optimization of convex finite sums, with a lower bound of Omega(n + n^{5/7} eps^{-2/7}). It gives a Taylor-corrected lazy Newton method whose complexity matches this bound up to logarithmic factors.
AI.motivation: Under averaged smoothness and convexity the minimax complexity is about n + n^{6/7} eps^{-2/7}; whether individual smoothness allows more acceleration was not settled.
AI.method: Establishing a lower bound under individual smoothness, deriving a novel second-order self-bounding inequality, designing a Taylor-corrected lazy Newton method, and applying optimal Monteiro-Svaiter acceleration.
AI.result: A lower bound of Omega(n + n^{5/7} eps^{-2/7}) under individual smoothness and an upper bound of O~(n + n^{5/7} eps^{-2/7}), matching up to logarithmic factors.
AI.conclusion: Individual smoothness provably enables acceleration beyond the averaged-smoothness minimax rate, and the proposed method is near-optimal under that assumption.

title: CausalWAM: Learning the Causes of Actions in World Action Models
summary: World action models (WAMs) learn latent variables from observations and use these to both predict the evolution of the scene and to generate actions. The prediction has to be of the whole scene, whereas only a portion of the scene causes actions. WAMs fitted to demonstrations do not, in general, guarantee that they will generate actions solely from the latent causes of the demonstrated actions (the action-relevant latent variables), as the model could just as well learn to imitate in this way whilst entangling the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance variables. We therefore separate out what causes action from what prediction depends on. We prove that under a sparsity constraint the latent variables used to generate actions are an invertible function of the action-relevant latent variables alone and the true structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables. This requires neither sufficient temporal dependence nor any assumptions on how the unobserved regimes evolve and holds even when the action-relevant latent variables are statistically dependent on the rest. We therefore propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which incorporates the constraint into a pretrained WAM by adding a sparse routing path to its action head, with the world modeling objective remaining unchanged. Experiments on both synthetic data and real-world robots validate the theory as well as showcase the improved efficiency in closed-loop success.

AI.tldr: CWAM adds a sparse routing path to the action head of a pretrained world action model so that actions are generated only from the latent variables that cause them, while the world-modeling objective stays unchanged. The paper proves identifiability under sparsity and reports better closed-loop efficiency on synthetic data and real robots.
AI.motivation: World action models fitted to demonstrations may generate actions from entangled nuisance variables, because prediction needs the whole scene while only part of the scene causes actions.
AI.method: Under a sparsity constraint the latent variables used to generate actions are shown to be an invertible function of the action-relevant latent variables alone, with the true structure identified up to permutation. This needs neither sufficient temporal dependence nor assumptions on how unobserved regimes evolve. CWAM implements the constraint by adding a sparse routing path to the action head of a pretrained WAM.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic data and real-world robots validate the theory and show improved efficiency in closed-loop success.
AI.conclusion: Separating what causes actions from what prediction depends on yields identifiable action-relevant latent variables and more efficient closed-loop control, even when those variables are statistically dependent on the rest.

title: Beyond Plausible Prediction: Safety Sufficiency in Web World Models
summary: Web world models increasingly predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, yet a plausible predicted future does not necessarily support the correct safety decision. In a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. However, several models exhibit highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour, combining low false-safe execution with poor recall of clarifiable ASK cases and a strong preference for BLOCK. This motivates safety sufficiency: whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required to distinguish actions that may be EXECUTED, require clarification through ASK, or should be BLOCKED. We introduce SafeWebWorld, a benchmark for evaluating safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains through action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions. Under a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol, evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. To determine whether this deterioration reflects loss of authorisation-sensitive score structure or a failure of the decision readout, we introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR). Frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, while paired recovery provides only a modest additional gain. Yet within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor, showing that aggregate recoverability does not imply robust fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Overall, plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recovery are each insufficient on their own to establish robust authorisation.

AI.tldr: SafeWebWorld benchmarks whether a predicted web future preserves enough policy-decisive evidence to correctly EXECUTE, ASK or BLOCK an action. In a matched human evaluation 86.1 percent of 3,000 predictions are judged plausible, yet authorisation decisions remain unreliable.
AI.motivation: Web world models predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, but a plausible prediction does not guarantee the correct safety decision, and plausibility alone does not measure whether the prediction supports that decision.
AI.method: Introduces safety sufficiency and the SafeWebWorld benchmark across five web-safety domains, with action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence and policy-conditioned decisions. Uses a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol and Latent Authorisation Recovery, which applies frozen-score recalibration and paired recovery to diagnose whether the decision readout or the score structure is at fault.
AI.result: Under the fine-tuning protocol evidence preservation improves substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. Frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, paired recovery adds only a modest further gain, and within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor. Several of the ten frozen open models show asymmetric authorisation behaviour, with low false-safe execution, poor recall of ASK cases and a strong preference for BLOCK.
AI.conclusion: Plausible prediction, evidence preservation and aggregate recoverability are each insufficient on their own to establish robust authorisation behaviour.

title: Circumventing the Computational Hardness of Computational Arbitrage
summary: AI model marketplaces host providers with heterogeneous costs and capabilities. These differences create an opportunity for computational arbitrage (Olmedo et al., 2026), in which an intermediary purchases inference from a portfolio of models and resells it to users at a profit. Beyond creating profit opportunities for the arbitrageur, computational arbitrage offers financial value to both consumers and providers and could therefore significantly influence AI model markets. While prior work empirically demonstrates the feasibility of computational arbitrage for small model pools, scaling it to large marketplaces requires arbitrage strategies that are both computationally tractable and inexpensive to identify and deploy. In this work, we formalize computational arbitrage as an allocation problem and prove that it is generally NP-hard. However, we show that the optimal allocation can be computed efficiently under a natural diminishing-returns condition on how model performance scales with inference spending. We further develop a sample-efficient method for estimating model performance from limited data, reducing the upfront cost of identifying arbitrage strategies. Our analysis also yields several economic insights: at the optimum, every funded model delivers the same marginal utility per dollar; arbitrage directs revenue away from providers offering little utility relative to their prices; and it rewards complementary specialization.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes computational arbitrage over AI model marketplaces as an allocation problem and proves it is generally NP-hard, but shows the optimum can be computed efficiently under a diminishing-returns condition. It also gives a sample-efficient method for estimating model performance and draws several economic insights.
AI.motivation: Arbitrage across providers with heterogeneous costs and capabilities could significantly influence AI model markets, but scaling it to large marketplaces requires strategies that are tractable and inexpensive to identify and deploy.
AI.method: Formalizing arbitrage as an allocation problem, proving general NP-hardness, and identifying a natural diminishing-returns condition on how performance scales with inference spending under which the optimal allocation is efficiently computable. A sample-efficient method estimates model performance from limited data.
AI.result: The allocation problem is generally NP-hard, while under diminishing returns the optimum is efficiently computable. At the optimum every funded model delivers the same marginal utility per dollar. Arbitrage directs revenue away from providers offering little utility relative to their prices and rewards complementary specialization.
AI.conclusion: Computational arbitrage is tractable under a natural condition, and it redistributes revenue toward providers that offer utility and specialize in complementary ways.

title: Incongruence-Aware Evaluation of Multimodal Speech Emotion Recognition in Audio Large Language Models
summary: Voice-interactive large language models process both what a speaker says and how they say it, yet the two channels do not always agree. We ask whether that disagreement degrades speech emotion recognition. Mapping text and audio into a shared valence-arousal-dominance space, we convert the distance between them into a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score with a two-component Gaussian mixture, and validate the score against human judgement. We evaluate three audiocapable models on acted, conversational and spontaneous speech (eNTERFACE'05, MELD and CMU-MOSEI). With the model held constant across modalities, incongruence raises the odds of error whenever audio is present, in every corpus, after controlling for the ground-truth emotion and for distance in the feature space. Supervised classifiers trained on the same features behave in the opposite way, which suggests that the difficulty lies in how these models combine raw evidence rather than in the signal itself. Text-only effects are unreliable: swapping only the model that reads the transcript reverses their sign on one corpus. Rebuilding the score without the emotion lexicon reproduces the central result, and among six simpler alternatives it is the only label-free score that predicts error in all three corpora. Code, data tables and prompts are released.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that disagreement between the transcript and the audio in audio LLMs raises the odds of speech emotion recognition errors whenever audio is present, across three corpora. The incongruence score is a threshold-free, label-free measure built from valence-arousal-dominance space and a two-component Gaussian mixture.
AI.motivation: Voice-interactive LLMs process both what a speaker says and how they say it, but it was unknown whether disagreement between these channels degrades speech emotion recognition.
AI.method: Mapping text and audio into a shared valence-arousal-dominance space, converting their distance into a continuous incongruence score with a two-component Gaussian mixture, validating the score against human judgement, and evaluating three audio-capable models on eNTERFACE'05, MELD and CMU-MOSEI while controlling for the ground-truth emotion and for feature-space distance.
AI.result: With the model held constant, incongruence raises the odds of error whenever audio is present, in every corpus. Supervised classifiers trained on the same features behave in the opposite way. Text-only effects are unreliable, reversing sign on one corpus when only the transcript-reading model is swapped. A score rebuilt without the emotion lexicon reproduces the central result and is the only label-free score among six alternatives that predicts error in all three corpora.
AI.conclusion: The difficulty lies in how audio LLMs combine raw evidence rather than in the signal itself, and incongruence is a useful diagnostic for evaluating them.

title: ChatGPT as a Surveillance Assistant? An Exploratory Case Study of AI-Assisted Surveillance Risks
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate detailed guidance, functional code, and persuasive text at scale. As one of the most widely used consumer language model products as of 2026, ChatGPT gives broad public access to these capabilities, motivating concerns about its potential use in surveillance-related tasks. We present an exploratory case study of what potentially harmful surveillance assistance looks like in ChatGPT's public web interface. We contribute a taxonomy of seven surveillance risk categories based on prior LLM risk research and reports of deployed surveillance systems, instantiated as 110 prompts, along with a manually reviewed analysis of ChatGPT's responses. Prompts were issued using two approaches: 55 jailbreak prompts drawing on five types of elicitation strategies, and 55 plain-language direct prompts, each run alone, and if unsuccessful, again with a short fixed prefix. We find that ChatGPT provides substantive surveillance guidance for 40 of the 55 jailbreak prompts and for 33 of the 55 direct prompts without any prefix. Compliant responses also rarely included policy mentions or suggestions for privacy-preserving alternatives. We manually review every response and find that even when ChatGPT states a refusal, it may still supply detailed instructions, working code, or architectural guidance alongside brief ethical caveats.

AI.tldr: An exploratory case study of 110 prompts across seven surveillance risk categories finds that ChatGPT's public web interface gives substantive surveillance guidance for 40 of 55 jailbreak prompts and 33 of 55 direct prompts without a prefix. Even stated refusals often came with detailed instructions or working code.
AI.motivation: Wide public access to ChatGPT raises concern about its use in surveillance-related tasks, and there was no systematic case study of what harmful surveillance assistance looks like in its public web interface.
AI.method: A taxonomy of seven surveillance risk categories instantiated as 110 prompts: 55 jailbreak prompts drawing on five types of elicitation strategy and 55 plain-language direct prompts, each run alone and, if unsuccessful, again with a short fixed prefix. Every response was manually reviewed.
AI.result: Substantive surveillance guidance for 40 of 55 jailbreak prompts and 33 of 55 direct prompts without any prefix. Compliant responses rarely included policy mentions or privacy-preserving alternatives. Even when ChatGPT stated a refusal it sometimes supplied detailed instructions, working code or architectural guidance alongside brief ethical caveats.
AI.conclusion: Refusal statements alone do not reliably prevent harmful surveillance assistance, so safeguards need to be judged on the content actually delivered.

title: Does Recursive Knowledge Construction Help Agents Verify Consensus Claims in Science?
summary: Recent scientific agents build knowledge recursively by retrieving evidence, constructing an intermediate state, and judging whether that state contains sufficient information. These agents are evaluated end-to-end, usually without ground truth, so the effect of each design choice is unknown. Here, we examined two design axes: (1) what the recursion builds (the state of evidence) and (2) what controls it (the judge that decides when to stop). To measure them, we defined consensus scientific claim verification and measured these effects on this task, where a system must establish a claim's consensus stance from the open literature. We built a new consensus claim dataset, ProClaim-eval, including 718 claims with SUPPORT and REFUTE gold labels from five expert-curated databases spanning molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy. Our instrument, ProClaim, persists an evidence state outside the model's context, so each axis can be studied with the other held fixed. Against verification systems and general-purpose agent harnesses, ProClaim ranks among the top three, with a significant advantage over the harnesses. We found that the evidence state improves performance over in-context accumulation, and it also matters what is stored in it. In addition, a trained judge that reads the evidence state performs better than fixed-round stopping. A judge trained separately and never exposed to ProClaim-eval achieves the highest agreement with the gold labels on three of five subsets, where it matches the off-the-shelf Claude Sonnet~4.6 judge and outperforms Claude Haiku~4.5. Our results support recursively maintaining a structured evidence state outside the model's context as an effective design for verifying claims in scientific agents.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that persisting an evidence state outside the model context, together with a trained judge that decides when to stop, improves scientific consensus claim verification. ProClaim ranks among the top three against verification systems and general-purpose agent harnesses on a new 718-claim dataset.
AI.motivation: Recent scientific agents build knowledge recursively, but they are evaluated end-to-end without ground truth, so the effect of each design choice, what the recursion builds and what controls it, is unknown.
AI.method: Defining consensus scientific claim verification and building ProClaim-eval, with 718 claims labeled SUPPORT or REFUTE from five expert-curated databases spanning molecular biology, nuclear physics and astronomy. Building ProClaim, which persists an evidence state outside the model context so that each design axis can be studied with the other held fixed.
AI.result: ProClaim ranks among the top three against verification systems and general-purpose agent harnesses, with a significant advantage over the harnesses. The evidence state improves performance over in-context accumulation, and what is stored in it matters. A trained judge reading the evidence state performs better than fixed-round stopping. A separately trained judge matches the off-the-shelf Claude Sonnet 4.6 judge on three of five subsets and outperforms Claude Haiku 4.5.
AI.conclusion: Recursively maintaining a structured evidence state outside the model context is an effective design for verifying claims in scientific agents.

title: Towards Portable Specification of the Agent Harness
summary: Large language models act only through the infrastructure that surrounds them. That infrastructure, the harness, determines what a model can accomplish and how it fails, yet it has no settled definition. To address this gap, we decompose the harness into eight functional components that can be specified and compared across systems, and we propose a portable specification framework that records which model ran in which harness. The record is needed because different harness configurations can yield several-fold differences in reported scores for the same model, and because much of an agent's attack surface lies in its harness. Existing model cards and agent cards provide release and operational information, but do not establish the sequence of effective configurations within a run. Harnesses can change between releases and between runs, and, where agents edit their own tools and configuration, within a run. Enacted AI laws contain documentation duties relevant to covered systems, subject to their respective scopes and application dates, but do not prescribe the common harness record proposed here. Therefore, the harness has to be explicitly described and specified as a versioned part of the system.

AI.tldr: The paper decomposes the agent harness into eight functional components and proposes a portable specification framework that records which model ran in which harness. It argues the harness must be explicitly described and versioned, since harness configuration can change reported scores several-fold for the same model.
AI.motivation: The harness determines what a model can accomplish and how it fails, yet it has no settled definition, and existing model cards and agent cards do not establish the sequence of effective configurations within a run.
AI.method: Decomposing the harness into eight functional components that can be specified and compared across systems, and proposing a portable specification framework that records the model and harness pairing, accounting for changes across releases, across runs and within a run when agents edit their own tools and configuration.
AI.result: Different harness configurations can yield several-fold differences in reported scores for the same model, and much of an agent's attack surface lies in its harness. The abstract notes that enacted AI laws contain documentation duties for covered systems but do not prescribe the proposed harness record.
AI.conclusion: The harness has to be explicitly described and specified as a versioned part of the system.

title: Agentic World Modeling for Agent Test-time Scaling without Environment Replica
summary: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model agents by sampling and selecting among multiple candidate trajectories, but common realizations assume that these trajectories can be executed in parallel. This assumption breaks in realistic deployments, where enterprise workspaces and cloud services are shared and persistent, costly or infeasible to replicate, and actions may introduce irreversible side effects or cross-trajectory interference. Existing generative world models avoid direct execution, but typically compress environment state into a single prompt, limiting their ability to reliably simulate transitions under partial observability. Instead, we introduce Agentic World Modeling (AWM), which reformulates next-observation prediction as a multi-turn evidence-acquisition task. For each hypothetical action, an agentic simulator adaptively queries the real environment through safe read-only interfaces, reasons over the returned evidence, and uses executable computation to construct the resulting observation without mutating shared state. Integrated with trajectory-level TTS, AWM enables parallel exploration over a single shared environment. Across $\tau$-bench, AppWorld, and OfficeBench, AWM outperforms a single-shot simulation baseline by 40.07% on average, and surpasses a trained world-model baseline by 12.36% on average. These results establish interactive, read-grounded simulation as a practical foundation for safe and scalable agentic test-time scaling in shared, non-resettable environments.

AI.tldr: Agentic World Modeling predicts the outcome of hypothetical actions by querying the real environment through safe read-only interfaces, which enables parallel test-time scaling in shared, non-resettable environments. It beats a single-shot simulation baseline by 40.07 percent and a trained world-model baseline by 12.36 percent on average.
AI.motivation: Test-time scaling assumes trajectories can run in parallel, which fails when environments are shared, persistent, costly to replicate or subject to irreversible side effects, while generative world models compress environment state into one prompt, which limits simulation under partial observability.
AI.method: Reformulating next-observation prediction as a multi-turn evidence-acquisition task in which an agentic simulator adaptively queries the environment through read-only interfaces, reasons over the returned evidence and uses executable computation to construct the resulting observation without mutating shared state, integrated with trajectory-level test-time scaling.
AI.result: Across tau-bench, AppWorld and OfficeBench, AWM outperforms a single-shot simulation baseline by 40.07 percent on average and surpasses a trained world-model baseline by 12.36 percent on average.
AI.conclusion: Interactive, read-grounded simulation is a practical foundation for safe and scalable agentic test-time scaling in shared, non-resettable environments.

title: DiRAFT: Privacy-Aware Financial Transcript Synthesis from Aggregate Discourse Priors
comment: 21 pages. Accepted at the Financial AI Security, Privacy and Safety Workshop at ICAIF 2026 (non-archival)
summary: Using customer conversations to train and evaluate financial language models raises confidentiality concerns because non-public financial facts can remain after direct identifiers are masked. Synthetic transcripts offer an alternative data source, but their discourse fidelity and residual confidentiality risks require assessment. We introduce DiRAFT (Discourse Realization from Aggregate First-order Transitions), which extracts financial concept graphs and records the order in which concepts are first introduced. It pools adjacent concept transitions across training records and samples new graph plans from aggregate transition, starting-concept, and plan-length priors. A discourse layer guides text realization without supplying an individual source passage or graph. We assess privacy-related risks through two complementary evaluations: corpus-level structural overlap and source-grounded checks for specific non-public investor facts. The structural assessment covers two financial corpora and three generation backends. The confidential-fact assessment uses human review of 1,400 investor-call outputs across seven strategies and two backends. We also evaluate transition fidelity, content recoverability, and trajectory diversity. Stochastic sampling provides a favorable balance between transition fidelity and structural overlap, with consistent advantages over greedy and top-3 on investor calls. The confidential-fact assessment likewise detects fewer matches for stochastic sampling than these alternatives on both backends covered by the fact assessment. These complementary assessments provide empirical evidence on residual confidentiality risks without establishing a formal guarantee.

AI.tldr: DiRAFT synthesizes financial transcripts by sampling new concept-introduction graph plans from aggregate discourse transition priors rather than from individual source passages. Stochastic sampling gives the best balance of transition fidelity and structural overlap, and the paper provides empirical rather than formal evidence on residual confidentiality risk.
AI.motivation: Customer conversations used to train financial language models carry confidentiality risk because non-public facts can remain after direct identifiers are masked, and synthetic transcripts need their discourse fidelity and residual risks assessed.
AI.method: Extracting financial concept graphs and the order in which concepts are first introduced, pooling adjacent concept transitions across training records, and sampling new graph plans from aggregate transition, starting-concept and plan-length priors, with a discourse layer guiding text realization. Privacy is assessed through corpus-level structural overlap and source-grounded human review of 1,400 investor-call outputs across seven strategies and two backends.
AI.result: Stochastic sampling gives a favorable balance between transition fidelity and structural overlap, with consistent advantages over greedy and top-3 decoding on investor calls. It detects fewer matches to specific non-public investor facts than these alternatives on both backends covered by the fact assessment.
AI.conclusion: The work provides empirical evidence on residual confidentiality risks of synthetic financial transcripts without establishing a formal privacy guarantee.

title: The First Few Tokens Matter: Understanding Chain-of-Thought Controllability
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising way to oversee increasingly capable agents. It succeeds in part because current models appear limited in their ability to control what they verbalize in their reasoning traces. We investigate the source of this limitation and link it to an entropy collapse in the first few tokens following the opening thinking tag. We exploit this mechanism to recover CoT controllability through two inference-time interventions on initial tokens: prefilling, where even a single token can substantially increase controllability, and banning frequent opening tokens combined with in-context examples, which improves average compliance by 34-41 percentage points across models. These interventions recover mainly addition and style controllability (adding or transforming information), while suppression controllability (avoiding or removing information) exhibits more varied responses, suggesting distinct underlying mechanisms. Consistent with this, the two groups behave as separate capabilities: across models, performance correlates positively within these groups, while cross-group correlations are mostly negative.
