Importantly, we find that the relationship with monitorability depends on the evaluation: addition and style controllability more consistently positively correlate with monitorability, while suppression often shows negative associations. Our findings motivate the development of controllability evaluations that distinguish difficulty initiating a specific opening from general limitations of the ability to alter reasoning content, alongside separate reporting of control tasks and categories.

AI.tldr: The paper traces the limited controllability of chain-of-thought reasoning to an entropy collapse in the first few tokens after the opening thinking tag, and recovers controllability with inference-time interventions on those initial tokens. Addition and style controllability respond most strongly, while suppression controllability behaves differently.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought monitoring partly relies on models' limited ability to control what they verbalize in their reasoning traces, and the source of that limitation was not understood.
AI.method: Linking the limitation to an entropy collapse in the initial tokens, then applying two interventions: prefilling, where even a single token can substantially increase controllability, and banning frequent opening tokens combined with in-context examples.
AI.result: Banning frequent opening tokens with in-context examples improves average compliance by 34 to 41 percentage points across models. The interventions mainly recover addition and style controllability, while suppression controllability gives more varied responses. The two groups behave as separate capabilities, with positive within-group and mostly negative cross-group correlations. Addition and style controllability more consistently correlate positively with monitorability, while suppression often shows negative associations.
AI.conclusion: Controllability evaluations should distinguish difficulty initiating a specific opening from general limitations in altering reasoning content, and should report control tasks and categories separately.

title: P-ContextBench: From Personal Fact Recall to Personalized Agent Behavior
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for personal tasks, yet evaluating their safe use of personal context remains difficult because such contexts are private, fragmented, dynamic, and socially situated. We introduce P-ContextBench, a realistic, verifiable, and scalable benchmark for evaluating personal-context understanding. P-ContextBench constructs population-structured, life-story-grounded digital humans from demographic seeds reflecting the U.S. population. Rather than using explicit, static profiles, P-ContextBench embeds traits, routines, goals, and constraints as implicit evidence across fragmented, evolving synthetic mobile-app records. It evaluates five capabilities: single-source fact recovery, multi-source fact recovery, temporal state tracking, inference of higher-level personal patterns from routine behavior, and safe handling of requests conflicting with persona-specific constraints through compliance, warning, clarification, or refusal. A multi-stage validation pipeline checks persona plausibility, context recoverability, information leakage, evidence preservation, test-case grounding, and human-judge agreement. We instantiate P-ContextBench with 100 personas, 10,088 hidden facts, 18,261 app-trace fragments, and 4,810 verified test cases. The pipeline supports configurable generation across scales and demographic groups. Cost-effective state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs relevant to personal agents achieve below 60% accuracy on temporal tracking, higher-level pattern inference, and constraint-aware action-boundary decisions, with fewer than 10% of test cases answered correctly across all three repeated runs. Even a high-performing SOTA model remains inconsistent on these capabilities. P-ContextBench provides measurable targets for improving the accuracy, reliability, and safety of LLM-based personal agents.

AI.tldr: P-ContextBench is a verifiable benchmark for personal-context understanding, built from 100 synthetic personas with 10,088 hidden facts and 4,810 verified test cases. Cost-effective state-of-the-art LLMs score below 60 percent on temporal tracking, higher-level pattern inference and constraint-aware action-boundary decisions.
AI.motivation: Evaluating the safe use of personal context by LLMs is difficult because such contexts are private, fragmented, dynamic and socially situated, and explicit static profiles do not capture this.
AI.method: Population-structured, life-story-grounded digital humans generated from U.S. demographic seeds, with traits, routines, goals and constraints embedded as implicit evidence across fragmented synthetic mobile-app records. Five capabilities are evaluated: single-source and multi-source fact recovery, temporal state tracking, inference of higher-level patterns from routine behavior, and safe handling of requests that conflict with persona constraints through compliance, warning, clarification or refusal. A multi-stage validation pipeline checks persona plausibility, recoverability, leakage and test-case grounding.
AI.result: The benchmark has 100 personas, 10,088 hidden facts, 18,261 app-trace fragments and 4,810 verified test cases. Cost-effective state-of-the-art LLMs reach below 60 percent accuracy on temporal tracking, higher-level pattern inference and constraint-aware action-boundary decisions, with fewer than 10 percent of test cases answered correctly across all three repeated runs. Even a high-performing model remains inconsistent on these capabilities.
AI.conclusion: P-ContextBench provides measurable targets for improving the accuracy, reliability and safety of LLM-based personal agents.

title: Nedimo: An Evidence-Grounded Multilingual Pipeline for AI-Generated Sleep Stories
summary: Generative audio systems can produce large libraries of personalized bedtime content, but ordinary media objectives (retention, completion, and novelty) are poorly aligned with the goal of supporting a transition toward sleep. Direct evidence for narrated bedtime audio in adults is mixed, and a recent active-controlled trial did not support such audio as a standalone treatment for sleep disturbance. We translate this uncertain evidence into conservative engineering requirements and present a multilingual pipeline for generating and narrating low-arousal sleep stories. The implemented prototype separates deterministic planning from large language model generation, represents content and delivery parameters explicitly, shapes each script through a four-phase attention taper, validates structural and lexical constraints, performs a bounded error-aware retry, and quarantines unresolved outputs. Provider-agnostic text-to-speech synthesis is followed by paragraph-aware joining, two-pass loudness normalization, and a publication gate that re-measures the saved, encoded file against fixed loudness, loudness-range, and true-peak limits. The product data model records stop position, replay, early abandonment, and completion while treating these events as ambiguous behavioral proxies rather than clinical outcomes. We contribute an evidence-to-requirement mapping, a traceable guardrail architecture with explicit acceptance thresholds, technical evaluation criteria, and a prospective protocol for testing sleep-onset effects. No clinical efficacy is claimed; the system is positioned as a relaxation and attentional-support tool whose benefit and possible reliance must be evaluated empirically.

AI.tldr: Nedimo is a multilingual pipeline that generates and narrates low-arousal AI sleep stories, combining deterministic planning, LLM script generation, guardrails and a loudness-based publication gate. It is positioned as a relaxation and attentional-support tool, and the paper claims no clinical efficacy.
AI.motivation: Ordinary media objectives such as retention, completion and novelty are poorly aligned with supporting a transition toward sleep, and evidence for narrated bedtime audio in adults is mixed, including a recent active-controlled trial that did not support it as a standalone treatment for sleep disturbance.
AI.method: Separating deterministic planning from LLM generation, representing content and delivery parameters explicitly, shaping scripts with a four-phase attention taper, validating structural and lexical constraints with a bounded error-aware retry and quarantine of unresolved outputs, and provider-agnostic text-to-speech with paragraph-aware joining and two-pass loudness normalization. A publication gate re-measures the saved, encoded file against fixed loudness, loudness-range and true-peak limits. The work also gives an evidence-to-requirement mapping and a prospective protocol.
AI.result: The abstract reports no empirical efficacy results. It contributes an evidence-to-requirement mapping, a traceable guardrail architecture with explicit acceptance thresholds, technical evaluation criteria and a prospective protocol for testing sleep-onset effects. The data model treats stop position, replay, early abandonment and completion as ambiguous behavioral proxies rather than clinical outcomes.
AI.conclusion: No clinical efficacy is claimed; the benefit of the system and any possible reliance on it must be evaluated empirically.

title: The psychophysics of affect in large language models
comment: 64 pages (26 main text, 25 Supplementary Information, 13 GUIDE-LLM reporting checklist), 5 figures. Code: this https URL ; data: this https URL
summary: Good decisions often require considering how outcomes will feel. Yet large language models (LLMs) increasingly enter decision workflows, despite little being known about how they map outcomes to feelings or use those mappings in choice. We tested how LLMs anticipated gambling or stock-trading outcomes would feel and whether they incorporated these ratings into choice. When outcomes were rated in isolation, ratings exhibited diminishing sensitivity to magnitude, resembling human value functions; but models rated gains more intensely than equivalent losses, an inversion of canonical loss aversion we call silicon gain amplification. When outcomes were rated together, enabling direct comparison, ratings linearised. In choice, the gain-loss asymmetry largely disappeared, and models' own ratings did not reliably explain their choices better than monetary utility did. These findings reveal malleable mappings from outcomes to affect, raising questions about whether and how agentic LLMs should incorporate anticipated feelings into decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper measures how LLMs map gambling and stock-trading outcomes to anticipated feelings and whether those ratings drive their choices. Ratings in isolation show a gain-amplifying inversion of loss aversion, which largely disappears in choice.
AI.motivation: LLMs increasingly enter decision workflows, but little is known about how they map outcomes to feelings or use those feelings in choice.
AI.method: Models rated anticipated feelings for gambling and stock-trading outcomes, both in isolation and jointly for direct comparison, and then made choices. The choices were compared with monetary utility as an explanation.
AI.result: Isolated ratings showed diminishing sensitivity to magnitude, like human value functions, but gains were rated more intensely than equivalent losses (silicon gain amplification). Joint ratings linearised, and in choice the gain-loss asymmetry largely disappeared; the models' own ratings did not explain choices better than monetary utility did.
AI.conclusion: LLM mappings from outcomes to affect are malleable, which raises the question of whether and how agentic LLMs should incorporate anticipated feelings into decisions.

title: Violet Teaming in Practice: Lessons from a Pilot Expert Workshop on Governing Complex AI Systems
summary: Violet teaming has been proposed as a method to integrate technical, policy, and societal considerations into the evaluation of emerging technologies. Here, we document a pilot expert workshop used to explore violet teaming as a governance methodology for biodefense-relevant AI capabilities and describe observations from the exercise. The workshop used a hypothetical technology scenario across three sequential stages - capability development, misuse potential, and implementation - while incorporating technical, security, operational, and policy perspectives. The sequential format provided an integrated way to examine potential benefits, misuse risks, and real-world implementation challenges, rather than considering these issues in isolation. The exercise surfaced non-obvious misuse pathways, expanded potential interventions beyond purely technical safeguards, and highlighted operational and policy constraints that could affect implementation. This report summarizes the workshop design, outputs, and lessons learned for applying violet teaming to the evaluation of complex, dual-use technologies.

AI.tldr: The paper documents a pilot expert workshop that applies violet teaming to the governance of biodefense-relevant AI capabilities, using a hypothetical technology scenario. The exercise surfaced non-obvious misuse pathways and interventions beyond purely technical safeguards.
AI.motivation: Violet teaming has been proposed to integrate technical, policy and societal considerations into the evaluation of emerging technologies, and this paper explores it for biodefense-relevant AI.
AI.method: A pilot expert workshop ran a hypothetical technology scenario through three sequential stages (capability development, misuse potential and implementation), incorporating technical, security, operational and policy perspectives.
AI.result: The sequential format surfaced non-obvious misuse pathways, expanded potential interventions beyond purely technical safeguards, and highlighted operational and policy constraints that could affect implementation.
AI.conclusion: The report summarizes the workshop design, outputs and lessons learned for applying violet teaming to the evaluation of complex, dual-use technologies.

title: ReplayRCA: Measuring Post-hoc Diagnosis and Live Oversight of Agent Failures by Counterfactual Replay
comment: 29 pages, 10 figures, 16 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: When a language-model agent fails a multi-step task, can another model find the decisive mistake and fix it with a single action? We introduce ReplayRCA, a benchmark that scores such diagnoses by intervention rather than by agreement with annotations: the environment is restored to the state preceding the chosen step, the proposed action replaces the agent's own, and the same agent continues. The score, causal repair, is the continuation success rate minus that of a paired placebo that replays the agent's original action through the same mechanism. Two tracks share this protocol: a post-hoc autopsy, where the diagnoser sees the whole failed run and is told that it failed, and live oversight, where a supervisor watches the run unfold and may intervene once, before an irreversible action, without knowing whether the run will fail. Tasks come from OpsWorld, a deterministic, procedurally generated back-office environment with six difficulty levels, the last of which is multimodal (QR codes, handwriting). On 62 calibrated systematic failures, the best of 13 frontier models (Grok 4.7) reaches a causal repair of +51.3 points; the top eight models are statistically indistinguishable, the flagship models of the two largest vendors rank 8th and 12th, and 5 items are repaired by no model. Forcing a strong model to intervene at the last step costs it 17.1 points, so the last-step shortcut of annotation-based attribution benchmarks does not transfer. On 87 runs, the two best live supervisors are statistically tied and one of them is a small open-weight model (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash); the supervisor that is among the best post-hoc diagnosers (GPT-6.1 Sol) is the weakest live one (-14.5 points on the same runs, p = 0.002), so post-hoc diagnostic performance can be a poor proxy for live oversight. The environment and the evaluation code are released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: ReplayRCA is a benchmark that scores diagnoses of LLM agent failures by intervention, replaying the run from the chosen step with the proposed action in place of the agent's own and comparing against a placebo. The best of 13 frontier models reaches a causal repair of +51.3 points, and post-hoc diagnostic skill is a poor guide to live oversight.
AI.motivation: Benchmarks that score attribution by agreement with annotations do not show whether a diagnosed mistake can actually be repaired.
AI.method: The environment is restored to the state before the chosen step, the proposed action replaces the agent's own, and the same agent continues. Causal repair is the continuation success rate minus that of a paired placebo replaying the original action. Two tracks are used: a post-hoc autopsy of a failed run, and live oversight in which a supervisor may intervene once before an irreversible action. Tasks come from OpsWorld, a deterministic procedurally generated back-office environment with six difficulty levels, the last of which is multimodal.
AI.result: On 62 calibrated systematic failures, the best of 13 frontier models (Grok 4.7) reaches +51.3 causal repair; the top eight are statistically indistinguishable, the flagship models of the two largest vendors rank 8th and 12th, and 5 items are repaired by no model. Forcing a strong model to intervene at the last step costs it 17.1 points. On 87 runs, the two best live supervisors are statistically tied, and GPT-6.1 Sol, among the best post-hoc diagnosers, is the weakest live one (-14.5 points, p = 0.002).
AI.conclusion: The last-step shortcut of annotation-based attribution benchmarks does not transfer, and post-hoc diagnostic performance can be a poor proxy for live oversight.

title: Capability-Grounded Agentic Planning
summary: LLM agents serve natural-language requests through tools, data sources, and other agents, and even simple requests often need several interdependent calls. Typically, the LLM picks these calls by trial and error, with no guarantee of an executable plan. We present Capability-Grounded Agentic Planning (CGAP), which instead reasons about what a request requires and what tools provide. CGAP compiles the tool catalog deterministically into a PDDL model, uses an LLM to turn the request into goals, and solves the model with a classical planner. Since tool outputs are unknown in advance, the model is abstract, tracking which inputs are available, not their values. During execution, an LLM adds entity-specific calls that abstract plans omit, and deterministic checks reject any that break the plan. Every argument is drawn from a cited source, such as a conversation span or an earlier tool response, and each requested result counts as delivered only after an LLM verifier checks it against the request. With three LLMs on ToolSandbox, ComplexFuncBench, BFCL multi-turn, and $\tau^2$-bench retail, CGAP outperforms a standard tool-calling agent by up to 28.9 points.

AI.tldr: CGAP is a planning approach for LLM agents that reasons about what a request requires and what tools provide, compiling the tool catalog into a PDDL model solved by a classical planner. It outperforms a standard tool-calling agent by up to 28.9 points.
AI.motivation: LLM agents usually pick tool calls by trial and error, with no guarantee that the calls form an executable plan, even when the request is simple.
AI.method: The tool catalog is compiled deterministically into a PDDL model, an LLM turns the request into goals, and a classical planner solves an abstract model that tracks which inputs are available rather than their values. During execution an LLM adds entity-specific calls that abstract plans omit, and deterministic checks reject any that break the plan. Every argument is drawn from a cited source, and an LLM verifier checks each requested result against the request.
AI.result: With three LLMs on ToolSandbox, ComplexFuncBench, BFCL multi-turn and tau^2-bench retail, CGAP outperforms a standard tool-calling agent by up to 28.9 points.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning over what requests need and what tools provide offers a route to executable and verifiable tool use for LLM agents.

title: LanG 2.0: Energy-Efficient Agentic AI for Semi-Automated Security Operations at Scale
summary: Security operations centers (SOCs) need to turn terabytes of alerts, logs and flows into trusted, affordable decisions to unveil hidden threats. We present LanG 2.0, an agentic system that detects threats, correlates evidence and writes rules, investigating whether small local models can replace frontier models affordably and safely when structural safeguards, not model accuracy, provide the guarantees. It incorporates entity-anchored correlation, human approval of rule changes and a tamper-evident ledger. Tests span eight flow datasets from five networks, real XDR alerts and multistage campaigns. Against its predecessor, campaign correlation precision rises from 18.75% to 51.81%, and rule acceptance from at most 60.00% to 98.33%. Against Claude Opus 5.5, scoring flows against each network's normal traffic detects attacks on unseen networks at 73.42% F1 without false positives, versus 58.10% with 49.00% false positives, for at least 650 times less energy. Finetuned models statistically match it on alert classification and rule writing for 5.6 to 59 times less energy. The work demonstrates LanG's practical scalability, processing 3.33 million records in 6.4 minutes, over 30 million hourly, and its safeguards resisted prompt injection, label poisoning and ledger tampering, so small local models can carry most SOC detection affordably and safely.

AI.tldr: LanG 2.0 is an agentic system for security operations that detects threats, correlates evidence and writes rules, showing that small local models can carry most detection when structural safeguards provide the guarantees. It improves on its predecessor and, on flow scoring, uses at least 650 times less energy than Claude Opus 5.5.
AI.motivation: Security operations centers must turn large volumes of alerts, logs and flows into trusted decisions, and it is unclear whether small local models can do this affordably and safely.
AI.method: The system combines entity-anchored correlation, human approval of rule changes and a tamper-evident ledger, and it scores flows against each network's normal traffic.
AI.result: Against its predecessor, campaign correlation precision rises from 18.75% to 51.81% and rule acceptance from at most 60.00% to 98.33%. Against Claude Opus 5.5, flow scoring detects attacks on unseen networks at 73.42% F1 without false positives, versus 58.10% with 49.00% false positives, for at least 650 times less energy. Finetuned models statistically match it on alert classification and rule writing for 5.6 to 59 times less energy. It processes 3.33 million records in 6.4 minutes, and its safeguards resisted prompt injection, label poisoning and ledger tampering.
AI.conclusion: Small local models can carry most SOC detection affordably and safely when structural safeguards, not model accuracy, provide the guarantees.

title: BABA-Bench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Patient-Advocacy Agents
summary: An LLM agent that helps a patient get care must do two things. It must reach the correct outcome, and it must follow the necessary procedure. For example, the agent must get the patient's permission before it shares the patient's records. We introduce BABA-Bench, a benchmark of 47 interactive worlds. We built each world from a de-identified, real patient advocacy case that expert advocates reviewed. In each world, the agent must find hidden information and coordinate insurers, clinics, suppliers, pharmacies, and community organizations. The engine checks each action at the time the agent does it. It checks if the agent has permission, if the agent has evidence for the action, and if the action is prohibited. We evaluated 14 frontier models with three runs on each world, for a total of 1,974 runs. Agents often reached the correct outcome by an invalid route. Of the 921 runs that reached all required outcomes, 254 (28%) did not follow the necessary procedure. Claude Opus 5 reached all required outcomes in 81.6% of its runs, but only 52.5% of its runs passed all checks. When we gave two models a verified route, their pass rates increased from 29.8% to 91.5% and from 44.0% to 97.2%. For these models, the main problem is to find a route, not to execute it.

AI.tldr: BABA-Bench is a benchmark of 47 interactive worlds for LLM agents acting as patient advocates, with each action checked for permission, evidence and prohibition. Agents often reach correct outcomes by invalid routes, and giving two models a verified route sharply raises their pass rates.
AI.motivation: A patient-advocacy agent must reach the correct outcome and also follow the required procedure, such as obtaining permission before sharing a patient's records.
AI.method: Each of the 47 worlds is built from a de-identified real patient advocacy case reviewed by expert advocates. Agents must find hidden information and coordinate insurers, clinics, suppliers, pharmacies and community organizations, and the engine checks permission, evidence and prohibitions at the time of each action. Fourteen frontier models were run three times per world, giving 1,974 runs.
AI.result: Of the 921 runs that reached all required outcomes, 254 (28%) did not follow the required procedure. Claude Opus 5 reached all required outcomes in 81.6% of its runs but passed all checks in only 52.5%. With a verified route, two models' pass rates rose from 29.8% to 91.5% and from 44.0% to 97.2%.
AI.conclusion: For these models the main difficulty is finding a valid route rather than executing one.

title: Optimization Techniques for Solving the Minimum Red--Blue Separating Set Problem with an Application to Human--AI Text Separation
summary: We study the so-called Minimum Red''Blue Separating Set Problem (MRBSSP) which arises from computational geometry. In particular, we propose a compact Set-Cover ILP formulation, safe preprocessing rules, a Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedure (GRASP), and two exact approaches: one is based on Logic-Based Benders Decomposition (LBBD) approach, and the second represents a novel Branch-and-Benders-Cut (BBC) approach. These two exact approaches are compared to ILP--alongside GRASP and the Variable Neighborhood Search (VNS) from literature. Experiments on 250 random graphs with up to 500 vertices reveal complementary strengths: ILP yields the best feasible solutions, LBBD provides the strongest lower bounds and smallest mean optimality gap, and BBC certifies optimality most frequently. We further introduce an NLP application distinguishing human- and AI-generated texts through vocabulary-based graph features. On 42 instances, BBC achieves the smallest mean optimality gap, certifying 16 optima, while GRASP outperforms VNS. Structural analysis of optimal vocabulary separators identifies 113 mandatory and 151 replaceable features across 272 tests, highlighting substantial variability among optimal solutions. Overall, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of complementary optimization strategies and the interpretability of optimal vocabulary-based discrimination.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a compact ILP, safe preprocessing, GRASP and two exact Benders-based methods for the Minimum Red-Blue Separating Set Problem, and applies them to separating human-written from AI-generated text. The methods have complementary strengths, and Branch-and-Benders-Cut certifies optimality most often.
AI.motivation: The Minimum Red-Blue Separating Set Problem arises in computational geometry and needs effective exact and heuristic solvers, and the paper also seeks an application to separating human- and AI-generated text.
AI.method: The approaches are a compact Set-Cover ILP formulation with safe preprocessing rules, a GRASP heuristic, a Logic-Based Benders Decomposition (LBBD) approach and a novel Branch-and-Benders-Cut (BBC) approach, compared with ILP, GRASP and the VNS from the literature. The text application uses vocabulary-based graph features.
AI.result: On 250 random graphs with up to 500 vertices, ILP yields the best feasible solutions, LBBD gives the strongest lower bounds and smallest mean optimality gap, and BBC certifies optimality most often. On 42 text instances, BBC has the smallest mean optimality gap, certifying 16 optima, and GRASP outperforms VNS. Structural analysis of optimal vocabulary separators identifies 113 mandatory and 151 replaceable features across 272 tests.
AI.conclusion: Complementary optimization strategies are effective, and optimal vocabulary-based separators are interpretable though substantially variable among optimal solutions.

title: Payroll Fraud Detection in Synthetic HR/ERP Graphs: An Inductive Comparison of Rules, Path Features, and Graph Neural Networks
summary: Payroll-fraud screening requires finding hidden employee--payee links while distinguishing suspicious relationships from legitimate ones. We formulate this problem as inductive link prediction and entity ranking on synthetic human-resources and enterprise resource planning (HR/ERP) graphs, with unseen organizations and a matched benign twin for every planted case. An original study on 24 held-out organizations and a prospectively frozen extension compare analyst rules, explicit path features and graph neural networks (GNNs). A tuned gradient-boosted model on chained-join features achieved the highest overall link average precision (AP; 0.823), above the GraIL-style GNN (0.663); its 4-hop AP was 0.646 versus 0.272. Thus, the observed multi-hop gain is not specific to GNNs. On a new synthetic cohort with 2.0% positive entities, chained-join boosting again led (AP 0.798); the relational entity GNN also exceeded record-aware rules (0.707 versus 0.504). At a 2% review budget, their precision was 0.695 versus 0.602. Under 40% failed identifier joins, the entity GNN ranked above chained-join boosting (AP 0.712 versus 0.683, descriptively). Structure-only auditing exposed a shortcut in the initial generator; matched twins reduced the audited twin-pool AUROC to 0.493--0.514. These results separate multi-hop candidate discovery, record-based discrimination and review prioritization within an explicit synthetic evaluation design. Code and data are available from the authors on request.

AI.tldr: The paper compares analyst rules, path features and graph neural networks for payroll-fraud link prediction on synthetic HR/ERP graphs. A gradient-boosted model on chained-join features achieves the highest overall average precision, and the multi-hop gain is not specific to GNNs.
AI.motivation: Payroll-fraud screening requires finding hidden employee-payee links while distinguishing suspicious relationships from legitimate ones.
AI.method: The problem is formulated as inductive link prediction and entity ranking on synthetic HR/ERP graphs with unseen organizations and a matched benign twin for every planted case. Analyst rules, explicit path features and GNNs are compared on 24 held-out organizations and on a prospectively frozen extension with 2.0% positive entities.
AI.result: A tuned gradient-boosted model on chained-join features achieves the highest overall link AP (0.823), above a GraIL-style GNN (0.663); its 4-hop AP is 0.646 versus 0.272. On the new cohort, chained-join boosting leads (AP 0.798), and the relational entity GNN exceeds record-aware rules (0.707 versus 0.504). At a 2% review budget, precision is 0.695 versus 0.602. Under 40% failed identifier joins, the entity GNN ranks above chained-join boosting (AP 0.712 versus 0.683, descriptively). Structure-only auditing exposed a shortcut, and matched twins reduced the twin-pool AUROC to 0.493-0.514.
AI.conclusion: Multi-hop candidate discovery, record-based discrimination and review prioritization are separated within an explicit synthetic evaluation design.

title: CIRCE Divines LLM Task Complexity from Constraint Structure
summary: Estimating whether a problem is too complex for a large language model (LLM) before the model attempts it can guide model routing, how to allocate test-time compute, and suggest the need for new tools to aid the agent. While existing estimators rely on the problem text, LLM-annotated task difficulty labels, or signals obtained after a model attempts to solve the problem, such as its hidden states, none explicitly leverage the constraint structure inherent in the problem: the variables to assign and how the constraints over them interact. We introduce CIRCE, which extracts a problem's structure by using a cheap LLM to construct a Constraint Intermediate Representation that deterministically compiles into the constraint graph. Across seven reasoning benchmarks (including SAT, logic, and math) and four LLMs, even a randomly initialized GNN encoder improves predictions of LLM response correctness, reducing negative log-likelihood from 0.465 to 0.423 and increasing AUROC from 0.691 to 0.727 relative to the strongest baseline for each metric.

AI.tldr: CIRCE estimates whether an LLM will answer a problem correctly before it attempts it, using the constraint structure of the problem. A cheap LLM builds a constraint intermediate representation that compiles into a constraint graph, and even a randomly initialized GNN encoder over that graph improves prediction.
AI.motivation: Estimating whether a problem is too complex for an LLM can guide model routing and test-time compute, but existing estimators rely on problem text, annotated difficulty labels or post-attempt signals, and none explicitly uses the constraint structure.
AI.method: A cheap LLM constructs a Constraint Intermediate Representation that deterministically compiles into a constraint graph, capturing the variables to assign and how the constraints over them interact. A GNN encoder operates on this graph to predict response correctness.
AI.result: Across seven reasoning benchmarks (including SAT, logic and math) and four LLMs, even a randomly initialized GNN encoder reduces negative log-likelihood from 0.465 to 0.423 and raises AUROC from 0.691 to 0.727, relative to the strongest baseline for each metric.
AI.conclusion: Constraint structure is a useful signal, available before any attempt, for predicting whether an LLM will get a task right.

title: Verifying Text-to-SQL Queries under Changing Business Semantics
summary: In text-to-SQL and AI-agent analytics, successful SQL execution does not establish semantic correctness under changing business definitions. We study revalidation of fixed queries after changes to refund attribution, tax treatment, eligible populations and exchange-rate dates. An executable verification profile binds the requested revision and knowledge cutoff to legal counterexample data and exact monetary comparison. A preregistered confirmation on 32 newly authored revision families and two local producer bundles retains 192 query-definition cells: 144 nonconforming, 36 finite-suite agreeing and 12 unresolved. Of the nonconforming cells, 63 agree on the current snapshot. At an eight-ledger budget, obligation-guided checking detects 137 discrepancies versus 127 for generic ordering, a paired difference of 6.9 percentage points (family bootstrap 95% interval [2.1, 13.6]; exact family sign-flip p=0.0156). Every ledger arm rejects zero of the 36 agreeing cells. Current-obligation and equal-weight scoring match the guided result, identifying coverage rather than revision-specific priority as the observed source of benefit. Controlled assays, a natural-query pilot and repeated samples provide separate mechanism and robustness evidence. A legal discrepancy refutes conformance; agreement remains restricted to the recorded suite. The study establishes an auditable business-semantic revalidation profile within its authored schema and local-model scope.

AI.tldr: The paper studies revalidation of fixed SQL queries after changes to business definitions such as refund attribution, tax treatment or exchange-rate dates. Obligation-guided checking detects more discrepancies than generic ordering at an eight-ledger budget.
AI.motivation: In text-to-SQL and AI-agent analytics, successful execution does not establish semantic correctness when business definitions change.
AI.method: An executable verification profile binds the requested revision and knowledge cutoff to legal counterexample data and exact monetary comparison. A preregistered confirmation on 32 newly authored revision families and two local producer bundles is complemented by controlled assays, a natural-query pilot and repeated samples.
AI.result: Of 192 query-definition cells, 144 are nonconforming, 36 agree with the finite suite and 12 are unresolved; 63 nonconforming cells agree on the current snapshot. At an eight-ledger budget, obligation-guided checking detects 137 discrepancies versus 127 for generic ordering (paired difference 6.9 points; family bootstrap 95% interval [2.1, 13.6]; exact sign-flip p = 0.0156). No ledger arm rejects any of the 36 agreeing cells.
AI.conclusion: Coverage rather than revision-specific priority appears to drive the benefit, and an auditable business-semantic revalidation profile is established within its authored schema and local-model scope, with agreement restricted to the recorded suite.

title: QUAL: Quantile Alignment Improves Zero-Shot Time-Series Foundation Models
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Foundation Models for Temporal Systems: From Forecasting to World Modeling
summary: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) provide zero-shot forecasts for unseen series, but their accuracy varies across datasets. Combining several models can reduce this variability, yet zero-shot deployment provides no target labels for selecting or weighting them. We find that a model pool is useful not only as a final ensemble, but also as a probability reference for transforming each member forecast. Aligning quantiles through this pool-relative reference improves every member forecast in aggregate. Motivated by this finding, we propose QUAL (Quantile alignment), a simple label-free framework for improving and combining diverse TSFMs. QUAL first produces aligned member forecasts, then applies Huber aggregation and rearrangement to obtain a robust combined forecast without training or model modification. On GIFT-Eval, quantile alignment reduces average member MASE and CRPS by 7.4% and 9.8%. The full framework remains robust when weak forecasters enter a candidate pool whose quality cannot be verified in advance. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: QUAL is a label-free framework that aligns the quantiles of each time-series foundation model's forecast to a pool-relative reference, then combines the forecasts with Huber aggregation and rearrangement. On GIFT-Eval it reduces average member MASE by 7.4% and CRPS by 9.8%.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot time-series foundation models vary in accuracy across datasets, and combining them reduces this variability, but zero-shot deployment provides no target labels for selecting or weighting members.
AI.method: The model pool serves as a probability reference for transforming each member forecast, aligning their quantiles. The aligned forecasts are then combined with Huber aggregation and rearrangement, without training or model modification.
AI.result: On GIFT-Eval, quantile alignment reduces average member MASE and CRPS by 7.4% and 9.8%. The full framework stays robust when weak forecasters enter a candidate pool whose quality cannot be verified in advance.
AI.conclusion: A model pool is useful both as a final ensemble and as a probability reference, giving a simple label-free way to improve and combine diverse TSFMs.

title: Calibration of Large Model Quantization based on HiFloat4 Format
summary: Quantization of Large Language Models (LLMs) has be- coming increasingly important for reducing the computa- tional costs and resource requirements for practical deploy- this http URL- nity to move beyond 8-bit quantization towards 4-bit preci- sion, leading to the development of customized 4-bit formats such as MXFP4 and NVFP4. Recently, HiFloat4 (HiF4) has emerged as a competitive alternative which adopts a Block Floating-Point(BFP)formatwithathree-levelscalinghierar- chy, thereby achieving a significantly larger dynamic range. While quantization can substantially reduce memory usage and accelerate inference, it frequently introduces accuracy degradation. Calibration is therefore essential for narrowing theperformancegapbetweenlow-precisionquantizedmodels and their full-precision counterparts. Nevertheless, existing calibration methods are mainly designed and validated us- ing integer-precision formats, such as INT4, lacking support for HiF4 due to its hierarchical BFP structure. In this paper, weinvestigatethreecalibrationapproaches,namelyHiGPTQ, HiAutoRound, and HiFlatQuant, to further enhance model this http URL demonstratethatallthreeproposedapproachesimproveinfer- ence accuracy compared with direct HiF4 conversion, reduc- ing the gap between HiF4 and BF16 to less than 1% and out- performing the state-of-the-art NVFP4 format across various models and downstream tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates three calibration methods, HiGPTQ, HiAutoRound and HiFlatQuant, for quantizing LLMs to the HiFloat4 format. All three improve accuracy over direct HiF4 conversion, narrowing the gap to BF16 to under 1% and outperforming NVFP4.
AI.motivation: Existing calibration methods were designed for integer formats such as INT4 and lack support for HiFloat4's hierarchical block floating-point structure, while 4-bit quantization is needed to reduce cost.
AI.method: Three calibration approaches are adapted to HiF4: HiGPTQ, HiAutoRound and HiFlatQuant.
AI.result: All three improve inference accuracy compared with direct HiF4 conversion, reducing the gap between HiF4 and BF16 to less than 1% and outperforming the state-of-the-art NVFP4 format across various models and downstream tasks.
AI.conclusion: With calibration, HiF4 becomes a competitive 4-bit format that narrows its gap to full precision and surpasses NVFP4 across models and tasks.

title: Predicting Human-Gain Curves under Local Proxy Optimization from Repeated Ratings
comment: 10-page main paper, 65 pages including references and supplementary material. Accepted as a Spotlight at NeurIPS 2026. Code: this https URL
summary: Optimizing a proxy objective can improve human-perceived quality, but the resulting gain can vary with optimization strength. Average proxy-human correlation alone does not reveal how human-perceived quality changes as optimization strength increases. We propose PACE (Proxy Alignment and Curvature Expansion), a pre-optimization diagnostic that uses repeated human ratings to predict the human-gain curve induced by a fixed proxy. The method models proxy optimization as a KL-regularized exponential tilt. At KL radius $d$, the local gain is approximated by $A\sqrt{d}+Bd$, where $A$ measures first-order proxy-human alignment and $B$ captures the leading second-order correction along the proxy-optimization path. We estimate $A$ and $B$ from repeated human ratings on calibration items and test the resulting gain-curve prediction on held-out evaluation items. Across SummEval, analysis-eligible WMT MQM clusters, an OpenMEVA-MAGS ROC/WP repeated-rating slice, and a GPT-4o judge proxy experiment, PACE consistently reduces held-out gain-prediction error relative to $A$-only, zero-gain, and reliability-only baselines. With the same pre-pool information, it is competitive with flexible proxy-conditional calibration, and a LoRA-DPO experiment provides a modest bridge to actual optimization. Transfer experiments across datasets and evaluation slices show that source coefficients are useful priors, but target calibration further improves prediction. The resulting diagnostic is local and one-sided: it characterizes gentle optimization along the positive tilt branch of a fixed item pool.

AI.tldr: PACE is a pre-optimization diagnostic that uses repeated human ratings to predict how human-perceived quality changes as a fixed proxy objective is optimized more strongly. It reduces held-out gain-prediction error relative to A-only, zero-gain and reliability-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Average proxy-human correlation does not reveal how human-perceived quality changes as optimization strength increases, and the resulting gain can vary with that strength.
AI.method: Proxy optimization is modelled as a KL-regularized exponential tilt. At KL radius d the local gain is approximated by A times sqrt(d) plus B times d, where A measures first-order proxy-human alignment and B the leading second-order correction. A and B are estimated from repeated human ratings on calibration items and tested on held-out evaluation items.
AI.result: Across SummEval, WMT MQM clusters, an OpenMEVA-MAGS repeated-rating slice and a GPT-4o judge proxy experiment, PACE consistently reduces held-out gain-prediction error relative to the baselines. It is competitive with flexible proxy-conditional calibration, and a LoRA-DPO experiment gives a modest bridge to actual optimization. Source coefficients are useful priors, but target calibration further improves prediction.
AI.conclusion: The diagnostic is local and one-sided, characterizing gentle optimization along the positive tilt branch of a fixed item pool.

title: Confident Fools or Careful Searchers? A Behavioural Study of When LLMs Search Beyond Their Static Internal Memory
summary: Agentic LLM assistants must repeatedly decide whether to answer from memory or to call a tool such as web search. Unnecessary searches cost latency and money; missing ones yield confident but unsupported answers. Prior work mostly measures verbalised confidence or trains new adaptive-retrieval methods, and rarely audits the search decisions that deployed products actually make. We introduce a benchmark of 400 multiple-choice questions that combines widely known inside-knowledge (IK) questions, which should be answered directly, with outside-knowledge (OK) questions about facts from news published after the models' training cut-offs (to our knowledge), which should trigger search or, without tools, abstention. Each item offers an abstain option, and two action-level scores, NAS and KIS, reward searching on OK questions and restraint on IK questions. Across five commercial LLMs with and without their vendors' web search, GPT-5 mini and Grok 4 Fast search on over 90% of OK but only 1% of IK questions, whereas Mistral Small searches on just 20% of OK questions, often abstaining instead of using its tool; one product's search indicator proved unusable. Searching is partly triggered by explicit temporal cues: on uncued OK questions, the NAS of the two selective models falls from about 0.72 to 0.57--0.58. The scores thus measure the search triggering of specific products, not metacognition in a strict sense.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a 400-question benchmark that tests whether LLM assistants search when they should, and finds large differences in search triggering between products. GPT-5 mini and Grok 4 Fast search on over 90% of outside-knowledge questions but only 1% of inside-knowledge ones, while Mistral Small searches on just 20% of outside-knowledge questions.
AI.motivation: Agentic assistants must decide whether to answer from memory or call a search tool, and prior work mostly measures verbalized confidence or trains new adaptive-retrieval methods rather than auditing the search decisions deployed products make.
AI.method: The benchmark has 400 multiple-choice questions, combining inside-knowledge (IK) questions, which should be answered directly, with outside-knowledge (OK) questions about news published after the models' training cut-offs, which should trigger search or abstention without tools. Each item has an abstain option, and two action-level scores, NAS and KIS, reward searching on OK questions and restraint on IK questions. Five commercial LLMs are tested with and without their vendors' web search.
AI.result: GPT-5 mini and Grok 4 Fast search on over 90% of OK questions but only 1% of IK questions, whereas Mistral Small searches on just 20% of OK questions, often abstaining instead. One product's search indicator proved unusable. Searching is partly triggered by explicit temporal cues: on uncued OK questions, the NAS of the two selective models falls from about 0.72 to 0.57-0.58.
AI.conclusion: The scores measure the search triggering of specific products rather than metacognition in a strict sense.

title: When Should AI Agents Ask? Clarification Requests Under Limited Human Attention
summary: AI agents increasingly carry out delegated tasks in parallel, with one person overseeing several of them at once. In practice, an agent often lacks information its task requires, such as an unstated preference, constraint, or specification. It can ask the human to clarify, or it can search for the information itself, for example in past records, which takes time and effort and may fail. In this paper, we study how to coordinate these decisions across several agents that share one human with limited attention. We build a stylized model in which each agent can search, ask, or continue the parts of its task that do not depend on the missing information, and we formulate the problem as a dynamic program. We first show that whether an agent should ask depends on more than its own uncertainty: an agent with other work to do can be better off asking earlier, and which question the human should answer first depends on all waiting questions, so no ranking computed agent by agent is optimal. We then propose the Pairwise Coordination Policy (PCP), which uses exact one- and two-task problems to estimate how pairs of tasks delay each other when they share the human. Theoretically, PCP is exactly optimal when at most two requirements remain unresolved and costs at most twice the optimum when every unresolved requirement must be resolved by the human. We evaluate PCP on 864 synthetic cases and in a case study with LLM agents. On the synthetic benchmark, PCP's mean gap to optimal cost is 0.07%, and it reduces cost by an average of 18-31% relative to three standard rules for when to ask. In the LLM case study, agents completed every task correctly, and PCP achieved the lowest mean cost in all tested settings.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when several AI agents sharing one human with limited attention should ask for clarification, and proposes the Pairwise Coordination Policy (PCP). PCP is near-optimal on synthetic cases and reduces cost by 18-31% relative to three standard rules.
AI.motivation: Agents often lack task-critical information and can either ask the human or search for it, but one human overseeing several agents has limited attention, so these decisions interact.
AI.method: Each agent can search, ask or continue the parts of its task that do not depend on the missing information, formulated as a dynamic program. PCP uses exact one- and two-task problems to estimate how pairs of tasks delay each other when they share the human.
AI.result: On 864 synthetic cases, PCP's mean gap to optimal cost is 0.07%, and it reduces cost by an average of 18-31% relative to three standard rules for when to ask. In an LLM case study, agents completed every task correctly and PCP achieved the lowest mean cost in all tested settings.
AI.conclusion: Whether an agent should ask depends on its other waiting work, and PCP is exactly optimal when at most two requirements remain unresolved and within twice the optimum when every unresolved requirement must be resolved by the human.

title: Counterfactual Pairwise Augmentation Improves Small Pointwise LLM Judges
comment: Accepted at Neurips'26 workshop of small language models for agentic systems
summary: Agentic systems increasingly gate individual steps with a pointwise judge that scores a response against a criterion. Small language models are attractive for this role because they can be served and specialized efficiently. Such a judge must locate the criterion's decision boundary, but pointwise labels under-determine that boundary in fine-tuning: labeled responses to different queries differ along many dimensions at once, so they do not reveal which features decide the label. We introduce CPA (Counterfactual Pairwise Augmentation), which makes the deciding difference explicit in training. For each pointwise item, CPA synthesizes and audits a counterfactual response to the same query intended to carry the opposite label. It frames the accepted pair as a pairwise task asking which of the two responses satisfies the criterion. The judge is fine-tuned jointly on both pointwise and pairwise datasets and deployed in pointwise mode only. A second-order analysis shows when this should outperform the prevailing strategy of merging separately trained pointwise and pairwise experts: merging moves every parameter direction toward the pairwise expert by the same fraction, whereas joint training can hold the pointwise optimum wherever the pairwise loss is flat and absorb its curvature where it is sharp. This is the regime that CPA's same-source, counterfactually minimal pairwise view is designed to produce. On separate Qwen3-8B LoRA adapters for six binary criteria, CPA improves criterion-averaged pointwise macro-F1 by 2.5 points over pointwise-only training and outperforms model merging on all six criteria at every tested merge weight. It also surpasses the strongest zero-shot frontier judge we evaluate, Gemini 3.6 Flash, by 11.8 points.

AI.tldr: CPA improves small pointwise LLM judges by synthesizing and auditing counterfactual responses that carry the opposite label, then fine-tuning jointly on pointwise and pairwise data. On Qwen3-8B LoRA adapters it adds 2.5 macro-F1 points over pointwise-only training and beats the strongest zero-shot frontier judge evaluated by 11.8 points.
AI.motivation: Pointwise labels under-determine a judge's decision boundary, because labeled responses to different queries differ along many dimensions at once and do not reveal which features decide the label.
AI.method: For each pointwise item, CPA synthesizes and audits a counterfactual response to the same query intended to carry the opposite label, and frames the accepted pair as a pairwise task. The judge is fine-tuned jointly on both datasets and deployed in pointwise mode only. A second-order analysis compares joint training with merging separately trained pointwise and pairwise experts.
AI.result: On separate Qwen3-8B LoRA adapters for six binary criteria, CPA improves criterion-averaged pointwise macro-F1 by 2.5 points over pointwise-only training and outperforms model merging on all six criteria at every tested merge weight. It also surpasses Gemini 3.6 Flash, the strongest zero-shot frontier judge evaluated, by 11.8 points.
AI.conclusion: Merging moves every parameter direction toward the pairwise expert by the same fraction, whereas joint training can hold the pointwise optimum where the pairwise loss is flat, so joint training on same-source counterfactual pairs can outperform merging.

title: Lifelong Learning of Scheduling Rules with Surrogate-assisted Genetic Programming for Dynamic Flexible Job Shop Scheduling
summary: Genetic programming (GP) has been widely used to learn scheduling rules for dynamic flexible job shop scheduling (DFJSS). However, trained rules tend to only generalise to tasks of similar scales and distributions, and when task characteristics change, learned rules often suffer significant performance degradation. Moreover, fine-tuning pre-trained rules on new tasks often leads to catastrophic forgetting, where prior knowledge is lost. This motivates the need for GP methods that can adapt to new tasks while preserving past knowledge, leading to a lifelong learning paradigm. However, lifelong learning in GP for DFJSS remains largely under-explored. To address this gap, this paper proposes a surrogate-assisted GP method for lifelong learning to handle sequential heterogeneous DFJSS tasks with job or batch arrivals. The framework includes three key components: an adaptive two-stage training strategy to balance plasticity and stability, a task-similarity-based weighting mechanism to regulate knowledge reuse, and an improved surrogate model with distance constraints to enhance estimation accuracy. Experimental results show that the proposed method effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting while maintaining strong adaptability, outperforming several compared methods and demonstrating the potential of lifelong GP in dynamic scheduling environments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a surrogate-assisted genetic programming method for lifelong learning of scheduling rules across sequential heterogeneous dynamic flexible job shop scheduling tasks. It mitigates catastrophic forgetting while maintaining adaptability and outperforms several compared methods.
AI.motivation: GP-learned scheduling rules generalize only to tasks of similar scale and distribution, and fine-tuning on new tasks causes catastrophic forgetting, yet lifelong learning in GP for DFJSS remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: An adaptive two-stage training strategy balances plasticity and stability, a task-similarity-based weighting mechanism regulates knowledge reuse, and an improved surrogate model with distance constraints enhances estimation accuracy.
AI.result: Experimental results show the method effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting while maintaining strong adaptability, outperforming several compared methods.
AI.conclusion: Lifelong GP shows potential for adapting to new dynamic scheduling tasks while preserving past knowledge.

title: FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D
summary: To accelerate materials discovery, language models must be able to address problems at the research frontier. Yet textbook- and examination-derived benchmarks primarily assess established knowledge, leaving performance on frontier research problems largely untested. We introduce FrontierMat, a benchmark of 330 problems drawn from frontier academic and industrial research in fields including aerospace, semiconductors, embodied intelligence and nuclear fusion. Every problem is validated by leading experimentalists and industry experts in its field. Each problem presents a real study and asks the model to infer a withheld outcome or draw a conclusion from selected experimental evidence. Problems are annotated by functional domain, material system and the scale of the governing mechanism; 130 require cross-scale reasoning. The strongest general-purpose model scores only 53.7%, and on matched problems, cross-scale problems score 8.7 points below single-scale ones. Half of the problems are solved by at most one model, and models fail chiefly by endorsing what is plausible rather than what was observed. A domain-adaptation study with meta-weighted continued pretraining and scale-modular self-distillation raises an open-weight model from 36.7% to 55.4%, matching the strongest proprietary model, with improvements on public materials benchmarks and no decline in aggregate performance on general benchmarks. FrontierMat provides a testbed for measuring progress toward language models that support frontier materials R&D.

AI.tldr: FrontierMat is a benchmark of 330 problems drawn from frontier materials research, each validated by experts and asking a model to infer a withheld outcome or draw a conclusion from experimental evidence. The strongest general-purpose model scores only 53.7%, and domain adaptation raises an open-weight model from 36.7% to 55.4%.
AI.motivation: Textbook- and exam-derived benchmarks mainly assess established knowledge, leaving performance on frontier materials research problems largely untested.
AI.method: The 330 problems come from frontier academic and industrial research in fields including aerospace, semiconductors, embodied intelligence and nuclear fusion, and are annotated by functional domain, material system and scale of the governing mechanism; 130 require cross-scale reasoning. A domain-adaptation study uses meta-weighted continued pretraining and scale-modular self-distillation.
AI.result: The strongest general-purpose model scores 53.7%, and on matched problems cross-scale items score 8.7 points below single-scale ones. Half of the problems are solved by at most one model, and models fail chiefly by endorsing what is plausible rather than what was observed. Domain adaptation raises an open-weight model from 36.7% to 55.4%, matching the strongest proprietary model, with improvements on public materials benchmarks and no decline in aggregate performance on general benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: FrontierMat provides a testbed for measuring progress toward language models that support frontier materials R&D.

title: LLM Detoxification via Transition-Aware Reward-Guided Representation Sampling
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate toxic content, motivating effective test-time detoxification. Existing representation steering methods often rely on static or coarse interventions and provide imprecise guidance because they inadequately model transitions between toxic and non-toxic generations. We propose Transition-Aware Reward-Guided Representation Sampling (TARGRS), a test-time framework that learns reward guidance over toxicity transitions in latent representation space. During exploration, progressive steering along the toxicity direction constructs trajectories from non-toxic to toxic states. Toxicity scores along these trajectories turn sparse annotations into dense, listwise supervision for a transition-aware token-level reward model. During inference, TARGRS uses this model to guide coarse-to-fine sampling along the opposite, non-toxic direction: coarse sampling identifies the intervention needed to reach non-toxic regions, and refinement selects a detoxified representation with minimal perturbation. Experiments on 10 LLMs across RealToxicityPrompts, BOLD, and AttaQ show that TARGRS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing toxicity by up to 69.38% on RealToxicityPrompts. TARGRS runs nearly as fast as the original LLM while preserving its core capabilities with minimal impact. By intervening in the language decoder space, TARGRS also extends to Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), reducing toxicity by up to 64.23% across 3 representative LVLMs.

AI.tldr: TARGRS is a test-time detoxification framework that learns reward guidance over toxicity transitions in latent representation space and samples a detoxified representation coarse-to-fine. It reduces toxicity by up to 69.38% on RealToxicityPrompts across 10 LLMs and by up to 64.23% across 3 LVLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing representation steering methods often use static or coarse interventions and give imprecise guidance because they do not model transitions between toxic and non-toxic generations.
AI.method: Progressive steering along the toxicity direction builds trajectories from non-toxic to toxic states, and the toxicity scores along them become dense listwise supervision for a transition-aware token-level reward model. At inference, coarse sampling finds the intervention needed to reach non-toxic regions, and refinement selects the representation with minimal perturbation. The intervention is applied in the language decoder space.
AI.result: Across 10 LLMs on RealToxicityPrompts, BOLD and AttaQ, TARGRS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing toxicity by up to 69.38% on RealToxicityPrompts. It runs nearly as fast as the original LLM while preserving its core capabilities with minimal impact, and reduces toxicity by up to 64.23% across 3 representative LVLMs.
AI.conclusion: Because the intervention acts in the decoder space, the method extends from LLMs to vision-language models with substantial toxicity reductions.

title: ImplicitHop: Evaluating knowledge integration across context and memory
summary: The ability to integrate new information and deduce its consequences is central to learning, understanding, and reasoning in large language models (LLMs). Whether information arrives during training or in-context, models must not only store local facts, but propagate their long-range implications globally. To explore information integration in LLMs, we introduce two complementary natural language benchmarks for large-scale evaluation of deductive reasoning as a function of inference depth. The first is a formal graph benchmark enabling controlled evaluation over a wide range of graph topologies and integration tasks; the second is a knowledge composition benchmark grounded in real-world knowledge graphs. We use these benchmarks to compare knowledge integration from information encoded in context versus information encoded in model weights during pretraining, evaluating a set of open models implicitly, without chain of thought. We find that accuracy decays sharply with increased composition length for both pretrained and in-context knowledge. Information presented in-context, however, substantially outperforms deduction over information encoded in weights. These results quantify a fundamental limitation of current models with direct implications for prompt-based control of agent behavior and for continual learning strategies, and they provide a foundation for developing training, prompting, and integration methods that support deeper reasoning.

AI.tldr: ImplicitHop introduces two natural-language benchmarks for deductive knowledge integration in LLMs, comparing information given in context with information encoded in weights. Accuracy decays sharply as composition length grows, and in-context information substantially outperforms deduction over information stored in weights.
AI.motivation: Models must not only store local facts but also propagate their long-range implications, whether the information arrives during training or in context.
AI.method: A formal graph benchmark allows controlled evaluation across graph topologies and integration tasks, and a knowledge composition benchmark is grounded in real-world knowledge graphs. Open models are evaluated without chain of thought, comparing knowledge encoded in context with knowledge encoded in weights during pretraining.
AI.result: Accuracy decays sharply with increased composition length for both pretrained and in-context knowledge. Information presented in context substantially outperforms deduction over information encoded in weights.
AI.conclusion: The results quantify a fundamental limitation of current models, with implications for prompt-based control of agent behavior and for continual learning, and they provide a foundation for training and integration methods that support deeper reasoning.

title: Researcher-in-the-Loop Evolutionary Discovery of Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Code Families
comment: 25 pages, 6 figures. Code, data and Lean proofs: this https URL
summary: LLM-guided program evolution can produce mathematical constructions, but validity, generality, and reproducibility require distinct evidence. We develop a researcher-in-the-loop discovery pipeline that combines program evolution, exact evaluation, mathematical generalization, certified nonexistence checks, and formal proof checking. We apply it to entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes (EAQECCs). Starting from tasks that did not specify a family formula, evolved programs produced finite qubit constructions whose structure researchers generalized to the family $[[n,1,n-1;n-q-1]]_q$ for prime powers $q\ge3$ at $n\ge2q+1$ and for $q=2$ at odd $n\ge5$. Lean checks the algebraic certificate underlying this family. Together with entanglement lifting, the family closes 54 gaps in archived EAQECC tables. The released evidence includes 115 verified code records, ten nonexistence results with checked DRAT proofs, family implementations, and preserved search programs for exact checks and seeded replay. In a controlled cohort of eight paired generation blocks, validation-selected iterative programs achieve success in 46.1% and 31.6% of held-out executions at unseen lengths $n=13,15$, compared with 19.5% and 3.1% for independently generated programs. In this setting, program evolution and researcher analysis turn finite computational discoveries into a proved family with independently checkable evidence.

AI.tldr: A researcher-in-the-loop pipeline combining LLM-guided program evolution, exact evaluation, mathematical generalization, nonexistence checks and Lean proof checking yields a proved family of entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes that closes 54 gaps in archived tables.
AI.motivation: LLM-guided program evolution can produce mathematical constructions, but validity, generality and reproducibility each require distinct evidence.
AI.method: A discovery pipeline that combines program evolution, exact evaluation, researcher-led generalization of evolved programs into the family [[n,1,n-1; n-q-1]]_q for prime powers q>=3 at n>=2q+1 and for q=2 at odd n>=5, certified nonexistence checks with DRAT proofs, and Lean verification of the algebraic certificate.
AI.result: The family, together with entanglement lifting, closes 54 gaps in archived EAQECC tables. The release includes 115 verified code records and ten nonexistence results with checked DRAT proofs. In eight paired generation blocks, validation-selected iterative programs succeed on 46.1% and 31.6% of held-out executions at n=13 and n=15, versus 19.5% and 3.1% for independently generated programs.
AI.conclusion: Program evolution combined with researcher analysis turns finite computational discoveries into a proved family with independently checkable evidence.

title: RTL-Interact: Training EDA-Interactive Models for Multi-Task RTL Design
summary: Large language models offer a promising route to register-transfer-level (RTL) design, but reliable implementations require checking and revision based on electronic design automation (EDA) tools' feedback. Existing RTL-specialized models often lack learned interaction with such EDA tools or rely on separate generation and repair components. We introduce RTL-Interact, a multi-task post-training framework that trains a single RTL-specialized model to generate RTL, construct task-appropriate EDA checks, and revise implementations using tool feedback. The framework combines automatically constructed multi-task demonstrations with staged supervision from chain-of-thought to tool-integrated reasoning. We further introduce Pattern-Aware Policy Optimization (PAPO) for multi-task reinforcement learning. PAPO augments Group Relative Policy Optimization with correctness-gated rewards that favor concise successful checking while rewarding effective revision, and uses task grouping to preserve coverage across objectives. On CVDP, RTL-Interact-32B achieves 48.7% weighted Pass@1 and 68.9% Pass@5, surpassing its teacher model, DeepSeek-V3.2, while RTL-Interact-8B achieves 44.9% weighted Pass@1. Additionally, we show that PAPO can reduce average tool calls by 63.8% while improving Pass@1. Both models also outperform all RTL-specialized baselines on VerilogEval v2 and RTLLM v2, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method.

AI.tldr: RTL-Interact trains a single RTL-specialized model to generate RTL, construct EDA checks and revise designs from tool feedback, using a new multi-task reinforcement learning method, PAPO. The 32B model reaches 48.7% weighted Pass@1 on CVDP, surpassing its teacher DeepSeek-V3.2.
AI.motivation: Reliable RTL generation needs checking and revision against EDA tool feedback, but existing RTL-specialized models often lack learned interaction with such tools or rely on separate generation and repair components.
AI.method: A multi-task post-training framework with automatically constructed demonstrations and staged supervision from chain-of-thought to tool-integrated reasoning, plus Pattern-Aware Policy Optimization (PAPO), which augments GRPO with correctness-gated rewards that favour concise successful checking and reward effective revision, and uses task grouping to preserve coverage.
AI.result: On CVDP, RTL-Interact-32B reaches 48.7% weighted Pass@1 and 68.9% Pass@5, and RTL-Interact-8B reaches 44.9% weighted Pass@1. PAPO reduces average tool calls by 63.8% while improving Pass@1. Both models outperform all RTL-specialized baselines on VerilogEval v2 and RTLLM v2.
AI.conclusion: Learned, tool-integrated multi-task training lets one model both generate and repair RTL, and PAPO shows that tool use can be made more efficient without losing accuracy.

title: TRIDENT and SHAKTI: A Framework and Benchmark for Hindi AI-Text Detection
summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become increasingly multilingual, distinguishing human-written from AI-generated text is essential for maintaining information integrity. However, research remains English-centric, with limited benchmarks for low-resource languages such as Hindi. To address this gap, we introduce SHAKTI, a large-scale Hindi benchmark covering four genres, eight LLM families, multiple prompting strategies, and adversarial transformations. We evaluate its quality through human annotation and analyze linguistic, grammatical, and sentiment-based differences between human- and AI-generated texts. Building on these findings, we propose TRIDENT, a round-trip translation-based detection framework with three variants: TRIDENT-S (static threshold), TRIDENT-D (dynamic threshold), and TRIDENT-C (logistic regression using multi-distance RTT features). TRIDENT leverages semantic consistency between original and round-trip translated texts to identify AI-generated content. Extensive experiments show that TRIDENT outperforms conventional and supervised baselines, with TRIDENT-S achieving the best overall performance. Further evaluations across seven languages, adversarial settings, and unseen LLMs demonstrate its multilingual applicability and robustness, while highlighting sensitivity to the translation model.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SHAKTI, a large Hindi benchmark for AI-text detection, and TRIDENT, a round-trip translation detection framework with three variants. TRIDENT-S, using a static threshold, performs best overall and beats conventional and supervised baselines.
AI.motivation: Research on distinguishing human from AI-generated text is English-centric, with few benchmarks for low-resource languages such as Hindi.
AI.method: SHAKTI covers four genres, eight LLM families, multiple prompting strategies and adversarial transformations, and its quality is checked by human annotation. TRIDENT detects AI-generated text by semantic consistency between original and round-trip translated text, in three variants: TRIDENT-S (static threshold), TRIDENT-D (dynamic threshold) and TRIDENT-C (logistic regression over multi-distance RTT features).
AI.result: TRIDENT outperforms conventional and supervised baselines, with TRIDENT-S achieving the best overall performance. It is evaluated across seven languages, adversarial settings and unseen LLMs, and its results are sensitive to the choice of translation model.
AI.conclusion: Round-trip translation consistency offers a multilingual detection signal that holds up under adversarial and unseen-model conditions, though its performance depends on the translation model.

title: Experts Exhibit Structured Redundancy: Structure-Preserving Expert Pruning for Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models
summary: Sparse MoE mechanism significantly improves the trade-off between model capacity and inference efficiency. However, practical deployment still requires storing all experts, resulting in substantial memory overhead. We show that expert outputs in MoE layers exhibit structured redundancy. Across different models and task categories, the stable rank and entropy effective rank of expert outputs are consistently far below the nominal number of experts, while expert output distributions also exhibit fewer effective modes. Motivated by these observations, we reformulate expert pruning as a structure-preserving expert subset selection problem and efficiently optimize it via a greedy strategy, rather than only independently scoring and ranking individual experts or exhaustively searching over expert combinations. We propose two expert pruning methods under the unified structure-preserving framework: Projection Energy Expert Pruning (PEEP), which preserves the functional subspace by maximizing weighted projection energy, and Distributional Coverage Expert Pruning (DCEP), which preserves the distributional geometry by minimizing weighted coverage error. Both methods incorporate router-derived weights as priors, enabling them to jointly preserve the global structural relationships among experts while accounting for the local importance of individual experts. Experiments on DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate that, at the expert retention ratios of 75% and 50%, our methods outperform the state-of-the-art baselines on the majority of benchmarks and consistently achieve the best average performance across both general tasks and mathematical reasoning tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that expert outputs in Mixture-of-Experts layers are structurally redundant and proposes two greedy, structure-preserving expert pruning methods, PEEP and DCEP. At 75% and 50% expert retention on DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B, they beat baselines on most benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Sparse MoE models still store all experts, which causes substantial memory overhead, and existing pruning methods typically score and rank individual experts independently.
AI.method: Expert pruning is reformulated as a structure-preserving expert subset selection problem and optimized greedily. PEEP preserves the functional subspace by maximizing weighted projection energy, while DCEP preserves the distributional geometry by minimizing weighted coverage error. Both use router-derived weights as priors to capture global structure and local importance.
AI.result: Expert outputs have stable rank and entropy effective rank far below the nominal number of experts, and fewer effective modes in their distributions. At 75% and 50% retention on DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B, the methods outperform state-of-the-art baselines on most benchmarks and achieve the best average on both general and mathematical reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: Pruning that preserves the joint structure among experts, as well as their individual importance, is a sound way to reduce MoE memory overhead.

title: MEMIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization
summary: Memory has become central to self-evolving LLM agents, which store and retrieve experience from past rollouts to guide future decisions. Existing systems represent this experience as free-form natural language and maintain it by rewriting, which fits tasks whose experience is narratable. However, in scientific discovery and optimization, experience is often a quantity measured by an oracle under a specific context. Rewriting it as text leaves no index for where a record should be, replaces a measurement with a description, and cannot express how interventions interact.
