To address this, we argue that agent memory for biomolecule optimization should instead be indexable, quantitative, and structured, and we introduce MEMIG. This memory construction framework realizes these three properties. In detail, MEMIG addresses each insight with a domain-grounded identifier and accumulates the quantitative effect measured by a property oracle, so that updates remain local and retrieval becomes an exact lookup. Next, MEMIG connects insights whose interventions are applied together and measures their epistasis by decomposing each evaluated set. Our results show that MEMIG improves performance in most settings across in silico antibody optimization tasks.

AI.tldr: MEMIG is a self-evolving memory framework for LLM agents in antibody optimization that stores indexed, quantitative records instead of rewritten natural-language experience. It improves performance in most settings across in silico antibody optimization tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing agent memory systems rewrite experience as free-form text, which leaves no index for where a record belongs, replaces measurements with descriptions and cannot express how interventions interact.
AI.method: MEMIG assigns each insight a domain-grounded identifier and accumulates the quantitative effect measured by a property oracle, so updates stay local and retrieval becomes an exact lookup. It links insights whose interventions are applied together and measures their epistasis by decomposing each evaluated set.
AI.result: MEMIG improves performance in most settings across in silico antibody optimization tasks. The abstract reports no specific numerical results.
AI.conclusion: Agent memory for biomolecule optimization should be indexable, quantitative and structured, since this enables exact retrieval and modelling of intervention interactions.

title: Rome Wasn't Built in One Turn: Replay-Grounded Reward Signals for Long-Horizon Freeciv Agents
comment: 22 pages, 3 figures, 12 tables. Code: this https URL ; Checkpoints: this https URL
summary: Training language-model agents to play long-horizon strategy games is hard because deterministic feedback is sparse and often arrives only at the end of a game. In-game scores can offer dense signals, but they do not reliably predict future outcomes: in 8-68% of position pairs across eight strategy games, the higher-scoring position leads to the worse outcome. We term this phenomenon scoreboard traps. In Freeciv, an open-source turn-based empire-building game where several players manage units, cities, and diplomacy over hundreds of turns, we look into better reward signals for gameplay agents. To facilitate this, we build CivHarness, an open system that saves current game states, branches on different decisions, and replays the game to future turns to provide measurable long-horizon feedback from saved positions. We use CivHarness to train CivTelescope, an LLM Judge that predicts which one of two game positions will yield the better outcome. On scoreboard-trap pairs, CivTelescope is 1.3-2.0 times more accurate than off-the-shelf language models, and it generalizes to new game starts, later turns, and unseen rules. We then train a Freeciv gameplay agent with CivTelescope as a dense reward, and call this recipe CivMarshmallow. When used in the middle stage of the game where scoreboard traps are common, CivMarshmallow reaches an average training phase gain of 8.94 points, 77% more than the best baseline, the end-of-game reward. Over the full 120-turn game, CivMarshmallow uses a hybrid reward that starts from the scoreboard or the end-of-game reward and shifts to CivTelescope as the game advances; this hybrid reward scores highest among the rewards we compare.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies scoreboard traps, where a higher in-game score predicts a worse outcome, and builds CivTelescope, an LLM judge that predicts which of two Freeciv positions will do better. Used as a dense reward, CivTelescope trains the CivMarshmallow agent.
AI.motivation: Gameplay agents for long-horizon strategy games receive sparse end-of-game feedback, and in-game scores do not reliably predict future outcomes: in 8-68% of position pairs across eight strategy games, the higher-scoring position leads to the worse outcome.
AI.method: CivHarness saves game states, branches on different decisions and replays the game to future turns to provide long-horizon feedback from saved positions. CivTelescope is trained on these outcomes as an LLM judge. CivMarshmallow trains a Freeciv agent using CivTelescope as a dense reward, with a hybrid reward that starts from the score or end-of-game reward and shifts to CivTelescope as the game advances.
AI.result: On scoreboard-trap pairs, CivTelescope is 1.3-2.0 times more accurate than off-the-shelf language models and generalizes to new game starts, later turns and unseen rules. In the middle game, where traps are common, CivMarshmallow reaches an average training phase gain of 8.94 points, 77% more than the best baseline, the end-of-game reward. Over the full 120-turn game, the hybrid reward scores highest among the rewards compared.
AI.conclusion: Judges trained on replayed outcomes can provide dense, long-horizon reward signals where raw in-game scores mislead.

title: From 1D Benchmarks to Complex 3D Geometries: Can Agents Reliably Specify Problems for Automated PDE Simulation?
summary: Turning an engineering request into a simulation requires consistent geometry, physics, boundary conditions, and numerical settings. Recent agent-assisted systems automate simulation setup, but successful execution alone does not establish whether the specification preserves the intended problem or correctly handles missing information. We study whether agents can reliably construct complete executable JSON specifications for automated geometry creation, meshing, PDE solving, and result export. Our workflow combines model extraction with deterministic scientific and capability checks, explicit clarification, and validated local patches that preserve unrelated accepted fields. We evaluate specification correctness, execution completion, and numerical verification separately. On 120 template-related requests, the full workflow achieves 98.3% correct first-turn specification and decision outcomes, compared with 92.5% for schema-assisted single shot and 82.5% for model-only: gains of 5.8 and 15.8 percentage points, respectively. It makes no false-ready decisions among the 42 requests requiring clarification or rejection. Component ablations identify contributions from scientific checks and conditional repair. Separate downstream studies cover 1D, 2D, and 3D steady and unsteady, linear and nonlinear problems, including flow and elasticity with complex three-dimensional wing geometries. A 30-case gallery demonstrates automated execution from retained JSON specifications, while 9 of 12 selected live user-to-results tests achieve joint specification, execution, export, and numerical-reference success (75.0%). These results support traceable, engineer-reviewed simulation assistance within the tested scope, while fresh-response regressions identify consistency as a priority for further improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether LLM agents can reliably write complete, executable JSON specifications for automated PDE simulation. A workflow with scientific checks, explicit clarification and conditional patching reaches 98.3% correct first-turn specification and decision outcomes on 120 requests.
AI.motivation: Successful execution does not show that an agent-built simulation specification preserves the intended problem or correctly handles missing information, so specification correctness needs separate evaluation.
AI.method: The workflow combines model extraction with deterministic scientific and capability checks, explicit clarification, and validated local patches that preserve unrelated accepted fields. Specification correctness, execution completion and numerical verification are evaluated separately, with component ablations and downstream studies from 1D to 3D problems.
AI.result: On 120 template-related requests, the full workflow achieves 98.3% correct first-turn specification and decision outcomes, compared with 92.5% for schema-assisted single-shot and 82.5% for model-only, gains of 5.8 and 15.8 percentage points. It makes no false-ready decisions among 42 requests needing clarification or rejection. In live tests, 9 of 12 selected requests achieve joint success (75.0%), and fresh-response regressions show consistency remains a priority.
AI.conclusion: Traceable, engineer-reviewed simulation assistance is supported within the tested scope, with consistency across fresh responses identified as the next priority.

title: SciGraphSelect: Auditable Scientific Data Selection through Knowledge--Reasoning Graphs
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: AI4Science
summary: Scientific data selection is typically driven by relevance or utility scores, providing limited insight into why a document is retained. We introduce SciGraphSelect, a reference-grounded framework for auditable scientific data selection. SciGraphSelect organizes domain-specific knowledge, reusable reasoning operations, and reference-attested relations into a typed knowledge--reasoning graph, then scores candidate documents using concept coverage, relation and path co-support, and directional alignment. To avoid over-interpreting document embeddings, rich relational structure is preserved on the reference side while candidate-side evidence is treated conservatively without assuming relation entailment. By exposing the reference-grounded evidence behind each selection, SciGraphSelect brings traceability to the upstream construction of scientific training corpora and complements downstream scientific verification.

AI.tldr: SciGraphSelect is a framework for auditable scientific data selection that scores candidate documents against a typed knowledge-reasoning graph built from reference material. Each selection exposes the reference-grounded evidence behind it.
AI.motivation: Scientific data selection is typically driven by relevance or utility scores, which give limited insight into why a document is retained.
AI.method: Domain-specific knowledge, reusable reasoning operations and reference-attested relations are organized into a typed knowledge-reasoning graph. Candidate documents are scored by concept coverage, relation and path co-support, and directional alignment. Rich relational structure is kept on the reference side, while candidate-side evidence is treated conservatively without assuming relation entailment.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The approach brings traceability to the upstream construction of scientific training corpora and complements downstream scientific verification.

title: Self-Improvement with Auxiliary Rewards: Learning from Verified Traces and Evaluating Transfer
summary: Answer-level rewards cannot distinguish reasoning traces with equally correct outcomes. We study whether auxiliary trajectory preferences improve small-language-model self-improvement and transfer under limited supervision. We compare confidence-based (SC) and entropy-based metrics (UID-Conj.), which combines global entropy variation and local smoothness, through online reward augmentation and offline training on correct responses. Online experiments adapt Qwen3-1.7B on 30 AIME problems without reference answers; offline experiments use historical AIME problems. UID-Conj. improves the online macro-average across the adaptation benchmark and three transfer benchmarks by 2.08 percentage points over unmodified TTRL. The strongest evidence comes from offline weighted SFT: UID-Conj. exceeds uniform weighting on the same response pool by 1.93 points, with a paired prompt-bootstrap 95\% CI of [0.44, 3.44]. Benefits are task-dependent: SC rewards judged trace quality and instruction following, while UID-Conj. rewards yield stronger training outcomes in several settings. We find that auxiliary preferences can expose learning value among equally correct traces not captured during inference time, motivating their evaluation through downstream gains.

AI.tldr: Auxiliary trajectory rewards based on confidence or entropy can improve self-improvement in a small language model. The entropy-based UID-Conj. variant adds 2.08 points over unmodified TTRL online and 1.93 points over uniform weighting offline.
AI.motivation: Answer-level rewards cannot distinguish reasoning traces that reach equally correct outcomes, so the learning value among them goes unused.
AI.method: Confidence-based (SC) and entropy-based (UID-Conj., combining global entropy variation and local smoothness) preferences are compared in two settings: online reward augmentation that adapts Qwen3-1.7B on 30 AIME problems without reference answers, and offline training on correct responses via weighted SFT using historical AIME problems.
AI.result: UID-Conj. improves the online macro-average across the adaptation benchmark and three transfer benchmarks by 2.08 points over unmodified TTRL. In offline weighted SFT it exceeds uniform weighting on the same response pool by 1.93 points, with a paired prompt-bootstrap 95% CI of [0.44, 3.44]. SC rewards judged trace quality and instruction following, while UID-Conj. rewards yield stronger training outcomes in several settings.
AI.conclusion: Auxiliary preferences can expose learning value among equally correct traces that inference-time evaluation misses, so they should be judged by downstream gains.

title: Subliminal Reinforcement Learning: traits travel through a judge's scores
comment: 37 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables, 2 Extended Data figures, 6 Extended Data tables; Supplementary Information included. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Subliminal learning, the transfer of a model's trait through data with no semantic trace of it, has been shown for students trained on a teacher's text. Post-training relies on group relative policy optimization with a language-model judge, where the student learns only from its own outputs and one judge's scores. We show this suffices: a student writes invented syllables or numbers, a judge made to prefer one animal scores them, and the student's preference moves toward that animal relative to a run whose judge prefers another. Of 48 design cells, two fail the validity gate and 17 establish the trait at 5% false-discovery rate, numbers-only cells included; elsewhere, our account gives the reason. Removing only the reward difference between judges removes transfer. We establish the principle as a chain of four stages: the trait must show in the judge's scores, favour strings that move the student, accumulate and reach the answers. Judges with the same preference built from other data, or on another model, place it on other strings, and transfer is not detected. Carried unchanged to AI-safety dispositions, the chain holds: undesirable dispositions reach the student's answers, and stages measured before training anticipate where, helping to prevent part of this risk.

AI.tldr: A student model trained with GRPO against a language-model judge acquires the trait that the judge prefers, even though its training strings carry no semantic trace of it. The trait transfers in 17 of 48 design cells at a 5% false-discovery rate, and the transfer follows a four-stage chain.
AI.motivation: Subliminal learning has been shown for students trained on a teacher's text, but post-training with a judge's scores, where the student learns only from its own outputs, has not been established.
AI.method: A student writes invented syllables or numbers, and a judge made to prefer one animal scores them. The paper traces transfer through a chain of four stages: the trait must show in the judge's scores, favour strings that move the student, accumulate, and reach the answers. Removing only the reward difference between judges removes transfer.
AI.result: Of 48 design cells, two fail the validity gate and 17 establish the trait at a 5% false-discovery rate, including numbers-only cells. The student's preference moves toward the favoured animal relative to a run whose judge prefers another. Judges with the same preference built from other data, or on another model, place the trait on other strings, and transfer is not detected. Carried to AI-safety dispositions, the chain holds, and stages measured before training anticipate where undesirable dispositions reach the answers.
AI.conclusion: The four-stage chain is offered as a principle for anticipating and partly preventing trait transfer through judge-based reinforcement learning.

title: SERIAL-7: Deriving, Realizing, and Preserving Machine-Verifiable Outputs Across Representations
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Verifiable Coding
summary: Large language models increasingly generate structured outputs consumed by programs and downstream systems, where semantic correctness alone does not guarantee reliable execution. We introduce SERIAL-7, a Korean-English benchmark built around an executable verification framework for machine-verifiable generation across seven representations. Using 177 validated canonical artifacts, SERIAL-7 separates semantic derivation (Derive), constrained artifact generation (Realize), and cross-representation preservation (Preserve). Its 43 atomic representation constraints are paired with executable checks over format, structure, and task-specific semantics, enabling progressively stricter verification from representation compliance to full artifact validity. Across ten models, REALIZE-L3 HSR ranges from 42.0% to 93.9%, while Full Compliance exposes additional artifact-level failures beyond correct final answers and valid representations. These results show that reliable structured generation requires explicit, executable verification of how artifacts are realized and preserved across representations.

AI.tldr: SERIAL-7 is a Korean-English benchmark for machine-verifiable structured output across seven representations, built on executable checks. Across ten models, REALIZE-L3 HSR ranges from 42.0% to 93.9%.
AI.motivation: LLM outputs consumed by programs and downstream systems need reliable execution, and semantic correctness alone does not guarantee it.
AI.method: The benchmark separates semantic derivation (Derive), constrained artifact generation (Realize) and cross-representation preservation (Preserve). It uses 177 validated canonical artifacts and 43 atomic representation constraints, each paired with executable checks over format, structure and task-specific semantics, enabling progressively stricter verification up to full artifact validity.
AI.result: Across ten models, REALIZE-L3 HSR ranges from 42.0% to 93.9%. Full Compliance exposes artifact-level failures beyond correct final answers and valid representations.
AI.conclusion: Reliable structured generation requires explicit, executable verification of how artifacts are realized and preserved across representations.

title: Do Transaction Prices Reflect Visual Preference? A Diagnostic Study with Multimodal Language Models
summary: Existing visual preference evaluation relies on costly human annotations or preference reward models, whereas online marketplace transaction prices are readily available and reflect real purchasing behavior, offering potential low-cost supervision. However, transaction prices conflate visual preferences with non-visual factors such as provenance, demand, and competition, making aggregate accuracy insufficient to distinguish model errors, unreliable price signals, and protocol confounds. To address this identifiability challenge, we introduce MarketImage, a diagnostic framework that identifies when transaction prices reflect visual preferences, where they fail, and whether multimodal language models can recover human-supported visual preference signals. MarketImage comprises three components: (i) MarketImageArt, 266 six-image comparison sets with transaction prices and price-blind human rankings; (ii) MarketImageLens, a tie-preserving protocol that partitions 3,990 within-set image pairs into price-human agreement, conflict, and price-tie regions while separately auditing presentation-order effects; and (iii) MarketValuator, six elicitation methods spanning direct comparison, independent scoring, budget constraints, and multi-agent aggregation to evaluate signal recovery by static visual scorers and three multimodal language models. Experiments show that only 24.2% of image pairs have a non-tied price direction, of which 34.7% agree with the human majority. Within this region, HPSv2 leads at 66.4% Recoverable Accuracy; Qwen's budgeted and aggregated variants trail baselines, while GPT interface gains remain statistically unresolved. Thus, transaction prices encode recoverable visual preferences only under limited conditions and should be treated as uncertain proxies rather than ground truth.

AI.tldr: MarketImage is a diagnostic study showing that marketplace transaction prices reflect visual preferences only under limited conditions. Only 24.2% of image pairs have a non-tied price direction, and of those, 34.7% agree with the human majority.
AI.motivation: Transaction prices are cheap supervision for visual preference, but they conflate visual merit with provenance, demand and competition, so aggregate accuracy cannot separate model error from unreliable prices and protocol confounds.
AI.method: MarketImageArt provides 266 six-image comparison sets with transaction prices and price-blind human rankings. MarketImageLens partitions 3,990 within-set pairs into price-human agreement, conflict and price-tie regions while auditing presentation-order effects. MarketValuator evaluates six elicitation methods for signal recovery by static visual scorers and three multimodal language models.
AI.result: Within the non-tied region, HPSv2 leads at 66.4% Recoverable Accuracy. Qwen's budgeted and aggregated variants trail the baselines, and GPT interface gains remain statistically unresolved.
AI.conclusion: Transaction prices should be treated as uncertain proxies rather than ground truth for visual preference.

title: LEAP: Efficient LLM Inference Scheduling with Generalizable Length Prediction
summary: Length-aware scheduling reduces request latency in LLM serving by prioritizing shorter requests. However, despite their large model sizes, length predictors can suffer degraded ranking performance under domain and task shifts, and adapting them can require costly retraining. Their prediction overhead can further offset the benefits of scheduling. To improve the generalization and efficiency of length-aware scheduling, we propose \textbf{LEAP}, a length prediction system with fast online adaptation and asynchronous CPU execution. LEAP reuses the serving model's prefill hidden states, which contain information about the output length, and extracts this signal through a linear readout. To adapt to substantial domain and task shifts, it updates the readout at test time through recursive least squares, using completed requests as supervision without gradient computation or historical-data replay. Prediction and updates run asynchronously on CPU, while prediction and initial batch ordering overlap the remaining GPU prefill. Across the evaluated cross-domain transfers, LEAP retains strong ranking performance, and online adaptation improves Spearman correlation by 64.7\% under a larger domain shift. Serving experiments show that LEAP reduces average per-token latency by 15.9--40.8\% compared with the evaluated length predictors, while achieving 1.9\% higher throughput with $30{,}569\times$ fewer predictor parameters than the strongest evaluated baseline.

AI.tldr: LEAP is a length-prediction system for LLM serving that reuses prefill hidden states, adapts online with recursive least squares, and runs asynchronously on CPU. It reduces average per-token latency by 15.9-40.8% compared with the evaluated length predictors.
AI.motivation: Length-aware scheduling reduces request latency, but length predictors degrade under domain and task shifts, adapting them requires costly retraining, and their prediction overhead can offset the scheduling benefit.
AI.method: A linear readout over the serving model's prefill hidden states predicts output length. At test time the readout is updated by recursive least squares, using completed requests as supervision without gradient computation or replay of historical data. Prediction and updates run asynchronously on CPU, overlapping with the remaining GPU prefill.
AI.result: Online adaptation improves Spearman correlation by 64.7% under a larger domain shift. Serving reduces average per-token latency by 15.9-40.8% compared with the evaluated predictors, while achieving 1.9% higher throughput with 30,569 times fewer predictor parameters than the strongest evaluated baseline.
AI.conclusion: Reusing the serving model's states with fast online adaptation makes length-aware scheduling both generalizable and cheap.

title: RECITE: Revising Eligibility Criteria Incorporating Textual Evidence
comment: 18 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Extended version of a paper in KDD 2026 (32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining). Code and data: this https URL
summary: Overly restrictive eligibility criteria contribute to widespread enrollment failure in clinical trials, yet published recommendations for how specific criteria should be broadened remain disconnected from trial design at scale. We introduce RECITE (Revising Eligibility Criteria Incorporating Textual Evidence), a framework for automated discovery, extraction, and implementation of evidence-based eligibility criteria revisions. RECITE uses protocol amendment documents from this http URL to construct a dataset of 11,913 curated instances across 5,735 trials, each pairing original criteria with documentary evidence and target revisions. We benchmark fifteen LLM configurations under truncated-to-context-window and retrieval-augmented generation conditions, on a 3,116-instance sample under an LLM-as-judge protocol validated against ten domain experts (judge vs. human quadratic-weighted Cohen's $\kappa_{qw} = 0.694 \pm 0.096$). The best open-weight model, Gemma 2 9B, achieves $\kappa_{qw}$-aligned ordinal score $3.0 \pm 0.9$ on a 0--4 scale (normalized 0.742) and the best closed-weight model, GPT-4o, reaches $3.0 \pm 0.8$ (normalized 0.745). Using an agentic literature discovery system, we then identified 44 paper--trial matches across five publications providing trial-design and EC-modification evidence. Our findings suggest that existing clinical knowledge can be operationalized into actionable trial design recommendations.

AI.tldr: RECITE builds a dataset of 11,913 instances pairing eligibility criteria with protocol-amendment evidence and benchmarks LLMs on revising them. The best open-weight model, Gemma 2 9B, and the best closed-weight model, GPT-4o, both reach a normalized score of about 0.74.
AI.motivation: Overly restrictive eligibility criteria contribute to widespread clinical trial enrollment failure, yet published recommendations for broadening them remain disconnected from trial design at scale.
AI.method: Protocol amendment documents are used to build 11,913 curated instances across 5,735 trials, each pairing original criteria with documentary evidence and target revisions. Fifteen LLM configurations are benchmarked under truncated-to-context-window and retrieval-augmented generation conditions on a 3,116-instance sample, using an LLM-as-judge protocol validated against ten domain experts. An agentic literature discovery system then identifies supporting publications.
AI.result: The judge agrees with human experts at quadratic-weighted Cohen's kappa 0.694 +/- 0.096. Gemma 2 9B achieves an ordinal score of 3.0 +/- 0.9 on a 0-4 scale (normalized 0.742), and GPT-4o reaches 3.0 +/- 0.8 (normalized 0.745). The agentic search identifies 44 paper-trial matches across five publications.
AI.conclusion: Existing clinical knowledge can be operationalized into actionable trial design recommendations.

title: Ask on Demand: Targeted Peer Communication for Parallel Agentic Systems
comment: Equal contribution: Haofu Yang and Hongyang Yin. Corresponding authors: Ran Bi and Faguo Wu
summary: Parallel LLM agents tackle complex tasks by exploring multiple trajectories, yet useful discoveries remain isolated in individual execution histories. Existing sharing methods often select or summarize information before other agents' needs become clear, potentially overlooking details that become important later. We propose Ask on Demand (AOD), a communication framework that enables agents to seek targeted peer assistance when specific information needs arise. Upon an approved request, AOD retrieves relevant evidence from peer execution histories, selects a suitable peer, and generates a response tailored to the request. To determine when such assistance is worthwhile, we train a lightweight gate using paired team continuations, with supervision derived from final team outcomes and inference cost. Experiments on AppWorld and WebShop demonstrate that AOD consistently improves task performance over independent parallel execution while achieving lower inference cost than existing information-sharing baselines. These findings highlight the benefits of aligning peer communication with agents' evolving information needs to achieve more effective and efficient collaboration.

AI.tldr: Ask on Demand lets parallel LLM agents request targeted assistance from peers when a specific information need arises, instead of pre-selecting or summarizing shared information. It improves task performance over independent parallel execution on AppWorld and WebShop at lower inference cost than information-sharing baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing sharing methods select or summarize information before other agents' needs are clear, potentially dropping details that become important later.
AI.method: Upon an approved request, AOD retrieves relevant evidence from peer execution histories, selects a suitable peer and generates a response tailored to the request. A lightweight gate, trained on paired team continuations with supervision from final team outcomes and inference cost, decides when peer assistance is worthwhile.
AI.result: AOD consistently improves task performance over independent parallel execution on AppWorld and WebShop, while achieving lower inference cost than existing information-sharing baselines.
AI.conclusion: Aligning peer communication with agents' evolving information needs makes parallel agent collaboration more effective and efficient.

title: Online Evidence-Containment Prediction over Text Spans under Distinct Queries
summary: Evidence-grounded NLP systems often verify nested text regions sequentially, so verifying one region constrains others. We formalize this as Online Evidence-Containment Prediction (OECP): each candidate is predicted before exact verification and queried at most once. Span containment is exactly a triangular 2D product order, making OECP distinct-query online isotonic regression. With multiple admissible targets, worst-case regret is near-linear, $\widetilde{\Theta}(m_{\mathrm{eff}})$, in the effective scale given by endpoint-rank compression; a single fixed target, as in standard QA, admits an explicit polynomial-time learner with optimal $\Theta(\log m_{\mathrm{eff}})$ regret, run on real NQ episodes. On Natural Questions, containment yields a large deductive gain plus a smaller learned gain on unresolved candidates, reproduced across two backbones and DPR hierarchies. Expected Search-space Reduction (ESR) turns these probabilities into decisions, localizing evidence in fewer verifier calls on SciFact, ERASER, and DPR hierarchies; on DPR hierarchies under call budgets it outperforms four recent external selectors and raises fixed-reader F1 over learned and generator-greedy scheduling.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes Online Evidence-Containment Prediction over nested text spans as distinct-query online isotonic regression, and introduces Expected Search-space Reduction to turn predictions into decisions that localize evidence in fewer verifier calls.
AI.motivation: Evidence-grounded NLP systems verify nested text regions sequentially, so verifying one region constrains the others.
AI.method: Each candidate is predicted before exact verification and queried at most once. Span containment is a triangular 2D product order, which makes the problem distinct-query online isotonic regression. With multiple admissible targets, worst-case regret is near-linear in the effective scale given by endpoint-rank compression; a single fixed target admits a polynomial-time learner with optimal logarithmic regret, run on real Natural Questions episodes.
AI.result: On Natural Questions, containment yields a large deductive gain plus a smaller learned gain on unresolved candidates, reproduced across two backbones and DPR hierarchies. ESR localizes evidence in fewer verifier calls on SciFact, ERASER and DPR hierarchies, and on DPR hierarchies under call budgets it outperforms four recent external selectors and raises fixed-reader F1 over learned and generator-greedy scheduling.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting span containment structure with expected search-space reduction makes evidence localization cheaper in verifier calls.

title: Cross-Interface Authorization for AI Computer-Use Agents
comment: 31 pages, 2 figures, and 7 tables. Includes formal results, two reference runtime mappings, mutation tests, commit-time race probes, source-shaped adapter checks, and a frozen external-source audit. Guarantees bind the registered deployment profile and declared effect semantics
summary: Computer-use agents act through graphical interfaces, command lines, APIs, scripts, and Model Context Protocol servers. A policy decision can be interface-invariant while its executable authorization is not: another route can bypass mediation, alter a security-relevant default, or commit after the authorized state has changed. We present a profile-bounded protocol for a fixed, versioned computer-use deployment. It enumerates effect-bearing routes and durable sinks, checks a route-to-sink enforcement cut, normalizes each concrete request to a canonical effect, issues a route-bound prepare ticket, and verifies the route, effect, grant, trace, profile, inventory, and authoritative state again at commit. A committed result requires an agreeing sink receipt. Under explicit assumptions, we prove profile-bounded refinement, matched-effect decision invariance, resistance to alternate-route laundering and declared cross-surface recomposition, commit-time state safety, and receipt-grounded outcomes. The reference profile registers 12 effect families, five interfaces, and 60 routes. Two structurally distinct runtime mappings produce 3,464 traces over 1,732 scenarios each: 960 commits, 2,312 denials, and 192 commits after re-preparation. An independent checker accepts every retained trace and pair and rejects 26/26 semantic regressions; coverage and normalizer suites reject 24/24 and 720/720 mutants; and 168/168 commit probes match their declared outcomes. A frozen-source audit passes 52 checks over 12 files from two independent hybrid runtimes and one public authorization substrate. Source-shaped adapter refinements commit 48/48 instrumented calls and reject 15/15 unbound cases. The resulting guarantees bind the declared profile and its effect semantics.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a profile-bounded protocol that keeps a computer-use agent's authorization consistent across GUI, command-line, API, script and MCP routes. The reference profile covers 12 effect families, five interfaces and 60 routes, and the guarantees are proved under explicit assumptions.
AI.motivation: A policy decision can be interface-invariant while its executable authorization is not, since another route may bypass mediation, alter a security-relevant default, or commit after the authorized state has changed.
AI.method: The protocol enumerates effect-bearing routes and durable sinks, checks a route-to-sink enforcement cut, normalizes each concrete request to a canonical effect, and issues a route-bound prepare ticket. At commit it verifies the route, effect, grant, trace, profile, inventory and authoritative state again, and a committed result requires an agreeing sink receipt.
AI.result: Two structurally distinct runtime mappings produce 3,464 traces over 1,732 scenarios each, with 960 commits, 2,312 denials and 192 commits after re-preparation. An independent checker accepts every retained trace and rejects 26/26 semantic regressions, mutant suites are rejected at 24/24 and 720/720, and 168/168 commit probes match their declared outcomes. A frozen-source audit passes 52 checks over 12 files, and adapter refinements commit 48/48 instrumented calls and reject 15/15 unbound cases.
AI.conclusion: The guarantees bind the declared profile and its effect semantics.

title: scAnyOmics: Foundation-Model Distillation for Any-to-Any Completion of Multi-omics Virtual Cells
summary: Recent advances in single-cell technologies have enabled the profiling of multiple molecular modalities, including transcriptomics, proteomics, and chromatin accessibility, providing a more comprehensive understanding of cellular states. However, integrating heterogeneous modalities and predicting missing molecular information remain challenging, particularly when paired measurements are limited. Here, we introduce scAnyOmics, a generative framework that distills knowledge from a frozen single-cell foundation model into a multimodal student model. scAnyOmics integrates scRNA-seq, protein-marker measurements, and scATAC-seq into a shared representation, enabling cross-modal prediction and reconstruction of missing modalities. We assembled 690,880 cells from six publicly available studies, covering both paired and partially paired multi-omics measurements, to systematically evaluate its predictive performance. We further evaluated scAnyOmics on held-out donor data, where it outperformed baseline methods across multiple evaluation metrics. Beyond cross-modal reconstruction, we explored its applications in cell-type annotation, perturbation-response prediction, and biological age estimation. Overall, scAnyOmics provides a unified framework for integrating incomplete single-cell multi-omics data and transferring pretrained biological knowledge, supporting the development of virtual cell models across diverse cellular contexts and experimental platforms.

AI.tldr: scAnyOmics distills a frozen single-cell foundation model into a multimodal student that integrates scRNA-seq, protein-marker and scATAC-seq data for cross-modal prediction of missing modalities. It is trained on 690,880 cells from six public studies.
AI.motivation: Integrating heterogeneous single-cell modalities and predicting missing molecular information remain challenging when paired measurements are limited.
AI.method: A generative framework distills knowledge from a frozen single-cell foundation model into a multimodal student model, which maps scRNA-seq, protein-marker measurements and scATAC-seq into a shared representation to enable cross-modal prediction and reconstruction of missing modalities.
AI.result: On held-out donor data, scAnyOmics outperforms baseline methods across multiple evaluation metrics. Its applications explored beyond cross-modal reconstruction include cell-type annotation, perturbation-response prediction and biological age estimation.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a unified way to integrate incomplete single-cell multi-omics data and transfer pretrained biological knowledge for virtual cell models.

title: CryoAtlas: A Large Curated Dataset and Unified Benchmark for Cryo-EM Atomic Model Building
summary: Deep learning has accelerated automated atomic model building from cryo-EM maps, yet progress remains limited by the lack of large, high-quality datasets and standardized evaluation benchmarks. We address this gap by introducing CryoAtlas, a rigorously curated dataset and unified benchmark for density-guided atomic model building of protein chains. By integrating and filtering EMDB and PDB entries (up to March 2026), CryoAtlas provides 17,809 map-model-sequence entries, including a curated 16,657-entry training split. From this resource, we construct a 618-target benchmark with a shared evaluation protocol that jointly assesses structural accuracy, model-to-map fit, and stereochemical validity. Using this framework, we benchmark state-of-the-art learning-based methods against Phenix and AlphaFold3, comprehensively analyzing the impact of map resolution, sequence length, protein category and sequence identity on modeling accuracy. As a case study, retraining the ModelAngelo CNN component on CryoAtlas improves performance on the benchmark. CryoAtlas provides an open, reproducible foundation for future cryo-EM atomic model building research. Project details and resource release updates are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: CryoAtlas is a curated cryo-EM dataset and unified benchmark for density-guided atomic model building, with 17,809 map-model-sequence entries and a 618-target benchmark. The paper benchmarks learning-based methods against Phenix and AlphaFold3.
AI.motivation: Progress in deep-learning-based atomic model building from cryo-EM maps is limited by the lack of large, high-quality datasets and standardized evaluation benchmarks.
AI.method: EMDB and PDB entries up to March 2026 are integrated and filtered into 17,809 map-model-sequence entries, including a curated 16,657-entry training split. A 618-target benchmark uses a shared protocol that jointly assesses structural accuracy, model-to-map fit and stereochemical validity.
AI.result: State-of-the-art learning-based methods are compared with Phenix and AlphaFold3, with analysis of how map resolution, sequence length, protein category and sequence identity affect accuracy. Retraining the ModelAngelo CNN component on CryoAtlas improves its benchmark performance.
AI.conclusion: CryoAtlas provides an open, reproducible foundation for future cryo-EM atomic model building research.

title: Evidence-Guided Recovery for AI Agents with Ambiguous Tool Outcomes and Partial Execution
comment: 24 pages, 1 figure, and 10 tables. Includes a finite recovery model, model-facing confirmation study with two local-model bundles, independent replay, and an explicit provider-capability scope
summary: Tool timeouts can leave AI agents facing ambiguous tool outcomes and partial execution: an action may have failed, committed or remained in flight while other workflow steps have already completed. We formulate evidence-guided task recovery over approved obligations, provider capabilities and states compatible with public evidence. A shared admissibility check handles key expiry, authorization timing, dependencies and residual effects; a terminal certificate separates actual goal satisfaction from publicly supported safe completion. The known-model implementation combines standard observation-contingent planning with a separately implemented effect-history adjudicator. In a finite study of 37 assignments, planning and three active controls each certify 28 completions; four saved synthetic fee units incur additional computation. A preregistered assignment-held-out comparison then evaluates planning advice against evidence prompting with two local model bundles. Across 58 paired units in 19 previously developed task families, advice certifies 30 completions versus 9, a 36.2-percentage-point difference (exact family sign-flip p=0.0078), using 272 proposals versus 399. All 116 trajectories pass independent replay. Both models exhibit a positive completion difference. The comparison measures the evaluated advice interface under a common shield; search-versus-rule advice requires a separate matched comparison. Unknown and handoff outcomes remain explicit, with guarantees tied to the declared provider capabilities rather than arbitrary third-party exactly-once execution.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes evidence-guided recovery for AI agents facing ambiguous tool outcomes and partial execution. In a preregistered comparison across 58 paired units, planning advice certifies 30 completions versus 9 for evidence prompting.
AI.motivation: Tool timeouts can leave an action failed, committed or still in flight while other workflow steps have already completed, so recovery must work from ambiguous outcomes.
AI.method: Recovery is formulated over approved obligations, provider capabilities and states compatible with public evidence. A shared admissibility check handles key expiry, authorization timing, dependencies and residual effects, and a terminal certificate separates actual goal satisfaction from publicly supported safe completion. The known-model implementation combines observation-contingent planning with a separately implemented effect-history adjudicator, and planning advice is compared with evidence prompting using two local model bundles.
AI.result: In a finite study of 37 assignments, planning and three active controls each certify 28 completions. In the preregistered comparison across 58 paired units in 19 task families, advice certifies 30 completions versus 9, a 36.2-percentage-point difference (exact family sign-flip p=0.0078), using 272 proposals versus 399. All 116 trajectories pass independent replay, and both models show a positive completion difference.
AI.conclusion: The comparison measures the evaluated advice interface under a common shield, not search-versus-rule advice, and guarantees are tied to declared provider capabilities rather than arbitrary third-party exactly-once execution.

title: EvoMCP: Co-evolving MCP agents and training data
summary: Supervised fine-tuning of Model Context Protocol (MCP) agents is typically conducted on a static data distribution, which fails to adapt to the student's evolving capabilities and leaves newly exposed weaknesses insufficiently addressed. To address these challenges, we propose \method, an agent--data mutual evolution framework that enables MCP agents to improve through a closed loop of task evolution, trajectory evolution, and supervised fine-tuning. Specifically, \method\ assesses the student's established capabilities and capability gaps from rollout feedback to identify learning targets. Task evolution then translates these targets into executable tasks by adapting the instructions and observable environment states of compatible verified seed tasks while keeping their verifiers aligned. To provide reliable and efficient demonstrations for these tasks, trajectory evolution uses reusable skills to recover failed teacher rollouts and refine successful ones. The resulting task--trajectory pairs are used to fine-tune the student, while accepted tasks seed subsequent evolution. To close the loop, we re-evaluate the updated student and use its feedback to guide the next round of data evolution. Experiments on Toolathlon, MCPMark, and MCP-Atlas demonstrate consistent improvements over the initial student, yielding absolute gains of 16.5\%, 10.2\%, and 12.6\%, respectively. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: EvoMCP is a closed loop that co-evolves training tasks and teacher trajectories with the student MCP agent during supervised fine-tuning. It gives absolute gains of 16.5%, 10.2% and 12.6% over the initial student on Toolathlon, MCPMark and MCP-Atlas.
AI.motivation: Supervised fine-tuning of MCP agents uses a static data distribution, which does not adapt to the student's evolving capabilities and leaves newly exposed weaknesses unaddressed.
AI.method: The student's established capabilities and gaps are assessed from rollout feedback. Task evolution adapts compatible verified seed tasks to these gaps while keeping their verifiers aligned, and trajectory evolution uses reusable skills to recover failed teacher rollouts and refine successful ones. The resulting task-trajectory pairs fine-tune the student, accepted tasks seed later rounds, and the re-evaluated student guides the next round of data evolution.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over the initial student on Toolathlon, MCPMark and MCP-Atlas, with absolute gains of 16.5%, 10.2% and 12.6% respectively.
AI.conclusion: Co-evolving the training data with the agent, rather than fixing it in advance, is a practical way to close an MCP agent's capability gaps in a closed loop.

title: Multi-Test Nation Bias Benchmarking of LLMs with Explicit Unbiased Baselines
comment: Published in Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics (TACL), 2026. 17 pages. Equal contribution: Jonghyeon Choi and Yeonjun Choi
summary: While prior work has highlighted that systematic nation-level bias in large language models (LLMs) can pose operational risks for international relations (IR) applications, many existing evaluations still lack a clearly specified unbiased reference (ground truth), limiting fully quantitative and cross-setting measurement. Using an expanded corpus of 722 official UN Security Council (UNSC) records, we measure nation-level bias with five complementary tests, thereby extending prior approaches to cover a broader set of bias expression channels: opinion ranking (WOW), association sorting (AK+-), vote simulation (PVS), opposition attribution (F-Oppose), and framing (Headliner). To enable grounded bias evaluation, we explicitly define an unbiased status for each test; in particular, for WOW and AK+- where ground truth is difficult to specify, we propose an action-based pseudo unbiased status derived from observable voting behavior to construct a quantifiable baseline. Benchmarking 4 LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.3-70B, Mistral-22B-Small, and Qwen3-30B) across the five permanent members of the UNSC, we find a test-agnostic macro-pattern: relative to the reference baselines defined for each test, model outputs lean toward the opposition (red) side for China and Russia and toward the supportive (blue) side for the U.K., the U.S., and France. These results underscore the need to audit IR-facing LLM deployments with grounded, multi-test benchmarks tied to explicit reference points.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks nation-level bias in four LLMs using 722 UN Security Council records and five tests, each with an explicit unbiased reference. Model outputs lean toward China and Russia's opposition side and toward the U.K., U.S. and France's supportive side.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of nation-level bias in LLMs for international relations often lack a clearly specified unbiased reference, which limits quantitative and cross-setting measurement.
AI.method: Five complementary tests cover opinion ranking (WOW), association sorting (AK+-), vote simulation (PVS), opposition attribution (F-Oppose) and framing (Headliner). Each test has an explicitly defined unbiased status, and for WOW and AK+- an action-based pseudo unbiased status is derived from observable voting behaviour.
AI.result: Benchmarking GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.3-70B, Mistral-22B-Small and Qwen3-30B across the five permanent UNSC members, the authors find a test-agnostic macro-pattern: relative to the reference baselines, China and Russia are pushed toward the opposition side, and the U.K., U.S. and France toward the supportive side.
AI.conclusion: IR-facing LLM deployments need auditing with grounded, multi-test benchmarks tied to explicit reference points.

title: Specification-Guided Generation for Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate structured outputs, but existing constrained-decoding methods mainly enforce syntax and cannot directly enforce satisfaction of a formal specification. We introduce a neuro-symbolic, specification-guided decoding framework that combines LLM generation with symbolic reasoning. At each step, the framework refines the decoding grammar by filtering out values that cannot be extended to an output satisfying the specification. We present a forward-only variant that guarantees specification satisfaction by construction, and a backtracking variant that revises earlier feasible choices when their downstream consequences leave only values that the LLM itself judges unsuitable. The framework is model-agnostic, requires no retraining, and builds on existing grammar-constrained decoding mechanisms. Experiments on configuration and constraint-solving benchmarks show that the forward-only variant reliably produces specification-compliant outputs while reducing repeated LLM inference compared with rejection sampling and incurring modest symbolic-reasoning overhead. The backtracking variant further reduces cases in which the model is forced to select values that it has itself judged unsuitable, thereby substantially improving adherence to the LLM's stated interpretation of the prompt.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a neuro-symbolic, specification-guided decoding framework that filters LLM token choices so the output satisfies a formal specification. It has a forward-only variant that guarantees compliance by construction and a backtracking variant that revises earlier choices.
AI.motivation: Existing constrained-decoding methods enforce syntax but cannot directly enforce satisfaction of a formal specification.
AI.method: At each decoding step the grammar is refined by filtering out values that cannot be extended to an output satisfying the specification, using symbolic reasoning. The forward-only variant guarantees satisfaction by construction, and the backtracking variant revises earlier feasible choices when their downstream consequences leave only values the LLM itself judges unsuitable. The framework is model-agnostic, needs no retraining, and builds on grammar-constrained decoding.
AI.result: On configuration and constraint-solving benchmarks the forward-only variant reliably produces specification-compliant outputs, with fewer repeated LLM inferences than rejection sampling and modest symbolic-reasoning overhead. The backtracking variant further reduces forced selections of values the model itself judged unsuitable, improving adherence to the LLM's stated interpretation of the prompt.
AI.conclusion: Specification satisfaction can be enforced during decoding without retraining, and backtracking further aligns outputs with the model's own interpretation of the prompt.

title: Verify--Backtrack Loop: Structured Precondition Recovery for Long-Horizon Language Agents
summary: Language agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks in interactive environments, where actions often depend on latent preconditions. The core difficulty is not trajectory length but recovery: when a prerequisite is missing or an earlier decomposition fails, trying another plausible action rarely helps. ReAct and later reflection or adaptive-planning methods support local correction, but express recovery as free-form text, with no explicit control state linking the terminal goal, the active goal, and the failure source. We introduce the Verify--Backtrack Loop (VBL), a training-free extension of ReAct that turns precondition discovery and failure diagnosis into structured planning-state updates. VBL maintains the task decomposition as a bounded goal stack and, on goal activation, execution failure, or material state change, jointly verifies two horizons---whether the active goal contributes to the terminal goal and whether it is feasible in the current state. These dual-horizon judgments, combined with typed failure attribution, trigger explicit operations---Push, Pop, retry, or BacktrackTo the parent. We evaluate VBL with Qwen3.5-9B, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek-V3.2 on AppWorld, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld. VBL improves over ReAct and reflection-based control on every backbone--benchmark pair. On the challenging AppWorld setting, it improves task success by up to 22.07 percentage points over ReAct. Ablations show that removing either verification or diagnosis degrades performance, in several settings below ReAct, confirming that the two mechanisms are complementary. These results show that reliable long-horizon interaction benefits from revising the planning state, not merely the next action.

AI.tldr: VBL is a training-free extension of ReAct that treats recovery as structured planning-state updates, using a bounded goal stack and dual-horizon verification with typed failure attribution. It improves over ReAct and reflection-based control on every backbone-benchmark pair tested, by up to 22.07 percentage points on AppWorld.
AI.motivation: In long-horizon language agents the core difficulty is recovery from missing preconditions or failed decompositions, and ReAct and reflection methods express recovery as free-form text with no explicit control state.
AI.method: VBL keeps the task decomposition as a bounded goal stack. On goal activation, execution failure or material state change, it jointly verifies whether the active goal contributes to the terminal goal and whether it is feasible in the current state, then uses typed failure attribution to trigger explicit operations: Push, Pop, retry or BacktrackTo the parent.
AI.result: Evaluated with Qwen3.5-9B, GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3.2 on AppWorld, ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, VBL improves over ReAct and reflection-based control on every backbone-benchmark pair, with task success up to 22.07 percentage points higher than ReAct on AppWorld. Ablations show removing verification or diagnosis degrades performance, in several settings below ReAct.
AI.conclusion: Reliable long-horizon interaction benefits from revising the planning state rather than only the next action, and verification and diagnosis are complementary.

title: Connectivity-Aware Client Selection in Decentralized Federated Learning
summary: Decentralized federated learning (DFL) has emerged as a scalable alternative to centralized federated learning, removing the single point of failure and communication bottleneck at the server. However, most existing decentralized approaches rely on full-neighborhood broadcasting, where each client transmits its model update to all of its neighbors in each communication round. While effective, this results in significant communication overhead and high energy consumption. This paper applies spectral graph tools as lightweight client selection methods that leverage the graph topology by analyzing the spectral properties of the graph Laplacian over a fixed communication graph. Specifically, we exploit eigenvector embeddings and heat/diffusion kernel similarities to guide each client in selecting only a subset of structurally relevant neighbors, i.e., those that are most beneficial for the convergence of the federation process. This topology aware randomization matches or outperforms uniform neighborhood subsampling and approaches the accuracy of full broadcasting. The largest gains, about $3$ percentage points, emerge under strong data heterogeneity on larger, structurally rich graphs, while the total number of transmitted messages is reduced by $50\%$ compared to naive broadcasting.

AI.tldr: The paper applies spectral graph tools to select a structurally relevant subset of neighbours for each client in decentralized federated learning. It matches or beats uniform neighbour subsampling, approaches full broadcasting accuracy, and cuts transmitted messages by 50%.
AI.motivation: Most decentralized federated learning methods broadcast each client's model update to all neighbours every round, which causes large communication overhead and energy consumption.
AI.method: Clients use eigenvector embeddings and heat or diffusion kernel similarities computed from the Laplacian spectrum of a fixed communication graph to select a subset of neighbours that are most beneficial for convergence.
AI.result: The topology-aware selection matches or outperforms uniform neighbourhood subsampling and approaches full broadcasting accuracy. The largest gains, about 3 percentage points, appear under strong data heterogeneity on larger, structurally rich graphs, and the number of transmitted messages drops by 50% compared with naive broadcasting.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight topology-aware client selection can substantially reduce communication cost in decentralized federated learning with little or no loss of accuracy.

title: Patch-Based Deep Kernel Learning for Data Assimilation and Bias Correction with Extremely Sparse Observations
summary: Data Assimilation (DA) reconstructs the state of a spatio-temporal system by combining sensor observations with the output of a numerical model. Since model states are high-dimensional while observations cover only a small fraction of the domain, DA is a challenging large-scale estimation problem, central to weather forecasting and oceanography. Classical variational methods such as 3D-Var rely on a hand-crafted background error covariance that assumes unbiased errors, and therefore cannot capture state-dependent correlations or systematic model biases. Moreover, their cost grows with the size of the domain. Deep learning (DL) methods can perform DA and bias correction (BC) non-linearly, but typically offer limited interpretability and no calibrated uncertainty estimates. We propose a hybrid framework that couples a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a learnable-kernel Gaussian Process (GP) to jointly perform DA and BC from extremely sparse observations. The model is trained end-to-end by maximizing the marginal log-likelihood, learns a data-driven covariance over the whole grid, and provides both the Maximum A Posteriori analysis and its uncertainty by design. A patch-based strategy reduces the $O(N^3)$ training cost of exact GPs over $N$ grid points to $O(N)$ for a fixed patch size. Inference remains exact and only requires solving a linear system whose $O(m^3)$ cost depends on the number of observations $m \ll N$, not on the domain. The learned covariance can also replace the hand-crafted one in 3D-Var, improving its accuracy without changing the variational formulation. Experiments on sea surface temperature and salinity, with both synthetic and real, extremely sparse in-situ observations, show that the framework outperforms 3D-Var, a classical GP and a competing DL model, while reducing inference time by more than 98% with respect to 3D-Var.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid CNN and learnable-kernel Gaussian Process that jointly performs data assimilation and bias correction from extremely sparse observations. It outperforms 3D-Var, a classical GP and a competing deep learning model while cutting inference time by more than 98% relative to 3D-Var.
AI.motivation: Classical variational methods such as 3D-Var rely on a hand-crafted background covariance that assumes unbiased errors and cannot capture state-dependent correlations or systematic biases, while deep learning methods offer limited interpretability and no calibrated uncertainty.
AI.method: A CNN is coupled with a learnable-kernel GP and trained end-to-end by maximising the marginal log-likelihood, learning a data-driven covariance over the whole grid. A patch-based strategy reduces the training cost of exact GPs from O(N^3) to O(N) for a fixed patch size, and inference requires solving an m-by-m linear system, where m is the number of observations. The learned covariance can also replace the hand-crafted one in 3D-Var.
AI.result: On sea surface temperature and salinity with synthetic and real extremely sparse in-situ observations, the framework outperforms 3D-Var, a classical GP and a competing DL model, and reduces inference time by more than 98% relative to 3D-Var.
AI.conclusion: A learned, uncertainty-aware covariance can improve both data assimilation and bias correction at a fraction of the cost of classical 3D-Var when observations are very sparse.

title: Real Computation or Merely Naming? A Pre-Registered Mechanism Audit of 25 Cognitive-Architecture Modules in an LLM-Based Agent System
comment: 40 pages. Static audit of 25 cognitive-architecture modules (18 carry no computed value to any production output), pre-registered interventions on 11 modules, 61 frozen criteria (53 confirmed / 5 falsified), two repair controls (0.028 -> 1.000 task success; -52% error). Artifact: this https URL
summary: Agent systems built on local large language models are increasingly marketed through the vocabulary of cognitive architecture: modules named global workspace, theory of mind, causal reasoning, or active inference are listed as features, and the presence of the name is taken as the presence of the mechanism. We ask the prior question -- does the named computation actually happen -- and contribute a transferable verification method for the claim-implementation gap: a four-question static audit protocol with line-number evidence and call-chain tracing, demonstrated on two systems. We audit a system claiming 25 cognitive mechanisms, pre-register falsifiable predictions for 11 modules and execute the interventions, replicate the protocol on the IIT-phi core of a second, independent system with its own pre-committed falsification criteria, and run two repair experiments as positive controls. In 18 of 25 modules the computed value never reaches any production output; three idle-wiring shapes new to the dead-code and code-smell literatures emerge (connected-but-never-called, called-but-inert, called-but-content-blind). Of 61 frozen criteria across 12 interventions, 53 were confirmed, two partially adjudicated, five falsified, one adjudication-ambiguous. Repairs raised planner task success from 0.028 to 1.000 and cut state-controller error by 52%. Module names and module computations must be audited as independent claims; the protocol and the five-class failure taxonomy are reusable for the claim-implementation gap at two-system, case-level depth.

AI.tldr: The paper audits whether 25 named cognitive-architecture modules in an LLM-based agent system perform the computation their names claim. It finds that in 18 of 25 modules the computed value never reaches any production output, and it contributes a transferable static audit protocol.
AI.motivation: Agent systems are marketed with cognitive-architecture vocabulary, and the presence of a module's name is taken as evidence of the mechanism, so the claim-implementation gap is rarely checked.
AI.method: A four-question static audit protocol with line-number evidence and call-chain tracing is applied to a system claiming 25 mechanisms. Falsifiable predictions are pre-registered for 11 modules and interventions are executed, the IIT-phi core of a second independent system is audited with its own pre-committed criteria, and two repair experiments serve as positive controls.
AI.result: In 18 of 25 modules the computed value never reaches any production output, and three new idle-wiring shapes are identified. Of 61 frozen criteria across 12 interventions, 53 were confirmed, two partially adjudicated, five falsified and one ambiguous. Repairs raised planner task success from 0.028 to 1.000 and reduced state-controller error by 52%.
AI.conclusion: Module names and module computations must be audited as independent claims, and the protocol and five-class failure taxonomy are reusable for the claim-implementation gap.

title: What Should LLMs Forget: Reinforcement Unlearning of Knowledge Associations
summary: Large language models (LLMs) acquire extensive factual knowledge during pre-training, which may include sensitive, private, or copyrighted information, motivating the development of unlearning methods that selectively remove specific knowledge while preserving general capabilities. However, existing approaches typically optimize entire responses without explicitly identifying the knowledge to be forgotten, resulting in coarse and uncontrolled forgetting. To address this, we revisit the forgetting target of LLM unlearning and introduce Knowledge Association (KA), which characterizes the association between a query context and its target knowledge and is instantiated by the corresponding conditional predictive distribution, as the fundamental target of forgetting. Based on KA, we propose Knowledge Association Reinforcement Unlearning (KARU), a unified reinforcement learning framework that suppresses forgotten knowledge associations while preserving retained ones. Specifically, KARU derives complementary mechanisms from the KA-based formulation: token-level reward construction for finer-grained forgetting supervision, distribution-level regularization for precise knowledge suppression, and proximity-aware retain sampling to mitigate collateral degradation. Experiments across diverse LLMs on representative benchmarks demonstrate that KARU consistently improves forgetting effectiveness over existing baselines while maintaining comparable retention performance and general utility.

AI.tldr: KARU is a reinforcement learning framework for LLM unlearning that targets knowledge associations, the conditional predictive distribution linking a query context to its target knowledge. It improves forgetting effectiveness over existing baselines while keeping retention and general utility comparable.
AI.motivation: Existing unlearning methods optimise entire responses without identifying the knowledge to forget, which leads to coarse and uncontrolled forgetting.
AI.method: Knowledge Association is adopted as the forgetting target. KARU combines token-level reward construction for finer forgetting supervision, distribution-level regularisation for precise suppression, and proximity-aware retain sampling to reduce collateral degradation.
AI.result: Across diverse LLMs and representative benchmarks, KARU consistently improves forgetting effectiveness over existing baselines while maintaining comparable retention performance and general utility.
AI.conclusion: Defining the forgetting target as knowledge associations gives more controlled unlearning that suppresses targeted knowledge without broadly degrading the model.

title: Chance-Constrained Inspection Viewpoint Sequencing for On-Orbit Servicing via Safe Reinforcement Learning
summary: Autonomous inspection of a target spacecraft is typically the initial step in on-orbit servicing. Planning close-proximity observation viewpoints involves a complex combinatorial problem constrained by coverage, fuel, and safety considerations. This paper models the viewpoint selection as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) and applies Proximal Policy Optimization with Lagrangian relaxation to solve it. The system combines a high-level planner, which sequences camera viewpoints on an observation sphere around the target, with a low-level model that assesses each transfer using the Clohessy--Wiltshire (CW) equations for relative motion. The deterministic constraints on single-impulse reachability and $\Delta v$ cap are enforced directly on the action set. Safety margins are affected by navigation and manoeuvre errors, making the actual clearance stochastic. To address this, a chance constraint on the realised trajectory is implemented, with a Lagrangian multiplier governed by PID control to adapt the penalty during training. The approach is tested on a Galileo-class navigation satellite in medium Earth orbit, modelled as a point cloud where visibility from each viewpoint considers field-of-view and line-of-sight occlusion. Across various risk budgets, the trained policy maintains the keep-out violation rate within the specified limit, achieving coverage close to its maximum and staying within the mission $\Delta v$ budget. Compared to the usual practice of applying a fixed margin to the keep-out radius and planning deterministically, the chance-constrained policy attains less than half the violation rate at comparable coverage. This makes the collision risk an explicit design parameter, eliminating the need for re-tuning per case. The learned policy selects a viewpoint without the repeated Monte Carlo risk estimates required by a greedy, chance-constrained planner at every decision point.

AI.tldr: The paper models viewpoint selection for autonomous inspection of a spacecraft as a constrained MDP, solved with PPO and Lagrangian relaxation plus a PID-controlled multiplier for a chance constraint on clearance. The trained policy keeps the keep-out violation rate within the specified limit while achieving near-maximum coverage.
AI.motivation: Close-proximity inspection planning is a combinatorial problem constrained by coverage, fuel and safety, and the usual fixed margin on the keep-out radius with deterministic planning is conservative and imprecise about collision risk.
AI.method: A high-level planner sequences camera viewpoints on an observation sphere, and a low-level model assesses each transfer with the Clohessy-Wiltshire equations. Single-impulse reachability and the delta-v cap are enforced on the action set, and a chance constraint on the realised trajectory handles stochastic clearance. Visibility accounts for field of view and line-of-sight occlusion on a point-cloud model of a Galileo-class satellite in MEO.
AI.result: Across risk budgets the policy keeps the violation rate within the limit, reaches coverage close to its maximum and stays within the delta-v budget. Compared with a fixed-margin deterministic approach, it attains less than half the violation rate at comparable coverage.
AI.conclusion: Collision risk becomes an explicit design parameter that does not require per-case re-tuning, and the learned policy avoids repeated Monte Carlo risk estimates at each decision.

title: Risk-Sensitive Mission Planning for Multi-Target On-Orbit Inspection via Distributional Reinforcement Learning
summary: Multi-target on-orbit servicing missions require planning tools that can adapt to evolving operational conditions while accounting for the outcome variability inherent to safety-critical spaceflight. This paper presents an adaptive planning approach for multi-target servicing campaigns in low Earth orbit and applies it to inspection missions flown by a low-thrust servicer. The approach is based on Distributional Reinforcement Learning, which learns the full distribution of mission returns and thereby supports explicit risk-sensitive decision-making at each planning step. Specifically, a Quantile-Regression Deep Q-Network (QR-DQN) agent selects which target to inspect next by jointly considering the expectation and the variance of the predicted return through a mean-variance criterion. The mission environment models circular orbits with a spread in inclination and uses Edelbaum's combined-manoeuvre low-thrust transfer estimates. The observation comprises the orbital elements, the visit history, the observed risk state of each target and the remaining mission-time budget. The risk state of each target changes stochastically during the campaign, making the outcome of an inspection uncertain and creating operationally meaningful distinctions between risk-neutral and risk-averse planning strategies. Because the mission-time budget generally admits only a subset of the candidate targets, the planner must also select which targets to inspect. Numerical experiments on scenarios with five target satellites show that one risk-aversion weight moves the policy across a range of mean return and return variance, over an unchanged environment and reward. Risk-averse agents reduce the variance of the episodic return by approximately one half relative to risk-neutral agents and lower the probability of a mission loss, at a cost in mean return. To validate the learned policies, the efficient frontier, which gives the highest mean return attainable at each level of return variance, is computed exactly by enumerating the admissible visit orders. At equal variance, the learned policies lie close to this frontier in mean return, and the risk-averse policies have a lower probability of a mission loss than the frontier policies.

AI.tldr: The paper applies distributional reinforcement learning with a QR-DQN agent and a mean-variance criterion to choose which targets to inspect in multi-target low-Earth-orbit servicing. A risk-aversion weight trades mean return against return variance, and risk-averse policies roughly halve return variance.
AI.motivation: Multi-target servicing needs planners that adapt to changing conditions and account for the outcome variability of safety-critical spaceflight, which risk-neutral planning does not capture.
AI.method: The agent learns the full return distribution and selects the next target by weighing expected return against variance. The environment uses circular orbits with a spread in inclination and Edelbaum low-thrust transfer estimates, and the observation includes orbital elements, visit history, stochastic per-target risk states and the remaining mission-time budget. The planner also chooses which subset of targets to visit.
AI.result: On scenarios with five target satellites, the risk-aversion weight moves the policy across a range of mean return and variance. Risk-averse agents reduce episodic return variance by about one half relative to risk-neutral agents and lower the probability of mission loss, at a cost in mean return. Learned policies lie close to the exact efficient frontier obtained by enumerating admissible visit orders.
AI.conclusion: A single risk-aversion parameter gives operators a controllable trade-off between expected mission return and the probability of mission loss.

title: Breaking Information Islands in Sparse Tuning via Small-World Connectivity
summary: Sparse tuning is widely used to adapt large language models due to its parameter efficiency. However, its effectiveness depends not only on the number of trainable parameters, but also on the feature-interaction topology of the sparse update's structural support. Limited or uneven connectivity in this support may isolate subsets of feature dimensions, forming information islands that restrict direct task-specific interactions through the trainable update. To address this issue, we propose Small-World Induced Fine-Tuning (SWIFT), a sparse tuning framework inspired by small-world connectivity. SWIFT combines block-diagonal sparse updates for local feature mixing with a fixed deterministic scattering permutation that routes the mixed outputs across feature groups without additional trainable parameters. We further show theoretically that certain random sparse-update models and block-diagonal updates can exhibit information islands, whereas a sufficiently scattering permutation guarantees positive block-level expansion when the trainable block-diagonal factor consists of equal-sized, structurally dense square blocks. Extensive experiments on commonsense reasoning, natural language generation, and image classification demonstrate that SWIFT outperforms the evaluated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) baselines on average and can match or surpass full fine-tuning. Implementation is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: SWIFT is a sparse fine-tuning method that combines block-diagonal updates with a fixed scattering permutation to avoid information islands in feature connectivity. It outperforms the evaluated PEFT baselines on average and can match or surpass full fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: The effectiveness of sparse tuning depends on the feature-interaction topology of the sparse update's support, and limited or uneven connectivity can isolate subsets of feature dimensions into information islands.
