AI.method: Small-world-inspired SWIFT pairs block-diagonal sparse updates for local feature mixing with a fixed deterministic permutation that routes mixed outputs across feature groups without adding trainable parameters. The authors show theoretically that random sparse-update models and block-diagonal updates can form information islands, while a sufficiently scattering permutation guarantees positive block-level expansion when the blocks are equal-sized and dense.
AI.result: Experiments on commonsense reasoning, natural language generation and image classification show that SWIFT outperforms the evaluated PEFT baselines on average and can match or surpass full fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Connectivity structure of the sparse update matters, and a fixed scattering permutation is a parameter-free way to improve parameter-efficient adaptation.

title: Radial Kernel Attention for Long-Range Modeling in Polymer Machine Learning Force Fields
summary: We introduce Radial Kernel Attention (RKA) for long-range modeling in polymer machine learning force fields. Local neighbor graphs constrain communication across polymer chains and their surrounding environments, while explicit all-pair attention incurs quadratic cost. RKA maps atomic distances from the cluster centroid to learned radial features and combines their overlap with content-dependent queries and keys. Factorized aggregation and readout enable global feature exchange at linear cost in atom count for fixed feature dimensions. We insert the invariant scalar update between EquiformerV3 local blocks and obtain conservative forces by differentiating the total energy, including its radial coordinate dependence. We evaluate energy and force prediction for finite polymer-derived clusters in OPoly26. Our models are trained on the official training split for 12 epochs and evaluated directly after training on the complete official validation split. A matched 5M comparison shows that RKA reduces per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%, respectively. The 20M RKA model is compared with UMA-S-1.2 and UMA-S-1.2.1 on the same validation structures. The 20M model attains a total-energy MAE of 15.81 meV and a force MAE of 2.619 meV/angstrom; its per-atom energy MAE is 0.1182 meV/atom. RKA provides a compact global communication pathway that improves energy and force prediction on the evaluated polymer-derived clusters.

AI.tldr: RKA is a radial kernel attention module that adds global, linear-cost communication between atoms in polymer machine learning force fields. Inserted into EquiformerV3, it reduces per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3% in a matched 5M comparison.
AI.motivation: Local neighbour graphs limit communication across polymer chains and their surroundings, while explicit all-pair attention has quadratic cost.
AI.method: RKA maps atomic distances from the cluster centroid to learned radial features and combines their overlap with content-dependent queries and keys. Factorised aggregation and readout give global feature exchange at linear cost in atom count. The invariant scalar update is inserted between EquiformerV3 local blocks, and conservative forces are obtained by differentiating the total energy, including its radial coordinate dependence.
AI.result: In a matched 5M comparison, RKA reduces per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%. The 20M RKA model reaches a total-energy MAE of 15.81 meV and a force MAE of 2.619 meV/angstrom on OPoly26 validation structures, with a per-atom energy MAE of 0.1182 meV/atom, and it is compared with UMA-S-1.2 and UMA-S-1.2.1 on the same validation set.
AI.conclusion: A compact global communication pathway improves energy and force prediction on the evaluated polymer-derived clusters.

title: Advancing Clinical Trial Outcome Prediction with Domain-Specific Large Language Models
summary: Clinical trial failures are a major barrier to efficient drug development, incurring substantial costs and delaying patient access to effective therapies. Structured approaches such as the Hierarchical Interaction Network (HINT) predict trial outcomes by explicitly modelling interactions between drugs, diseases and protocols, but make limited use of the free text in trial registrations. We evaluate two domain-specific language models, BioBERT (108M parameters) and BioMistral (7B parameters), for phase-level outcome prediction on the TOP benchmark (12,477 trials), representing each trial as text built from ten this http URL fields. We compare fine-tuning (full fine-tuning for BioBERT, low-rank adaptation for BioMistral) with probing, in which the pretrained model is frozen and only a lightweight classifier is trained on its embeddings. On the held-out test set of each phase, all four language-model variants achieved higher ROC-AUC (0.613--0.772) and PR-AUC (0.649--0.901) than the published HINT results, corresponding to relative PR-AUC gains of 10--20\%. F1 differences were small and mixed, and no model, including HINT, clearly exceeded the F1 of a trivial classifier that predicts success for every trial. Under the configurations tested, probing performed comparably to fine-tuning: fine-tuned models scored highest on ROC-AUC and PR-AUC in Phases I and II, and frozen BioMistral embeddings in Phase III (ROC-AUC 0.772; PR-AUC 0.901), although most differences between variants were below 0.03 and were not tested for significance. These results suggest that pretrained biomedical representations already encode signal relevant to trial outcome, and that probing is a computationally cheaper alternative to fine-tuning for this task.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates BioBERT and BioMistral on clinical trial phase outcome prediction using the TOP benchmark, and all four language-model variants beat the published HINT results on ROC-AUC and PR-AUC. F1 gains are small and mixed, and no model clearly beats a trivial always-success classifier on F1.
AI.motivation: Clinical trial failures are costly, and the HINT model uses structured interactions but makes limited use of the free text in trial registrations.
AI.method: Each trial is represented as text built from ten registration fields. Two domain-specific models are compared, BioBERT (108M parameters) with full fine-tuning and BioMistral (7B parameters) with low-rank adaptation, against probing, in which the pretrained model is frozen and only a lightweight classifier is trained on its embeddings.
AI.result: On the held-out test set of each phase, all four variants reach ROC-AUC 0.613 to 0.772 and PR-AUC 0.649 to 0.901, relative PR-AUC gains of 10 to 20% over HINT. Probing performs comparably to fine-tuning, and most differences between variants are below 0.03 and were not tested for significance.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained biomedical representations already encode signal about trial outcomes, and probing is a computationally cheaper alternative to fine-tuning for this task.

title: Multimodal In-Context Learning with Explicit Rule Induction
summary: A central challenge in multimodal in-context learning (MICL) arises from tasks that are ill-defined without context and require uncovering the underlying rules from demonstrations. Existing methods predominantly treat MICL as direct input-output mapping, overlooking the importance of explicitly inducing and reasoning over such rules, limiting both performance and interpretability. We propose ERIM, Explicit Rule-Induction for Multimodal In-Context Learning, a unified framework that enhances MICL by explicitly inducing the latent rules governing demonstration samples. Leveraging the reasoning ability of multi-modal large language model (MLLM), ERIM constructs rule-centric MICL datasets, introduces explicit supervision for rule induction, and fine-tunes MLLM to perform explicit rule-induction via a two-stage training strategy that combines mixed cold-start supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments show consistent performance improvements across diverse MICL settings and demonstrate that correctly inducing underlying rules directly leads to stronger and more stable performance.

AI.tldr: ERIM improves multimodal in-context learning by explicitly inducing the latent rules behind demonstrations and reasoning over them. It uses rule-centric datasets and a two-stage training scheme of cold-start supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal in-context learning treats tasks as direct input-output mapping and ignores that many tasks are ill-defined without uncovering the underlying rules from demonstrations, which limits performance and interpretability.
AI.method: Using an MLLM, ERIM builds rule-centric MICL datasets, adds explicit supervision for rule induction, and fine-tunes the model in two stages: mixed cold-start supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning.
AI.result: The authors report consistent performance improvements across diverse MICL settings, and state that correctly inducing the underlying rules leads to stronger and more stable performance. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Explicit rule induction is a useful route to better and more interpretable multimodal in-context learning.

title: Clinical-Protocol-Aware Cyber Resilience for Connected Clinical Technologies Under AI-Enabled Adversarial Conditions
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Healthcare increasingly relies on connected medical devices, clinical information systems, cloud services, and distributed-care technologies, creating cybersecurity risks across clinical workflows. AI-enabled capabilities can accelerate vulnerability discovery and attack-path analysis, increasing the need to limit compromise propagation. This paper proposes a clinical-protocol-aware cyber-resilience framework based on bounded clinical micro-networks and controlled interconnections. The framework integrates clinical factors into cybersecurity design, management, and evaluation, covering prevention, containment, and incident response. A parameterized Monte Carlo simulation distinguishes technical cyber exposure from modeled clinical consequence. Experiments investigate architectural connectivity, adversarial capability, security controls, protocol dependency, risk alignment, communication directionality, lifecycle integration, and response timing. Under the simulation assumptions, connected architecture increases mean cyber exposure by 56.3% relative to segmented architecture, while combined prevention and containment reduce exposure by 60.1% relative to no controls. Increasing protocol dependency raises the modeled clinical-impact index from 1.021 to 7.567 without changing mean cyber exposure, demonstrating that technical exposure and clinical consequence can diverge. Risk-alignment experiments further indicate higher modeled clinical impact when greater technical risk corresponds to greater clinical significance. The findings support comparative architectural analysis, not calibrated estimates of real-world cyber risk, control effectiveness, or patient harm. The framework provides a clinical-context-aware approach to security-boundary design, control prioritization, and coordinated containment in connected healthcare environments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a clinical-protocol-aware cyber-resilience framework based on bounded clinical micro-networks and controlled interconnections, evaluated with a parameterised Monte Carlo simulation. Connected architectures raise mean cyber exposure by 56.3% over segmented ones, and increasing protocol dependency raises the modelled clinical-impact index without changing exposure.
AI.motivation: Connected medical devices, clinical information systems and cloud services create cybersecurity risks across clinical workflows, and AI-enabled attack-path analysis increases the need to limit compromise propagation.
AI.method: The framework integrates clinical factors into the design, management and evaluation of prevention, containment and incident response. A parameterised Monte Carlo simulation separates technical cyber exposure from modelled clinical consequence, and experiments vary architectural connectivity, adversarial capability, controls, protocol dependency, risk alignment, communication directionality, lifecycle integration and response timing.
AI.result: Under the simulation assumptions, connected architecture increases mean cyber exposure by 56.3% relative to segmented architecture, and combined prevention and containment reduce exposure by 60.1% relative to no controls. Raising protocol dependency lifts the clinical-impact index from 1.021 to 7.567 with unchanged mean exposure, and greater risk alignment yields higher modelled clinical impact.
AI.conclusion: Technical exposure and clinical consequence can diverge, so security-boundary design and control prioritisation should be clinically informed, though the results are comparative and not calibrated estimates of real-world risk or patient harm.

title: Whose Values, Which Contexts, and What Signals? Grounding Cultural Value Alignment with Re3Culture
summary: Cultural value alignment requires not only model optimization but also a well-specified target grounded in real-human evidence. Yet how such targets should be grounded in human data remains largely unexplored, raising three fundamental questions: (1) whose values should be represented? (2) where should cultural values be observed? and (3) what signals reveal underlying values? We investigate these questions through Re3Culture, a large-scale dataset linking (i) Representative communities: 700+ human participants across four cultures recruited through cultural-affiliation screening and demographic-aware sampling; (ii) Realistic scenario: culturally sensitive scenarios selected by community members, e.g., family and kinship; and (iii) Revealed value signals: 1,400+ value surveys, 20,000+ topic-grounded behavioral principles and explicit value priorities with responses for 6,000+ situated questions. Our analysis shows why these choices matter for defining the target, with three implications. First, estimating cultural values requires both community affiliation and broad internal coverage. Substituting other cultures or restricting subgroup coverage shifts value estimates. LLM simulations also disproportionately reflect particular subgroups. Second, values must be observed in concrete, community-guided situations. Abstract questionnaire profiles weakly recover situated priorities, and communities differ in which scenarios they identify as culturally value-revealing. Third, value priorities should be elicited explicitly, not learned from response preferences or bottom-line answers alone. Preferences conflate value agreement with other response-level qualities, and similar answers can be derived from different value priorities. By addressing these requirements, Re3Culture provides the first human-grounded resource that explicitly informs target definition for cultural value alignment.

AI.tldr: Re3Culture is a human-grounded dataset of 700+ participants across four cultures, linking community-selected scenarios with revealed value signals for cultural value alignment. The analysis shows that who is represented, where values are observed and how they are elicited each change the estimated target.
AI.motivation: Cultural value alignment needs a well-specified target grounded in real human evidence, but how such targets should be grounded in human data has been largely unexplored.
AI.method: The dataset links representative communities recruited through cultural-affiliation screening and demographic-aware sampling, realistic culturally sensitive scenarios selected by community members, and revealed value signals including 1,400+ value surveys, 20,000+ topic-grounded behavioural principles and explicit value priorities for 6,000+ situated questions.
AI.result: Substituting other cultures or restricting subgroup coverage shifts value estimates, and LLM simulations disproportionately reflect particular subgroups. Abstract questionnaire profiles weakly recover situated priorities, and preferences conflate value agreement with other response qualities, so priorities should be elicited explicitly.
AI.conclusion: Re3Culture is presented as the first human-grounded resource that explicitly informs target definition for cultural value alignment.

title: RECAST: REconstruction of Chain-of-Thought via Auditable Structured Traces
summary: Large closed-source reasoning models expose only their final answers. The intermediate reasoning that produces those answers is hidden behind API surfaces, tool-call policies, and safety filters. Existing chain-of-thought (CoT) extraction methods assume a side channel: a visible reasoning field, a scratchpad carried through tool calls, or a signed/encrypted reasoning block. We reproduce three representative state-of-the-art extraction methods and find that, on Claude-Sonnet-5.5 accessed through the standard chat-completions interface, all three return zero CoT tokens. The failure is structural rather than a bug: the reasoning field is absent, named tool selection is rejected, free-text scratchpad arguments are filtered, and no replayable reasoning block is exposed. We therefore take a different route. We present RECAST, a reconstruction-based framework that conditions a decoder on the question and the target model's final answer, reconstructs a first-person structured rationale, cleans it, and builds SFT-ready data. To the best of our knowledge, RECAST is the first system to reconstruct CoT from frontier closed models such as Claude-Sonnet-5.5, GPT-6.1, and Gemini 3 without using hidden reasoning channels. We instantiate RECAST on Claude-Sonnet-5.5 and additionally obtain successful qualitative reconstructions on GPT-6.1 and Gemini 3 with the same answer-only protocol. The system is open-source and packaged as an agent skill: one prompt deploys it and runs the complete pipeline to produce SFT-ready CoT data. This preprint describes the system, its threat model, and a controlled artifact validation; it does not claim large-scale benchmark improvements.

AI.tldr: RECAST reconstructs chain-of-thought from closed frontier models using only their final answers, since three existing extraction methods return zero CoT tokens on Claude-Sonnet-5.5 through the standard chat interface. It conditions a decoder on the question and answer to produce cleaned, SFT-ready rationales, and is packaged as an open-source agent skill.
AI.motivation: Closed reasoning models expose only final answers, and existing CoT extraction methods depend on a side channel such as a visible reasoning field, a tool-call scratchpad or a replayable reasoning block, which the tested interface does not provide.
AI.method: A decoder conditioned on the question and the target model's final answer reconstructs a first-person structured rationale, which is then cleaned and turned into SFT-ready data. The threat model and pipeline are described, and the whole pipeline runs from one prompt.
AI.result: The authors report that all three reproduced state-of-the-art extraction methods return zero CoT tokens on Claude-Sonnet-5.5, and that RECAST yields reconstructions on Claude-Sonnet-5.5, with successful qualitative reconstructions on GPT-6.1 and Gemini 3. The preprint describes a controlled artifact validation and claims no large-scale benchmark improvement.
AI.conclusion: Frontier model reasoning can be reconstructed from answers alone without hidden channels, though the evidence is qualitative and the downstream benefit remains untested at scale.

title: ReuScope: Auditing Data Reuse and Evaluation Sensitivity in Capsule Vision 2024
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets. 39 pages, 3 figures. Code and data: this https URL
summary: We develop ReuScope, a protocol for auditing data reuse and evaluation sensitivity, using Capsule Vision 2024 as a case study. It combines measurements of data relationships with two comparisons: changing the evaluation population while holding predictions fixed, and changing training data while holding evaluation fixed. Byte-identical files cross the public training-validation boundary, and all 41 Kvasir-Capsule recordings that contribute frames occur in both partitions. Shared source recordings establish cross-split overlap; missing cross-recording patient identifiers prevent counting unique shared patients. Across ten paired seeds, removing all training rows attributed to Kvasir-Capsule, plus five rows from other sources flagged as near-matches to it, lowers public-validation balanced accuracy from 82.5% to 61.2%. Evaluating the same fitted models on the validation rows of the other sources reverses the comparison: removal improves balanced accuracy by 1.38 percentage points. The public-validation drop measures sensitivity to source removal, not an amount of leakage-induced inflation. Matched controls show that sample size and class counts alone do not explain the observed score differences. An exploratory experiment removes the training neighbors of validation frames that have close training matches, or equally many distant training rows, and yields a difference-in-differences estimate, relative to matched unflagged frames, of -0.355 percentage points in true-class probability; the paired-t interval for accuracy spans zero. The resulting procedure distinguishes observed reuse from conditional performance sensitivity and specifies the population, class support and uncertainty unit for each conclusion.

AI.tldr: ReuScope is an auditing protocol that separates observed data reuse from conditional performance sensitivity, applied to Capsule Vision 2024. Removing training rows from the Kvasir-Capsule source drops public-validation balanced accuracy from 82.5% to 61.2%, but the same comparison on other sources reverses.
AI.motivation: Public benchmark splits may share source recordings and near-duplicate files, so high validation scores can reflect reuse rather than generalisation, and this needs a principled audit.
AI.method: The protocol combines measurements of data relationships with two comparisons: changing the evaluation population while holding predictions fixed, and changing training data while holding evaluation fixed. Ten paired seeds are used, matched controls check sample size and class counts, and an exploratory experiment removes training neighbours of close validation frames to obtain a difference-in-differences estimate.
AI.result: Byte-identical files cross the public training-validation boundary, and all 41 Kvasir-Capsule recordings contributing frames occur in both partitions. Removing Kvasir-Capsule rows and five flagged near-matches lowers public-validation balanced accuracy from 82.5% to 61.2%, while on the other sources' validation rows removal improves balanced accuracy by 1.38 percentage points. The exploratory difference-in-differences estimate is -0.355 percentage points and its paired-t interval spans zero.
AI.conclusion: The public-validation drop measures sensitivity to source removal rather than leakage-induced inflation, and conclusions must specify population, class support and uncertainty unit.

title: Dynamical Memory Transformer: Selective Recurrent Memories with Constant Cost Attention
summary: Transformers retain an explicit history of the sequence, allowing attention to directly retrieve past representations. However, the size of the KV-Cache and the cost of a new token increase with the context length. State Space Models compress the past into a fixed-size recurrent state, at the cost of reduced addressability. We present the Dynamical Memory Transformer (DMT), a hybrid architecture that separates sequence encoding from information reading. The encoder uses several memory units, each implemented by a dynamical system with a complex diagonal recurrent matrix. An input-dependent leak rate controls their updates. The decoder then uses attention to read and combine their outputs, without going through the token history. The formulation of the recurrence allows an associative scan with O(T ) total work and O(log T ) parallel depth, with fixed dimensions. During autoregressive inference, the recurrent states and the convolution cache remain fixed in size. We compare DMT with Mamba and Transformer on cognitive and language modeling tasks, and show its strengths and limitations: DMT achieves the best results on several cognitive tasks and language modeling performance close to that of Transformer, but remains behind Mamba in language modeling. On selective copy, DMT also shows stronger length extrapolation than Mamba and Transformer. These results demonstrate that parallel dynamical memory units are a promising mechanism for retaining and using information over sequences.

AI.tldr: The Dynamical Memory Transformer is a hybrid architecture that encodes sequences with complex-diagonal dynamical memory units and reads them with attention, keeping recurrent state fixed in size during inference. It achieves the best results on several cognitive tasks and stronger length extrapolation on selective copy, but remains behind Mamba on language modelling.
AI.motivation: Transformer KV caches grow with context length, while state space models compress history into a fixed-size state at the cost of reduced addressability.
AI.method: The architecture separates sequence encoding from information reading. The encoder uses several memory units, each a dynamical system with a complex diagonal recurrent matrix and an input-dependent leak rate, and the decoder uses attention over their outputs rather than over the token history. The recurrence admits an associative scan with O(T) total work and O(log T) parallel depth.
AI.result: DMT achieves the best results on several cognitive tasks and language modelling performance close to Transformer, but remains behind Mamba on language modelling. On selective copy it shows stronger length extrapolation than Mamba and Transformer.
AI.conclusion: Parallel dynamical memory units are a promising mechanism for retaining and using information over long sequences, with the stated strengths and limitations.

title: Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents
summary: Video director agents orchestrate multistage production to realize users' creative visions. Emerging research on their self-evolution advances screenplay planning effectively. However, the mutual reinforcement between directing and user interaction remains largely overlooked. Improved interaction clarifies user intent and informs workflow refinement, while more reliable execution shifts collaboration from troubleshooting to creative decisions. To this end, we introduce LIT (Learning to Interact and DirecT), a framework comprises a director agent, a simulated user, and a meta engineer. Simulated user assigns creative tasks to probe the director's weaknesses, while the meta engineer uses the task traces to revise the director's interaction and production strategy. Although this approach can address discovered interaction and production issues, it still relies on passive attribution by the meta agent. This limits its ability to adapt to broader user interaction patterns and production techniques. To solve this problem, we equip LIT with a co-evolution paradigm. The meta agent proactively learns external knowledge, thereby improving its ability to discover problems and propose solutions. The meta agent, simulated user, and director together form an evolutionary closed loop, collaboratively enhances the system's directing and interaction capabilities. Across the Test and OOD Test splits, LIT improves production and Interaction scores by 19.1% and 32.0%, respectively, relative to the initial pipeline. Controlled ablations reveal the correlation between improvements in production and interaction, where the co-evolution mechanism further encourage directing skill and interaction mode exploration.

AI.tldr: LIT is a co-evolving framework for video director agents, with a director, a simulated user and a meta engineer that jointly improve directing and user interaction. It raises production and interaction scores by 19.1% and 32.0% over the initial pipeline on the Test and OOD Test splits.
AI.motivation: Prior self-evolving director agents improve screenplay planning but overlook the mutual reinforcement between directing and user interaction, and their meta agent relies on passive attribution that limits adaptation to broader interaction patterns and production techniques.
AI.method: A simulated user assigns creative tasks to probe the director's weaknesses, and a meta engineer uses the task traces to revise the director's interaction and production strategy. The meta agent proactively learns external knowledge, and the meta agent, simulated user and director form an evolutionary closed loop.
AI.result: Across the Test and OOD Test splits, LIT improves production and interaction scores by 19.1% and 32.0% relative to the initial pipeline. Controlled ablations show a correlation between production and interaction improvements, and co-evolution further encourages exploration of directing skill and interaction modes.
AI.conclusion: Co-evolving the director, the simulated user and the meta agent is a route to more reliable directing and interaction, with the gains tied to proactive external knowledge acquisition.

title: Fuzzy selective state model for forecasting the dynamics of consumer preferences
summary: We consider forecasting the dynamics of consumer preferences of retail chain customers. A customer's preference is described by a triangular fuzzy number. The evolution of the preference over time is governed by a Mamba-type selective state space model whose hidden state is a triangular number, with computations carried out in M.G.~Matveev's two-component algebra of fuzzy numbers. The recurrence parameters are computed from crisp features, while the fuzzy part of the model remains linear with non-negative coefficients. We show that the state then always remains a proper triangular number and is a convex combination of past observations, so that the fuzziness of the forecast does not accumulate over time and the algebraic computations coincide with Zadeh's extension principle. On a synthetic example with competitor promotions and customer switching, a lightweight 107-parameter model reaches a mean absolute error of the forecast centre of 0.154 versus 0.163 for the constant-inertia evolution operator and 0.179 for the naive forecast, matches a crisp model of the same architecture and additionally provides a linguistically interpretable estimate of forecast vagueness. We also show how the linguistic readout of the forecast can be used to detect a permanent switch of a customer to a competitor.

AI.tldr: Forecasts retail customers' preferences, modelled as triangular fuzzy numbers, with a Mamba-type selective state space model whose hidden state is itself a triangular fuzzy number. On a synthetic example it lowers the forecast-centre mean absolute error to 0.154, against 0.163 for constant inertia and 0.179 for the naive forecast, and gives a linguistic readout of forecast vagueness.
AI.motivation: Forecasting how retail customers' preferences evolve calls for representing them as fuzzy quantities, so that the vagueness of a forecast is expressed and can be interpreted rather than dropped.
AI.method: A Mamba-style selective state space model whose hidden state is a triangular fuzzy number, computed in Matveev's two-component algebra of fuzzy numbers. The recurrence parameters are computed from crisp features, while the fuzzy part stays linear with non-negative coefficients, so the state remains a proper triangular number and a convex combination of past observations.
AI.result: On a synthetic example with competitor promotions and customer switching, a 107-parameter model reaches a forecast-centre MAE of 0.154, versus 0.163 for a constant-inertia evolution operator and 0.179 for the naive forecast. It matches a crisp model of the same architecture, and the fuzziness of the forecast does not accumulate over time. The linguistic readout can also detect a permanent switch of a customer to a competitor.
AI.conclusion: The fuzzy state space model gives a lightweight forecaster with an interpretable estimate of forecast vagueness, and its linguistic output can flag customers who have switched to competitors.

title: Automated Keyword Generation Using LLMs in a High-Volume Data Virtualization Service
summary: In modern data infrastructure, a data virtualization service (DVS) allows users to create many versions of source datasets for different processing tasks. For example, a multivariate or multi-modality dataset can be used for different machine learning tasks (e.g., classification, detection, segmentation, forecasting, and so on). Data selection, participation, integration, and preprocessing in different tasks result in many virtual datasets [Khan et al., SSC 2026]. Meanwhile, different users need to discover existing virtual datasets frequently and easily to avoid duplicate efforts. To enable an effective search engine in a DVS, it is desirable to automatically generate keywords for each virtual dataset. In this work, we present a solution for generating keywords for virtual datasets using large language models (LLMs). We propose five strategies for selecting different collections of text data for processing by the LLMs. We applied the five strategies to virtual datasets created in five application case studies with different source datasets. We conducted experiments with three LLM generators and two embedding techniques. The experiments show that the performances of the five strategies depend on the quality of the text descriptions. The results help us adopt a multi-strategy implementation of a new keyword generation service (KGS) as part of an extended DVS. The work demonstrates that the capability of automated keyword generation is indispensable for a high-volume DVS that is dataset-rich and frequently accessed.

AI.tldr: Generates keywords for virtual datasets in a data virtualization service with LLMs, using five strategies for choosing which text to feed the model. Experiments with three LLM generators and two embedding techniques show that the strategies' performance depends on the quality of the text descriptions.
AI.motivation: In a high-volume data virtualization service, users repeatedly duplicate effort because existing virtual datasets are hard to discover, so an effective search engine needs keywords generated automatically for each virtual dataset.
AI.method: Five strategies select different collections of text data for processing by LLMs. They were applied to virtual datasets created in five application case studies with different source datasets.
AI.result: Across three LLM generators and two embedding techniques, the performance of the five strategies depends on the quality of the text descriptions. The results support a multi-strategy implementation of a new keyword generation service as part of an extended data virtualization service.
AI.conclusion: Automated keyword generation is indispensable for a high-volume, dataset-rich data virtualization service that is frequently accessed.

title: Using Machine Learning to Measure Self-Efficacy Belief Through Learners' Interaction Traces in Technology-Enhanced Learning
summary: Self-efficacy beliefs play a critical role in learners' performance, academic choices, and, more broadly, in their future career trajectories. As Technology-Enhanced Learning (TEL) environments have demonstrated strong potential for supporting both performance and motivation, investigating self-efficacy within such environments is of particular interest, especially for implementing remedial practices as early as possible to support learners' self-efficacy beliefs. Our research aims to develop a system capable of detecting low self-efficacy based on learners' interaction traces while they solve exercises in a TEL system. In this paper, we present initial results and future perspectives on a detection approach based on data mining and machine learning techniques to identify features indicative of low self-efficacy beliefs. Because the detection of learners' self-efficacy beliefs through their use of TEL systems remains largely unexplored, this work is exploratory in nature. To this end, we conducted an experiment across two universities to collect interaction traces and self-reported measures of self-efficacy. We then developed a machine learning pipeline comprising multiple classification models, enabling us to highlight the importance of closely monitoring of learners' self-efficacy beliefs for improved prediction performance, given their highly dynamic nature during learning.

AI.tldr: Explores detecting low self-efficacy from learners' interaction traces in a technology-enhanced learning system, using data mining and machine learning. In an exploratory experiment across two universities, self-efficacy was tracked with self-reported measures alongside the traces.
AI.motivation: Self-efficacy beliefs shape learners' performance, academic choices and career trajectories, and early remedial support requires detecting them, yet their detection from use of technology-enhanced learning systems remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: A machine learning pipeline with multiple classification models, trained on features from learners' interaction traces while they solve exercises, with self-reported self-efficacy measures collected in the experiment.
AI.result: The abstract reports no specific metrics. It states that monitoring learners' self-efficacy beliefs closely, given their highly dynamic nature during learning, improves prediction performance.
AI.conclusion: The work is exploratory and suggests that self-efficacy should be monitored over time in technology-enhanced learning systems; the authors outline future work toward a detection system.

title: ReX-GG: a LLM Ensemble Pipeline for Relation-extraction and Graph Generation
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, accepted at KG&LLM @ LREC 2026
summary: Current LLM ensemble frameworks focus on multi-step setups with additional modules for answer ranking, often opting for token and span analysis rather than structured outputs, leading to heavyweight architectures with potential fail states along the pipeline. Faster, lighter solutions are more vulnerable to hallucination propagation and can lack output control in more complex pipelines. This paper proposes a customisable, lightweight ensemble workflow of coordinated Large Language Models that leverages JSON-structured outputs and anonymous peer-review ranking to mitigate hallucinatory outputs and single-model failure points. The pipeline is demonstrated on a relation extraction task applied to popular science articles in English, targeting four ontologically-grounded relation types (strong causation, weak causation, contrastive, and compositional), with semantic node canonicalisation and interactive, colour-coded HTML causal graphs as the final output. Performance is evaluated through an anonymous user study, achieving an average perceived accuracy of 0.778 against a human-annotated gold standard. The modular architecture supports flexible deployment across both API-based and in-house LLM setups, and the full framework is released under an open license to foster reproducibility and collaborative research.

AI.tldr: Presents ReX-GG, a lightweight ensemble of coordinated LLMs that extracts causal relations from popular science articles and produces interactive, colour-coded HTML causal graphs. An anonymous user study gives an average perceived accuracy of 0.778 against a human-annotated gold standard.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM ensemble frameworks are multi-step and heavyweight, with ranking modules and token or span analysis, while faster and lighter solutions are more prone to hallucination propagation and offer less output control.
AI.method: A customisable ensemble workflow that uses JSON-structured outputs and anonymous peer-review ranking to mitigate hallucinatory outputs and single-model failure points. It extracts four relation types (strong causation, weak causation, contrastive, compositional), canonicalises semantic nodes, and renders the result as HTML causal graphs. The architecture supports both API-based and in-house LLMs.
AI.result: An anonymous user study gives an average perceived accuracy of 0.778 against a human-annotated gold standard on relation extraction from English popular science articles.
AI.conclusion: The modular, lightweight design offers flexible deployment, and the full framework is released under an open license to support reproducibility and collaborative research.

title: Structure-Aware Skill Retrieval and Arbitration for Optimization Modeling
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) can turn natural-language optimization tasks into solver-checked answers, but current agents remain brittle under narrative rewrites and often store reusable experience at the instance level. We introduce \textsc{ArchOR}, an archetype-centric skill agent that builds on \textsc{OptSkills} by adding two retrieval-focused modules. \emph{Centroid-Aware Representation Learning} (CARL) refines the ordering of cached skill representations through a low-rank prototype residual. \emph{Signature-Guided Retrieval} (S\textsuperscript{3}R) attaches open-dimensional structural signatures to skills, prioritizes candidates by weighted Jaccard overlap, and bounds semantic re-ranking to a top-$K$ set. A baseline-preserving arbitration rule determines when the structural route should replace the original selector. With the same DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone and released skill library, \textsc{ArchOR} reaches 65.00\% Micro-Avg.\ Pass@1 across five benchmarks, improving over \textsc{OptSkills} by 1.64~pp Micro-Avg.\ and 2.68~pp Macro-Avg.

AI.tldr: Introduces ArchOR, an archetype-centric skill agent that adds two retrieval modules to OptSkills for LLM-based optimization modelling. With the same DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone it reaches 65.00% Micro-Avg. Pass@1 across five benchmarks, improving on OptSkills by 1.64 and 2.68 percentage points on Micro-Avg. and Macro-Avg.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents for optimization modelling are brittle under narrative rewrites, and they store reusable experience at the instance level rather than at the level of problem archetypes.
AI.method: ArchOR adds two modules to OptSkills. Centroid-Aware Representation Learning (CARL) refines the ordering of cached skill representations through a low-rank prototype residual. Signature-Guided Retrieval (S3R) attaches structural signatures to skills, ranks candidates by weighted Jaccard overlap, and bounds semantic re-ranking to a top-K set. A baseline-preserving arbitration rule decides when the structural route should replace the original selector.
AI.result: With the same backbone and released skill library, ArchOR reaches 65.00% Micro-Avg. Pass@1 across five benchmarks, improving over OptSkills by 1.64 percentage points on Micro-Avg. and 2.68 percentage points on Macro-Avg.
AI.conclusion: Archetype-level structural retrieval, combined with a baseline-preserving arbitration rule, improves the reuse of skills for optimization modelling.

title: Sensorium: An Open-Source Multimodal Data Collection and Curation Library for Embodied Surgical AI
comment: GenAI for Health Workshop @ NeurIPS 2026, Sydney
summary: Embodied surgical AI requires reliable multimodal data, yet surgical data collection remains costly, difficult to repeat, and strongly dependent on the hardware setup. We present Sensorium, an open-source Python library for recording, processing, annotating, and curating multimodal surgical data from configurable robot and sensor streams using the Robot Operating System (ROS) and ROS2 middleware. The library combines operator-facing data acquisition, configurable processing, semantic annotation, and episodic dataset generation. We evaluate Sensorium across 1516 recordings of phantom, ex vivo, and in vivo porcine experiments involving multiple surgical tasks and sensing configurations, and report preliminary usability feedback.

AI.tldr: Presents Sensorium, an open-source Python library for recording, processing, annotating and curating multimodal surgical data from robot and sensor streams via ROS and ROS2. It is evaluated on 1516 recordings of phantom, ex vivo and in vivo porcine experiments.
AI.motivation: Embodied surgical AI needs reliable multimodal data, but surgical data collection is costly, hard to repeat, and strongly dependent on the hardware setup.
AI.method: The library combines operator-facing data acquisition, configurable processing, semantic annotation and episodic dataset generation over configurable robot and sensor streams, built on the Robot Operating System (ROS) and ROS2 middleware.
AI.result: Evaluated across 1516 recordings of phantom, ex vivo and in vivo porcine experiments with multiple surgical tasks and sensing configurations, with preliminary usability feedback reported. The abstract gives no quantitative performance metrics.
AI.conclusion: The library is offered as an open-source tool for building repeatable multimodal surgical datasets for embodied surgical AI.

title: Prune Gradually, Adapt Sparsely: Efficient Pruning of Large Language Models at Extreme Sparsity
summary: Weight pruning can reduce the storage and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), but preserving quality at high sparsity levels remains challenging. Existing methods face a quality-cost trade-off in this regime. One-shot pruning is cheap but degrades sharply as sparsity increases, even when followed by post-pruning recovery. A growing line of work instead optimizes the mask directly from the dense model under the end-to-end objective; among these methods, [Lee et al.,2026], the recent state of the art at extreme sparsity, reaches high quality but at the cost of model-sized optimizer state and auxiliary variables. To address this gap, we propose ETAPS, which prunes gradually and adapts sparsely: it tightens a global sparsity constraint in progressive stages while training a sparse delta with a small, fixed budget. Our key observation is that gradual weight removal keeps each pruning step small enough for sparse adaptation to compensate, allowing the adapted model to provide end-to-end gradients that guide the next pruning decision without model-sized optimizer state. Across six models from 125M to 13B parameters, ETAPS achieves lower perplexity than ELSA at every evaluated sparsity from 50% to 90%, with perplexity reductions of up to 42%. ETAPS is also far cheaper: at 90% sparsity, it prunes LLaMA2-7B on a single H200, where ELSA uses four, with $5.0\times$ smaller total persistent state and 49% fewer GPU-hours. Together, our findings point to a promising direction for achieving high quality in demanding regimes such as extreme sparsity at substantially lower cost.

AI.tldr: Proposes ETAPS, which prunes LLMs gradually while training a sparse delta under a small fixed budget, avoiding model-sized optimizer state. Across six models from 125M to 13B parameters it achieves lower perplexity than ELSA at every sparsity from 50% to 90%, with reductions of up to 42%.
AI.motivation: One-shot pruning degrades sharply as sparsity increases, and mask-optimization methods such as ELSA reach high quality at extreme sparsity only at the cost of model-sized optimizer state and auxiliary variables.
AI.method: ETAPS tightens a global sparsity constraint in progressive stages while training a sparse delta with a small, fixed budget. Gradual removal keeps each pruning step small enough for sparse adaptation to compensate, and the adapted model supplies end-to-end gradients that guide the next pruning decision.
AI.result: ETAPS achieves lower perplexity than ELSA at every evaluated sparsity from 50% to 90%, with reductions of up to 42%. At 90% sparsity it prunes LLaMA2-7B on a single H200 where ELSA uses four, with 5.0x smaller total persistent state and 49% fewer GPU-hours.
AI.conclusion: Gradual pruning combined with sparse adaptation points to a route to high quality at extreme sparsity at substantially lower cost.

title: When Does Test-Time Search Help World Action Models? An Empirical Audit of Candidate Selection and Simulator Integrity
summary: World-action models increasingly apply test-time scaling, spending extra inference computation on candidate selection and adaptive allocation to improve control. Such gains are credible only when candidates carry exploitable signal, nominal compute savings become real speedup, and evaluation stays reliable. We audit all three on Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa with a premise-first, pre-registered methodology. On clean data, a learned value selector is 1.66 pp worse than random; a hindsight oracle gains only 1.40 pp, with an episode-level interval spanning zero; and 82% of states show identical candidate outcomes, leaving little selection headroom. Token pruning cuts per-forward FLOPs by up to 47% but yields at most a measured 1.15$\times$ end-to-end speedup on the deployed path (1.25$\times$ on a decode-excluded path), short of a 1.5$\times$ target, and our adaptive-allocation experiment is inconclusive under a power gate. We further identify and fix a silent rendering corruption whose rate rises sharply along compute-heavy planning paths while leaving the official direct-policy result unaffected, and release a detector, fix, and scripts. These findings show why test-time scaling should be audited as a chain of premises (decision signal, realized efficiency, evaluationintegrity) rather than by success rate alone. Conclusions are scoped to the tested configuration.

AI.tldr: Audits test-time search for world-action models on Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa along three premises: candidate selection signal, realised efficiency, and evaluation integrity. A learned value selector is 1.66 percentage points worse than random, and token pruning yields at most a 1.15x end-to-end speedup, short of a 1.5x target.
AI.motivation: Test-time scaling gains for world-action models are credible only if candidates carry exploitable signal, nominal compute savings become real speedup, and evaluation stays reliable.
AI.method: A premise-first, pre-registered audit of the three premises. It compares a learned value selector with random selection and a hindsight oracle, measures per-forward FLOPs and end-to-end speedup for token pruning, tests adaptive allocation under a power gate, and identifies and fixes a silent rendering corruption on compute-heavy planning paths.
AI.result: On clean data the learned selector is 1.66 percentage points worse than random, and the hindsight oracle gains only 1.40 percentage points, with an episode-level interval spanning zero. In 82% of states all candidates have identical outcomes. Token pruning cuts per-forward FLOPs by up to 47% but gives at most a 1.15x end-to-end speedup on the deployed path (1.25x on a decode-excluded path). The adaptive-allocation experiment is inconclusive, and the rendering fix leaves the official direct-policy result unaffected.
AI.conclusion: Test-time scaling should be audited as a chain of premises rather than by success rate alone, and the conclusions are scoped to the tested configuration. A detector, fix and scripts are released.

title: ID2Pattern: Pretraining Generalizable Identity Behavior Patterns for Transaction Risk Foundation Models
summary: Large-scale behavioral pretraining offers a promising route to generalizable representations in online payment systems. However, high-cardinality identity fields such as card, device, and account IDs, though rich in behavioral signals, remain underexploited. Their continually growing vocabularies and limited semantic meaning make existing vocabulary-based and semantics-based encodings ill-suited. Their generalizable signal lies not in specific values, but in the identity behavior patterns they exhibit across a transaction sequence. Building on this insight, we propose ID2Pattern, a pretraining framework that brings these patterns into transaction foundation models. ID2Pattern first encodes identity fields with a Local Anonymous ID (LAID) tokenizer, which captures how each identity appears and recurs within the sequence, independent of its specific value. It then pretrains a multi-scale pattern codebook on unlabeled sequences, which abstracts LAID sequences into discrete behavior patterns for downstream prediction. Experiments on an industrial dataset with over 100M sequences and six public datasets show that ID2Pattern consistently outperforms strong baselines, improving industrial by 4.13% and public datasets by 8.83% on average. Notably, ID2Pattern remains equally effective even when all identity values are unseen during training, highlighting its potential to generalize to new users and markets.

AI.tldr: Proposes ID2Pattern, a pretraining framework that encodes high-cardinality card, device and account IDs by the behaviour patterns they show across a transaction sequence rather than by their values. It outperforms strong baselines on an industrial dataset and six public datasets, by 4.13% and 8.83% on average respectively.
AI.motivation: High-cardinality identity fields are rich in behavioural signal but remain underexploited, because their continually growing vocabularies and limited semantic meaning make vocabulary-based and semantics-based encodings ill-suited.
AI.method: A Local Anonymous ID (LAID) tokenizer captures how each identity appears and recurs within a sequence, independent of its specific value. A multi-scale pattern codebook is pretrained on unlabeled sequences to abstract LAID sequences into discrete behaviour patterns for downstream prediction.
AI.result: Experiments on an industrial dataset with over 100M sequences and six public datasets show improvements over strong baselines of 4.13% on the industrial dataset and 8.83% on average on the public datasets. The method remains equally effective when all identity values are unseen during training.
AI.conclusion: Identity behaviour patterns carry generalizable signal for transaction risk foundation models, with potential to generalize to new users and markets.

title: DAMI: Dual-Axis Memory Initialization for Enhanced Long-Context Retrieval in Gated Linear Attention
summary: Linear attention scales linearly with sequence length, but its finite-state memory can limit long-context retrieval. In gated linear recurrences, memory retention depends on state decay, which is shaped jointly by gate parameters A_log and dt_bias and by input activations. In controlled Gated DeltaNet (GDN) experiments, both parameters remain highly correlated with their initial values after training, highlighting the importance of initialization. Therefore, we introduce Dual-Axis Memory Initialization (DAMI), which jointly configures these parameters before training. DAMI assigns geometric timescales across heads for varied retrieval distances and a low-high-low input-sensitivity profile across layers. A small activation sample calibrates the GDN-family implementation to match both behavioral targets without adding trainable parameters. Across GDN, KDA, GDN2, Mamba-2, and RWKV-7, DAMI improves average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29 to 16.71 percentage points over the corresponding random-initialization baselines. Performance on language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and 2K real-world retrieval remains broadly comparable to those baselines. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Introduces Dual-Axis Memory Initialization (DAMI), which configures the gate parameters A_log and dt_bias before training to set memory timescales in gated linear attention. Across GDN, KDA, GDN2, Mamba-2 and RWKV-7 it improves average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29 to 16.71 percentage points over random initialization.
AI.motivation: Finite-state memory limits long-context retrieval in linear attention, and in controlled Gated DeltaNet experiments the gate parameters remain highly correlated with their initial values after training, so initialization matters.
AI.method: DAMI jointly configures the gate parameters before training: it assigns geometric timescales across heads for varied retrieval distances, and a low-high-low input-sensitivity profile across layers. A small activation sample calibrates the GDN-family implementation to match both targets, without adding trainable parameters.
AI.result: DAMI improves average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29 to 16.71 percentage points over random-initialization baselines across five architectures. Performance on language modelling, commonsense reasoning and 2K real-world retrieval remains broadly comparable to those baselines.
AI.conclusion: Initialization of memory-decay parameters is an effective, parameter-free lever for long-context retrieval in gated linear recurrences.

title: TradeWar: A Benchmark for Execution-Grounded Trade Negotiation with Adaptive LLM Agents
summary: Multi-turn negotiation remains a challenging problem for large language model (LLM) agents. While LLMs can conduct natural-language dialogue, existing benchmarks predominantly assess only agreement rates, overlooking whether negotiated commitments actually create value once executed. To address this gap, we introduce TradeWar, a multi-country simulation benchmark that translates negotiation dialogues into concrete tariff and trade-share policies, enforces capacity and network constraints during settlement, and evaluates outcomes via an Economic Health Index (EHI). To solve this execution-grounded task, we propose TACTIC (Trade-aware Adaptive Consolidation and Theory-of-mind for International Commerce), an agent that iteratively refines its negotiation strategy across episodes-without updating base LLM weights-by leveraging prior experience, opponent behavior, and past settlement outcomes. Despite using zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, PromptLLM attains a 75% agreement rate but only 57.1 final EHI (*100), whereas TACTIC reaches 68.8. Across 20 sequential episodes and three seeds, TACTIC's final EHI improves from 58.2 to 73.2, compared with 65.2 for an ablation without cross-episode updates. Under technology-controls and energy-crisis shocks, TACTIC also exhibits smaller performance degradation than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM. These results indicate that CoT deliberation and interaction memory alone do not fully address delayed execution feedback, whereas settlement-grounded adaptation improves long-horizon negotiation in TradeWar.

AI.tldr: Introduces TradeWar, a multi-country simulation benchmark that turns negotiation dialogues into tariff and trade-share policies and scores outcomes by an Economic Health Index (EHI). TACTIC, an agent that adapts across episodes without updating base LLM weights, raises final EHI from 58.2 to 73.2 over 20 sequential episodes.
AI.motivation: Existing negotiation benchmarks mainly measure agreement rates and overlook whether negotiated commitments create value once executed, so delayed execution feedback goes unassessed.
AI.method: TradeWar enforces capacity and network constraints during settlement and evaluates outcomes via the EHI. TACTIC iteratively refines its negotiation strategy across episodes, using prior experience, opponent behaviour and past settlement outcomes.
AI.result: PromptLLM attains a 75% agreement rate but only 57.1 final EHI, while TACTIC reaches 68.8. Across 20 sequential episodes and three seeds, TACTIC's final EHI improves from 58.2 to 73.2, compared with 65.2 for an ablation without cross-episode updates. Under technology-control and energy-crisis shocks, TACTIC degrades less than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM.
AI.conclusion: Chain-of-thought deliberation and interaction memory alone do not fully address delayed execution feedback, whereas settlement-grounded adaptation improves long-horizon negotiation.

title: Same Question, Different Answers: Auditing Persona-Dependent Variation in Six LLMs on Smoking-Cessation Advice
summary: Hundreds of millions of people now ask large language model (LLM) chatbots for health advice, which raises a question that is simple to pose and hard to answer: does everyone get the same advice? We audit six widely deployed LLMs from four providers on smoking cessation, a domain with codified clini- cal guidance and substantial public-health stakes, by putting the same four cessation questions to twelve user personas that differ in life stage, self-described expertise, and smoking history, for a total of 2,880 responses. What the models say depends on who appears to be asking. Every model named FDA-approved prescription cessation medications less often to teen personas than to adult personas, by 32 to 67 percentage points, and in five of six models a persona presenting health- care expertise received fewer facts than a persona presenting none. We then evaluate one deployable intervention: a short system prompt specifying a factual floor, the set of core med- ical facts every user should receive when they are relevant, while leaving tone, vocabulary, and framing free to adapt. The prompt narrows persona differences in every model, but its effect on overall fact coverage varies in both magnitude and direction across models, so a prompt validated on one system cannot be assumed to transfer to another. Two cautions frame these results. Equal mention rates are not always the correct clinical target, because prescription cessation pharmacother- apy is not recommended for minors, so a defensible factual floor must be age-aware rather than uniform. And because our personas vary on several attributes at once, we report scenario- level differences rather than isolated effects of age or expertise. We release all 2,880 responses and the analysis code.

AI.tldr: Audits six LLMs from four providers on smoking-cessation advice by putting the same four questions to twelve user personas, for 2,880 responses. Every model names FDA-approved prescription cessation medications less often to teen personas than to adult personas, by 32 to 67 percentage points.
AI.motivation: People increasingly ask LLM chatbots for health advice, and it is unclear whether everyone receives the same advice, in a domain with codified clinical guidance and substantial public-health stakes.
AI.method: The same four cessation questions are put to twelve personas that differ in life stage, self-described expertise and smoking history. The authors then evaluate a system prompt that sets a factual floor of core medical facts while leaving tone, vocabulary and framing free to adapt.
AI.result: Five of six models gave a healthcare-expertise persona fewer facts than a persona presenting no expertise. The factual-floor prompt narrows persona differences in every model, but its effect on overall fact coverage varies in magnitude and direction across models.
AI.conclusion: A prompt validated on one model cannot be assumed to transfer to another, and a defensible factual floor must be age-aware, since prescription cessation pharmacotherapy is not recommended for minors. All 2,880 responses and the analysis code are released.

title: The Knowledge Layer Model (KLM): Evidence-Visible AI Output, Routing Diagnostics, and Negative Results
comment: 47 pages, 1 figure, 14 tables. Includes Appendix A
summary: AI answers require more than apparent correctness: reviewers need to inspect their recorded basis. We introduce the Knowledge Layer Model (KLM), an open, implementation-neutral specification for inference records with versioned epistemic assessments, evidence relations, and explicit unknowns. SEDIM, the knowledge and evidence architecture of Nage AI OS, is a reference implementation. We reference KLM v0.3 (repository tag v0.3.0). Empirical material consists of separate internal experiments, not end-to-end validation. A historical platform-domain routing benchmark reports 137/150 classifications across 15 classes (91.3%; nominal 95% Wilson interval 85.7-94.9%); the numerator is recovered from a rounded summary, and historical example membership is unverified. A native-model weight-path configuration yielded 0/15 successful answers in a corrected two-source test. A capacity-growth comparison could not establish a reliable effect because of a defective legacy scorer and missing original outputs. Lexical and scoped diagnostics each yielded AUC 0.008 for silent-versus-contradicted examples, below the registered minimum of 0.65. Legacy packing lost gold-containing text in 118/221 selected cases; repaired packing retained it in 221/221. These measure text presence, not answer quality. Python and TypeScript verifiers reportedly agreed on six checks per synthetic fixture; a separate production disclosure was not accepted. Restoration, re-derivation, human-rubric support, boundary isolation, and bounded-response evaluations remain proposed. Findings are internal and author-reported; historical observations are distinguished from later reproductions. Evidence visibility does not establish correctness, causal reliance, security, or regulatory compliance. Independent replication and a complete public audit package remain future work.

AI.tldr: Introduces the Knowledge Layer Model (KLM), an open, implementation-neutral specification for inference records with versioned epistemic assessments, evidence relations and explicit unknowns, with SEDIM as a reference implementation. The internal experiments are mixed, and the paper does not claim end-to-end validation.
AI.motivation: Reviewers need to inspect the recorded basis of AI answers, not merely their apparent correctness.
AI.method: KLM specifies inference records with versioned epistemic assessments, evidence relations and explicit unknowns. SEDIM, the knowledge and evidence architecture of Nage AI OS, is a reference implementation, and the empirical material consists of separate internal experiments.
AI.result: A historical platform-domain routing benchmark reports 137/150 correct classifications across 15 classes (91.3%; nominal 95% Wilson interval 85.7-94.9%), with the numerator recovered from a rounded summary. A native-model weight-path configuration gave 0/15 successful answers, and lexical and scoped diagnostics each gave AUC 0.008 for silent-versus-contradicted examples, below the registered minimum of 0.65. Repaired packing retained gold-containing text in 221/221 selected cases, against 118/221 lost by legacy packing; these measure text presence, not answer quality.
AI.conclusion: Evidence visibility does not establish correctness, causal reliance, security or regulatory compliance, and restoration, re-derivation and bounded-response evaluations remain proposed, with independent replication as future work.

title: ACCT: Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer
summary: In real-world deployments, large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly evolving from single-model invocation toward heterogeneous deployments in which different models are dynamically invoked for inference. When the same context is reused across models, however, each newly selected target model typically has to process it again, repeatedly incurring substantial computational costs. Therefore, we propose ACCT (Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer), which targets KV cache transfer between models of different scales within the same model family. ACCT transforms the KV cache produced by a source model into sparse KV states that can be directly consumed by a target model, thereby enabling cross-model reuse of context computation and decoupling context computation from downstream inference. ACCT consists of three lightweight components: the Cartographer identifies query-relevant context tokens for each target layer and KV head; the Allocator determines how many context tokens each target layer and KV head retains under a shared total KV budget; and the Compiler transforms selected source KV into sparse target KV. The target model can therefore perform inference using the transferred KV without reprocessing the original context. We evaluate ACCT in two complementary settings comprising five general-capability benchmarks and six highly context-dependent tasks. Experiments show that ACCT matches or exceeds the target model's original inference performance even when reducing the KV cache size by 75%. At a context length of approximately 19K tokens, ACCT's KV conversion achieves a 6.5-21.2 times speedup over target context prefill. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transferring context computation across models under a limited KV budget.

AI.tldr: Proposes ACCT, which transfers KV cache between LLMs of different scales in the same model family by converting the source model's cache into sparse KV states that the target model can consume directly. It matches or exceeds the target's original inference performance while reducing KV cache size by 75%, with a 6.5 to 21.2 times speedup over target context prefill at about 19K tokens.
AI.motivation: When heterogeneous deployments reuse the same context across dynamically invoked models, each newly selected target model must reprocess that context, incurring substantial repeated computational cost.
AI.method: ACCT has three components. The Cartographer identifies query-relevant context tokens for each target layer and KV head, the Allocator sets how many tokens each layer and head retains under a shared total KV budget, and the Compiler transforms selected source KV into sparse target KV, so the target can infer without reprocessing the original context.
AI.result: Across five general-capability benchmarks and six highly context-dependent tasks, ACCT matches or exceeds the target model's original inference performance even when the KV cache is reduced by 75%. At a context length of about 19K tokens, its KV conversion achieves a 6.5 to 21.2 times speedup over target context prefill.
AI.conclusion: Context computation can be transferred across models under a limited KV budget, decoupling context computation from downstream inference.

title: Latent Sparse Attention: Towards Subquadratic Ultra-Long Context Attention
summary: Agentic workflows are increasingly shifting towards long-horizon tasks, such as open-ended scientific work, where models benefit from long context windows. However, at ultra-long context (above 1M tokens), full attention is prohibitively expensive. A promising approach is sparse attention, in which a dedicated indexer selects a subset of keys for the attention. Yet current methods of indexing either still have quadratic cost in context size or lose accuracy at ultra-long context scale. We address this with Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), an efficient attention method that maintains accuracy at ultra-long context. In LSA, keys are hierarchically clustered in a learned latent space, and queries score the hierarchy of clusters instead of scoring every key, making prefill, decode and training faster at long context. We propose two variants, Distilled-LSA (D-LSA), which can be applied to pre-trained models via distillation, and Native-LSA (N-LSA), which is trained natively on the next-token loss alone. On GLM-5.3-FLASH (QWEN-3.8-27B) at 10M tokens, D-LSA speeds up one attention layer by 22.7x (72.4x) in prefill and 4.6x (42.5x) in decode over its original sparse attention (full attention), while keeping similar accuracy across a variety of tasks. N-LSA matches the accuracy of full attention with a training speedup of 1.6x per layer at 128k tokens. LSA offers practical and efficient attention for models to benefit from ultra-long context.

AI.tldr: Proposes Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), which clusters keys hierarchically in a learned latent space so that queries score clusters rather than every key, aiming at subquadratic attention for ultra-long context. At 10M tokens, Distilled-LSA speeds up one attention layer by 22.7x in prefill and 4.6x in decode over its original sparse attention, while keeping similar accuracy.
AI.motivation: Above 1M tokens full attention is prohibitively expensive, and current indexers for sparse attention either still scale quadratically with context size or lose accuracy at ultra-long context scale.
AI.method: LSA hierarchically clusters keys in a learned latent space, and queries score the cluster hierarchy instead of every key, which speeds up prefill, decode and training at long context. Distilled-LSA (D-LSA) is applied to pretrained models via distillation, and Native-LSA (N-LSA) is trained natively on the next-token loss alone.
AI.result: On GLM-5.3-FLASH (QWEN-3.8-27B) at 10M tokens, D-LSA speeds up one attention layer by 22.7x in prefill (72.4x over full attention) and 4.6x in decode (42.5x over full attention) relative to its original sparse attention, with similar accuracy across tasks. N-LSA matches the accuracy of full attention with a 1.6x per-layer training speedup at 128k tokens.
AI.conclusion: LSA offers practical and efficient attention for models that benefit from ultra-long context.

title: Characterizing LLM Agent Behaviors in Module Shadowing Environments
summary: LLM agents operating in untrusted workspaces face the risk of untrusted code execution during routine tasks, yet final reports and workspace states alone cannot reliably establish whether execution occurred. We introduce an evaluation framework that codes observation, reasoning, execution, and response behaviors from agent trajectories and aligns them with independent environmental records to reconstruct execution histories and verify final reports. We apply this framework to module shadowing, in which a local file is loaded in place of a trusted module during import, enabling untrusted code execution without adversarial prompts. Across 90 trials with 15 models, the payload executed in 51% of direct shadowing trials and 87% of indirect shadowing trials. Even explicit recognition of the shadowing mechanism did not ensure prevention, as the payload ran in 10 of the 29 trials with recorded recognition. These failures were often omitted from final reports, as 49 of the 62 triggered trials ended without mention of the security issue. Three reports even denied execution, including one from a trial in which independent logs recorded 19 payload executions. Final workspace states also obscured prior execution when agents deleted or overwrote the payload marker in 10 triggered trials. These findings demonstrate that combining behavioral coding with independent environmental auditing enables rigorous and transparent evaluation of agent safety.

AI.tldr: Introduces an evaluation framework that codes LLM agent behaviours from trajectories and aligns them with independent environmental records to reconstruct execution and verify final reports. In module shadowing across 90 trials with 15 models, the payload executed in 51% of direct and 87% of indirect trials, and many final reports omitted or denied the execution.
AI.motivation: LLM agents in untrusted workspaces may run untrusted code during routine tasks, yet final reports and workspace states alone cannot reliably establish whether execution occurred.
AI.method: Observation, reasoning, execution and response behaviours are coded from agent trajectories and aligned with independent environmental records to reconstruct execution histories and verify final reports. It is applied to module shadowing, in which a local file is loaded in place of a trusted module during import, without adversarial prompts.
AI.result: The payload executed in 51% of direct and 87% of indirect shadowing trials. Explicit recognition of the mechanism did not ensure prevention, as the payload ran in 10 of 29 trials with recorded recognition. Of 62 triggered trials, 49 ended without mention of the security issue, and three reports denied execution, one despite independent logs recording 19 payload executions. Workspace states also obscured prior execution in 10 triggered trials.
AI.conclusion: Combining behavioural coding with independent environmental auditing enables rigorous and transparent evaluation of agent safety.

title: MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection
summary: LLM agents are increasingly used to automate vulnerability detection, but reliable detection is challenging because agents must distinguish subtle, security-relevant fixes from benign code variation. While underlying LLM capability has improved significantly, the accuracy of the agent still depends heavily on the harness: the code that defines the scaffolding around the LLM. Harnesses are typically fixed, and largely hand-written, limiting adaptation to evaluator feedback. Additionally, when harnesses are static, improvements on one dataset or model may not transfer to others. To address these challenges, we introduce MetaVul, a self-improving framework for harness discovery in vulnerability detection. Starting from a seed structured reasoning scaffold, MetaVul uses a workflow-based optimization loop to iteratively refine the harness using feedback from paired vulnerable and patched functions, while preserving the structured reasoning and verdict format. At each iteration, it searches over the history of prior harnesses, with access to their trajectories, logs, and metrics, and it returns a set of Pareto-optimal harnesses. We apply MetaVul to discover agent harnesses for various architectures. A validation set (202 pairs) is used for optimization, while an unseen dataset (430 pairs) is kept as the held-out set. We test whether harnesses learned from one model transfer to others not seen during optimization. Results on both frontier and small LLMs show that the optimized harnesses improve pairwise vulnerability detection up to 23.3 percentage points on the validation set and up to 25.8 points on the held-out set with a Pareto-frontier harness. Harnesses learned with one model also transfer to others. We show that harnesses optimized with one model transfer to another, improving held-out pairwise accuracy by 14.7 points without further optimization.

AI.tldr: Presents MetaVul, a self-improving framework that uses a workflow-based optimization loop to discover agent harnesses for LLM vulnerability detection from paired vulnerable and patched functions. Optimized harnesses improve pairwise detection by up to 23.3 points on the validation set and up to 25.8 points on the held-out set.
AI.motivation: Vulnerability detection accuracy depends heavily on the harness around the LLM, which is typically fixed and largely hand-written, and static harnesses may not transfer across datasets or models.
AI.method: Starting from a seed structured reasoning scaffold, MetaVul iteratively refines the harness using feedback from paired vulnerable and patched functions. It searches over the history of prior harnesses, with their trajectories, logs and metrics, and returns a set of Pareto-optimal harnesses while preserving the structured reasoning and verdict format. A validation set of 202 pairs is used for optimization and an unseen set of 430 pairs is held out.
AI.result: Optimized harnesses improve pairwise vulnerability detection by up to 23.3 points on the validation set and up to 25.8 points on the held-out set with a Pareto-frontier harness. A harness optimized with one model improves held-out pairwise accuracy by 14.7 points on another model without further optimization.
AI.conclusion: Harnesses optimized for one model transfer to others, which suggests that harness design need not be fixed or hand-written.
