title: RiskyPy: Toward Model-Calibrated Prompt Generation for Joint Security and Functionality Evaluation of LLM-Generated Code
summary: Evaluating approaches that improve the security of LLM code generation requires datasets that jointly assess security and functionality and remain adapted to the capabilities of the models being studied. However, existing benchmarks are costly to produce and are generally not calibrated to a chosen range of model capabilities. We introduce RiskyPy, an automated pipeline that generates security-oriented code-generation datasets calibrated to model proficiency using functionality and vulnerability canaries. We instantiate RiskyPy for Python using domains covering 18 CWEs from the 2025 CWE Top 25, producing 101 prompts. Experiments on Qwen3-4B and Seed-Coder-8B show that the generated tasks remain functionally accessible, with 57-72% of prompts yielding functional code, while only 5-10% of generations are free of Bandit findings, leaving room for joint evaluation of security and functionality of security improvement approaches.

AI.tldr: Introduces RiskyPy, an automated pipeline that generates security-oriented Python code-generation prompts calibrated to model proficiency, using functionality and vulnerability canaries. It produces 101 prompts covering 18 CWEs, with 57-72% of prompts yielding functional code on the tested models while only 5-10% of generations are free of Bandit findings.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for evaluating security in LLM code generation are costly to produce and generally not calibrated to the range of model capabilities being studied.
AI.method: An automated pipeline generates prompts calibrated to model proficiency through functionality and vulnerability canaries. It was instantiated for Python across domains covering 18 CWEs from the 2025 CWE Top 25, producing 101 prompts.
AI.result: On Qwen3-4B and Seed-Coder-8B, 57-72% of prompts yield functional code, while only 5-10% of generations are free of Bandit findings.
AI.conclusion: The generated tasks remain functionally accessible and leave room for joint evaluation of the security and functionality of security-improvement approaches.

title: CLIC: Closed-Loop Intent Consistency for Securing LLM-Driven Control in Open RAN
summary: With the progressive capabilities of large language models (LLMs), researchers are finding ways to integrate them into the control loops of Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) to enable slicing and resource management through user intents. However, integration of LLMs in the O-RAN control loop via the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) makes the system vulnerable to \textit{runtime prompt injection threats}, which manipulate control decisions without violating interface authentication, and \textit{residual virtual prompt injection (VPI)} attacks that plant trigger mechanisms to silently steer the behaviour during fine-tuning. Existing studies address only the runtime threat and do not enforce consistency across the full control path, i.e. from the certified A1 intent, through the multi-step LLM trajectory, to the final E2 action. We propose a closed-loop intent-consistency layer (CLIC) that jointly mitigates both threats. The proposed CLIC defines a formal consistency score using a small quantized language model, which is deployed as a Non-RT rApp for model-integrity certification along with a Near-RT xApp for runtime enforcement. We implement CLIC on the OpenAI Cellular (OAIC) platform and evaluate it under domain-adapted JailbreakBench, AdvBench, and VPI workloads. The experimental results show that the proposed CLIC reduces the attack success rate from 0.92 to 0.29 and residual VPI attacks from 0.37 to 0.04, while improving isolation and fairness at slightly higher latency costs, i.e. approximately 27 ms.

AI.tldr: Proposes CLIC, a closed-loop intent-consistency layer that secures LLM-driven control in Open RAN against runtime prompt injection and residual virtual prompt injection (VPI) attacks. On the OpenAI Cellular platform it reduces attack success from 0.92 to 0.29 and residual VPI attacks from 0.37 to 0.04, at about 27 ms extra latency.
AI.motivation: Integrating LLMs into the O-RAN control loop exposes it to runtime prompt injection and to residual VPI attacks that plant triggers during fine-tuning. Existing studies address only the runtime threat and do not enforce consistency across the full control path.
AI.method: CLIC defines a formal consistency score using a small quantized language model, deployed as a Non-RT rApp for model-integrity certification and as a Near-RT xApp for runtime enforcement. It checks consistency from the certified A1 intent, through the multi-step LLM trajectory, to the final E2 action.
AI.result: On the OAIC platform under domain-adapted JailbreakBench, AdvBench and VPI workloads, CLIC reduces attack success rate from 0.92 to 0.29 and residual VPI attacks from 0.37 to 0.04, while improving isolation and fairness at approximately 27 ms higher latency.
AI.conclusion: A closed-loop consistency layer can jointly mitigate runtime and residual threats to LLM-driven O-RAN control at a modest latency cost.

title: Safin-1.5: Safety-Native Architecture and Verifiable Reasoning for Recursive Safety Improvement
summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) enables large language models to advance their capabilities through successive updates, but these updates can also introduce new risks and weaken existing safeguards. In line with the AI-45° Law, we pursue Safety RSI, in which safety develops as an intrinsic capability alongside general model capabilities through continual risk discovery and repair, while preserving utility and limiting over-refusal. We introduce Safin-1.5, a model built on a safety architecture and trained through recursive safety improvement, with an inference-time harness that extends its capabilities to formal reasoning. Our approach comprises three components: i) The safety architecture combines persistent safety states with hazardous-knowledge disentanglement. The former retains and selectively invokes safety knowledge, while the latter relocates targeted hazardous knowledge into removable experts, enabling its removal with minimal impact on general capabilities. ii) Recursive safety improvement establishes a discovery-evaluation-repair loop. The loop identifies new vulnerabilities and uses experimental feedback to develop repair strategies. It accepts updates only when they improve safety while preserving general capabilities and limiting over-refusal. iii) The formal reasoning harness combines the model's language understanding with symbolic inference and verification. Proof-obligation-guided semantic bridging recovers missing relations in formal representations, enabling symbolic solvers to construct checkable proofs under formalized premises and accepted semantic bridges. Experimental results demonstrate that Safin-1.5 achieves safety and reasoning performance, outperforming frontier models.

AI.tldr: Introduces Safin-1.5, a model built on a safety architecture and trained through recursive safety improvement, with an inference-time harness that extends it to formal reasoning. The authors report that it outperforms frontier models on safety and reasoning.
AI.motivation: Recursive self-improvement can introduce new risks and weaken existing safeguards, so safety should develop alongside general capability while preserving utility and limiting over-refusal.
AI.method: Three components: a safety architecture with persistent safety states and hazardous-knowledge disentanglement into removable experts; a discovery-evaluation-repair loop that accepts updates only when they improve safety while preserving general capabilities and limiting over-refusal; and a formal reasoning harness that combines language understanding with symbolic inference and proof-obligation-guided semantic bridging.
AI.result: The abstract states that Safin-1.5 achieves safety and reasoning performance outperforming frontier models, without giving specific numbers, datasets or baselines.
AI.conclusion: Safety is presented as an intrinsic capability developed through continual risk discovery and repair, with hazardous knowledge kept in removable experts as a route to safer models.

title: "Shall We Approve?" Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents increasingly rely on automated approvers to decide whether a proposed shell command may run. Existing approvers, from rule-based checkers to guardrail models and deployed permission classifiers, base their decisions on the text of the request and command. Yet a command's behavior depends on the code it invokes and the state of the workspace, and systems that observe file changes leave the assessment to the agent or a human after execution. We present Caper, a consequence-aware approval mechanism that pre-executes each command in a snapshotted sandbox, provides an independent approver with a bounded report of its observed effects, commits allowed commands, and rolls back blocked ones with a reason the agent can act on. Compared with six existing systems, Caper achieves the lowest harmful-outcome rate on SABER (6.7% versus at least 14.8%) and YoloFS-Ext, a benchmark we build in which harmful behavior is hidden inside invoked tools (7.8% versus at least 35.3%), while blocking 1.0% of the safe twins of the dangerous tasks in YoloFS-Ext.

AI.tldr: Caper is a consequence-aware approval mechanism for coding-agent shell commands that pre-executes each command in a snapshotted sandbox and lets an independent approver judge the observed effects before committing or rolling back. On SABER and the authors' YoloFS-Ext benchmark it has the lowest harmful-outcome rate of six compared systems.
AI.motivation: Existing automated approvers for agent shell commands judge the request and command text, which does not capture what the invoked code does to the workspace, and systems that observe file changes leave the assessment to the agent or a human after execution.
AI.method: Each command is pre-executed in a snapshotted sandbox; an independent approver receives a bounded report of the observed effects; allowed commands are committed and blocked commands are rolled back with a reason the agent can act on.
AI.result: Compared with six existing systems, Caper reaches a 6.7% harmful-outcome rate on SABER (versus at least 14.8%) and 7.8% on YoloFS-Ext (versus at least 35.3%), where harmful behavior is hidden inside invoked tools, while blocking 1.0% of the safe twins of the dangerous tasks in YoloFS-Ext.
AI.conclusion: Judging commands by their observed consequences rather than by their text lowers the harmful-outcome rate at a small cost in blocked safe tasks, a route to safer autonomous coding agents.

title: The Generative Gap Between Speculative Drafter and Continuous Diffusion Language Model
summary: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) and speculative drafters offer efficient language generation but are typically evaluated differently: CDLMs generate independently through iterative refinement, whereas drafters propose text for target-model verification and correction. We compare their architectures without verification, using LangFlow for CDLMs and adapting DSpark's Markov and recurrent-head architectures for standalone generation. All models are trained from scratch for unconditional, single-block OpenWebText generation at lengths 16, 128, and 1024, without target features or verification, using common preprocessing, backbone dimensions, and training-update budgets. We evaluate generation perplexity (GenPPL) with an external language model and distributional similarity to reference text with MAUVE. With default denoising steps equal to sequence length, LangFlow outperforms both DSpark variants on both metrics at lengths 128 and 1024, while DSpark-RNN leads at 16. A conditional KL analysis characterizes dependencies excluded by the Markov head's previous-token conditioning. Recurrent memory removes this restriction and improves both metrics, but the longer-sequence gap persists. Teacher probability matching further lowers Markov GenPPL without observed MAUVE gains. Increasing LangFlow's denoising steps at fixed weights improves both metrics at lengths 16 and 128, changing the length-128 ordering relative to DSpark-RNN. These results establish LangFlow's longer-sequence advantage under the evaluated budgets and highlight iterative full-sequence refinement as a route to improving standalone generation beyond gains from recurrent head memory.

AI.tldr: The paper compares continuous diffusion language models (LangFlow) with speculative drafters (DSpark variants) on standalone unconditional generation under matched training budgets. LangFlow gives better GenPPL and MAUVE at lengths 128 and 1024, while DSpark-RNN leads at length 16.
AI.motivation: Continuous diffusion language models and speculative drafters are efficient text generators but are evaluated differently, so their quality as standalone generators, without target-model verification, has not been compared directly.
AI.method: LangFlow is used for the diffusion models and DSpark's Markov and recurrent-head architectures are adapted for standalone generation; all models are trained from scratch for unconditional single-block OpenWebText generation at lengths 16, 128 and 1024, with common preprocessing, backbone dimensions and update budgets, and are scored by GenPPL with an external language model and by MAUVE; a conditional KL analysis probes the dependencies the Markov head excludes.
AI.result: With denoising steps equal to sequence length, LangFlow beats both DSpark variants on GenPPL and MAUVE at lengths 128 and 1024, and DSpark-RNN leads at length 16. Recurrent memory improves both metrics for DSpark but the longer-sequence gap persists; teacher probability matching lowers Markov GenPPL without MAUVE gains; raising LangFlow's denoising steps at fixed weights improves both metrics at lengths 16 and 128 and changes the length-128 ordering relative to DSpark-RNN.
AI.conclusion: Under the evaluated budgets LangFlow has a longer-sequence advantage, and iterative full-sequence refinement is a promising route to better standalone generation beyond what recurrent head memory provides.

title: STAR: Steering Action Representations during Inference
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions, showing strong capabilities across robotic manipulation tasks. However, in our probing experiment, we find that action representations near the action output do not fully preserve task-relevant visual grounding. Motivated by this late-layer grounding gap, we introduce STAR, for STeering Action Representations, a training-free inference method for pre-trained VLAs. STAR applies an exponential moving average over late-layer residual updates, allowing later action representations to inherit object-aware update directions from earlier layers without model updates or architectural changes. It further uses recent proprioceptive states to adapt the mixing strength, using conservative mixing when execution dynamics change rapidly. Experiments on robot manipulation benchmarks show that STAR improves late-layer object awareness and increases average task success rates by 4.0 percentage points. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: STAR is a training-free inference method for pre-trained vision-language-action models that mixes late-layer residual updates through an exponential moving average to restore object-aware grounding in action representations. It raises average task success by 4.0 percentage points on robot manipulation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: A probing experiment shows that action representations near the action output do not fully preserve task-relevant visual grounding, a late-layer grounding gap.
AI.method: STAR applies an exponential moving average over late-layer residual updates so that later representations inherit object-aware update directions from earlier layers, with no model updates or architectural changes; it adapts the mixing strength from recent proprioceptive states and mixes conservatively when execution dynamics change rapidly.
AI.result: On robot manipulation benchmarks STAR improves late-layer object awareness and increases average task success rate by 4.0 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Late-layer grounding can be strengthened at inference time without retraining, a cheap way to improve pre-trained VLAs.

title: Dreams Are Cheaper Than Flights: Curated World-Model Data Improves Aerial Detection
summary: Robot perception is increasingly data driven, yet field data is slow, costly, and sometimes disruptive to collect. Video world models offer a cheaper source: seeded with real frames, they extend a recorded scene into new footage with the deployment's sensor, altitude, and environment. We ask whether such synthetic data matches the utility of real field data and whether detectors trained with it perform in the field. Seeding a 7B-parameter world model with wildlife drone video, we more than double the training set with curated frames. On held-out videos from the same drones, mAP@50--95 rises 4.3\% when these frames are added to real data and 10.3\% when they replace it, and up to 33.5\% on an urban benchmark. Although an expert rejects an estimated 87.5\% of generated clips, the data costs about \$1,100 of GPU time, against more than \$3,200 of field labor alone for a less useful real training set. Synthetic data thus shifts data costs from fieldwork to compute.

AI.tldr: Synthetic frames from a 7B-parameter video world model seeded with wildlife drone footage improve aerial object detection, and raise mAP by 10.3% when they replace real training data. The synthetic data costs about $1,100 of GPU time, against more than $3,200 of field labor for a less useful real training set.
AI.motivation: Field data for robot perception is slow, costly and sometimes disruptive to collect, so the authors ask whether synthetic world-model data matches the utility of real field data and whether detectors trained on it work in the field.
AI.method: A 7B-parameter video world model seeded with real wildlife drone video extends the recorded scene into new footage with the deployment's sensor, altitude and environment; the training set is more than doubled with curated frames, and detectors are evaluated on held-out videos from the same drones and on an urban benchmark.
AI.result: mAP@50-95 rises 4.3% when the curated frames are added to real data and 10.3% when they replace it, and by up to 33.5% on an urban benchmark. An expert rejects an estimated 87.5% of the generated clips.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic data shifts data costs from fieldwork to compute, making world-model generation a practical alternative to field collection for training detectors.

title: WebOverlay: High-Throughput Vision-Only Distillation for Extreme Aspect-Ratio Web Overlay Detection
summary: Web overlays, such as cookie consent banners, newsletter prompts, and age gates, obstruct automated web crawlers and degrade downstream document representations. While proprietary multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can accurately identify overlays, their latency and inference cost preclude web-scale ingestion. Conversely, lightweight vision models struggle with full-page renderings characterized by extreme vertical aspect ratios, where standard isotropic resizing collapses critical text features and causes false positives. In this work, we present WebOverlay, a high-throughput vision-only detector trained via distillation from a frontier vision-language teacher. We establish a dynamic tiling strategy that partitions extreme aspect-ratio web renders into aspect-preserving patches with spatial overlap, coupled with an aspect-ratio-aware boundary adjudication mechanism to eliminate boundary artifacts. To eliminate cross-modal latency overheads, our student model relies purely on visual cues, bypassing DOM tree parsing. WebOverlay significantly outperforms DOM-based heuristics and achieves competitive precision and recall against heavy proprietary MLLM baselines while delivering multiple orders of magnitude higher throughput and substantially reduced deployment costs.

AI.tldr: WebOverlay is a vision-only detector, distilled from a frontier vision-language teacher, that finds web overlays such as cookie banners and age gates in full-page renderings. It reaches precision and recall competitive with heavy proprietary MLLMs at far higher throughput.
AI.motivation: Proprietary MLLMs identify overlays accurately but are too slow and costly for web-scale ingestion, while lightweight vision models fail on full-page renders with extreme vertical aspect ratios, where isotropic resizing collapses text and causes false positives.
AI.method: Dynamic tiling partitions extreme aspect-ratio renders into aspect-preserving patches with spatial overlap, and an aspect-ratio-aware boundary adjudication removes boundary artifacts; the student relies purely on visual cues and bypasses DOM tree parsing, and is trained by distillation from a frontier vision-language teacher.
AI.result: WebOverlay significantly outperforms DOM-based heuristics and achieves competitive precision and recall against heavy proprietary MLLM baselines, with multiple orders of magnitude higher throughput and substantially lower deployment cost.
AI.conclusion: A visual-only student distilled from a strong teacher can make overlay detection practical at web scale without DOM parsing or costly model inference.

title: Accept Changes, Reject Attacks: Robust Memory Management for LLM Agents
summary: Since large language model (LLM) agents rely on long-term memory, what they store now shapes what they do later. A memory manager decides how each input changes this memory and which records the agent acts on. It can fail in two ways: keeping a fact that has since changed (outdated memory), or storing a planted passage or injected instruction (memory poisoning). Most prior work studies them separately, yet they call for opposite write decisions, so no fixed write rule handles both. We therefore formalize memory robustness as handling both without doing worse on other inputs. Since accuracy checks only the answer, we measure robustness with evidence-conditioned accuracy (ECA), which also checks that the records the manager selects include all the evidence the answer needs, updated and free of attacks. However, existing memory systems and defenses are not more robust than an untuned manager on our test sets. We improve robustness with a simple one-shot recipe that fine-tunes the manager on episodes synthesized around a single conversation with inserted changes and attacks. On three backbones, it improves every category score on our test sets and more than doubles the untuned manager's overall ECA, though robustness remains incomplete.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes memory robustness for LLM agents as handling both outdated memory and memory poisoning without doing worse on other inputs, and measures it with evidence-conditioned accuracy. A one-shot fine-tuning recipe on synthesized episodes more than doubles the untuned manager's overall ECA, though robustness remains incomplete.
AI.motivation: A memory manager can keep a fact that has since changed or store a planted passage or injected instruction; prior work studies these failures separately even though they call for opposite write decisions, and existing memory systems and defenses are no more robust than an untuned manager.
AI.method: Robustness is measured by evidence-conditioned accuracy (ECA), which also requires the selected records to include all the evidence the answer needs, updated and free of attacks; the manager is fine-tuned in one shot on episodes synthesized around a single conversation with inserted changes and attacks.
AI.result: On three backbones the recipe improves every category score on the authors' test sets and more than doubles the untuned manager's overall ECA.
AI.conclusion: A simple training recipe substantially improves memory robustness, although the authors note that robustness remains incomplete.

title: One Verdict Is Not Enough: Regression Testing Learned World Models and Their Test Harnesses
summary: Learned world models ship as software components whose model versions, preprocessing, and test harnesses change between releases. Work on model updates already counts per-sample regressions, or negative flips, that an accuracy check hides. Two problems remain: a test can pass under one configuration and fail under another, and a harness fault can produce erroneous scores and wrong verdicts without a crash. We present TetraState, a regression-testing protocol for paired possible/impossible video tests. Each test runs under four fixed model-native configurations; its number of correct verdicts assigns one of four outcome classes. Inconclusive tests and failed executions are reported separately alongside the verdict rate. Revisions are compared by per-test outcome transitions, and the harness is versioned as part of the system under test. On all 506 IntPhys 2 Main tests and two heterogeneous systems, Cosmos 3 Nano and V-JEPA 2, two V-JEPA 2 harness revisions move modal accuracy by only 0.2 and 2.6 points yet change 11 and 214 test labels; in the second, accuracy rises although fewer tests are judged correctly, and 43 regressions keep the modal verdict, so a modal-verdict flip check misses them. These results outline a research agenda on configuration-level regression oracles for learned components.

AI.tldr: TetraState is a regression-testing protocol for learned world models that runs paired possible/impossible video tests under four fixed configurations and assigns each test one of four outcome classes. On IntPhys 2 Main it shows that harness revisions can change many test labels while barely moving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Learned world models ship as software whose model versions, preprocessing and test harnesses change between releases; accuracy hides per-sample regressions, a test can pass under one configuration and fail under another, and a harness fault can produce wrong verdicts without a crash.
AI.method: Each paired possible/impossible video test runs under four fixed model-native configurations, and the number of correct verdicts assigns one of four outcome classes; inconclusive tests and failed executions are reported separately alongside the verdict rate; revisions are compared by per-test outcome transitions, and the harness is versioned as part of the system under test.
AI.result: On all 506 IntPhys 2 Main tests with Cosmos 3 Nano and V-JEPA 2, two V-JEPA 2 harness revisions move modal accuracy by only 0.2 and 2.6 points yet change 11 and 214 test labels. In the second revision accuracy rises although fewer tests are judged correct, and 43 regressions keep the modal verdict, which a modal-verdict flip check misses.
AI.conclusion: Learned components need configuration-level regression oracles, because aggregate accuracy and modal-verdict checks can miss regressions.

title: When Disclosure Is Compulsory: Evaluating Ride-Hailing Rebalancing Policies with Self-Interested LLM Driver Agents
summary: The EU Platform Work Directive, to be transposed by December 2026, requires ride-hailing platforms to state in plain language the main parameters of their automated decisions and how a worker's behaviour affects them. Such rules are exactly what a large language model (LLM) can read, so drivers will be able to let one decide for them. We compare two main families of rebalancing policy once their rules are public: a reactive policy (R) that sends idle drivers to cover requests just lost, and an anticipatory policy (A) that plans moves on a demand forecast. Each driver is an LLM agent maximizing its own net income, given no rules (N) or the rules at the directive's level of detail (L). We test two LLMs, Claude Haiku 5.5 and Jev, which understand the rules equally well, in a three-zone model and in Manhattan. With the rules disclosed, drivers follow the platform more closely: in Manhattan, the share of relocation offers they decline falls from about four in five to one in four under both policies. Yet the effects differ by policy. For the platform, disclosure costs R 3.7% of its profit in Manhattan, as R now pays for moves drivers used to make for free, while A's profit is unchanged; the two policies, which tie on profit under full compliance, end 6.1% apart. For drivers, disclosure raises income in the small model under both policies and LLMs; for users, it raises the service rate there by 10 to 18 percentage points. In Manhattan, self-interested drivers also make A a win-win-win against full compliance, raising driver income, platform profit and service rate by 10 to 12% each. Rebalancing policies that perform equally well under full compliance can thus show opposite results under mandatory disclosure. The study offers a framework to evaluate such policies under the new requirement and is, to our knowledge, the first to do so with LLM agents.

AI.tldr: LLM driver agents that maximize their own income respond to mandatory disclosure of ride-hailing rebalancing rules, and the effect depends on the policy. Disclosure costs the reactive policy 3.7% of platform profit in Manhattan while leaving the anticipatory policy's profit unchanged, and the two policies that tie under full compliance end 6.1% apart.
AI.motivation: The EU Platform Work Directive requires platforms to state the main parameters of their automated decisions in plain language, and an LLM can read such rules and decide for drivers, so the effect of disclosure on rebalancing policies needs evaluating with LLM agents.
AI.method: A reactive policy (R) sends idle drivers to cover lost requests and an anticipatory policy (A) plans moves on a demand forecast; each driver is an LLM agent maximizing net income, given either no rules (N) or rules at the directive's level of detail (L); two LLMs, Claude Haiku 5.5 and Jev, are tested in a three-zone model and in Manhattan.
AI.result: With rules disclosed, drivers follow the platform more closely, and in Manhattan the share of declined relocation offers falls from about four in five to one in four under both policies. Disclosure costs R 3.7% of platform profit in Manhattan while A's profit is unchanged. Disclosure raises driver income in the small model under both policies and LLMs and raises the service rate there by 10 to 18 percentage points. In Manhattan, A is a win-win-win against full compliance, raising driver income, platform profit and service rate by 10 to 12% each.
AI.conclusion: Policies that perform equally under full compliance can show opposite results under mandatory disclosure, so the framework for evaluating rebalancing policies must account for the disclosure requirement.

title: Lineage Is Memory: Parent Inheritance and Feedback Disclosure in Short-Budget LLM-Guided Optimization
comment: 17 pages, 2 figures, 10 tables. Code, pre-registrations, and 1,750 run logs at this https URL
summary: Iterative language-model optimizers refine prompts and programs by evaluating a candidate, showing a proposer model a sample of failing cases, and keeping revisions that improve performance. Recent work attributes the limits of this loop to narrow single-round reflection, introducing full-set error clustering, targeted minibatches, or larger proposer models so the optimizer sees more failure modes per step. Yet every existing evaluation tests these mechanisms exclusively inside lineage-preserving search, where each revision edits a surviving parent, leaving the contribution of parent inheritance confounded with the breadth of per-round feedback. Across 1,750 pre-registered runs spanning nine prompt and program synthesis benchmarks, we separate parent inheritance from feedback disclosure under matched evaluation budgets. We find that greedy parent inheritance drives the vast majority of optimization progress, outperforming seed-reset resampling even when seed-reset proposals receive a clustered summary of all failures in every round or use a larger proposer model. While full-set error clustering and diverse failure selection improve single-step rewrites from the seed and accelerate the opening rounds of search, sequential parent inheritance rapidly closes this gap as solved error modes are retained in the candidate and filtered from subsequent failure lists. Moreover, decomposing token expenditure in GEPA reveals that proposer reflection accounts for only a small fraction of total cost whereas validation and minibatch gating consume nearly the entire budget, showing that greedy parent inheritance over raw failures captures the gains of complex reflective loops at a fraction of their compute.

AI.tldr: Across 1,750 pre-registered runs on nine prompt and program synthesis benchmarks, greedy parent inheritance drives most of the progress in LLM-guided optimization and beats seed-reset resampling even when resampling gets richer feedback or a larger proposer. Feedback-breadth mechanisms mainly speed up the opening rounds.
AI.motivation: Recent work attributes the limits of iterative LLM optimizers to narrow single-round reflection and proposes full-set error clustering, targeted minibatches or larger proposers, but these were tested only inside lineage-preserving search, which confounds parent inheritance with feedback breadth.
AI.method: Under matched evaluation budgets, parent inheritance is separated from feedback disclosure: greedy parent inheritance is compared with seed-reset resampling, including variants given a clustered summary of all failures in every round or a larger proposer model; full-set error clustering and diverse failure selection are also tested, and GEPA's token expenditure is decomposed.
AI.result: Greedy parent inheritance outperforms seed-reset resampling even when the seed-reset proposals receive a clustered failure summary or a larger proposer. Full-set clustering and diverse failure selection improve single-step rewrites from the seed and accelerate the opening rounds, but sequential inheritance closes this gap as solved error modes are retained and filtered out of later failure lists. In GEPA, proposer reflection is a small fraction of total cost, whereas validation and minibatch gating consume nearly the entire budget.
AI.conclusion: Greedy parent inheritance over raw failures captures the gains of complex reflective loops at a fraction of their compute.

title: ARK: Avoiding Routing Collisions for KV Cache Transfer in Disaggregated LLM Inference
comment: 7 pages. Published in the Proceedings of the ACM SIGCOMM 2026 Conference (SIGCOMM '26)
summary: Disaggregated LLM inference separates the prefill and decode phases across GPU pools, generating massive KV-cache transfers. Because these transfers last hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, they behave as mega elephant flows that dominate link bandwidth utilization. In this regime, stateless ECMP can perform poorly: hash collisions may overload one spine link while leaving others idle, stretching transfer times by seconds. Yet this same persistence makes coordination practical. Since these flows are long-lived, even lightweight one-to-all coordination can be amortized over their lifetime. We present ARK, a distributed elephant-flow path reservation mechanism. ARK coordinates senders to choose source ports whose hashes map concurrent flows onto distinct spines, without requiring switch changes or receiver-side packet reordering. Packet-level RDMA simulations show that ARK reduces mean and P95 FCT by up to 27.3% and 34.0% under moderate load, and further reduces mean TTFT by up to 12.9%.

AI.tldr: ARK is a distributed elephant-flow path reservation mechanism for KV-cache transfers in disaggregated LLM inference: senders coordinate their source-port choices so that concurrent flows hash onto distinct spine links. Packet-level RDMA simulations show mean and P95 flow completion time reductions of up to 27.3% and 34.0% under moderate load.
AI.motivation: KV-cache transfers in disaggregated inference are long-lived mega elephant flows that dominate link bandwidth, and stateless ECMP can overload one spine link through hash collisions, stretching transfer times by seconds.
AI.method: Because the flows are long-lived, lightweight one-to-all coordination can be amortized over their lifetime; ARK coordinates senders to choose source ports whose hashes map concurrent flows onto distinct spines, without switch changes or receiver-side packet reordering.
AI.result: Packet-level RDMA simulations show that ARK reduces mean and P95 flow completion time by up to 27.3% and 34.0% under moderate load, and further reduces mean time to first token by up to 12.9%.
AI.conclusion: Coordinating path choice among senders at the endpoints can cut KV-cache transfer times without modifying switches or receivers.

title: ROSTrans: Empirically Benchmarking LLMs for ROS1-to-ROS2 Migration
summary: Although large language models have shown strong capabilities in domain-specific code generation, their performance in robotics software development, especially for the Robot Operating System (ROS), remains largely unexplored. ROS code generation presents distinctive challenges, including complex inter-node coordination, middleware configuration, and lifecycle semantics that go far beyond standard coding benchmarks, and many important correctness properties become observable only once migrated nodes are launched and communicate. We present ROSTrans, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on ROS1-to-ROS2 code migration, a representative and practically important setting for ROS code generation. ROSTrans comprises 108 scaffolded completion tasks drawn from a diverse set of 70+ open-source ROS1 repositories and organized into a hierarchical taxonomy assessing interface-level, behavioral-level and system-level correctness. For every task we establish an executable reference: a verified ROS2 implementation, a runtime test suite that launches the nodes and exercises their topics, services, actions and parameters, and a container ensuring reproducibility. Candidates are scored by injecting only their target files into an otherwise fixed copy of the reference package, so a candidate can neither supply nor weaken the tests it is judged by. Evaluating six frontier LLMs over five stochastic generations per task, we find pass@1 below 10.9%, and that 56.5% of all samples build successfully and then fail at runtime,and 32.0% fail runtime assertions on the migrated interfaces, a class of error no compile-only oracle can detect. Execution-guided repair further improves task success, reaching 49.1% and 47.2% for Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.5 after three rounds, respectively.

AI.tldr: ROSTrans is a benchmark of 108 scaffolded tasks for evaluating LLMs on ROS1-to-ROS2 migration, with executable references and runtime tests. Six frontier LLMs reach pass@1 below 10.9%, and execution-guided repair lifts Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.5 to 49.1% and 47.2%.
AI.motivation: LLM code generation for the Robot Operating System is largely unexplored, and ROS has distinctive challenges such as inter-node coordination, middleware configuration and lifecycle semantics that standard coding benchmarks do not test, with correctness visible only once migrated nodes launch and communicate.
AI.method: The benchmark has 108 scaffolded completion tasks drawn from over 70 open-source ROS1 repositories, organized into a hierarchical taxonomy of interface-level, behavioral-level and system-level correctness; each task has a verified ROS2 implementation, a runtime test suite that launches the nodes and exercises topics, services, actions and parameters, and a reproducible container; candidates are scored by injecting only their target files into a fixed reference package, and six frontier LLMs are evaluated over five stochastic generations per task.
AI.result: pass@1 is below 10.9%; 56.5% of all samples build successfully and then fail at runtime, and 32.0% fail runtime assertions on the migrated interfaces, an error class no compile-only oracle can detect. Execution-guided repair reaches 49.1% and 47.2% task success for Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.5 after three rounds.
AI.conclusion: Execution-based evaluation is needed for ROS code generation, since compile-only checks would miss a large class of interface errors.

title: Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation is becoming agentic. A search harness writes queries, reads results, reformulates, and decides when to stop. This largely solves accuracy: a harness with only BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% on multi-hop FRAMES in our runs, without compiled or vector indexes. It exposes a context problem: an undisciplined loop repeats queries, rereads documents, and fills the window with unused passages. The missing layer is knowledge compilation: a configurable ingestion pipeline where LLMs enrich documents with context no chunk contains alone--navigation hierarchies with claim-evidence leaves, entity graphs, timelines, mind maps, ontologies, wikis, and memory. Compilation is not a better retriever: under a competent harness, structural artifacts gave no detectable accuracy gain on FRAMES, and a PageIndex-style outline degraded at scale. It is a supply layer. A navigation tree whose leaves are claim-evidence pairs--the mechanism we measure--cuts query tokens by 91% when evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not, a 38% average reduction; this implies a 2% break-even sufficiency rate and a measured rate near 43%. A decision gate cuts latency from 140 s to 30 s, though substitution's token saving is bought with retrieval rounds and carries its own latency cost. Other artifacts--ontology, graph, wiki, timeline, mind map, memory--pay off in deployment (governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, continuity) where accuracy benchmarks cannot see them. We describe RAGFlow's pipeline and harness (open source at this https URL), which turns the loop into five disciplined stations and keeps the context entering the model the smallest sufficient set; together they form an agent-native database: a store that hands the agent compiled, governed context instead of a ranked list of passages.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that agentic retrieval needs knowledge compilation, a supply layer that enriches documents with navigation trees, entity graphs and other artifacts, rather than a better retriever. A claim-evidence navigation tree cuts average query tokens by 38%, while other artifacts pay off in governance and onboarding that accuracy benchmarks do not measure.
AI.motivation: A search harness with only BM25 or grep already answers most multi-hop questions, but an undisciplined loop repeats queries, rereads documents and fills the context window with unused passages.
AI.method: Knowledge compilation is a configurable ingestion pipeline in which LLMs enrich documents with context no chunk holds alone, including navigation hierarchies with claim-evidence leaves, entity graphs, timelines, mind maps, ontologies, wikis and memory; the RAGFlow pipeline and harness run the loop through five stations and keep the context entering the model the smallest sufficient set.
AI.result: With BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 the harness answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% of multi-hop FRAMES without compiled or vector indexes. Under a competent harness, structural artifacts gave no detectable accuracy gain on FRAMES, and a PageIndex-style outline degraded at scale. A claim-evidence navigation tree cuts query tokens by 91% when evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not, a 38% average reduction, against a 2% break-even sufficiency rate and a measured sufficiency rate near 43%. A decision gate cuts latency from 140 s to 30 s, although substitution's token saving is bought with retrieval rounds and its own latency cost.
AI.conclusion: Compilation acts as a supply layer for context rather than a retrieval improvement, and the authors frame the result as an agent-native database that hands agents compiled, governed context instead of a ranked list of passages.

title: Beyond CLIP: Calibrated (Few-Shot) Defect Detection With System One Decision Models
summary: Cameras and vision sensors are widely used for product and process inspection in manufacturing environments. Traditionally, this process required thousands of images of both nominal and defective products to train such models. Recent research shows that vision transformer (ViT) models, such as CLIP, can reduce this requirement to 50-100 images per nominal and defective class. However, collecting even 50 defective images can be difficult in high-yield or low-volume manufacturing processes. In this paper, we examine the utility of two recently proposed structured decision models (Jev and Clef-Flash) in applications using as few as k=2 reference images per class at inference. In the process, we provide three main contributions: (a) a framework for k-shot learning of these models for image classification/inspection applications; (b) an agentic approach for automatically refining the text descriptions that guide image classification in these decision models; and (c) an approach to calibrate the resulting defect probabilities to improve their reliability for inspection decisions. We test these contributions in five manufacturing case studies. Using two reference images per class, both Jev and Clef-Flash outperform CLIP's test accuracies with the same references (0.75-1.00 [Jev] and 0.71-0.99 [Clef-Flash] vs 0.67-0.84 [CLIP]). Furthermore, we show that our agentic refinement of text descriptions significantly improves accuracy across 6 of 8 model-application combinations, and our calibration approach reduces the Brier score in 13 of the 15 model-application configurations. To support the reproducibility of our work, we provide our replication code and have created the R "decisions" package for evaluating additional models. We also provide a publicly available web app that allows practitioners to inspect their own images with no code.

AI.tldr: The paper tests two structured decision models, Jev and Clef-Flash, for defect detection with as few as two reference images per class and shows that both beat CLIP given the same references. It adds k-shot learning, agentic refinement of text descriptions and calibration of defect probabilities.
AI.motivation: Manufacturing inspection often lacks enough defective images for training, and CLIP-style vision transformers need 50-100 images per class, which can be infeasible in high-yield or low-volume processes.
AI.method: Three contributions: a framework for k-shot learning of these decision models for classification and inspection, an agentic approach that automatically refines the text descriptions guiding classification, and a calibration approach for the resulting defect probabilities; the models are tested in five manufacturing case studies with k=2 reference images per class at inference.
AI.result: With two references per class, Jev reaches 0.75-1.00 and Clef-Flash 0.71-0.99 test accuracy, versus 0.67-0.84 for CLIP. Agentic refinement significantly improves accuracy across 6 of 8 model-application combinations, and calibration reduces the Brier score in 13 of 15 configurations. The authors release replication code, an R package "decisions" and a public web app.
AI.conclusion: Structured decision models with few-shot adaptation, refined descriptions and calibration are a practical option for inspection when defective images are scarce.

title: From Evaluation to Evolution: Benchmarking Image Editing and Evolving Image Models
summary: Real-world image editing requires coordinating multiple visual transformations with content preservation and reference constraints, yet aggregate scores can readily obscure unmet local requirements. Effective evaluation must therefore identify local failures and translate them into priorities for subsequent model improvement. We introduce WeGenEditBench, comprising 2,740 evaluation instances and 148 task types across single-image, text-intensive, and multi-reference editing. Pre-generated checklists shared across models decompose each request into atomic requirements; item-level deductions and visual evidence are established first and then summarized into scores for edit execution, preservation, visual quality, and task-specific correctness. To support the experience-acquisition component of recursive self-improvement (RSI), we develop WeGenEvoStudio, a unified multi-agent harness for RSI-oriented learning that integrates model-conditioned failure diagnosis, retrieval-grounded data construction, supervised adaptation, and re-evaluation. Among 15 evaluated configurations, GPT-Image-2 leads single-image editing with an Overall score of 4.076, while Seedream-5.0-Pro leads text-intensive editing at 4.291. Evolution experiments across four generation and editing benchmarks demonstrate substantial targeted gains: on their report-selected Top-5 single-image targets, FLUX.2 [dev] improves Overall from 1.083 to 3.517, while Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 gains 13.2%. Together, our benchmark and harness provide a foundation for developing more reliable image models through interpretable evaluation and feedback-driven learning.

AI.tldr: WeGenEditBench is a benchmark of 2,740 image-editing instances across 148 task types that uses checklist-based scoring to expose local failures, and WeGenEvoStudio is a multi-agent harness for recursive self-improvement. Evolution experiments give large targeted gains, for example FLUX.2 [dev] rises from 1.083 to 3.517 Overall on the report-selected Top-5 single-image targets.
AI.motivation: Aggregate scores can hide unmet local requirements in image editing, so evaluation should locate local failures and turn them into priorities for subsequent model improvement.
AI.method: Pre-generated checklists shared across models decompose each request into atomic requirements; item-level deductions and visual evidence are established first and then summarized into scores for edit execution, preservation, visual quality and task-specific correctness; WeGenEvoStudio integrates model-conditioned failure diagnosis, retrieval-grounded data construction, supervised adaptation and re-evaluation.
AI.result: Among 15 evaluated configurations, GPT-Image-2 leads single-image editing with an Overall score of 4.076 and Seedream-5.0-Pro leads text-intensive editing at 4.291. Across evolution experiments on four generation and editing benchmarks, the targeted gains are substantial: FLUX.2 [dev] improves from 1.083 to 3.517 Overall on the Top-5 single-image targets, and Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 gains 13.2%.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable, checklist-based evaluation combined with feedback-driven adaptation provides a foundation for more reliable image models.

title: Coarse3D: Controllable and Faithful Sparse Structure Generation for Image-to-3D
summary: Coarse-to-fine 3D-native generation relies heavily on the first-stage sparse structure, which determines the global orientation and overall geometry for subsequent refinement. However, existing coarse generators suffer from two key limitations: their orientation is difficult to control due to ambiguous semantic canonicalization, and their structures are often inconsistent with input images due to weak 2D-3D grounding. We propose Coarse3D, a sparse-structure generation model that produces orientation-controllable and structurally faithful voxel geometry from arbitrary unposed images. Coarse3D introduces three designs: a first-frame anchored canonical space that aligns generation with the first input view while preserving object-centric normalization; a dual-tower DiT that couples generation with auxiliary feed-forward reconstruction to learn spatially grounded features; and spatial-prior guided attention that regularizes cross-attention with pixel-to-voxel correspondence. Coarse3D can directly replace the coarse stage of existing pipelines. Experiments show that it substantially improves sparse structure quality and consistently enhances final 3D generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: Coarse3D is a sparse-structure generator for image-to-3D that produces orientation-controllable, structurally faithful voxel geometry from unposed images. It can replace the coarse stage of existing pipelines, and it improves final 3D generation to state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Coarse-to-fine 3D generation depends on the first-stage sparse structure, but existing coarse generators are hard to orient because of ambiguous semantic canonicalization, and their structures are often inconsistent with the input because of weak 2D-3D grounding.
AI.method: Three designs: a first-frame anchored canonical space that aligns generation with the first input view while keeping object-centric normalization; a dual-tower DiT that couples generation with auxiliary feed-forward reconstruction to learn spatially grounded features; and spatial-prior guided attention that regularizes cross-attention with pixel-to-voxel correspondence.
AI.result: Coarse3D substantially improves sparse structure quality and consistently enhances the final 3D generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.conclusion: A better first-stage sparse structure improves the whole pipeline, and the model can directly replace the coarse stage of existing pipelines.

title: ANGLER: Verifier-Grounded Benchmarking with an Adaptive Attacker for Web Agents
summary: Web agents are increasingly deployed to complete tasks autonomously on real websites, where adversarially injected content can induce them to perform unauthorized actions. Existing evaluations primarily use fixed attacks or focus on a single attack type, and evaluate attacks at the text level rather than through real state changes, thus underestimating how vulnerable agents are to diverse attacks. To address the gap, we introduce REEF, a benchmark of red-teaming executable environments with faithful verification for measuring the security vulnerabilities of web agents. REEF covers 9 verifier-grounded websites spanning travel, commerce, productivity, media, and communication, and pairs every authentic benign task with a malicious objective delivered through 5 attack types at both the user and the environment level. REEF's state-based verifiers provide the execution feedback that drives ANGLER, an adaptive near-miss-guided lure evolution framework for red-teaming. Rather than evaluating a fixed attack set, ANGLER uses outcomes from prior rollouts to guide LLM-based attack mutation and candidate selection, prioritizing near-miss seeds during refinement. Across 8 VLM-based web agents, ANGLER achieves an end-to-end attack success rate (ASR) of 20.36%, compared with 15.24% for the non-adaptive setting. Compared with attack-free execution on the same benign tasks, attacks generated by ANGLER reduce benign task success rate (BSR) from 61.9% to 44.4%.

AI.tldr: REEF is a red-teaming benchmark of 9 verifier-grounded websites with state-based verification, and ANGLER is an adaptive attacker that evolves injected lures guided by near-miss outcomes. Across 8 VLM-based web agents, ANGLER reaches a 20.36% attack success rate versus 15.24% for a non-adaptive setting.
AI.motivation: Existing web-agent evaluations use fixed attacks or a single attack type and judge attacks at the text level rather than through real state changes, which underestimates how vulnerable agents are to diverse attacks.
AI.method: REEF covers 9 verifier-grounded websites across travel, commerce, productivity, media and communication, pairing each benign task with a malicious objective delivered through 5 attack types at both the user and environment levels; its state-based verifiers give the execution feedback that drives ANGLER, which uses prior rollout outcomes to guide LLM-based attack mutation and candidate selection, prioritizing near-miss seeds.
AI.result: Across 8 VLM-based web agents, ANGLER achieves an end-to-end attack success rate of 20.36%, compared with 15.24% for the non-adaptive setting. Attacks generated by ANGLER reduce benign task success rate from 61.9% under attack-free execution to 44.4%.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, state-verified red-teaming uncovers more web-agent vulnerabilities than fixed attack sets, which matters for agents that act autonomously on real websites.

title: ART of PIV: Agentic Real-Time Particle Image Velocimetry for Active Flow Control
summary: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measures fluid motion from images of tracer particles, but its accuracy depends on choices throughout the estimation pipeline, including image preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing. These choices are typically left to expert tuning, and a fixed configuration can become less accurate as conditions change. This matters especially when PIV supplies feedback for real-time control, where measurements must be both accurate and fast, and flow conditions vary. We introduce ART of PIV -- short for Agentic Real-Time and also a nod to the art of tuning a PIV pipeline -- which automates pipeline choice for each image pair. A learned agent selects a configuration according to a chosen measurement objective from a library assembled for a specified speed budget. Across cross-correlation, classical optical-flow, and learning-based estimators, ART of PIV reduces average end-point error (AEPE) by 12.2-22.4 % relative to the best single estimator at matched speed, with gains extending to 1000-4000 image pair/s. In a simulated local velocity regulation task, it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24-13.59 percentage points relative to a tuned fixed estimator, with the same classical controller in both cases. In a tabletop water channel, we illustrate two ways to tune ART of PIV for a fluidic pinball of three rotating cylinders: selecting between complementary optical-flow tunings for accuracy, and selecting regions of interest with coherent rotation or shear using a common flow estimator. For the first variant, we train a DreamerV3 reinforcement learning controller directly in the physical world and demonstrate tracking of a prescribed flow field in the wake of a fluidic pinball.

AI.tldr: ART of PIV is an agent that selects a particle image velocimetry pipeline configuration for each image pair from a library, according to a chosen measurement objective and speed budget. It reduces average end-point error by 12.2-22.4% relative to the best single estimator at matched speed and lowers closed-loop cost in a simulated velocity regulation task.
AI.motivation: PIV accuracy depends on expert-tuned choices in preprocessing, flow estimation and postprocessing, and a fixed configuration becomes less accurate as flow conditions change, which matters when PIV provides feedback for real-time control.
AI.method: A learned agent selects a configuration per image pair according to a chosen measurement objective from a library assembled for a specified speed budget, spanning cross-correlation, classical optical-flow and learning-based estimators; in a tabletop water channel the authors also select between optical-flow tunings and regions of interest, and train a DreamerV3 reinforcement learning controller directly in the physical world.
AI.result: ART of PIV reduces AEPE by 12.2-22.4% relative to the best single estimator at matched speed, with gains extending to 1000-4000 image pairs/s. In a simulated local velocity regulation task it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24-13.59 percentage points relative to a tuned fixed estimator. In the water channel the DreamerV3 controller tracks a prescribed flow field in the wake of a fluidic pinball of three rotating cylinders.
AI.conclusion: Automatic per-pair pipeline selection improves PIV accuracy and speed for closed-loop flow control, an advantage over fixed, expert-tuned pipelines.

title: Erase the Injected Region: Multimodal Prompt-Injection Defense with On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: Multimodal indirect prompt injection embeds malicious instructions in external media that also contains information needed for the user's task. Existing defenses can block the attack yet impair the model's use of that information, leaving a gap between attack defense and task preservation. We propose ERASE, an on-policy self-distillation method that constructs its reference by erasing the injected region in place. Modality-appropriate blank content replaces the injection while the surrounding media is preserved. A student reading attacked media learns from a frozen base model reading the erased view through full-distribution token-level feedback on its own rollouts. Across image, audio, and video on two model sizes, ERASE records near-zero observed attack success on the evaluated benchmark while retaining task utility close to the undefended clean-input level. On 3B audio, ERASE reaches 60.1% attacked-input accuracy compared with ARGUS's 33.1%, within 0.5 points of the undefended clean-input level. Experiments show that ERASE reduces injection dependence from 6.26 to 0.0095 on 3B audio while staying close to the base model on the erased input. Out-of-domain accuracy also stays near the base level. Our code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: ERASE defends multimodal models against indirect prompt injection by erasing the injected region from the media and using the erased view as the reference for on-policy self-distillation. It reaches near-zero observed attack success while keeping task utility close to the clean-input level across image, audio and video.
AI.motivation: Existing defenses can block an injection but impair the model's use of the information the same external media carries for the user's task, leaving a gap between attack defense and task preservation.
AI.method: ERASE builds its reference by replacing the injected region with modality-appropriate blank content while preserving the surrounding media; a student reading the attacked media learns from a frozen base model reading the erased view, through full-distribution token-level feedback on its own rollouts.
AI.result: Across image, audio and video on two model sizes, ERASE records near-zero observed attack success on the evaluated benchmark and keeps task utility close to the undefended clean-input level. On 3B audio it reaches 60.1% attacked-input accuracy versus 33.1% for ARGUS, within 0.5 points of the undefended clean-input level, and reduces injection dependence from 6.26 to 0.0095; out-of-domain accuracy stays near the base level.
AI.conclusion: Erasing the injected region and distilling from the erased view defends against multimodal injection while preserving utility, at least on the evaluated benchmark.

title: GenDSR: Transferring Representations from Video Generation Models for Dynamic Spatial Reasoning
summary: Dynamic spatial reasoning is essential for connecting visual intelligence to thephysical world, yet remains challenging for vision-language models (VLMs), which must preserve scene state while tracking how spatial relations evolve over time. Meanwhile, video generation models (VGMs), trained to synthesize temporally coherent world dynamics, offer a rich source of spatiotemporal representations. We present GenDSR, a framework that transfers intermediate representations from VGM into VLM for dynamic spatial reasoning. Rather than treating a VGM feature as a monolithic prior, GenDSR constructs two complementary branches: a raw branch preserving holistic generative context and a delta branch emphasizing temporal variation. Task-conditioned tokenwise gates then fuse both signals and inject the result into the native visual representation. On DSR-Bench, GenDSR achieves 67.2%, surpassing the previous best result and establishing a new state of the art.

AI.tldr: GenDSR transfers intermediate representations from a video generation model into a vision-language model to improve dynamic spatial reasoning. It reaches 67.2% on DSR-Bench, surpassing the previous best result and setting a new state of the art.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models must preserve scene state while tracking how spatial relations evolve over time, and video generation models, trained to synthesize temporally coherent dynamics, offer rich spatiotemporal representations.
AI.method: GenDSR builds two complementary branches from a video generation model feature: a raw branch that preserves holistic generative context and a delta branch that emphasizes temporal variation; task-conditioned tokenwise gates fuse both signals and inject the result into the native visual representation of the VLM.
AI.result: GenDSR achieves 67.2% on DSR-Bench, surpassing the previous best result.
AI.conclusion: Splitting video generation features into raw and temporal-variation components and gating them per task can strengthen the dynamic spatial reasoning of vision-language models.

title: With foundation-model features, aggregator complexity does not improve cross-hospital discrimination in gastric whole-slide image classification
summary: Whole-slide image classifiers are usually developed within one hospital and often go untested at unseen hospitals. We assembled 5,036 haematoxylin-and-eosin-stained gastric slides from five Korean hospitals, scanned at 20x and 40x, and compared multiple-instance learning aggregators under leave-one-hospital-out validation on frozen pathology foundation-model features. A hierarchical patch-region-slide graph aggregator (CHIME-MIL) with site alignment and two-scale fusion reached a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.837, above six conventional attention and transformer aggregators trained without these steps. Under a matched recipe it did not exceed attention-based pooling, and global max pooling given the same alignment and fusion was better (AUC 0.855, P = 0.0002). The alignment, which subtracts each hospital's mean feature vector without labels, onboarded a new hospital from ten unlabelled slides and cost 0.002 AUC without held-out-hospital data, but its accuracy gains were small and inconsistent. The model had low top-label calibration error (0.053) but under-confident malignancy probabilities, and removing its most-attended patches lowered the malignancy probability far more than removing random patches. With these features, more complex aggregators did not improve discrimination; what a deployable system adds is label-free onboarding, calibration checks and auditable evidence.

AI.tldr: On 5,036 gastric slides from five Korean hospitals, a complex hierarchical aggregator (CHIME-MIL) does not beat attention-based pooling under a matched recipe, and global max pooling with the same alignment and fusion does better. With frozen foundation-model features, the authors conclude that deployment value lies in label-free onboarding, calibration checks and auditable evidence rather than in aggregator complexity.
AI.motivation: Whole-slide image classifiers are usually developed within one hospital and often go untested at unseen hospitals, so their cross-hospital generalization needs assessment.
AI.method: Multiple-instance learning aggregators are compared under leave-one-hospital-out validation on frozen pathology foundation-model features; the hierarchical patch-region-slide graph aggregator CHIME-MIL uses site alignment, which subtracts each hospital's mean feature vector without labels, and two-scale fusion, and is compared with six conventional attention and transformer aggregators.
AI.result: CHIME-MIL reaches a mean AUC of 0.837, above the six conventional aggregators trained without these steps. Under a matched recipe it does not exceed attention-based pooling, while global max pooling with the same alignment and fusion is better (AUC 0.855, P = 0.0002). Alignment onboarded a new hospital from ten unlabelled slides and cost 0.002 AUC without held-out-hospital data, with small, inconsistent accuracy gains. The model has low top-label calibration error (0.053) but under-confident malignancy probabilities, and removing its most-attended patches lowers the malignancy probability far more than removing random patches.
AI.conclusion: With these features more complex aggregators did not improve cross-hospital discrimination; what a deployable system adds is label-free onboarding, calibration checks and auditable evidence.

title: Pinching Antennas for ISAC: Waveguide Architectures, Solutions, and Future Directions
summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is a core design principle for sixth-generation (6G) wireless systems, yet fixed antenna geometry limits its performance. Pinching antenna systems (PASS) guide electromagnetic waves along dielectric waveguides and radiate them through position-adaptive antennas, allowing communication links and sensing observations to benefit from spatial reconfiguration. This article reviews PASS-enabled ISAC through single-waveguide, multi-waveguide, and segmented-waveguide architectures, comparing their feed structures, spatial degrees of freedom, operating protocols, and uplink/downlink support. We organize solution pathways around physics-consistent modeling, joint spatial-signal optimization, dynamic channel acquisition, and stable real-time control. A segmented waveguide-enabled pinching-antenna array (SWAN) case study demonstrates joint segment selection, antenna po?sitioning, and transmit beamforming using segment-hysteresis reinforcement learning. The results illustrate how waveguide loss and per-segment aperture gain create communication-sensing tradeoffs. We conclude with research directions in joint transmit?receive operation, measurement-calibrated digital twins, and trustworthy control.

AI.tldr: This review surveys pinching-antenna systems (PASS) for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) in 6G, covering single-waveguide, multi-waveguide and segmented-waveguide architectures, and illustrates them with a SWAN case study that uses segment-hysteresis reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Fixed antenna geometry limits ISAC performance in 6G systems, and the design space of reconfigurable pinching-antenna architectures for joint sensing and communication has not been organized into a unified review.
AI.method: The paper compares single-, multi- and segmented-waveguide PASS architectures by feed structure, spatial degrees of freedom, operating protocols and uplink/downlink support, and organizes solution pathways around physics-consistent modeling, joint spatial-signal optimization, dynamic channel acquisition and real-time control. The SWAN case study jointly optimizes segment selection, antenna positioning and transmit beamforming using segment-hysteresis reinforcement learning.
AI.result: The SWAN case study illustrates how waveguide loss and per-segment aperture gain create communication-sensing tradeoffs under joint segment selection, antenna positioning and beamforming.
AI.conclusion: The paper identifies research directions in joint transmit-receive operation, measurement-calibrated digital twins and trustworthy control for PASS-enabled ISAC.

title: From prediction error to sparse events: Biologically inspired signed-dyadic coding for Mandarin keyword spotting
summary: In continuous spiking keyword spotting, temporally correlated acoustic frames can repeatedly trigger memory access and neural computation at a dense input interface, even when hidden activity is sparse. Predictive processing and sensory adaptation suggest retaining predictable input locally and responding selectively to deviations. Inspired by this mechanism, we propose Predictive Signed-Dyadic Coding (PG). PG maintains a local prediction for each input channel and transmits an event only when the residual exceeds a learned threshold. Each event carries a sign and a finite power-of-two magnitude, and the receiver reconstructs it with fixed-point shifts and additions. In Mandarin keyword spotting, INPUT-PG reaches 90.00% accuracy while reducing mean SRAM reads by 33.87% and inference cycles by 32.77%. PG provides a hardware interface for research on low-power continuous speech processing and event-based sensory systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Predictive Signed-Dyadic Coding (PG), an event-driven input coding scheme for continuous spiking keyword spotting that transmits only residuals above a learned threshold, reaching 90.00% accuracy on Mandarin keyword spotting with fewer memory reads and inference cycles.
AI.motivation: In continuous spiking keyword spotting, temporally correlated acoustic frames repeatedly trigger memory access and computation at the dense input interface even when hidden activity is sparse, which wastes energy.
AI.method: PG keeps a local prediction for each input channel and emits an event only when the prediction residual exceeds a learned threshold. Each event carries a sign and a finite power-of-two magnitude, which the receiver reconstructs with fixed-point shifts and additions.
AI.result: On Mandarin keyword spotting, INPUT-PG reaches 90.00% accuracy while reducing mean SRAM reads by 33.87% and inference cycles by 32.77%.
AI.conclusion: PG provides a hardware interface for low-power continuous speech processing and event-based sensory systems.

title: ProSearch: Benchmarking Multi-Constraint Protocol Retrieval in Experimental Science
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track). 48 pages, 4 figures. Wenliang Liang and Zhiyuan Ning contributed equally. Code: this https URL. Data: this https URL
summary: In AI for Science scenarios, experimental design and method reproduction require retrieving protocols that satisfy multiple interdependent constraints, yet existing benchmarks lack systematic evaluation of this capability. To address this gap, we introduce ProSearch, a benchmark for multi-constraint protocol retrieval in experimental science. ProSearch has three key features: (1) realism, with queries grounded in real experimental records and expert-defined templates; (2) complexity, with 60 experimental fields and their dependencies; and (3) diagnosticity, with 3-5 explicit constraints per query, including numerical and negation constraints. We construct ProSearch through LLM-based extraction, data-driven constraint selection, controlled query generation, and evidence-based relevance validation. The resulting benchmark contains 1,515 queries across six experimental science domains. We conduct extensive experiments on ProSearch with 19 representative retrievers and complementary analyses. The best-performing retriever achieves an average nDCG@10 of only 0.290, which improves to 0.474 with reranking. Structured diagnostic analysis shows that explicit constraint matching provides a strong ranking signal, while manual error analysis identifies joint constraint binding as a key bottleneck. ProSearch provides a testbed for systematically evaluating scientific retrieval systems.

AI.tldr: ProSearch is a benchmark of 1,515 queries for multi-constraint protocol retrieval across six experimental science domains, where the best of 19 retrievers reaches an average nDCG@10 of only 0.290, rising to 0.474 with reranking.
AI.motivation: Experimental design and method reproduction in AI for Science require retrieving protocols that satisfy several interdependent constraints, but existing benchmarks do not systematically evaluate this capability.
AI.method: The benchmark is built through LLM-based extraction, data-driven constraint selection, controlled query generation and evidence-based relevance validation. Queries are grounded in real experimental records and expert-defined templates, span 60 experimental fields with their dependencies, and carry 3-5 explicit constraints, including numerical and negation constraints.
AI.result: The best of 19 representative retrievers achieves an average nDCG@10 of 0.290, improving to 0.474 with reranking. Explicit constraint matching is a strong ranking signal, and manual error analysis identifies joint constraint binding as the key bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: ProSearch provides a testbed for systematically evaluating scientific retrieval systems, and its results point to joint constraint binding as the main obstacle for current retrievers.

title: Distilling Knowledge from Search: Decoder Model Factory for Quantum LDPC Codes
summary: We introduce GraphMP, a learning-based message-passing decoder for quantum low-density parity-check codes that transfers without fine-tuning across code families, code sizes, physical error rates, and noise models. GraphMP uses local message passing to keep computation scalable as the decoding graph grows. Guided by its predictions, beam search progressively refines candidate error patterns, trading additional decoding time for lower logical error rates. We develop the decoder model factory as a paradigm for training successive models on experience generated by earlier models during decoding. Model-guided search supplies verified trajectories for knowledge distillation, folding computation spent on decoding into reusable training data. Repeated collection and distillation improve the decoder across generations and adapt its strategy as the noise changes. These results motivate a coupled quantum--classical architecture with two interacting cycles: rapid decoding protects quantum information, while slower learning renews the models from operating experience. The long-term vision is a scalable decoder model factory that produces high-performance, low-latency decoders and continually adapts them to evolving quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: GraphMP is a learning-based message-passing decoder for quantum LDPC codes that transfers across code families, code sizes, physical error rates and noise models without fine-tuning, and it is combined with beam search and repeated distillation in a decoder model factory.
AI.motivation: Decoders for quantum LDPC codes must scale as decoding graphs grow and keep adapting as noise changes, and the paper seeks to turn computation spent during decoding into reusable training data.
AI.method: GraphMP uses local message passing, and beam search guided by its predictions refines candidate error patterns, trading extra decoding time for lower logical error rates. The decoder model factory trains successive models on verified trajectories generated by earlier models during decoding, through knowledge distillation over repeated collection and distillation rounds.
AI.result: The abstract reports that the decoder transfers without fine-tuning across code families, code sizes, physical error rates and noise models, and that repeated collection and distillation improve it across generations and adapt its strategy as noise changes, without giving numerical results.
AI.conclusion: The authors propose a coupled quantum-classical architecture with a fast decoding cycle and a slower learning cycle, with the long-term goal of a scalable decoder model factory that adapts to evolving quantum hardware.

title: When Safety Checks Become Privacy Risks: A Privacy-Preserving Paradigm for LLM Agent Safety Auditing
summary: Large language model agents interact with online services through tool calls that may access private data or perform sensitive actions. Specialized providers can supply and maintain pre-execution safety auditing capabilities for agent operators. However, sending task descriptions, call arguments, and interaction histories to an external auditor may expose sensitive user information.
