In this work, we propose a paradigm for privacy-preserving safety auditing that separates delegated audit computation from plaintext access and execution authority. Grounded in a three-domain auditing model, the paradigm connects trusted representation construction, encrypted audit computation, and trusted decision and execution through explicit interfaces. These interfaces accommodate alternative representations and scorers, while encrypted computation protects audit inputs from a semi-honest auditor. We instantiate this paradigm in SealCall, a framework combining learned audit representations, CKKS-based encrypted similarity computation, and execution control bound to audited tool calls. Evaluated on 1,252 public binary candidates, SealCall achieves a mean F1 score of 0.840 under grouped nested evaluation, while preserving plaintext audit decisions in all measured cases. A representative configuration completes each encrypted scoring operation in 0.176 s.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a privacy-preserving paradigm for pre-execution safety auditing of LLM agent tool calls, instantiated as SealCall, which uses CKKS encrypted similarity computation and reaches a mean F1 of 0.840 on 1,252 public binary candidates.
AI.motivation: Sending task descriptions, call arguments and interaction histories to an external safety auditor may expose sensitive user information, so outsourced auditing conflicts with privacy.
AI.method: The paradigm separates delegated audit computation from plaintext access and execution authority, connecting trusted representation construction, encrypted audit computation and trusted decision and execution through explicit interfaces. SealCall combines learned audit representations, CKKS-based encrypted similarity computation and execution control bound to audited tool calls, and protects audit inputs from a semi-honest auditor.
AI.result: On 1,252 public binary candidates, SealCall achieves a mean F1 of 0.840 under grouped nested evaluation and preserves plaintext audit decisions in all measured cases. A representative configuration completes each encrypted scoring operation in 0.176 s.
AI.conclusion: The paradigm shows that safety auditing of LLM agents can be delegated to an external auditor without exposing plaintext inputs to it, while decisions and execution stay under trusted control.

title: BlindToChange: AI Agents Can Find Changes When Asked But Do They Look When Needed?
summary: Given that AI agents can search the web broadly and deeply in real time, it is tempting to conclude that their outputs account for recent world events. We show that this conclusion does not hold in practice. While agents can search and easily find recent changes, the correctness of their responses depends on whether they search and what they search for. Popular agentic search benchmarks like BrowseComp cannot expose failures wherein agents do not recognize their own assumptions that should be verified, since these benchmarks explicitly state what needs to be found. In contrast, many user requests state only the final information need (e.g., an itinerary for a trip), leaving the agent to discover relevant changes (e.g., the temporary closure of a museum) and account for their consequences. To highlight such gaps, we introduce BlindToChange, a benchmark that measures whether agents proactively discover recent events that affect their responses. Our benchmark comprises requests for recommendations where an obvious candidate is no longer applicable due to a recent real-world event. These events are drawn automatically from Wikidata, allowing BlindToChange to be periodically refreshed. Strikingly, we find a big gap -- as high as 27.5 points, even at high reasoning effort -- in systems' performance, when the recent event is not explicitly mentioned compared to when we ask about it directly. Analyzing search trajectories, we learn that more than half of the failures can be attributed to the fact that agents do not directly search to verify whether a relevant fact has changed. Our benchmark highlights, and tracks, a new axis of progress, wherein systems account for recent information that is not explicitly mentioned in the user request.

AI.tldr: BlindToChange is a benchmark showing that AI search agents often fail to proactively discover recent real-world events that invalidate an obvious recommendation, with performance gaps of up to 27.5 points when the event is not mentioned in the request compared with when it is asked about directly.
AI.motivation: Benchmarks such as BrowseComp state explicitly what must be found, so they cannot reveal whether agents recognize their own unstated assumptions that need verification, while many real user requests leave that discovery to the agent.
AI.method: The authors build requests for recommendations where an obvious candidate is no longer applicable because of a recent event, with events drawn automatically from Wikidata so the benchmark can be refreshed periodically. They compare performance when the event is explicitly mentioned against when it is not, and analyze search trajectories.
AI.result: The gap reaches 27.5 points even at high reasoning effort when the event is not explicitly mentioned. More than half of the failures are attributed to agents not directly searching to verify whether a relevant fact has changed.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark highlights a new axis of progress, namely whether systems account for recent information that the user request does not explicitly mention.

title: KEEPER: Learning Control-Sufficient Textual Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Recursive textual memory can carry earlier errors into later updates, yet task performance alone does not establish memory reliability. We define self-consistency bias as the persistence of incorrect claims already present in the incoming memory. We present KEEPER, a comparative analysis of four auxiliary objectives along information-content and update-sensitivity axes within a shared recursive interface, examining how supervision targets relate to agent performance. Among evaluated conditions, reward-related prediction achieve the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning, outperforming joint supervision. A claim-level analysis of one baseline trajectory documents error persistence despite corrective observations. Together, these analyses motivate evaluating error persistence and valid-information retention alongside task outcomes.

AI.tldr: KEEPER compares four auxiliary objectives for recursive textual memory in long-horizon LLM agents and finds that reward-related prediction gives the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning, while error persistence in memory remains a concern.
AI.motivation: Recursive textual memory can carry earlier errors into later updates, and task performance alone does not establish memory reliability, so the paper defines self-consistency bias as the persistence of incorrect claims already present in the incoming memory.
AI.method: Within a shared recursive interface, the authors compare four auxiliary objectives along information-content and update-sensitivity axes and examine how each supervision target relates to agent performance. A claim-level analysis of one baseline trajectory documents how errors persist.
AI.result: Reward-related prediction achieves the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning, outperforming joint supervision. The claim-level analysis documents error persistence despite corrective observations.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that error persistence and valid-information retention should be evaluated alongside task outcomes when assessing textual memory in agents.

title: Sparse Text Diffusion under Dual Budgets: Context Connectivity and Expert Activation
summary: Long-context diffusion repeatedly pays for both token interaction and feed-forward computation. We formulate these costs as two separate budgets: the edges available to an attention graph and the experts activated for each token. This view connects local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming that sparsity alone preserves document-level information. We specify normalized masked attention, distinguish denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derive graph and compute bounds. A reported sparse-expert configuration, denoted DualBudget, is analyzed across scientific summarization, multi-hop question answering, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction. All supplied table measurements are retained. The length study shows gains over the listed baselines through 16K, together with measurable degradation as length increases. Ablations reveal mixed changes across the three reported scores, while the cost record indicates a 20% reduction relative to DiffuSeq under an unspecified timing convention. The analysis separates these observations from unmeasured claims about training speed, absorbing states, global coherence, and deployment memory.

AI.tldr: DualBudget is a sparse text diffusion model that separates attention-edge and expert-activation budgets for long-context generation, with the abstract reporting gains over the listed baselines through 16K length and a 20% cost reduction relative to DiffuSeq under an unspecified timing convention.
AI.motivation: Long-context diffusion models repeatedly pay for both token interaction and feed-forward computation, and sparsity alone is not assumed to preserve document-level information.
AI.method: The paper treats the two costs as separate budgets, the edges available to an attention graph and the experts activated per token, and connects local, dilated and global attention with conditional expert computation. It specifies normalized masked attention, distinguishes denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derives graph and compute bounds.
AI.result: DualBudget is evaluated on scientific summarization, multi-hop question answering, dialogue and sentence-pair prediction. It shows gains over the listed baselines through 16K and measurable degradation as length increases, ablations show mixed changes across the three reported scores, and the cost record indicates a 20% reduction relative to DiffuSeq under an unspecified timing convention.
AI.conclusion: The reported measurements support the gains within the stated length range, while claims about training speed, absorbing states, global coherence and deployment memory are not measured.

title: Qistas: A Pre-Registered, Portable Protocol for Fairness Evaluation of Large Language Models
comment: 19 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Protocol paper; no model results. Pre-registration: this https URL. Reference implementation: this https URL
summary: Fairness benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) are overwhelmingly English-born and American in their social categories; translated versions carry those categories into societies where they do not apply, and almost none fix their hypotheses before the models are run. We present Qistas (Arabic qistas, "the just balance"), a protocol for evaluating how LLMs treat the social, confessional, and regional constituencies of a society, portable across countries and instantiated first for Iraq. In its pilot form it measures only what needs no verdict on contested truth: procedural symmetry across matched counterfactual pairs, differential refusal, stereotype reliance under ambiguity, and terminological framing of documented events. Every measurement is paired by construction and analysed with paired machinery (sign-flip permutation tests, exact McNemar tests, template-clustered bootstrap intervals, Holm-corrected families), with a power analysis that states, before any data exist, the smallest effect each axis can detect after the design effect of template clustering. We release the authoring apparatus (a pruned 3x5 taxonomy with four cells closed by design, per-type checklists, a cumulative rulings log, a structural audit, and a human review notebook) and report its first field test: a semantic review of a 58-item seed bank in which 24 of 25 template groups failed at least one check. The defect patterns it exposed (evaluation criteria leaking into prompts, token-level swaps that break Arabic agreement, epistemically unbalanced pairs, single-theme refusal probes, unwritten dialect twins counted as coverage) are, we argue, general hazards of counterfactual fairness benchmarks. This is a protocol paper, not a results paper: no model has been evaluated, and the accompanying pre-registration commits the hypotheses, metrics, exclusion rules, and analysis plan that the pilot will follow.

AI.tldr: Qistas is a pre-registered, portable protocol for evaluating how LLMs treat a society's social, confessional and regional groups, instantiated first for Iraq; this paper reports the protocol and a pilot field test of its authoring apparatus, with no model evaluated.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM fairness benchmarks are overwhelmingly English-born and American in their social categories, translated versions carry those categories into societies where they do not apply, and almost none fix their hypotheses before the models are run.
AI.method: The pilot protocol measures procedural symmetry across matched counterfactual pairs, differential refusal, stereotype reliance under ambiguity and terminological framing of documented events. Measurements are paired by construction and analyzed with sign-flip permutation tests, exact McNemar tests, template-clustered bootstrap intervals and Holm correction, with a power analysis fixed before data exist. The authors release the authoring apparatus, including a pruned 3x5 taxonomy, per-type checklists, a rulings log, a structural audit and a human review notebook.
AI.result: In a semantic review of a 58-item seed bank, 24 of 25 template groups failed at least one check. The exposed defect patterns include evaluation criteria leaking into prompts, token-level swaps that break Arabic agreement, epistemically unbalanced pairs, single-theme refusal probes and unwritten dialect twins counted as coverage.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue these defect patterns are general hazards of counterfactual fairness benchmarks, and the pre-registration commits the hypotheses, metrics, exclusion rules and analysis plan that the pilot will follow.

title: CoFiBreak: A Coarse-to-Fine Diversity Reward for Effective Multi-Turn Jailbreak
comment: 10 pages main text, 24 pages total, 8 figures, 12 tables
summary: Automated red teaming trains an attacker large language model (LLM) to elicit harmful responses from a victim LLM, but reinforcement learning can collapse attackers onto a narrow set of prompts when attack success is the only reward. Such a collapse of attack diversity can bias safety evaluation toward repeatedly testing near-duplicate attack patterns rather than the underlying harmful intents. Existing methods often trade off attack success or inference cost for greater content or strategy diversity. We propose CoFiBreak, a coarse-to-fine diversity reward for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) that improves attack diversity while preserving strong attack effectiveness and low inference cost. The coarse reward broadens which strategies the attacker uses by encouraging strategies underrepresented within each GRPO group, while the fine reward broadens how those strategies are realized by discouraging reuse of the same personas, framings, and output formats after harmful-intent information is removed from prompt embeddings. Diversity rewards apply only to attacks that already exceed an effectiveness threshold, so diversity cannot be gained through ineffective attacks. Since both rewards are computed only during training, CoFiBreak also retains inference efficiency. Trained with Llama3.1-8B-Instruct as the victim, CoFiBreak discovers 1.6-2.0x as many distinct successful fine-grained strategies as the strongest baseline across frontier victims on HarmBench. It reaches 98.8% ASR@10 (attack success rate with 10 generations per intent) on AdvBench with the highest diversity score among all compared methods, which is 2.1x that of the strongest-attacking baseline. The resulting attacks transfer to unseen frontier LLMs, reaching 71.0% ASR@10 on AdvBench with the unseen victim Claude-Opus-4.6. The code will be released.

AI.tldr: CoFiBreak is a coarse-to-fine diversity reward for GRPO-trained red-teaming attackers that discovers more distinct successful jailbreak strategies than the strongest baseline while keeping attack success high and inference cost low.
AI.motivation: RL-trained automated red teamers can collapse onto a narrow set of prompts when attack success is the only reward, which biases safety evaluation toward near-duplicate attack patterns rather than the underlying harmful intents.
AI.method: CoFiBreak adds a coarse reward that favors strategies underrepresented within each GRPO group and a fine reward that discourages reuse of the same personas, framings and output formats after harmful-intent information is removed from prompt embeddings. Diversity rewards apply only to attacks above an effectiveness threshold and are computed only during training.
AI.result: Trained with Llama3.1-8B-Instruct as the victim, CoFiBreak finds 1.6-2.0x as many distinct successful fine-grained strategies as the strongest baseline on HarmBench across frontier victims. On AdvBench it reaches 98.8% ASR@10 with the highest diversity score, 2.1x that of the strongest-attacking baseline, and its attacks transfer to the unseen victim Claude-Opus-4.6 at 71.0% ASR@10.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest that diversity-aware training can broaden red-teaming coverage without sacrificing attack effectiveness or inference efficiency, and the code will be released.

title: Adaptive Personalization Under Preference Epistemic Uncertainty
summary: Human preferences change over time: an established preference may remain valid over time, become uncertain as context shifts, or be explicitly revised. Effective personalization requires conversational AI to adapt its response strategy to evolving preferences rather than relying on passive memory retrieval. We formalize this capability as adaptive personalization under epistemic uncertainty. A human preference study further confirms that people favor state-contingent response strategies as preference uncertainty changes. To evaluate whether language models mirror this adaptation, we create a multilingual benchmark spanning 250 personas, 5 languages, and 25K conversational turns that decouples strategy selection from response execution. Across eight closed- and open-weight models, we uncover a recognition-generation gap: models reliably identify appropriate strategies when selecting among candidate options, but collapse during open-ended generation, suffering a 35-46% drop in strategy calibration. Crucially, this failure is systematic: models default to exploit-first behavior, over-relying on existing preferences regardless of preference epistemic uncertainty. We show this failure is addressable: while prompting interventions fail, targeted training that supervises models' internal strategy representations toward state-conditional human preferences narrows the user acceptability generalization gap by a third on out-of-distribution personas and conversational styles.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes adaptive personalization under preference epistemic uncertainty and shows that LLMs select appropriate response strategies when given candidate options but collapse during open-ended generation, with a 35-46% drop in strategy calibration; targeted training narrows the acceptability gap by a third on out-of-distribution personas.
AI.motivation: Conversational AI needs to adapt its response strategy as preferences evolve rather than relying on passive memory retrieval, but it is unclear whether language models mirror the state-contingent adaptation that people show.
AI.method: The authors formalize adaptive personalization under epistemic uncertainty and run a human preference study. They build a multilingual benchmark with 250 personas, 5 languages and 25K conversational turns that decouples strategy selection from response execution, and evaluate eight closed- and open-weight models. They also train models to supervise internal strategy representations toward state-conditional human preferences.
AI.result: Models reliably identify appropriate strategies among candidate options but collapse during open-ended generation, with a 35-46% drop in strategy calibration, defaulting to exploit-first behavior. Prompting interventions fail, while the targeted training narrows the user acceptability generalization gap by a third on out-of-distribution personas and conversational styles.
AI.conclusion: The recognition-generation gap is systematic but addressable, and supervising internal strategy representations offers a route beyond prompting.

title: Better Retrievers, Worse Labels: How Incomplete Relevance Judgments Distort Abstention Evaluation in Conversational RAG
summary: Conversational RAG benchmarks such as MTRAG and RETECO evaluate retrieval and generation end to end: each system answers from its own retrieval, so abstention must be scored against whether each retrieved context is sufficient. A convenient shortcut reads sufficiency off the relevance judgments and treats a context without gold documents as unanswerable. We re-run the official baselines exactly and test this shortcut on RECOR (RETECO track~2) with four retrievers (nDCG@10 from .18 to .59) and three Qwen3 readers. Two open LLM judges and a panel of four small open models label each context by content, and a model of another family audits 250 contexts blind, with adjudication. The stronger the retriever, the larger the share of no-gold contexts that still contain the answer (28\% to 72\%) and the lower the shortcut's precision (.68 to .10; .70 to .21 under the audit). A reader agrees: Qwen3-4B answers 62--67\% of these false misses correctly, against 23--30\% of no-gold contexts judged insufficient and 1\% with no documents. In most false misses, the answer comes from a hard negative mined for the same question, another turn's gold or a neighbouring chunk of the gold page. On MTRAG, whose judgments come from annotators, precision drops from .72 to .50. Under the shortcut, answerability AUROC is up to .19 too low, and the best sufficiency detector appears to be a retrieval score that never reads the documents. We release code, runs and labels, and recommend scoring refusals against content labels, not the presence of gold.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that scoring abstention in conversational RAG by the presence of gold documents misclassifies many answerable contexts, with the shortcut's precision falling from .68 to .10 as retrievers get stronger on RECOR, and recommends scoring refusals against content labels instead.
AI.motivation: Conversational RAG benchmarks score abstention against whether each retrieved context is sufficient, and a common shortcut treats a context without gold documents as unanswerable without testing that assumption.
AI.method: The authors re-run official baselines and test the shortcut on RECOR with four retrievers (nDCG@10 from .18 to .59) and three Qwen3 readers. Two open LLM judges and a panel of four small open models label each context by content, and a model from another family audits 250 contexts blind, with adjudication.
AI.result: The stronger the retriever, the larger the share of no-gold contexts that still contain the answer (28% to 72%) and the lower the shortcut's precision (.68 to .10; .70 to .21 under the audit). Qwen3-4B answers 62-67% of these false misses correctly, against 23-30% of no-gold contexts judged insufficient and 1% with no documents. On MTRAG, precision drops from .72 to .50, and under the shortcut answerability AUROC is up to .19 too low.
AI.conclusion: Refusals should be scored against content labels rather than the presence of gold documents, and the best sufficiency detector found appears to be a retrieval score that never reads the documents; code, runs and labels are released.

title: Do Open Language Models Invent Scripture? BILAL-BENCH: Benchmarking Islamic-Source Fabrication in Bengali
comment: 15 pages, 6 tables. Accepted at the 7th Muslims in ML (MusIML) Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. Code and dataset: this https URL
summary: When a language model invents a Qur'anic verse or hadith, it gives false authority to text that readers may treat as sacred. Existing Islamic hallucination benchmarks are largely Arabic and often closed-ended, while Bengali resources mainly study general-domain hallucination or factual knowledge. We introduce BILAL-BENCH, a 240-question expert-verified benchmark for open-ended Islamic-source fabrication in Bengali. It covers Qur'anic attribution, hadith, fiqh, contemporary issues, and adversarial false-premise prompts, and uses a two-axis rubric that separates source errors from assertiveness. We evaluate seven open-weight models from 1B to 120B on 1,680 double-annotated responses. Six of the seven models confidently fabricate on 79.3-95.3% of source-production questions, with no monotonic improvement from scale. Hadith provenance is the weakest category across models: only two of 315 responses are correct and correctly sourced. The two 8B BanglaLLaMA variants have similar confident-fabrication rates but different error profiles. Models vary far more in whether they withhold a claim they cannot support than in source accuracy: appropriate abstention or false-premise correction ranges from 6 to 46 responses across the benchmark, and does not track parameter count.

AI.tldr: BILAL-BENCH is a 240-question expert-verified benchmark for open-ended Islamic-source fabrication in Bengali, in which six of seven open-weight models confidently fabricate sources on 79.3-95.3% of source-production questions.
AI.motivation: Models that invent Qur'anic verses or hadith lend false authority to sacred text, yet existing Islamic hallucination benchmarks are largely Arabic and often closed-ended, while Bengali resources mainly study general-domain hallucination or factual knowledge.
AI.method: The benchmark covers Qur'anic attribution, hadith, fiqh, contemporary issues and adversarial false-premise prompts, and uses a two-axis rubric that separates source errors from assertiveness. Seven open-weight models from 1B to 120B are evaluated on 1,680 double-annotated responses.
AI.result: Six of seven models confidently fabricate on 79.3-95.3% of source-production questions, with no monotonic improvement from scale. Hadith provenance is the weakest category, with only two of 315 responses correct and correctly sourced. Appropriate abstention or false-premise correction ranges from 6 to 46 responses across the benchmark and does not track parameter count.
AI.conclusion: Models differ far more in whether they withhold unsupported claims than in source accuracy, so abstention behavior appears to be a separate axis from factual sourcing.

title: Language Models Show Conformity Bias in RAG: When the Majority Endorses a Poisoned Claim
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can expose language models to misleading evidence in retrieved documents. We investigate whether increasing the number of mutually agreeing poisoned documents affects a model's ability to detect misinformation. We evaluate 200 randomly selected questions from SciFact (random seed 38), comparing contexts with one poisoned and six healthy documents against contexts with six mutually agreeing poisoned documents and one healthy document. For Gemma-3-12b, poison-detection rates decrease from 25% (50/200) in the minority condition to 10% (20/200) in the majority condition. Among the 38 questions with different outcomes across conditions, 34 change from detected to undetected, while only four change in the opposite direction (exact McNemar test, p = 6.04e-7). This pattern is consistent with a conformity-like response to a majority of mutually agreeing poisoned documents. Our results provide initial evidence of conformity bias in RAG-based misinformation detection: Gemma-3-12b is substantially less likely to detect poisoned claims when they dominate the retrieved evidence.

AI.tldr: Gemma-3-12b detects poisoned claims less often when six mutually agreeing poisoned documents dominate the retrieved context than when one poisoned document is outnumbered by six healthy ones, which the authors interpret as conformity bias in RAG on SciFact.
AI.motivation: RAG can expose language models to misleading retrieved evidence, and it was unknown whether a majority of mutually agreeing poisoned documents impairs their ability to detect misinformation.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 200 randomly selected SciFact questions (random seed 38), comparing contexts with one poisoned and six healthy documents against contexts with six mutually agreeing poisoned documents and one healthy document, and test the paired outcomes with an exact McNemar test.
AI.result: For Gemma-3-12b, poison-detection rates fall from 25% (50/200) in the minority condition to 10% (20/200) in the majority condition. Of 38 questions with differing outcomes, 34 change from detected to undetected and four change in the opposite direction (p = 6.04e-7).
AI.conclusion: The results provide initial evidence of conformity-like bias in RAG-based misinformation detection, although the evidence comes from a single model and a single dataset.

title: EDU-Jev Training System-One Decision Models for Education
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Work in progress
summary: Many automated decisions in education involve choosing from a fixed set of options: assigning a rubric score, checking whether an answer meets a marking criterion, or identifying the first wrong step in a solution. Generative language models are increasingly used to make these decisions, but their responses require parsing, longer outputs increase inference costs, and confidence expressed in words does not necessarily reflect the probability of being correct. We present EDU-Jev, a family of single-pass ("System One") decision models at 0.8B, 2B and 4B parameters. Given an assessment context and a question with predefined answer options, the model returns a probability distribution over those options without generating text. A pointer head scores a marker for each option, ensuring the predictions are restricted to the allowed choices. Training uses a single supervised stage with soft cross-entropy against the available target label distributions; calibration is assessed empirically. Across twelve education benchmarks, EDU-Jev 4B achieves an average accuracy of 67.6%, exceeding the strongest of five commercial decision APIs by 9.4 percentage points and the best open 4B decision model by 18.7 points. On four cross-domain education sets, it matches the strongest API, which remains ahead on general decision-making and reasoning tasks. The 2B model processes about 150 decisions per second on a single H100 GPU.

AI.tldr: EDU-Jev is a family of single-pass 0.8B, 2B and 4B decision models for education that output a probability distribution over fixed options without generating text, and EDU-Jev 4B averages 67.6% accuracy across twelve benchmarks, 9.4 points above the strongest of five commercial decision APIs.
AI.motivation: Automated educational decisions choose among fixed options, but generative models require output parsing, longer outputs raise inference cost, and verbal confidence does not necessarily reflect the probability of being correct.
AI.method: A pointer head scores a marker for each predefined option, restricting predictions to the allowed choices. Training uses a single supervised stage with soft cross-entropy against the available target label distributions, and calibration is assessed empirically.
AI.result: Across twelve education benchmarks, EDU-Jev 4B averages 67.6% accuracy, exceeding the strongest of five commercial decision APIs by 9.4 points and the best open 4B decision model by 18.7 points. On four cross-domain education sets it matches the strongest API, which stays ahead on general decision-making and reasoning tasks. The 2B model processes about 150 decisions per second on a single H100 GPU.
AI.conclusion: Single-pass option-scoring models can be competitive for educational decisions at low latency, although they do not surpass commercial APIs on general decision-making and reasoning tasks.

title: Language Models Show a "Women-Are-Wonderful" Effect in Blame Attribution That is Not Just Leniency
summary: This paper investigates the Women-Are-Wonderful (WaW) effect in language-model blame attribution: a favorable bias in which women receive more positive evaluations than men. Using 11,270 interpersonal conflicts from r/AmItheAsshole, we construct matched counterfactuals that vary the gender of the person being judged (the original poster) and the person affected (the counter-party). Across four language models, gender changes a minority of verdicts, but those changes consistently favor women. The effect is strongly role-dependent. Making the original poster a woman reduces the odds of blame by 9--52%, while making the counter-party a woman multiplies them by 2.7--9.2X. Counter-party WaW also varies across conflict types, strengthening in communication and relationship conflicts and weakening in family conflicts. Exploratory probes suggest that counter-party gender can shift judgments of sympathy, reasonableness, harm and protection. WaW is therefore not just leniency toward women being judged: models also judge conduct more harshly when it affects a woman.

AI.tldr: Across four language models, judging blame in r/AmItheAsshole conflicts shows a Women-Are-Wonderful effect: the gender changes that do occur favor women, and making the counter-party a woman multiplies the odds of blame by 2.7-9.2x.
AI.motivation: Whether the favorable bias toward women in language-model blame attribution reflects leniency toward the person being judged, or something broader, is unclear.
AI.method: The authors use 11,270 interpersonal conflicts from r/AmItheAsshole and build matched counterfactuals that vary the gender of the original poster and of the counter-party across four language models, with exploratory probes of sympathy, reasonableness, harm and protection.
AI.result: Gender changes a minority of verdicts, but those changes consistently favor women. Making the original poster a woman reduces the odds of blame by 9-52%, while making the counter-party a woman multiplies them by 2.7-9.2x. Counter-party effects are stronger in communication and relationship conflicts and weaker in family conflicts.
AI.conclusion: The effect is strongly role-dependent, and models judge conduct more harshly when it affects a woman, so the Women-Are-Wonderful effect is not just leniency toward women being judged.

title: HyperRepair: Recovering Forgotten General Capabilities of Fine-Tuned Language Models
summary: Fine-tuning improves a language model's performance in a target domain but can weaken its general capabilities. Existing methods often face a trade-off between general capabilities and domain specialization, making it difficult to preserve both. We introduce HyperRepair, a framework for recovering general capabilities while retaining domain specialization at only inference cost. To make recovery generalizable across models sharing a pretrained backbone, HyperRepair learns a hypernetwork from repairs trained on source models. The hypernetwork uses activation fingerprints that summarize changes from the pretrained backbone to generate a tailored Repairing Side Net (RSN), whose prompt-conditioned gate applies corrections selectively. This enables recovery on models from unseen adaptation domains without target-domain examples or additional optimization. We evaluate HyperRpair across two model families, 12 LoRA adaptation datasets, and 15 general benchmarks. On the default split, HyperRepair achieves 93.4% of the base models' average general score while retaining 99.5% of the fine-tuned models' average domain score.

AI.tldr: HyperRepair uses a hypernetwork trained on repairs from source models to generate a tailored repair side network from activation fingerprints, recovering general capabilities of fine-tuned language models while retaining 99.5% of their domain score, without target-domain examples.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning improves target-domain performance but can weaken general capabilities, and existing methods face a trade-off between general capabilities and domain specialization that makes it hard to preserve both.
AI.method: A hypernetwork is learned from repairs trained on source models. It takes activation fingerprints summarizing changes from the pretrained backbone and generates a Repairing Side Net whose prompt-conditioned gate applies corrections selectively, enabling recovery on unseen adaptation domains at inference cost only.
AI.result: On the default split, across two model families, 12 LoRA adaptation datasets and 15 general benchmarks, HyperRepair achieves 93.4% of the base models' average general score while retaining 99.5% of the fine-tuned models' average domain score.
AI.conclusion: The approach recovers general capabilities across models that share a pretrained backbone without additional optimization or target-domain examples, while preserving most of the domain specialization.

title: S2TDR: Structured Multimodal Reconstruction for Sticker-Aware Dialogue Understanding
summary: Stickers are widely used in social media dialogues to express affect, stance, and intent beyond literal text. Their meanings are often non-literal and context-dependent, making them difficult to handle with generic visual fusion or standalone captioning. We propose Sticker-to-Text Dialogue Reconstruction (S2TDR), a structured multimodal reconstruction framework that converts sticker turns into contextually appropriate textual utterances. S2TDR decomposes sticker interpretation into visual cue extraction, affective-intent inference, and context-aware dialogue reconstruction, using OCR text only as an auxiliary cue when available. The reconstructed dialogue can then be consumed by existing text-based dialogue models. Experiments on sentiment analysis, intent recognition, and dialogue summarization show that S2TDR generally improves multiple downstream models over direct sticker integration methods. Further analyses on component ablations, OCR-empty stickers, and reconstruction quality indicate that structured reconstruction provides an interpretable and effective way to integrate sticker semantics into dialogue understanding.

AI.tldr: S2TDR reconstructs sticker-bearing dialogue turns into textual utterances through visual cue extraction, affective-intent inference and context-aware reconstruction, so that existing text-based dialogue models can consume them, and it generally improves several downstream models over direct sticker integration.
AI.motivation: Stickers express affect, stance and intent in non-literal, context-dependent ways, which generic visual fusion or standalone captioning struggles to handle.
AI.method: S2TDR decomposes sticker interpretation into visual cue extraction, affective-intent inference and context-aware dialogue reconstruction, using OCR text only as an auxiliary cue when available. The reconstructed dialogue is then consumed by existing text-based dialogue models.
AI.result: Experiments on sentiment analysis, intent recognition and dialogue summarization show that S2TDR generally improves multiple downstream models over direct sticker integration methods. Component ablations, OCR-empty stickers and reconstruction quality are analyzed.
AI.conclusion: Structured reconstruction offers an interpretable and effective way to integrate sticker semantics into dialogue understanding.

title: TraceSpec: Understanding and Improving Speculative Decoding for LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents execute tasks through repeated model calls over evolving histories of reasoning, actions, and tool feedback. Aggregate speculative-decoding metrics merge these distinct decisions, providing limited guidance on where draft supervision is needed. We present TraceSpec, a framework connecting trajectory evaluation with adaptive draft training. It combines dynamic execution with fixed-prefix replay and introduces TraceSpec-Traj, a corpus of 10,000 training states and 2,500 test states spanning browsing and software engineering. Analysis of five speculative baselines reveals that aggregate acceptance can rise with context length while declining within matched late browsing actions. Workload and phase further distinguish these trends, motivating supervision guided by trajectory conditions. TraceSpec trains on intermediate assistant turns and allocates a fixed prediction budget using state-conditioned estimates of prefix-aware acceptance gaps. Across three target sizes and two temperatures, it improves replay throughput by 12.5% to 22.6% over its DSpark base. Qwen3-4B ablations show that adaptive allocation increases accepted length by 3.3% to 10.0% over fixed full-turn supervision, with additional comparisons substantiating the roles of state conditioning and consecutive-token agreement. The resulting evaluation resources, trajectory findings, and training strategy connect the analysis of agent execution to practical draft improvement.

AI.tldr: TraceSpec connects trajectory-level evaluation with adaptive draft training for speculative decoding in LLM agents, allocating a fixed prediction budget by state-conditioned prefix-aware acceptance gaps and improving replay throughput by 12.5% to 22.6% over its DSpark base.
AI.motivation: Aggregate speculative-decoding metrics merge distinct agent decisions made over evolving histories of reasoning, actions and tool feedback, giving limited guidance on where draft supervision is needed.
AI.method: TraceSpec combines dynamic execution with fixed-prefix replay and introduces TraceSpec-Traj, a corpus of 10,000 training states and 2,500 test states spanning browsing and software engineering. It trains on intermediate assistant turns and allocates a fixed prediction budget using state-conditioned estimates of prefix-aware acceptance gaps.
AI.result: Across three target sizes and two temperatures, TraceSpec improves replay throughput by 12.5% to 22.6% over its DSpark base. On Qwen3-4B, adaptive allocation increases accepted length by 3.3% to 10.0% over fixed full-turn supervision. Analysis of five speculative baselines shows that aggregate acceptance can rise with context length while declining within matched late browsing actions.
AI.conclusion: The evaluation resources, trajectory findings and training strategy connect the analysis of agent execution to practical draft improvement, and supervision guided by trajectory conditions is motivated.

title: Beyond Response Scoring: An AI-aware Cognitive Supervision Framework for Automated Mathematical Short Answer Grading
summary: Transformer-based language models have achieved remarkable success in automated short answer grading (ASAG). However, current methods in ASAG struggle to comprehend, reason about and evaluate complex mathematical answers involving symbols and formulas. These score-only methods fail to generalize across diverse responses and skill states associated with identical scores. Moreover, they ignore the potential upward bias introduced by generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) usage in assessing students' performance and knowledge mastery. To address these limitations, we propose AICG (AI-aware Cognitive-supervised Grading), a two-branch multi-task framework. The first branch combines RoBERTa-based regression, ordinal, and classification heads for individual-answer grading. The second branch uses an expert-designed Q-matrix to associate responses with assessed skills and jointly predicts G-DINA-derived skill mastery and learning gain. Through the shared encoder, these skill-level targets provide cognitive supervision for answer grading beyond score labels. AICG further uses a Gen-AI detector, trained through supervised contrastive pretraining followed by linear classification, to estimate assistance probabilities and convert them into reliability weights, attenuating unreliable cognitive evidence during learning assessment. We conduct experiments on 49,402 instructor-graded responses spanning 19 academic semesters. Relative to RoBERTa regression, AICG reduces mean absolute error (MAE) by 50.3% and improves quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) from 0.798 to 0.927. Ablations identify Q-matrix-guided cognitive supervision as the primary source of improvement, while AI-aware weighting further reduces overall MAE by 4.2% over the unweighted cognitive model and consistently improves MAE and QWK across the four most recent post-Gen-AI semesters.

AI.tldr: AICG is a two-branch multi-task framework for mathematical short answer grading that adds cognitive supervision from a Q-matrix and G-DINA skill-mastery targets plus an AI-usage reliability weight, reducing MAE by 50.3% relative to RoBERTa regression and raising QWK from 0.798 to 0.927.
AI.motivation: Score-only transformer grading struggles with complex mathematical answers involving symbols and formulas, fails to generalize across responses and skill states that share the same score, and ignores the upward bias introduced by generative AI use.
AI.method: A RoBERTa-based regression, ordinal and classification head grades individual answers, while a second branch uses an expert-designed Q-matrix to predict G-DINA-derived skill mastery and learning gain through a shared encoder. A Gen-AI detector, trained with supervised contrastive pretraining and linear classification, estimates assistance probabilities that become reliability weights attenuating unreliable cognitive evidence.
AI.result: On 49,402 instructor-graded responses from 19 academic semesters, AICG reduces MAE by 50.3% relative to RoBERTa regression and improves QWK from 0.798 to 0.927. Q-matrix-guided cognitive supervision is the primary source of improvement, and AI-aware weighting further reduces MAE by 4.2% over the unweighted cognitive model, consistently improving MAE and QWK across the four most recent post-Gen-AI semesters.
AI.conclusion: Cognitive supervision beyond score labels, together with AI-aware weighting, improves automated math grading and the reliability of learning assessment in the post-Gen-AI setting.

title: PsyInterviewee: Informational Invariance and Relational Adaptivity in Mental Health Interview Simulation
comment: 38 pages, including appendices. Code: this https URL
summary: LLM-based simulated interviewees support interviewer training and the evaluation of mental health interviewing systems. Existing studies have primarily focused on improving human-likeness through richer patient profiles and behavioral modeling. However, human-likeness alone does not establish their reliability. Reliable simulation requires preserving profile-grounded clinical facts (informational invariance) while adapting disclosure and interaction behavior to the interview (relational adaptivity). To this end, we introduce PsyInterviewee, which separates a protected truth channel from a dynamic interaction channel and verifies generated clinical claims against the profile. Specifically, asymmetric write permissions allow dialogue context to update disclosure and behavioral states without authorizing new clinical facts; these states guide what profile-supported information is revealed and how it is expressed. In an automated evaluation of interactions between LLM-based interviewers and interviewees, PsyInterviewee achieves higher scores than four representative baselines on most metrics across both axes, as assessed by two LLM judges. Ablations suggest that the two channels contribute to clinical grounding and response modulation, respectively.

AI.tldr: PsyInterviewee is an LLM-based simulated interviewee for mental health interviews that separates a protected truth channel from a dynamic interaction channel, so it stays clinically grounded while adapting disclosure to the interview. In automated evaluation with two LLM judges it outperforms four representative baselines on most metrics across both axes.
AI.motivation: Existing simulated interviewees are tuned for human-likeness, which does not establish that they preserve profile-grounded clinical facts, so their reliability for interviewer training and evaluation is unproven.
AI.method: Asymmetric write permissions let dialogue context update disclosure and behavioral states without authorizing new clinical facts, and these states select which profile-supported information is revealed and how it is expressed. Generated clinical claims are verified against the profile.
AI.result: In automated evaluation of interactions between LLM-based interviewers and interviewees, PsyInterviewee scores higher than four representative baselines on most metrics across both informational and relational axes, as assessed by two LLM judges. Ablations show that the two channels contribute to clinical grounding and response modulation, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Human-likeness alone does not make simulated interviewees reliable, and separating fact preservation from adaptive interaction is a route to reliable simulation for interviewer training and evaluation.

title: From Transcription to Reformulation: Defining and Benchmarking Grounded Generative Speech Recognition
summary: Speech language models have expanded automatic speech recognition (ASR) from transcription to general speech-to-text generation. Yet existing benchmarks still assume a single ground-truth transcript per utterance, an assumption that struggles when models produce readable, formatted, or structured outputs. In this work, we introduce Grounded Generative Speech Recognition (GSR), reformulating speech recognition as generating semantically grounded text instead of a single transcript. We define a grounded reformulation space that characterizes all valid textual realizations supported by the input speech, and establish a four-level hierarchy of reformulation capabilities, including literal transcription, canonical reformulation, semantic reformulation and speech-grounded structuring. Based on this formulation, we present GSR-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate generative speech recognition systems beyond exact transcript matching. GSR-Bench covers diverse scenarios including refined meeting transcription, cross-dialect translation, context-aware speech understanding, and robustness under silent or noisy acoustic conditions. To address the limitations of word-level evaluation metrics, we develop a multi-dimensional evaluation framework combining speech grounding assessment and LLM-based semantic judgment, whose reliability is validated through human preference studies. Extensive experiments across representative architectures, ranging from conventional ASR systems to end-to-end Speech-LLMs, reveal fundamental trade-offs between transcription fidelity and generative reformulation ability. Our analysis further identifies critical failure modes, including acoustic hallucination, unsupported generation, and instruction drift, providing insights into the design and evaluation of future grounded generative speech systems.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates speech recognition as generating semantically grounded text rather than producing a single ground-truth transcript, and introduces GSR-Bench to evaluate generative speech recognition beyond exact transcript matching. Experiments reveal trade-offs between transcription fidelity and generative reformulation ability.
AI.motivation: Existing ASR benchmarks assume one ground-truth transcript per utterance, which does not fit models that produce readable, formatted or structured outputs, and word-level metrics cannot judge such outputs well.
AI.method: The authors define a grounded reformulation space of all valid textual realizations supported by the input speech, and a four-level hierarchy: literal transcription, canonical reformulation, semantic reformulation and speech-grounded structuring. GSR-Bench covers refined meeting transcription, cross-dialect translation, context-aware understanding and silent or noisy conditions, and is scored by a multi-dimensional framework that combines speech grounding assessment with LLM-based semantic judgment validated by human preference studies.
AI.result: Experiments across conventional ASR systems and end-to-end Speech-LLMs reveal fundamental trade-offs between transcription fidelity and generative reformulation ability. The analysis identifies failure modes including acoustic hallucination, unsupported generation and instruction drift.
AI.conclusion: Speech recognition evaluation needs to move beyond exact transcript matching, and the findings on grounding and failure modes inform the design and evaluation of future grounded generative speech systems.

title: Comparative Evaluation of LLM-Based Review Paradigms for Academic Paper Quality Assessment
summary: Growing submission volumes have renewed interest in using large language models (LLMs) to support peer review. It remains unclear how such evaluation should be structured, how much the model matters, and whether LLM scores predict research impact. We evaluate five paradigms across three input representations and three LLMs on 232 stratified ICLR 2025 submissions. Direct absolute rating matches comparative ranking on rank correlation with human scores, yet compresses most predictions above the accept threshold, flagging almost none of the papers reviewers scored below it. A base-rate-matched recalibration control locates the cause: comparative ranking supplies placement, not better ordering, and after recalibration Direct Rating reaches higher agreement than Elo while making 24% as many API calls. Abstract-only input beats full-paper summarization, and model choice matters as much as paradigm choice. Replicating on all 11,513 scored submissions reproduces these patterns, shows absolute agreement depends on the evaluated set's score spread, and finds none beating an always-reject baseline in accuracy. Human scores track citations better than any paradigm, with one exception: Group Rating retains its citation correlation after controlling for human scores, and alone ranks within the accepted pool. Ranking quality alone cannot assess review quality; calibration, thresholds, model, and target outcome all matter.

AI.tldr: The paper compares five LLM review paradigms, three input representations and three LLMs on 232 stratified ICLR 2025 submissions, and finds that Direct Rating after recalibration reaches higher agreement with human scores than Elo while making 24% as many API calls. A replication on all 11,513 scored submissions reproduces these patterns, and no paradigm beats an always-reject baseline in accuracy.
AI.motivation: Growing submission volumes make LLM-assisted peer review attractive, but it is unclear how evaluation should be structured, how much the model matters, and whether LLM scores predict research impact.
AI.method: Five paradigms are evaluated across three input representations and three LLMs, with a base-rate-matched recalibration control to separate placement from ordering. Abstract-only input is compared with full-paper summarization, and the outputs are checked against human scores and citation outcomes, with a replication on all 11,513 scored submissions.
AI.result: Direct absolute rating matches comparative ranking on rank correlation with human scores, but it compresses predictions above the accept threshold and flags almost none of the papers reviewers scored below it. After recalibration, Direct Rating reaches higher agreement than Elo with 24% as many API calls. Abstract-only input beats full-paper summarization. Human scores track citations better than any paradigm, except that Group Rating keeps its citation correlation after controlling for human scores. In the replication, absolute agreement depends on the evaluated set's score spread, and no paradigm beats an always-reject baseline in accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Ranking quality alone cannot assess review quality, so calibration, thresholds, model choice and target outcome must all be considered when evaluating LLM-based review.

title: Enhancing Knowledge Entity Relation Extraction in Abstracts and Full-text Content of Academic Articles Using Large Language Models
summary: This study investigates the effectiveness of large pre-trained language models (LLMs) for knowledge entity relation extraction (KERE) from academic papers. Existing studies have examined individual types of LLM-based strategies and evaluated model performance using metrics such as precision and recall. To provide a broader evaluation, this study investigates multiple strategies, including closed-source LLM-based CoT prompting, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, LLM-enhanced small pre-trained language models (SLMs), and SLM-enhanced closed-source LLMs. In addition, this study introduces two strategies, namely SLM-enhanced open-source LLMs and closed-source LLM-enhanced open-source LLMs. These strategies are evaluated from multiple perspectives, including metrics, their ability to mitigate errors observed in SLMs, and potential directions for model optimization. This study manually constructs two annotated datasets in the NLP domain, covering Abstract and Full-Text datasets. Experimental results show that the LoRA-adapted T5 model achieves the highest macro F1 scores of 0.7408 and 0.7013 on the Abstract and Full-Text datasets, respectively. SLMs also benefit from LLM-generated entity descriptions under the LLM-enhanced SLM strategy. Error analysis further reveals that the effectiveness of LLM-based strategies in mitigating SLM errors varies across error types. Based on the identified limitations and error patterns of these strategies, several optimization directions are proposed. In addition, combining strategies with different error patterns further improves KERE performance.

AI.tldr: The paper compares LLM-based strategies for knowledge entity relation extraction from academic papers on two newly annotated NLP datasets, one of abstracts and one of full text. A LoRA-adapted T5 model achieves the highest macro F1, 0.7408 on abstracts and 0.7013 on full text, and combining strategies with different error patterns further improves performance.
AI.motivation: Earlier studies examined individual LLM-based strategies with precision and recall, without a broad comparison or an analysis of how well each strategy mitigates the errors of small pre-trained language models.
AI.method: The study evaluates closed-source LLM chain-of-thought prompting, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, LLM-enhanced small pre-trained language models, and SLM-enhanced closed-source LLMs, and introduces two further strategies: SLM-enhanced open-source LLMs and closed-source LLM-enhanced open-source LLMs. Two datasets covering abstracts and full text are manually annotated.
AI.result: The LoRA-adapted T5 model achieves the highest macro F1 scores, 0.7408 on the abstract dataset and 0.7013 on the full-text dataset. SLMs benefit from LLM-generated entity descriptions under the LLM-enhanced SLM strategy, and the effectiveness of LLM strategies in mitigating SLM errors varies by error type. Combining strategies with different error patterns further improves performance.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based strategies have error-type-dependent strengths, and the identified limitations and error patterns point to concrete directions for optimizing them and for combining them.

title: CEFR Level Assessment across Languages and Text Granularities
summary: Automatic assessment of textual CEFR levels is an important task in educational natural language processing. However, accurate CEFR level prediction remains challenging due to the naturally imbalanced distribution of CEFR levels and the ambiguous boundaries between adjacent levels. To address these challenges, we propose a unified training objective that combines focal loss with supervised contrastive learning. Focal loss mitigates class imbalance by emphasizing underrepresented and difficult examples, while supervised contrastive learning learns more discriminative representations by encouraging intra-class compactness and inter-class separation. We evaluate the proposed method on sentence- and document-level CEFR assessment in both monolingual and multilingual settings. Experimental results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms strong baselines across all settings, establishing new state-of-the-art performance on multiple CEFR assessment benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes training CEFR level assessment with a combined focal loss and supervised contrastive learning objective to handle class imbalance and ambiguous level boundaries. The method consistently outperforms strong baselines at sentence and document level, in monolingual and multilingual settings, and sets new state-of-the-art results on multiple CEFR benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Accurate CEFR level prediction is hard because the levels are naturally imbalanced and the boundaries between adjacent levels are ambiguous.
AI.method: A unified training objective combines focal loss, which emphasizes underrepresented and difficult examples, with supervised contrastive learning, which encourages intra-class compactness and inter-class separation.
AI.result: The method consistently outperforms strong baselines on sentence- and document-level CEFR assessment in both monolingual and multilingual settings, and establishes new state-of-the-art performance on multiple CEFR assessment benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Combining an imbalance-aware loss with contrastive representation learning is an effective approach to CEFR assessment across text granularities and languages.

title: Digital sovereignty in professional translation workflows: a case study of migrating from Windows to Linux
comment: 14 pages, submitted for formal peer review at the 47th Translating and the Computer conference (Luxembourg) 8/10 December 2026
summary: This study examines digital sovereignty in professional translation through a screening of computer-assisted translation tools and translation management systems, and a case study of migrating a translator's workstation from Windows to Linux. The framework combines three principles - Control, Continuity and Exit - with three practical requirements: native Linux operation, independence from mandatory external services, and independent access to essential data and resources. Drawing on documentary evidence and the limited number of responses received from providers, the ecosystem screening distinguishes Linux accessibility from operational independence: browser-based platforms may remain dependent on provider-controlled infrastructure. The migration case demonstrates the feasibility of reconstructing one professional workflow around a locally operable Linux core, using LoopCAT, LibreOffice and locally run TranslateGemma, alongside tools for optical character recognition, communication, credential management and backup. Selected cloud services remained available where needed. The findings suggest that digital sovereignty depends on how workflow dependencies are organized, rather than on individual applications or operating systems. It does not require technological isolation, but meaningful control over essential components, continuity of work and practical exit options. The framework is tailored to the case examined here and may require adaptation to other professional workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper examines digital sovereignty in professional translation through a screening of CAT tools and translation management systems and a case study of moving a translator's workstation from Windows to Linux. It concludes that sovereignty depends on how workflow dependencies are organized, not on individual applications or operating systems.
AI.motivation: Translators depend on CAT tools and management systems, many of them browser-based and possibly reliant on provider-controlled infrastructure, so Linux accessibility alone does not establish independence from those providers.
AI.method: A framework combines three principles, Control, Continuity and Exit, with three practical requirements: native Linux operation, independence from mandatory external services, and independent access to essential data and resources. A documentary screening, supplemented by the limited responses from providers, is combined with a migration of one workflow to a locally operable Linux core built on LoopCAT, LibreOffice and locally run TranslateGemma, plus OCR, communication, credential management and backup tools.
AI.result: The migration shows that one professional workflow can be rebuilt around a locally operable Linux core, with selected cloud services still available where needed. The screening distinguishes Linux accessibility from operational independence.
AI.conclusion: Digital sovereignty does not require technological isolation, only meaningful control over essential components, continuity of work and practical exit options, and the framework may need adaptation to other professional workflows.

title: Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B: Adapting a 2.6B Hybrid Model to Tajik Tool Calling, and What Continued Pretraining Takes Away
comment: 12 pages, 9 tables, 3 figures. Technical report. Model: this https URL
summary: We release Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B, a Tajik adaptation of the 2.6B-parameter hybrid model LFM2.5-2.6B-Base, built for tool calling in Tajik on modest hardware. The recipe has two stages: LoRA continued pretraining (CPT) on 1,485,319 cleaned Tajik web documents for 3 epochs, then one epoch of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a mix of machine-translated Tajik tool calls, English tool calls kept as replay, and Tajik instructions. On a 174-item tool-calling test set built from BFCL v3 and machine-translated to Tajik, strict full-call accuracy on Tajik prompts rises from 20.69 for the base model to 64.14 (paired difference +43.45 points, 95% interval +35.2 to +51.7); a lenient parser that also accepts the base model's own call formats puts the base at 31.72. English shows no detectable change (76.55 and 77.24). Every CPT checkpoint scores zero: CPT removes the native tool-call format and, as the lenient re-scoring shows, part of the skill itself. Outside tool calling, accuracy on a Tajik knowledge benchmark rises from 28.0 to 35.0, Belebele Tajik shows no significant change, and English MMLU falls from 60.8 to 52.5. The model is not a general Tajik assistant. It almost never declines when no tool fits (6.9% correct on Tajik, against 31.0% for the base under the lenient parser), it is weak at multi-turn calls, and its calls should be checked before they are executed. We describe the data, the training settings and every evaluation in enough detail to repeat them.

AI.tldr: The paper releases Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B, a 2.6B-parameter hybrid model adapted to Tajik tool calling through LoRA continued pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning. Strict full-call accuracy on Tajik prompts rises from 20.69 to 64.14, while English tool-calling accuracy shows no detectable change.
AI.motivation: Tool calling in Tajik needs an adapted model that runs on modest hardware, and continued pretraining is known to disrupt the native tool-call format.
AI.method: The recipe is LoRA continued pretraining on 1,485,319 cleaned Tajik web documents for three epochs, then one epoch of supervised fine-tuning on a mix of machine-translated Tajik tool calls, English tool calls kept as replay, and Tajik instructions. Evaluation uses a 174-item tool-calling test set built from BFCL v3 and machine-translated to Tajik.
AI.result: Strict full-call accuracy on Tajik prompts rises from 20.69 for the base model to 64.14, a paired difference of +43.45 points (95% interval +35.2 to +51.7), while a lenient parser puts the base at 31.72. English tool-calling accuracy shows no detectable change (76.55 and 77.24). Every CPT checkpoint scores zero. Tajik knowledge benchmark accuracy rises from 28.0 to 35.0, Belebele Tajik shows no significant change, and English MMLU falls from 60.8 to 52.5.
AI.conclusion: The model is not a general Tajik assistant: it rarely declines when no tool fits, is weak at multi-turn calls, and its calls should be checked before execution, while CPT removes the native tool-call format and part of the skill itself.

title: When Steering Shifts Discourse: Identifying and Intervening on Discourse-Level Changes due to Activation Steering in LLMs
summary: Activation steering is an inference-time technique used to control or modify the behavior, tone, or safety properties of a large language model (LLM) without retraining the model's weights or editing its input prompt, but simply by adding a vector to its residual-stream activations. However, activation steering also changes the generated text in unintended ways, unrelated to intended behavior change, that are not well understood. Prior work has measured these changes only through coarse signals such as perplexity. In this work, we show that steering systematically produces significant changes in discourse dimensions of the generated text, such as its formality, use of evidence, and ambiguity. We present a way of countering this by adding a second, complementary vector that targets the affected discourse dimension. This intervention restores about 78% of the unintended discourse changes while preserving the intended steering behavior in about 93% of the generations.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that activation steering, which adds a vector to residual-stream activations to control LLM behavior, also shifts discourse-level properties of generated text such as formality, use of evidence and ambiguity. A second, complementary vector that targets the affected discourse dimension restores about 78% of the unintended changes while preserving the intended steering in about 93% of generations.
AI.motivation: Prior work measured the side effects of steering only through coarse signals such as perplexity, so the unintended changes to generated text were poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors measure discourse dimensions of steered generations and counter the unintended shifts by adding a second, complementary vector that targets the affected discourse dimension.
AI.result: Steering systematically produces significant changes in discourse dimensions such as formality, use of evidence and ambiguity. The complementary vector restores about 78% of the unintended discourse changes while preserving the intended steering behavior in about 93% of generations.
AI.conclusion: Steering side effects are at the discourse level and can be partly corrected with a second vector, so steering evaluations should look beyond perplexity.

title: Precision--Recall Trade-off on the Inference Level for LLMs in Grammatical Error Correction
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have recently been adopted for Grammatical Error Correction (GEC), achieving strong performance via both full fine-tuning and prompt-based approaches. As probabilistic sequence models, LLMs expose inference-time parameters that directly modify token generation behavior; however, their potential for controlling GEC-specific trade-offs has not been systematically studied. In this work, we investigate decoding strategies for grammatical error correction. We show that the repetition penalty parameter enables controllable adjustment of the precision--recall trade-off at inference time, without modifying the model architecture, training procedure, or prompt. Through experiments on standard GEC benchmarks, we demonstrate that repetition-penalty-based decoding enables inference-time control of the precision--recall balance, conceptually related to methods previously proposed for sequence-to-sequence GEC models, such as Align-and-Predict Decoding (APD), while remaining simple and broadly applicable to existing LLMs that expose inference-time decoding penalties.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the repetition penalty at decoding time gives LLMs an inference-time control over the precision-recall trade-off in grammatical error correction, without changing the model, its training or the prompt. Experiments on standard GEC benchmarks confirm this controllability.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for GEC, but their inference-time parameters have not been studied as a means of controlling GEC-specific precision-recall trade-offs.
AI.method: The authors investigate decoding strategies for GEC and adjust the repetition penalty to control the precision-recall balance at inference time. The approach is conceptually related to Align-and-Predict Decoding for seq2seq GEC models, but applies to any LLM that exposes decoding penalties.
AI.result: Experiments on standard GEC benchmarks show that repetition-penalty-based decoding enables controllable adjustment of the precision-recall balance at inference time.
AI.conclusion: Decoding penalties offer a simple, broadly applicable way to control GEC precision and recall in existing LLMs without retraining or prompt changes.

title: GraphNIAH: A Benchmark for Long-Context Reasoning over Real-World Graphs
summary: The needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) benchmark was introduced as a test for measuring a model's ability to find small relevant facts within a very large body of input text. However, existing NIAH benchmarks each suffer from one or more of the following limitations: (1) reliance on synthetic data, so their evaluations may not generalize to real-world settings; (2) reuse of previously published datasets, leading to the risk of benchmark contamination; (3) dependence on manual annotation, which requires human effort to create and update data and is prone to future benchmark contamination; and (4) unrealistic simplification of long-context multi-hop reasoning where each next step is trivial given previous steps, while real-world reasoning often requires planning over multiple possible proof paths. To address these limitations, we introduce \Benchmark, a dynamic benchmark built from real citation relationships among scientific papers published after the evaluated models' knowledge cutoff date, which utilizes real-world information while ensuring no benchmark contamination. The fully automated benchmark construction pipeline samples representative subgraphs of the citation graph formed by these papers and converts each subgraph into a long-context QA example with a verifiable answer. We use GraphNIAH to evaluate eight LLMs from the GPT-5.6, Gemini-3, and Qwen3.5 families. We find that accuracy falls as questions require longer reasoning paths: at question depths of 16 and 32, the GPT-5.6 and Qwen3.5 models answer YES/NO questions no better than random guessing, mostly by answering NO; four of the eight models answer no counting example correctly, and the others model get worse as the subgraph size increases. These findings suggest that current LLMs often stop searching the citation relationships in their context before they reach the answer, even though every fact they need is in the context.

AI.tldr: GraphNIAH is a dynamic long-context benchmark built automatically from real citation relationships among papers published after the evaluated models' knowledge cutoff. Evaluating eight LLMs shows that accuracy falls as reasoning paths lengthen, and that models often stop searching their context before reaching an answer that is present.
AI.motivation: Existing needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks rely on synthetic data, reuse published datasets with contamination risk, depend on manual annotation, or oversimplify multi-hop reasoning where each step is trivial.
AI.method: The pipeline samples representative subgraphs of the citation graph formed by post-cutoff scientific papers and converts each subgraph into a long-context QA example with a verifiable answer. Eight LLMs from the GPT-5.6, Gemini-3 and Qwen3.5 families are evaluated.
AI.result: Accuracy falls as questions require longer reasoning paths. At question depths of 16 and 32, the GPT-5.6 and Qwen3.5 models answer YES/NO questions no better than random guessing, mostly by answering NO. Four of the eight models answer no counting example correctly, and the others get worse as subgraph size increases.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs often stop searching the citation relationships in their context before reaching the answer, even though every fact they need is present in that context.

title: Stepwise-Querying: Distilling Reasoning without Access to Teacher Chain-of-Thought
summary: Reasoning distillation is widely used to transfer the reasoning capabilities of large language models to smaller students through teacher-generated supervision. In the black-box setting, however, teachers may expose only final answers and brief solutions, leaving intermediate calculations and validity conditions unavailable and thus limiting the reasoning supervision available for distillation. We propose Stepwise Querying, which elicits step-specific explanations without requiring access to the teacher's internal chain-of-thought (CoT) traces. Independent queries to the same teacher request intermediate derivations, validity checks, and corrections for individual steps, the assembled solutions are then used for standard supervised fine-tuning. Across two teachers, two students, and four mathematics and code benchmarks, our method achieves the highest score in 14 of 16 comparisons with three baselines. We further introduce Stepwise Explanation Information Gain (SEIG), a diagnostic based on the log-ratio of a frozen student's probabilities of correct step completion under stepwise and global explanations. Analyses on GSM8K show that incorrect-answer trajectories can remain useful when they preserve valid intermediate reasoning, while further decomposition yields limited additional gains.

AI.tldr: Stepwise Querying distills reasoning from a black-box teacher that exposes only final answers and brief solutions, by making independent queries for step-specific explanations. The method achieves the highest score in 14 of 16 comparisons with three baselines, across two teachers, two students and four math and code benchmarks.
AI.motivation: In the black-box setting, teachers expose only final answers and brief solutions, so intermediate calculations and validity conditions are unavailable as reasoning supervision.
AI.method: Independent queries to the same teacher request intermediate derivations, validity checks and corrections for individual steps, and the assembled solutions are used for standard supervised fine-tuning. The paper also introduces SEIG, a diagnostic based on the log-ratio of a frozen student's probabilities of correct step completion under stepwise and global explanations.
AI.result: Across two teachers, two students and four mathematics and code benchmarks, the method achieves the highest score in 14 of 16 comparisons with three baselines. On GSM8K, incorrect-answer trajectories remain useful when they preserve valid intermediate reasoning, while further decomposition yields limited additional gains.
AI.conclusion: Step-specific querying recovers useful reasoning supervision without access to teacher chain-of-thought, and the diagnostic shows that incorrect-answer trajectories can still be useful when their intermediate reasoning is valid.

title: Iterated Integrals as Lexical Fingerprints: Path Signature Embeddings for Lexical Similarity
