summary: While sentence embeddings are primarily designed for semantic generalization, their latent geometry implicitly encodes surface-level lexical properties, a relationship that remains poorly understood. Shallow pooling methods discard word order, while deep Transformer models obscure these lexical alignments behind computational complexity and uninterpretable spaces. We propose constructing sentence embeddings via the path signature of Word2Vec trajectories, leveraging the iterated integrals of rough path theory to create representations that explicitly capture sequential and lexical structure in a geometrically tractable manner. Through extensive ablations spanning Word2Vec dimensions, signature depths, and PCA compression, we correlate embedding distances against five lexical string metrics: Levenshtein, Jaro-Winkler, word Jaccard, phoneme Levenshtein, and character TF-IDF. We reveal that while average pooling almost entirely fails to capture character-level edit distances, path signatures strongly align with them, with depth 2 signatures optimally balancing character and word-level sensitivities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the critical lexical variance is concentrated in a highly compact PCA subspace, and unlike pooling, signatures structurally preserve and quantify word order. These findings establish path signatures not as semantic generalizers, but as rigorous mathematical lenses that explicitly encode discrete lexical structures and word order, offering an interpretable alternative to opaque deep learning for lexical tracking.

AI.tldr: The paper builds sentence embeddings from the path signature of Word2Vec word trajectories and shows that they track character-level and word-level lexical similarity, unlike average pooling. Depth-2 signatures balance character and word sensitivity best.
AI.motivation: Sentence embeddings are designed for semantic generalization, and their lexical geometry is poorly understood. Shallow pooling discards word order, while deep Transformers hide lexical alignment behind computational complexity and uninterpretable spaces.
AI.method: Sentence embeddings are built from the path signature of Word2Vec trajectories, using iterated integrals from rough path theory. Ablations vary Word2Vec dimensions, signature depth and PCA compression, and embedding distances are correlated with five lexical string metrics: Levenshtein, Jaro-Winkler, word Jaccard, phoneme Levenshtein and character TF-IDF.
AI.result: Average pooling almost entirely fails to capture character-level edit distances, while path signatures strongly align with them, and depth-2 signatures optimally balance character- and word-level sensitivity. The critical lexical variance is concentrated in a compact PCA subspace, and unlike pooling, signatures preserve and quantify word order.
AI.conclusion: Path signatures act as interpretable lexical lenses that encode discrete lexical structure and word order rather than as semantic generalizers, offering an alternative to opaque deep models for lexical tracking.

title: SimXAI: A Simple Drop-in Layer Increases Interaction Quality and Understanding in Conversational XAI
summary: Conversational explainable AI (ConvXAI) agents often use GUS-style architectures with separate modules for intent recognition, dialogue management, and template-based response generation. While faithful to the underlying XAI methods, these pipelines are hard to adapt and often struggle with context-dependent follow-up questions. We present SimXAI, a lightweight LLM-centric conversational layer that replaces these modules with a single tool-calling LLM that bridges access to existing XAI resources. Rather than a standalone agent, SimXAI serves as a modular interface that enables conversational access to external XAI resources. We further introduce an evaluation suite for single- and multi-turn parsing, faithfulness, and contextualization. Across existing and new datasets, SimXAI achieves strong function-selection accuracy and high faithfulness while better handling context-dependent requests. In a user study replacing only the conversational layer of TalkToModel, a representative GUS-based agent, users completed tasks more accurately and in fewer turn. Overall, SimXAI improves GUS-based design while preserving faithfulness and improving conversational quality.

AI.tldr: SimXAI replaces the intent recognition, dialogue management and template modules of GUS-style conversational XAI agents with a single tool-calling LLM layer that accesses existing XAI resources. In a user study replacing only the conversational layer of TalkToModel, users completed tasks more accurately and in fewer turns.
AI.motivation: GUS-style conversational XAI pipelines are faithful to the underlying XAI methods but are hard to adapt and struggle with context-dependent follow-up questions.
AI.method: SimXAI is a lightweight LLM-centric conversational layer that uses one tool-calling LLM as a modular interface to existing XAI resources, rather than as a standalone agent. An evaluation suite covers single- and multi-turn parsing, faithfulness and contextualization.
AI.result: Across existing and new datasets, SimXAI achieves strong function-selection accuracy and high faithfulness while handling context-dependent requests better. In a user study that replaced only the conversational layer of TalkToModel, users completed tasks more accurately and in fewer turns.
AI.conclusion: SimXAI improves GUS-style design by preserving faithfulness while improving conversational quality, and it works as a drop-in conversational layer.

title: Aligning MLLMs with the Latent Structure of Human Cognition via Behavior-Derived Semantic Dimensions
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations and decision criteria align with the latent structure of human cognition. In this work, we propose a novel framework to align MLLMs with the multidimensional mental representations underlying human similarity judgements. We build on a previously established behavior-derived semantic embedding space, in which objects are represented along 66 interpretable dimensions derived from 4.70 million human Odd-One-Out (O1O) judgements. For each triplet, we infer the most salient decision dimension and convert it into a dimension-grounded linguistic rationale. This enables MLLMs to learn both the final choice and a justification consistent with the inferred behavioral criterion. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves model consistency with human similarity judgements while retaining competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks. Furthermore, using searchlight Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) on an independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we observe increased representational alignment between model and human. Ultimately, our findings point to a data-driven route for incorporating human cognitive structure into MLLMs alignment. The code is available \href{this https URL}{here}.

AI.tldr: The paper aligns MLLMs with human similarity judgements by training them to output a dimension-grounded linguistic rationale derived from a behavior-based semantic space of 66 dimensions, built from 4.70 million odd-one-out judgements. The approach improves agreement with human judgements, keeps competitive benchmark performance and increases representational alignment with human fMRI data.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether MLLM internal representations and decision criteria align with the multidimensional latent structure behind human similarity judgements.
AI.method: For each odd-one-out triplet, the most salient decision dimension is inferred from a behavior-derived embedding space with 66 interpretable dimensions and converted into a dimension-grounded linguistic rationale. MLLMs learn both the final choice and a justification consistent with that criterion.
AI.result: The approach improves consistency with human similarity judgements while retaining competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks. Searchlight RSA on the independent NSD fMRI dataset shows increased representational alignment between model and human.
AI.conclusion: The work points to a data-driven route for incorporating human cognitive structure into MLLM alignment.

title: TurnTurk-GPT: Text-Based Turn-Taking Prediction for Turkish
summary: This paper presents TurnTurk-GPT, a text-based turn-taking predictor for Turkish obtained by fine-tuning a Turkish GPT-2 model with the TurnGPT objective on synthetic and real dialogue, and evaluates it on real Turkish conversation against rule baselines, a zero-shot Turkish language model and a widely used multilingual end-of-turn detector. Evaluation uses word-level decision points on unpunctuated, lower-cased text approximating the output of streaming speech recognisers, recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint folds, nested threshold selection and paired cluster bootstrap tests. TurnTurk-GPT outperforms the multilingual detector under both recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation. It outperforms the zero-shot language model only when the test speakers occur in training; on unseen speakers the two are statistically indistinguishable. Removing the suffixes of the turn-final word reduces AP by up to 44%, against 2% for a sentence-internal word, locating the Turkish end-of-turn cue in verb-final morphology. Synthetic dialogue alone yields the weakest trained model, and when a speaker pauses the zero-shot and multilingual baselines remain close to chance. The model and the evaluation protocol are publicly released.

AI.tldr: TurnTurk-GPT is a text-based turn-taking predictor for Turkish, obtained by fine-tuning a Turkish GPT-2 with the TurnGPT objective. It outperforms a multilingual end-of-turn detector under both recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation, but on unseen speakers it is statistically indistinguishable from a zero-shot language model.
AI.motivation: Turn-taking prediction in Turkish needs a text-based predictor that is compared with rule baselines, a zero-shot Turkish language model and a widely used multilingual end-of-turn detector on output resembling streaming speech recognition.
AI.method: The model fine-tunes a Turkish GPT-2 on synthetic and real dialogue with the TurnGPT objective. Evaluation uses word-level decision points on unpunctuated, lower-cased text approximating streaming recogniser output, with recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint folds, nested threshold selection and paired cluster bootstrap tests.
AI.result: TurnTurk-GPT outperforms the multilingual detector under both recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation. It beats the zero-shot language model only when test speakers appear in training. Removing the suffixes of the turn-final word reduces AP by up to 44%, against 2% for a sentence-internal word. Synthetic dialogue alone yields the weakest trained model, and when a speaker pauses, the zero-shot and multilingual baselines stay close to chance.
AI.conclusion: The Turkish end-of-turn cue is located in verb-final morphology, and the model and evaluation protocol are publicly released.

title: Asynchronous Flow Map Language Models
comment: Code available at: this https URL
summary: The order in which tokens are predicted in language modeling has a profound impact on the quality of generated sequences. Autoregressive and masked diffusion models iteratively fill in tokens and can exploit such orderings across generation steps, but how to leverage an ordering for one-step parallel language modeling is unclear. We introduce asynchronous flow map language models (aFMLMs), which incorporate prediction order into one-step modeling by learning the flow maps of asynchronous flows. These flows specify an ordering through a tokenwise time schedule that controls the relative denoising progress of tokens. We formulate a general class of asynchronous flows that admit both prescribed and learned, state-adaptive schedules, show that they define valid flow maps, and develop new methods for their flow map distillation. The resulting models can generate all tokens in a single forward pass by internalizing the ordering encoded in the flow into their hidden computations. On Sudoku solving and code generation for GSM8K math word problems, aFMLM establishes new state-of-the-art one-step performance.

AI.tldr: Asynchronous flow map language models (aFMLMs) incorporate prediction order into one-step parallel language modeling by learning flow maps of asynchronous flows with tokenwise time schedules. They establish new state-of-the-art one-step performance on Sudoku solving and on code generation for GSM8K math word problems.
AI.motivation: The order in which tokens are predicted strongly affects generation quality, but autoregressive and masked diffusion models exploit ordering only across iterative steps, and it is unclear how to use an ordering in one-step parallel language modeling.
AI.method: aFMLMs learn flow maps of asynchronous flows, which specify an ordering through a tokenwise time schedule that controls the relative denoising progress of tokens. The authors formulate a general class of such flows with prescribed and learned, state-adaptive schedules, show that they define valid flow maps, and develop new flow map distillation methods.
AI.result: The models generate all tokens in a single forward pass by internalizing the ordering into their hidden computations. On Sudoku solving and code generation for GSM8K math word problems, aFMLM establishes new state-of-the-art one-step performance.
AI.conclusion: Prediction order can be internalized into single-pass language models through asynchronous flow maps.

title: CRoS: Causality Reward on Scrambled CoTs Improves Accuracy and Reasoning Faithfulness
comment: 17 pages, 3 figures, 14 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become the standard method for training language models to reason. However, RLVR typically relies solely on outcome correctness, which does not guarantee that the CoT causally contributes to the final answer. Without this connection, outcome rewards may fail to reinforce high-quality reasoning. Existing causality metrics assess CoT causality by perturbing the CoT, such as deleting reasoning steps or injecting errors, and measuring changes in the final answer. However, these perturbations inevitably alter information in each step. Consequently, high causality scores may reflect sensitivity to information changes introduced by perturbation rather than true causality. Such confounding effects further induce undesirable reasoning behaviors when these metrics are used as training rewards, including generating less informative CoTs and reducing exploration and self-correction. To address this problem, we propose CRoS (Causality Reward on Scrambled CoTs), a novel CoT causality metric that perturbs the order of reasoning steps without altering content, thereby preserving information within each step. On Reasoning Gym with Gemma-3-4B, CRoS outperforms existing causality and outcome rewards in out-of-domain accuracy, CoT quality, and CoT faithfulness. Specifically, CRoS achieves 46.8% accuracy on five unseen logic and games datasets, outperforming the strongest baseline (43.8%). It also achieves better CoT quality, consistently outperforming baselines in CoT-Pass@K from K=1 to 128, averaging 43.4% vs. 41.4%. For CoT faithfulness, CRoS achieves a hint acknowledgment score of 34.0% vs. 20.2%.

AI.tldr: CRoS is a reward for RLVR that measures CoT causality by reordering reasoning steps without changing their content, avoiding the information loss of deletion or error-injection perturbations. On Reasoning Gym with Gemma-3-4B it improves out-of-domain accuracy, CoT quality and faithfulness over existing causality and outcome rewards.
AI.motivation: RLVR rewards only outcome correctness, which does not ensure that the CoT causally contributes to the answer, and existing causality metrics perturb content in ways that confound causality with information change, inducing behaviors such as less informative CoTs and reduced exploration.
AI.method: CRoS scrambles the order of reasoning steps without altering their content, so the information within each step is preserved, and uses the resulting causality score as a training reward.
AI.result: On Reasoning Gym with Gemma-3-4B, CRoS achieves 46.8% accuracy on five unseen logic and game datasets, versus 43.8% for the strongest baseline. Its CoT-Pass@K averages 43.4% against 41.4% for baselines across K from 1 to 128, and its hint acknowledgment score is 34.0% against 20.2%.
AI.conclusion: Order-scrambling causality rewards improve accuracy, CoT quality and faithfulness without the confounds of content-perturbing metrics.

title: PersonaChatBench: Evaluating Chat Assistants with Diverse Simulated Users
summary: Conversational assistants are expected to help people with diverse backgrounds, preferences, and communication styles. Yet evaluations centered on a single cooperative user provide limited insight into how reliably an assistant serves users with different personas. We introduce PersonaChatBench, a framework for evaluating task competence and responsiveness to diverse user needs. PersonaChatBench pairs the same underlying task with multiple simulated users, each guided by a private persona card that specifies distinct needs, preferences, and interaction behaviors. By holding the task fixed while varying the user, the framework examines how assistant performance changes across user conditions. We evaluate 20 language models across six domains, separately assessing native task outcomes, fulfillment of expressed persona needs, and simulator fidelity. Our results show that task performance and need fulfillment vary across personas and domains. Strong task performance does not necessarily translate into satisfying individual needs, and models' relative strengths in meeting those needs are not consistent across domains. PersonaChatBench makes these differences measurable, revealing gaps obscured by aggregate scores and helping identify which users an assistant serves well and where adaptation is needed. It provides a basis for evaluating consistency across users and guiding the development of assistants that better accommodate diverse needs in everyday applications.

AI.tldr: PersonaChatBench evaluates chat assistants by holding the task fixed while pairing it with multiple simulated users, each guided by a private persona card. Evaluating 20 language models across six domains shows that task performance does not guarantee satisfying individual needs, and relative strengths shift across domains.
AI.motivation: Evaluations centred on a single cooperative user give limited insight into whether assistants serve users with different backgrounds and communication styles reliably.
AI.method: The framework pairs the same underlying task with multiple simulated users, each guided by a private persona card that specifies distinct needs, preferences and interaction behaviors, and separately assesses native task outcomes, fulfillment of expressed persona needs and simulator fidelity.
AI.result: Task performance and need fulfillment vary across personas and domains. Strong task performance does not necessarily satisfy individual needs, and models' relative strengths in meeting those needs are not consistent across domains.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark exposes gaps hidden by aggregate scores and identifies which users an assistant serves well, providing a basis for evaluating consistency across users.

title: RangeSWA: Training-Free Length Extrapolation for Continuous Diffusion Language Models
summary: Continuous diffusion language models show promising potential in text generation tasks, but are prone to problems such as text repetition, semantic drift, and generation quality degradation when the generation length exceeds the training length. To address these challenges, we propose RangeSWA, a training-free length extrapolation method. The method combines local sliding-window attention, remote block summaries, and dynamic content retrieval to preserve local details and support long-range context access. In addition, generation degradation caused by length extrapolation is mitigated through positional remapping, conditioning attention correction, and denoising-stage-adaptive window scheduling. We conducted experiments on multiple continuous diffusion language models, and the results show that RangeSWA can effectively reduce generative perplexity and text repetition rates in long-text generation.

AI.tldr: RangeSWA is a training-free length extrapolation method for continuous diffusion language models, combining local sliding-window attention, remote block summaries and dynamic content retrieval. It reduces generative perplexity and text repetition in long-text generation beyond the training length.
AI.motivation: Continuous diffusion language models suffer from text repetition, semantic drift and quality degradation when generation exceeds the training length.
AI.method: RangeSWA combines local sliding-window attention, remote block summaries and dynamic content retrieval to preserve local detail and support long-range context access. Degradation caused by extrapolation is mitigated through positional remapping, conditioning attention correction and denoising-stage-adaptive window scheduling.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple continuous diffusion language models show that RangeSWA effectively reduces generative perplexity and text repetition rates in long-text generation.
AI.conclusion: RangeSWA offers a training-free route to longer generation with continuous diffusion language models.

title: Subquadratic Attention with a Hierarchical Tree-Structured Indexer
summary: The quadratic scaling of attention is a fundamental bottleneck limiting the long-context capabilities of large language models (LLMs). A variety of approaches have attempted to circumvent this, but they either fail to match attention's expressiveness (e.g., sliding-window or linear attention variants with fixed-size state) or only achieve constant-factor speedups (e.g., sparse attention methods whose indexers themselves scale quadratically). In this paper, we derive an asymptotically subquadratic sparse attention method based on a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer, which we call Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA). ZHA constructs a tree of recursively compressed key summaries over the KV cache, which future queries traverse from the top down to retrieve a sparse subset of keys. Crucially, by iteratively growing the tree's depth, the total cost including routing and final attention grows sublinearly in sequence length, resulting in overall subquadratic (but superlinear) scaling for attention. We demonstrate that ZHA can be cheaply applied to existing pretrained models with only a short KL distillation training stage over a few billion tokens, and maintains performance on long-context retrieval and challenging reasoning, mathematical, and agentic coding evaluation tasks. Moreover, we show that our method is highly robust to tree geometry including very deep trees of up to 6 levels. Finally, we develop a detailed performance model and show that our approach scales subquadratically, dramatically outperforms competing methods beyond 1 million context, and ultimately has the potential to extend effective context windows to the hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.

AI.tldr: Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA) is a sparse attention method whose tree-structured indexer routes each query down recursively compressed key summaries, giving overall subquadratic but superlinear attention cost. It can be applied to pretrained models with a short KL distillation stage and maintains performance on long-context and reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: The quadratic scaling of attention limits long-context LLMs. Sliding-window and linear variants with fixed-size state lose attention's expressiveness, and sparse methods with quadratically scaling indexers achieve only constant-factor speedups.
AI.method: ZHA builds a tree of recursively compressed key summaries over the KV cache, which queries traverse top-down to retrieve a sparse subset of keys. Increasing tree depth makes the total cost, including routing and final attention, grow sublinearly in sequence length.
AI.result: ZHA can be applied to existing pretrained models with only a short KL distillation stage over a few billion tokens and maintains performance on long-context retrieval and challenging reasoning, mathematical and agentic coding tasks. It is robust to tree geometry, including trees up to 6 levels deep, and the performance model indicates it outperforms competing methods beyond 1 million context.
AI.conclusion: The approach scales subquadratically and has the potential to extend effective context windows to hundreds of millions or billions of tokens, though this is a projection rather than a demonstrated result.

title: DecisionRank: On-Policy Distillation for Decision-Model Rerankers
summary: Decision models target structured tasks by directly predicting choices or scores, avoiding autoregressive decoding latency. However, transferring a generative LLM's ranking knowledge to a decision model remains challenging: the teacher expresses preferences through a ranked list of document ID sequences, while the student determines the ranking using scores from the first-token position. To bridge this gap, we introduce DecisionRank, a decision model trained through item-space on-policy distillation (OPD). Item-space OPD constructs the student's rollout by sorting its document scores into a ranked sequence. A generative teacher takes the resulting ranking list as inputs and provides conditional feedback to directly supervise those scores. Combined with offline ranking supervision, DecisionRank achieves state-of-the-art performance on both general and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks such as TREC DL, BEIR, and BRIGHT. Across four benchmarks, item-space OPD consistently outperforms alternative training objectives. Even at 1.7B parameters, DecisionRank surpasses its 27B generative teacher on TREC DL19--23. At 8B, it outperforms its generative listwise counterpart while running $24.5\times$ faster on TREC DL and $16.7\times$ faster on BRIGHT.

AI.tldr: DecisionRank trains a decision-model reranker with item-space on-policy distillation, in which the student's document scores are sorted into a ranked sequence that a generative LLM teacher supervises, and it reaches state-of-the-art retrieval results.
AI.motivation: Transferring a generative LLM's ranking knowledge to a decision model is hard because the teacher expresses preferences as ranked lists of document ID sequences, while the student ranks documents using scores from the first-token position.
AI.method: Item-space on-policy distillation (OPD) constructs the student's rollout by sorting its document scores into a ranked sequence; a generative teacher takes that ranking as input and gives conditional feedback that directly supervises the scores. This is combined with offline ranking supervision.
AI.result: DecisionRank achieves state-of-the-art performance on TREC DL, BEIR and BRIGHT, and item-space OPD consistently outperforms alternative training objectives across four benchmarks. At 1.7B parameters it surpasses its 27B generative teacher on TREC DL19-23; at 8B it outperforms its generative listwise counterpart while running 24.5 times faster on TREC DL and 16.7 times faster on BRIGHT.
AI.conclusion: Decision models can inherit the ranking knowledge of a generative LLM teacher while avoiding autoregressive decoding latency, which matters for latency-critical structured retrieval tasks.

title: Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking
comment: 20 pages. Project page: this https URL
summary: Decision models such as Jev have emerged as a highly promising paradigm for LLM agent systems, providing lightweight and reliable categorical reasoning for rapid System One execution. However, existing generation-oriented inference engines fail to support these workloads effectively, suffering from severe prefix recomputation overheads or distorted output probabilities. To address this challenge, we propose Flide, an efficient and exact inference engine that decouples the logical tree structure of a decision request from its physical execution within a single flattened token stream. Through ForkAttention, Flide navigates request dependencies using GPU-resident indices across both standard attention and recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers, guaranteeing in exact arithmetic that every query branch evaluates identically to an isolated forward pass. By expressing branch topologies directly in GPU-resident metadata, Flide accommodates diverse request mixtures with a compact set of pre-recorded execution graphs while enabling expanding agent histories to resume from checkpoints saved in earlier passes. Extensive evaluations on public hybrid and decision models demonstrate that Flide answers queries up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang while staying closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance. By unifying physical execution throughput with mathematical exactness, Flide establishes a principled foundation for scalable, latency-critical decision intelligence in agent systems.

AI.tldr: Flide is an exact inference engine for decision-model workloads that uses ForkAttention to decouple the logical branch structure of a decision request from its physical execution in one flattened token stream, answering queries up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang.
AI.motivation: Existing generation-oriented inference engines handle decision-model workloads poorly, suffering either from severe prefix recomputation overheads or from distorted output probabilities.
AI.method: Flide decouples the logical tree of a decision request from its physical execution within a single flattened token stream. ForkAttention uses GPU-resident indices to navigate request dependencies across standard attention and recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers, and it uses a compact set of pre-recorded execution graphs with checkpoints that let expanding agent histories resume from earlier passes.
AI.result: On public hybrid and decision models, Flide answers queries up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang while staying closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance, and every query branch evaluates identically to an isolated forward pass in exact arithmetic.
AI.conclusion: Unifying physical execution throughput with mathematical exactness provides a principled basis for scalable, latency-critical decision intelligence in LLM agent systems.

title: Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations
comment: Accepted to the 9th annual workshop for Machine Learning & the Physical Sciences (ML4PS). A starter code is available on this https URL
summary: Calibrating a cosmological simulation is an expensive, high-dimensional parameter optimization task. Previous works employ Bayesian optimization for automation, which treats the simulator as a black box and precludes the incorporation of human domain knowledge or workflow into the selection policy. We propose AgenticTuner, an agentic calibration pipeline with a present-day large language model serving as the optimizer who proposes the next parameter trial. We show that these agents can achieve competitive calibration performance at a fraction of the CPU cost when they are given informal, human-readable priors (such as codebase, documentation, and heuristic guides that seasoned scientists may possess). We hope this work serves as an early step toward AI scientists that can carry out complex, long-horizon scientific tasks.

AI.tldr: AgenticTuner is an agentic pipeline in which a present-day LLM acts as the optimizer that proposes the next parameter trial when calibrating a cosmological simulation, reaching competitive calibration performance at a fraction of the CPU cost.
AI.motivation: Calibrating a cosmological simulation is an expensive, high-dimensional parameter optimization task, and prior Bayesian optimization approaches treat the simulator as a black box, which precludes using human domain knowledge or workflow in the selection policy.
AI.method: An LLM serves as the optimizer that proposes each next parameter trial, and it is given informal, human-readable priors such as the codebase, documentation and heuristic guides that practitioners would normally possess.
AI.result: The agents achieve competitive calibration performance at a fraction of the CPU cost when given these informal, human-readable priors.
AI.conclusion: The work is presented as an early step toward AI scientists that can carry out complex, long-horizon scientific tasks.

title: Prevented is Not Protected: What Attack Success Rate Hides about RAG
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is vulnerable to knowledge poisoning, where adversaries manipulate retrieved evidence to influence model outputs. Existing defenses are primarily evaluated using attack success rate (ASR), which obscures defense-induced failures and the mechanisms behind apparent attack prevention. To address this issue, this work introduces \textbf{Aligned RAG Evaluation}, a matched-query protocol that jointly examines clean and poisoned responses, with and without defense. By combining matched conditions analysis, LLM-judge endorsement, and retrieval dependence controls, the proposed framework distinguishes prevented from introduced failures, target mentions from LLM endorsement, and single-passage influence from evidence composition. Experiments on HotpotQA and Natural Questions reveal that existing defenses can introduce unexpected target-positive answers, although they can prevent some attacks, while evaluation criteria can also change defense rankings. Our findings expose critical blind spots in ASR-based evaluation and motivate a more comprehensive assessment of RAG poisoning defenses. The code and the evaluation artifact are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Aligned RAG Evaluation, a matched-query protocol that jointly examines clean and poisoned responses with and without defense, and shows that attack success rate hides failures introduced by existing RAG poisoning defenses.
AI.motivation: RAG poisoning defenses are mainly evaluated by attack success rate (ASR), which obscures defense-induced failures and the mechanisms behind apparent attack prevention.
AI.method: The protocol combines matched-condition analysis, LLM-judge endorsement, and retrieval dependence controls to distinguish prevented from introduced failures, target mentions from LLM endorsement, and single-passage influence from evidence composition.
AI.result: On HotpotQA and Natural Questions, existing defenses can introduce unexpected target-positive answers even though they prevent some attacks, and evaluation criteria can change defense rankings.
AI.conclusion: The findings expose blind spots in ASR-based evaluation and motivate a more comprehensive assessment of RAG poisoning defenses.

title: Hybrid Computer Use: A Unified Programmatic, Semantic, and Visual Interface for General Agents
summary: Computer-use agents increasingly tackle tasks ranging from everyday desktop activities to long-horizon professional workflows. Yet interfaces centered on screenshots and mouse-and-keyboard actions can impose a human-interaction prior, requiring repeated screen interpretation while leaving the computer's semantic and programmatic capabilities underexposed. We argue for exposing these capabilities and letting models choose and combine them. We introduce Hybrid Computer Use (HCU), a unified interface for general agents that combines three complementary channels: programmatic interaction through code and command-line tools, semantic interaction through accessibility (AX), and visual interaction through graphical user interfaces (GUI). Our HCU supports efficient AX interaction and guards against stale-state actions during channel switching. A supplementary HCU skill guides agents in selecting and coordinating channels to use the unified interface effectively. Our designed AX tools return compact observations, execute actions in batches, and report their effects as AX diffs, so the model needs fewer round trips. On OSWorld 2.0, HCU achieves the highest Partial and Binary scores among the compared systems. Analyzing agent trajectories, we find that all evaluated models improve with HCU yet allocate work across the channels differently and consistently outperform compared baselines in terms of both efficiency and task success, highlighting the value of unified computer-use interfaces that allow flexible channel selection and combination.

AI.tldr: Hybrid Computer Use (HCU) is a unified interface for general computer-use agents that combines programmatic, accessibility (AX) and visual GUI channels, and it achieves the highest Partial and Binary scores on OSWorld 2.0 among the compared systems.
AI.motivation: Screenshot and mouse-and-keyboard interfaces impose a human-interaction prior that forces repeated screen interpretation and leaves a computer's semantic and programmatic capabilities underexposed.
AI.method: HCU combines three channels: programmatic interaction through code and command-line tools, semantic interaction through accessibility (AX), and visual interaction through GUIs. It guards against stale-state actions during channel switching, and its AX tools return compact observations, execute actions in batches and report effects as AX diffs; a supplementary HCU skill guides channel selection and coordination.
AI.result: On OSWorld 2.0, HCU achieves the highest Partial and Binary scores among the compared systems. All evaluated models improve with HCU, allocate work across channels differently, and consistently outperform compared baselines in both efficiency and task success.
AI.conclusion: Unified computer-use interfaces that allow flexible channel selection and combination are valuable for general agents.

title: SCRBench: Beyond Equivalence Checking for Semantic Change Reasoning in Code
summary: Understanding how code changes affect program semantics is a core aspect of code reasoning in language models. It is commonly evaluated by asking whether two programs are semantically equivalent, but a yes/no answer does not reveal whether a model knows which code change caused a semantic difference, or which sequence of code changes produced the modified program. We study two tasks that ask these questions directly, diagnosing semantic change and reconstructing sequences of code changes, alongside detecting semantic equivalence. We build SCRBench, 67,658 Python program pairs generated by applying sequences of code changes that preserve or alter program semantics, and evaluate five language models on a stratified subset of 4,500 pairs. Detecting semantic equivalence exposes weaker models, whose accuracy declines as changes accumulate, but the strongest models remain near the ceiling. Diagnosing semantic change reveals weaknesses that equivalence accuracy hides: a model with 94.71% equivalence accuracy diagnoses only 54.44% of semantic changes. Reconstructing sequences of code changes is much harder: the best model reconstructs the exact sequence for only 39.27% of pairs, and no model exceeds 1.11% when five changes are applied. High equivalence accuracy therefore overestimates how well models reason about the semantic effects of code changes.

AI.tldr: SCRBench is a benchmark of 67,658 Python program pairs that tests semantic change diagnosis and reconstruction of code-change sequences beyond yes/no equivalence checking, and shows that high equivalence accuracy overestimates how well models reason about code changes.
AI.motivation: Code reasoning is usually evaluated by asking whether two programs are semantically equivalent, which does not reveal whether a model knows which change caused a semantic difference or which sequence of changes produced the modified program.
AI.method: The authors build SCRBench from program pairs generated by applying sequences of code changes that preserve or alter semantics, and they study three tasks: detecting semantic equivalence, diagnosing semantic change, and reconstructing sequences of code changes. Five language models are evaluated on a stratified subset of 4,500 pairs.
AI.result: Weaker models' equivalence accuracy declines as changes accumulate, while the strongest models stay near the ceiling. A model with 94.71% equivalence accuracy diagnoses only 54.44% of semantic changes; the best model reconstructs the exact sequence for only 39.27% of pairs, and no model exceeds 1.11% when five changes are applied.
AI.conclusion: High equivalence accuracy overestimates how well models reason about the semantic effects of code changes, so diagnosis and sequence reconstruction are needed to assess that ability.

title: GRIT: Gradient Masking for Visually Misgrounded Tokens in Text-Rich Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has recently been extended to vision-language models (VLMs), yet its effectiveness remains limited for text-rich reasoning tasks. We highlight a key factor contributing to this limitation: models frequently arrive at correct final answers despite misperceiving visual information during intermediate steps. We define this phenomenon as Correct-but-Visually-Misgrounded Reasoning (CVMR). Because standard RLVR rewards only final-answer correctness, it fails to differentiate between properly grounded and misgrounded reasoning, reinforcing both equally. Through token-level analysis, we reveal that CVMR tokens exhibit distinct attention patterns that differ systematically from well-grounded ones. Based on this observation, we propose GRIT, a training framework that incorporates visual grounding into RLVR to mitigate the impact of CVMR. Furthermore, to address the lack of text-rich reasoning benchmarks that allow for systematic evaluation across text length and reasoning depth, we introduce GRIT-Bench. Experiments demonstrate that GRIT significantly improves both reasoning accuracy and grounding fidelity over existing RLVR methods.

AI.tldr: GRIT is a training framework that adds visual grounding to RLVR for vision-language models to penalize correct-but-visually-misgrounded reasoning, and it introduces GRIT-Bench, a text-rich reasoning benchmark that varies text length and reasoning depth.
AI.motivation: Standard RLVR rewards only final-answer correctness, so for text-rich reasoning it fails to distinguish well-grounded reasoning from reasoning that reaches correct answers despite misperceiving visual information in intermediate steps, and no benchmark allows systematic evaluation across text length and reasoning depth.
AI.method: Token-level analysis shows that Correct-but-Visually-Misgrounded Reasoning (CVMR) tokens have attention patterns that differ systematically from well-grounded ones, and GRIT incorporates visual grounding into RLVR to mitigate the impact of CVMR. GRIT-Bench is introduced to evaluate across text length and reasoning depth.
AI.result: GRIT significantly improves both reasoning accuracy and grounding fidelity over existing RLVR methods.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating visual grounding into RLVR mitigates the effect of misgrounded yet correct reasoning in text-rich VLM tasks.

title: How Much Can Tool Calls Reveal About You? Privacy Leakage from Tool-Call Traces
comment: 24 pages, 12 figures, 8 tables, including references and appendices
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents interact with external tools through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), producing tool-call traces that may expose behavioral signals about users. In this work, we systematically study the risk of user-profile inference from MCP tool-call traces, where observers infer user attributes from protocol-valid tool interactions without access to user conversations. We introduce PrivacyTrace, a benchmark containing 1,000 synthetic user profiles and 4,000 agent trajectories across four domains, generated with real MCP tools from 25 servers. Experiments with four mainstream LLM attackers show that tool-call traces enable a 26.25% attack success rate for profile inference, compared with 17.97% from prior-based guessing. Further analysis reveals that tool arguments and returned results provide the main trace-grounded evidence, while linking traces across sessions further amplifies profiling risk. These findings demonstrate that MCP tool-call traces can act as effective behavioral side channels for user profiling, motivating the development of privacy-aware mechanisms for agent-tool interactions. Code and data are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that tool-call traces from MCP-based LLM agents leak user attributes, with PrivacyTrace, a benchmark of 1,000 synthetic user profiles and 4,000 agent trajectories, yielding a 26.25% attack success rate for profile inference against 17.97% for prior-based guessing.
AI.motivation: LLM agents that call external tools through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) produce traces that may expose behavioral signals about users, and the risk of user-profile inference from these traces without access to conversations had not been systematically studied.
AI.method: The authors introduce PrivacyTrace, built from 1,000 synthetic user profiles and 4,000 agent trajectories across four domains, generated with real MCP tools from 25 servers. Four mainstream LLM attackers infer user attributes from protocol-valid tool interactions, and the analysis examines tool arguments, returned results and linking traces across sessions.
AI.result: Tool-call traces enable a 26.25% attack success rate for profile inference, compared with 17.97% from prior-based guessing. Tool arguments and returned results provide the main trace-grounded evidence, and linking traces across sessions further amplifies profiling risk.
AI.conclusion: MCP tool-call traces can act as effective behavioral side channels for user profiling, which motivates privacy-aware mechanisms for agent-tool interactions.

title: Completeness and Cost of Retrieval Structures for Multi-Tool Requests in LLM Agents
summary: An agent that must call several tools to fulfill a request fails when the tool retriever omits any one of them, yet tool retrievers are mostly built and evaluated on queries requiring a single tool. We compare representatives of six retrieval structures (flat lexical and dense retrieval, LLM query decomposition, LLM-navigated hierarchies, server-then-tool matching, dependency graphs, and trained set-level retrievers) across two multi-tool testbeds: 345 AppWorld queries with expert dependency labels and 103 MCP-Bench tasks over 257 MCP tools. We measure completeness@k, the share of queries whose entire required tool set appears in the top k, alongside the LLM calls, tokens, and latency that each structure incurs at retrieval time. A motivating analysis on all 7,961 ToolRet queries shows that aggregate completeness mixes two regimes: completeness at 10 is .58 to .67 on single-target queries and .08 to .17 on queries with four or more targets, and the ordering of retrievers on single-target queries reverses on multi-target ones. Across the two testbeds, none of the compared structures that is untrained on the testbed and makes at most one LLM call per query completes more than 10% of AppWorld queries at k = 16. The two structures that do better incur different costs: a set-level retriever trained on 75 to 90 in-domain queries reaches .33 on AppWorld and .58 on MCP-Bench with no LLM calls, while an LLM-navigated hierarchy reaches .30 and .40 with a median of 31 to 38 LLM calls and about five minutes per query. Their failure modes also differ: the trained retriever mostly ranks the missing tools just below the cutoff, whereas the hierarchy finds the target API and stops before collecting its prerequisites. In a downstream check with the official AppWorld agent, tasks with a complete retrieved set succeeded 21 of 21 times, whereas incomplete ones succeeded 2 of 39 times.

AI.tldr: On multi-tool requests, no untrained retrieval structure that makes at most one LLM call completes more than 10% of AppWorld queries at k = 16, and a set-level retriever trained on 75 to 90 in-domain queries performs best at zero LLM calls.
AI.motivation: An agent fails when its tool retriever omits any one of several required tools, yet tool retrievers are mostly built and evaluated on single-tool queries.
AI.method: The authors compare representatives of six retrieval structures (flat lexical and dense retrieval, LLM query decomposition, LLM-navigated hierarchies, server-then-tool matching, dependency graphs, and trained set-level retrievers) on 345 AppWorld queries with expert dependency labels and 103 MCP-Bench tasks over 257 MCP tools. The measure is completeness@k, the share of queries whose entire required tool set appears in the top k, together with the LLM calls, tokens and latency each structure incurs.
AI.result: Completeness at 10 is .58 to .67 on single-target queries but .08 to .17 on queries with four or more targets. The trained set-level retriever reaches .33 on AppWorld and .58 on MCP-Bench with no LLM calls, while an LLM-navigated hierarchy reaches .30 and .40 with a median of 31 to 38 LLM calls and about five minutes per query. In a downstream check with the official AppWorld agent, complete retrieved sets succeeded 21 of 21 times and incomplete ones 2 of 39 times.
AI.conclusion: Aggregate completeness hides different regimes, and completeness of the retrieved tool set strongly predicts task success, so multi-tool retrieval needs dedicated design and evaluation.

title: DyCraft: An Agentic System for Long-Horizon 4D Scene Generation
summary: While frontier coding agents can generate high-quality 3D scenes and articulated assets, they struggle to create coherent long-horizon animations. When equipped with general-purpose harnesses, they frequently produce physically implausible outputs, generating objects that interpenetrate, lack physical support, or move unnaturally. Such bare agents struggle to repair these errors because they default to scripting the full animation in one pass, making it difficult to verify their work and disentangle complex spatiotemporal constraints. Drawing on the practice of human animators, we introduce DyCraft, a system for animated 3D scene generation that breaks animation into steps that coding agents can more reliably solve. DyCraft first expands the user's prompt into a detailed plan and builds a static scene. It then creates a 3D storyboard of key animation poses, where each frame is a static 3D scene that the agent can build and debug in isolation. Storyboarding decomposes the problem into pairs of verified start and end states, allowing the agent to author local motion between them with a collection of motion authoring tools. We evaluate DyCraft on 24 long-horizon, multi-shot animation tasks covering humanoid robots, human and animal characters, and physical mechanisms. Compared with a native GPT-6 agent in Codex and prior agentic baselines, DyCraft substantially reduces physical violations and generates higher-quality animated 3D scenes that are more often preferred by human raters.

AI.tldr: DyCraft is an agentic system that generates long-horizon animated 3D scenes by breaking animation into a verified 3D storyboard of key poses, and it substantially reduces physical violations compared with a native GPT-6 agent in Codex and prior agentic baselines.
AI.motivation: Frontier coding agents with general-purpose harnesses produce physically implausible long animations, with interpenetrating or unsupported objects and unnatural motion, because they script the full animation in one pass, which makes verification and repair difficult.
AI.method: DyCraft expands the prompt into a detailed plan and builds a static scene, then creates a 3D storyboard of key animation poses in which each frame is a static scene built and debugged in isolation. Each pair of verified start and end states lets the agent author local motion with a set of motion authoring tools.
AI.result: On 24 long-horizon, multi-shot animation tasks covering humanoid robots, human and animal characters, and physical mechanisms, DyCraft substantially reduces physical violations and generates higher-quality animated 3D scenes that human raters more often prefer.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing animation into verified key-pose storyboards makes long-horizon 4D scene generation by coding agents more reliable.

title: Drone-PUR: From Visual Clue Discovery to Understanding and Reasoning in UAV Scenes
summary: The reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) can be limited by incomplete or inaccurate visual observations in the general domain. In unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) scenes, small targets, subtle attributes, and changing viewpoints further complicate perception and understanding. Therefore, we introduce Drone-PUR, a dataset and benchmark organized around visual clue discovery, interpretation, and integration, corresponding to the three capability dimensions of perception, understanding, and reasoning. Reasoning samples are designed to require models to combine multiple visual clues to derive visually grounded conclusions. Its 11 tasks provide 175k training and 20k test samples spanning single images, image sequences, cross-modal images, and multiple viewpoints. All test samples undergo human review. Evaluating 22 general-purpose VLMs reveals persistent limitations in spatial judgment and cross-modal and cross-view reasoning. Across models, stronger perception is associated with better reasoning, while single-task fine-tuning further reveals selective bidirectional transfer between these capabilities. To examine domain adaptation, we develop UAV-PUR from Qwen3-VL through staged fine-tuning with auxiliary supervision. Its 4B and 8B variants improve overall multiple-choice accuracy by 18.33 and 17.52 percentage points over their pretrained counterparts, respectively. The dataset and project resources are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Drone-PUR is a dataset and benchmark for UAV scene understanding with 175k training and 20k test samples across 11 tasks, and UAV-PUR, a Qwen3-VL model fine-tuned for this domain, improves multiple-choice accuracy by 18.33 and 17.52 percentage points at 4B and 8B.
AI.motivation: VLM reasoning is limited by incomplete or inaccurate visual observations, and small targets, subtle attributes and changing viewpoints in UAV scenes complicate perception and understanding.
AI.method: The benchmark is organized around visual clue discovery, interpretation and integration, corresponding to perception, understanding and reasoning, with samples covering single images, image sequences, cross-modal images and multiple viewpoints. UAV-PUR is built from Qwen3-VL through staged fine-tuning with auxiliary supervision, and all test samples undergo human review.
AI.result: Evaluating 22 general-purpose VLMs reveals persistent limitations in spatial judgment and in cross-modal and cross-view reasoning. Stronger perception is associated with better reasoning, and single-task fine-tuning shows selective bidirectional transfer between the two. The 4B and 8B UAV-PUR variants improve overall multiple-choice accuracy by 18.33 and 17.52 percentage points over their pretrained counterparts.
AI.conclusion: Current general-purpose VLMs are limited in spatial and cross-view reasoning for UAV imagery, and domain-specific staged fine-tuning gives large gains.

title: EgoHSI3R: Online 4D Hand-Scene Interaction Reconstruction from Egocentric Video
summary: Egocentric videos offer an abundant source of hand-scene interactions for embodied learning, which requires recovering hands, camera, and scene consistently in a shared 3D world. Existing methods focus on either camera-frame hands or world-space hand trajectories, without jointly recovering the scene pointmaps or interaction information. Building a complete reconstruction from such specialized predictions therefore typically requires per-sequence optimization. We propose EgoHSI3R, a unified feed-forward framework for online 4D hand-scene interaction reconstruction from egocentric monocular video. To jointly recover these components, it maintains a recurrent scene representation that accumulates geometric evidence over time and provides a shared world space and scale. We introduce hand-centric prompts that fuse pretrained hand priors and local scene context, while MANO vertex queries attend to scene features to predict dense per-vertex contact. These designs enable a single network to jointly estimate camera motion, dense scene geometry, world-space bilateral MANO hands, and per-vertex hand contact. Despite operating causally, EgoHSI3R achieves the lowest world-space hand joint error on ARCTIC among the evaluated methods, while offering faster inference than existing world-space hand reconstruction pipelines and competitive camera and scene reconstruction accuracy.

AI.tldr: EgoHSI3R is a unified feed-forward framework that jointly reconstructs camera motion, dense scene geometry, world-space bilateral MANO hands and per-vertex hand contact online from egocentric monocular video.
AI.motivation: Existing methods recover either camera-frame hands or world-space hand trajectories, and building a complete reconstruction from such specialized predictions usually requires per-sequence optimization.
AI.method: A recurrent scene representation accumulates geometric evidence over time to provide a shared world space and scale. Hand-centric prompts fuse pretrained hand priors with local scene context, and MANO vertex queries attend to scene features to predict dense per-vertex contact.
AI.result: On ARCTIC, EgoHSI3R achieves the lowest world-space hand joint error among the evaluated methods, while running faster than existing world-space hand reconstruction pipelines and remaining competitive on camera and scene reconstruction accuracy.
AI.conclusion: A single causal network can jointly estimate hands, camera and scene for egocentric hand-scene interaction without per-sequence optimization.

title: Spatial Atlas-Informed Loss Ensembles for Whole-Body PSMA PET/CT Metastasis Segmentation
summary: Existing whole-body PSMA PET/CT prostate metastasis segmentation methods generally rely on images alone, without explicitly incorporating where metastases tend to occur. We investigate whether a population metastasis atlas can improve lesion detection when integrated into model training. We constructed voxel-wise mean and standard deviation maps from 375 expert-annotated training scans and used them to weight the cross-entropy loss of an nnU-Net. The additional penalties for missed lesions and false positives depend on spatial atlas statistics and diminish as predictions become confidently correct. Seven configurations were compared on validation data; three were combined by majority voting into SAILS (Spatial Atlas-Informed Loss enSemble). We compared SAILS with a baseline nnU-Net and inference-time atlas fusion on AutoPET~III (110 disease-positive cases) and Deep-PSMA (100 external cases). No atlas or registration is needed at inference. Results: On AutoPET~III, SAILS improved whole-body Dice (0.531 vs. 0.520; p=0.006), reduced missed-lesion volume (9.5 vs. 12.1 cc/case; p<0.01), and increased pooled lesion sensitivity (0.857 vs. 0.843; p=0.004). On Deep-PSMA, SAILS detected 126 additional reference lesions (sensitivity 0.769 vs. 0.751; p<0.001), without a significant whole-body Dice change (-0.009; p=0.36). High-risk bone Dice improved in both cohorts (0.576 vs. 0.552 and 0.667 vs. 0.653; both p<0.01). False-positive volume increased by 2.3 and 18.2 cc/case, respectively (p<0.001). Atlas-weighted training improves lesion detection, especially in high-risk bone, without test-time atlas registration, but increases false positives.

AI.tldr: SAILS is a loss ensemble that weights the cross-entropy loss of an nnU-Net with voxel-wise population metastasis atlas statistics, improving lesion detection for whole-body PSMA PET/CT metastasis segmentation without atlas registration at inference.
AI.motivation: Existing whole-body PSMA PET/CT metastasis segmentation methods rely on images alone and do not explicitly use where metastases tend to occur.
AI.method: Voxel-wise mean and standard deviation maps are computed from 375 expert-annotated training scans and used to weight the cross-entropy loss, with extra penalties for missed lesions and false positives that diminish as predictions become confidently correct. Three of seven validated configurations are combined by majority voting into SAILS.
AI.result: On AutoPET III, SAILS improves whole-body Dice from 0.520 to 0.531 (p=0.006), reduces missed-lesion volume from 12.1 to 9.5 cc per case and raises pooled lesion sensitivity from 0.843 to 0.857. On Deep-PSMA, SAILS detects 126 additional reference lesions (sensitivity 0.769 versus 0.751) without a significant whole-body Dice change, and high-risk bone Dice improves in both cohorts, while false-positive volume increases by 2.3 and 18.2 cc per case.
AI.conclusion: Atlas-weighted training improves lesion detection, especially in high-risk bone, without test-time atlas registration, at the cost of more false positives.

title: Sparse Autoencoders for Expert-Assisted Interpretation of Histopathology Foundation Model Embeddings
summary: Histopathology foundation models learn rich embedding representations, but their internal structure remains difficult to inspect. Concept-level interpretability is particularly relevant in computational pathology because pathologists reason through recurring morphological and tissue-level patterns, including tissue architecture, cellular morphology, staining variation, and artifacts. In this work, we investigate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose embeddings from histopathology foundation models into sparse latent features suitable for expert-assisted interpretation. We train vanilla and Batch-TopK SAE variants on NCT-CRC embeddings, using CONCH as the primary foundation model and UNI2-h as an additional robustness evaluation, and characterize the resulting latent features through reconstruction fidelity, sparsity, coherence, label enrichment, and downstream class-signal preservation. The learned sparse representations preserve most downstream tissue-class information, and their latent features retrieve more coherent and label-concentrated patch groups than raw embedding dimensions or PCA components. Discussions with pathology experts further motivated a WSI-level latent visualization workflow that places feature activations into larger tissue context. Overall, the additional UNI2-h evaluation suggests that the observed behavior is not specific to CONCH, supporting the use of sparse autoencoders for expert-assisted analysis of histopathology foundation-model embeddings, while emphasizing that latent features should be treated as candidate concepts requiring pathological assessment rather than automatically validated histopathological concepts.

AI.tldr: The paper uses sparse autoencoders to decompose histopathology foundation model embeddings into sparse latent features, which retrieve more coherent and label-concentrated patch groups than raw dimensions or PCA components while preserving most tissue-class information.
AI.motivation: Histopathology foundation models learn rich embeddings whose internal structure is hard to inspect, and pathologists reason through recurring morphological and tissue-level patterns, which makes concept-level interpretability relevant.
AI.method: Vanilla and Batch-TopK sparse autoencoders are trained on NCT-CRC embeddings, with CONCH as the primary foundation model and UNI2-h as a robustness check. Latent features are characterized by reconstruction fidelity, sparsity, coherence, label enrichment and downstream class-signal preservation, and a WSI-level latent visualization workflow was motivated by discussions with pathology experts.
AI.result: The learned sparse representations preserve most downstream tissue-class information, and their latent features retrieve more coherent and label-concentrated patch groups than raw embedding dimensions or PCA components. The UNI2-h evaluation suggests the behavior is not specific to CONCH.
AI.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders support expert-assisted analysis of histopathology foundation-model embeddings, but latent features should be treated as candidate concepts requiring pathological assessment rather than validated histopathological concepts.

title: Coupled or Independent? Fault Coupling in Agentic Medical Vision Systems
summary: Vision-language agents equipped with tools expose intermediate outputs for inspection and comparison with the model's reasoning, which may offer safety benefits over single-shot models. This paper tests that potential benefit when the sensor reading itself is untrusted, so that the tool and reasoning channels share a common visual fault. We consider a dermatology agent based on segmentation, contrastive retrieval, and an iterative vision-language reasoner and define a coupling taxonomy that distinguishes single-channel errors from joint errors that agree or disagree. On PAD-UFES-20, we show that typographic injection produces detectable directional retrieval capture, whereas physical corruption does not. Crop-first retrieval preserves the payload at a readable scale and produces 55% joint wrong agreement across all cases (71% of faulty cases); full-image retrieval produces 35% (43%). Under a binary decision, if both channels are wrong, their predictions must agree, so hard-label channel comparison cannot detect joint failures, limiting disagreement recall to 0.29 (crop-first) versus 0.57 (full-image). The direction of the order effect is reproduced on the independent HIBA test set.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that in a tool-using dermatology vision-language agent, a shared visual fault can make tool and reasoning channels fail jointly, and that crop-first retrieval produces far more joint wrong agreement than full-image retrieval, so hard-label channel comparison cannot detect such failures.
AI.motivation: Tool-using vision-language agents are assumed to gain safety from inspecting intermediate outputs, but this benefit is untested when the sensor reading itself is untrusted and the tool and reasoning channels share a common visual fault.
AI.method: The authors study a dermatology agent built from segmentation, contrastive retrieval and an iterative vision-language reasoner, and define a coupling taxonomy that separates single-channel errors from joint errors that agree or disagree. Typographic injection and physical corruption are tested on PAD-UFES-20, with crop-first and full-image retrieval compared.
AI.result: Typographic injection produces detectable directional retrieval capture, whereas physical corruption does not. Crop-first retrieval produces 55% joint wrong agreement across all cases (71% of faulty cases), against 35% (43%) for full-image retrieval. Disagreement recall is 0.29 for crop-first and 0.57 for full-image, and the order effect is reproduced on the independent HIBA test set.
AI.conclusion: Under a binary decision, joint failures of both channels necessarily agree, so hard-label channel comparison cannot detect them, and the benefit of tool inspection depends on how the shared sensor input is handled.

title: Let LiDAR Decide Where to Look: Geometry-Measured Token Selection for Efficient Sparse Latent World Models
summary: Vision-centric autonomous driving models encode thousands of image tokens per frame, yet most depict sky, buildings, or empty road---content irrelevant to planning. Worse, these tokens dilute the planner's attention: we show that randomly discarding 75% of tokens already outperforms the dense model, because the planner can concentrate on the remaining driving-critical content. Building on this finding, we present Geometry-Aware Token Selection (GATS), which uses LiDAR and radar point projections to select a small fraction of image tokens before the vision backbone runs. Because the selector operates on measured 3D geometry rather than visual features, the backbone encodes only the selected patches, cutting end-to-end FLOPs by up to $18\times$. Each kept token receives a 3D anchor from its LiDAR point and is fed to a self-supervised latent world model that predicts future features and 3D displacements without box annotations. At 25% budget, GATS achieves a 3-sec L2 displacement error of 0.520 m on nuScenes and an EPDMS of 88.9 on NAVSIM---surpassing the dense baseline (0.573 m / 85.9) at $6.6\times$ fewer total FLOPs. At an extreme 10% budget (24 GFLOPs, $18\times$ reduction), it still beats the dense baseline on both nuScenes (0.537 m vs. 0.573 m L2) and NAVSIM (87.9 vs. 85.9 EPDMS). On 739 intent-critical scenarios, GATS covers 95.8% of hazardous vehicles and achieves a 0.09% collision rate---73.5% lower than the dense model (0.34%).

AI.tldr: GATS is a token selector that uses LiDAR and radar point projections to keep a small fraction of image tokens before the vision backbone runs, cutting end-to-end FLOPs by up to 18 times while beating the dense baseline on nuScenes and NAVSIM.
AI.motivation: Vision-centric driving models encode thousands of image tokens per frame, most of which show content irrelevant to planning, and these tokens dilute the planner's attention.
AI.method: Geometry-Aware Token Selection (GATS) selects image tokens from measured 3D geometry rather than visual features, so the backbone encodes only the selected patches. Each kept token receives a 3D anchor from its LiDAR point and is fed to a self-supervised latent world model that predicts future features and 3D displacements without box annotations.
AI.result: At a 25% budget, GATS achieves a 3-second L2 displacement error of 0.520 m on nuScenes and an EPDMS of 88.9 on NAVSIM, against 0.573 m and 85.9 for the dense baseline at 6.6 times fewer total FLOPs. At 10% budget it still beats the dense baseline on both benchmarks, and on 739 intent-critical scenarios it covers 95.8% of hazardous vehicles with a 0.09% collision rate, 73.5% lower than the dense model.
AI.conclusion: Selecting tokens by measured geometry rather than visual features both reduces computation and improves planning, since the planner can focus on driving-critical content.

title: UFMF: Radar-Guided Kinematic Priors for Real-Time 4D Occupancy Forecasting
summary: Real-time 4D occupancy forecasting requires reliably extrapolating both ego motion and surrounding actor motion under strict latency budgets. Recent occupancy world models improve long-horizon fidelity through generative decoders and 3D volumetric modeling, yet their computational cost makes real-time deployment challenging. Light-weight BEV forecasters meet latency requirements but often blur or suppress fast-moving actors at longer horizons. We present UFMF (Ultra-Fast Multi-modal Forecaster), a real-time forecaster that keeps an attention-free diagonal state-space temporal core while injecting targeted kinematic and geometric structure where lightweight models typically fail. A radar-guided velocity-aware dynamic prior (VADP) decomposes future displacement into a linear extrapolation plus a learned horizon-dependent residual. The resulting per-cell flow fields transport a compact dynamic latent subspace during rollout. Two auxiliary training constraints complement this branch: world-frame dynamic supervision enforces inter-horizon trajectory coherence, and class-conditioned vertical-profile supervision regularizes BEV-to-3D lifting. UFMF operates at 122 FPS on a single RTX 4090 and reaches 0.45 fast-displacement mIoU on nuScenes, outperforming recent occupancy world models at a fraction of their computational cost.

AI.tldr: UFMF is a real-time 4D occupancy forecaster that uses a radar-guided velocity-aware dynamic prior and an attention-free diagonal state-space core, running at 122 FPS on a single RTX 4090 and reaching 0.45 fast-displacement mIoU on nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Real-time occupancy forecasting must extrapolate ego and actor motion under strict latency budgets, but occupancy world models are too costly for real-time use, while lightweight BEV forecasters blur or suppress fast-moving actors at longer horizons.
AI.method: The forecaster keeps an attention-free diagonal state-space temporal core. A radar-guided velocity-aware dynamic prior (VADP) decomposes future displacement into a linear extrapolation plus a learned horizon-dependent residual, producing per-cell flow fields that transport a compact dynamic latent subspace during rollout. Two auxiliary constraints add world-frame dynamic supervision and class-conditioned vertical-profile supervision.
AI.result: UFMF runs at 122 FPS on a single RTX 4090 and reaches 0.45 fast-displacement mIoU on nuScenes, outperforming recent occupancy world models at a fraction of their computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Targeted kinematic and geometric structure can make lightweight forecasters accurate for fast-moving actors while meeting real-time requirements.

title: AVID: A Weakly Aligned RGB-Infrared Dataset and Perturbation Benchmark for Tiny Aerial Targets
summary: Long-range detection of small drones is complicated by their visual similarity to birds and by the limited detail available from ground-based cameras. Combining visible and infrared observations offers complementary information, but their usefulness depends on target size, cross-modal alignment, and image quality. We present AVID, a benchmark for studying these factors using real RGB-infrared bird-drone surveillance footage originating from the Drone Detection Dataset and curated for the IEEE ICIP 2025 Video and Image Processing Cup. AVID comprises 32,040 corresponding frame pairs from 115 videos, with 35,952 existing bird and drone annotations at $320\times256$ resolution. Targets occupy an unusually narrow size range: 68.1\% have a geometric-mean bounding-box side of 8--16 pixels, and 99.0\% meet the COCO small-object criterion. To characterize the geometric difficulty of combining the modalities, we introduce an object-relative alignment ratio and an alignment burden curve. In a sample of 300 frame pairs, 32.3\% have estimated global translations greater than 5 pixels; among the 264 pairs with matching annotations, 16.3\% exceed one median target side. We further introduce AVID-C, which simulates seven families of image degradation at five severity levels independently in RGB, infrared, or both. A fixed-feature analysis examines how scale, degradation, and added cross-modal shifts affect fitted bird-drone class overlap. At 12--16 pixels, the Bhattacharyya error bounds are 0.148 for RGB, 0.198 for infrared, and 0.046 for their combined features. These values describe separation in the specified feature and density models, not detector accuracy. Together, AVID and AVID-C support scale-aware, alignment-aware, and sensor-specific studies of tiny aerial targets.

AI.tldr: AVID is a benchmark of 32,040 aligned RGB-infrared frame pairs of tiny drones and birds, with a degradation suite AVID-C, and its fixed-feature analysis shows that combining both modalities gives much lower class overlap than either alone at 12 to 16 pixels.
AI.motivation: Long-range detection of small drones is complicated by their visual similarity to birds and by limited detail in ground-based cameras, and the usefulness of combining visible and infrared observations depends on target size, cross-modal alignment and image quality.
AI.method: AVID is built from real RGB-infrared bird-drone surveillance footage from the Drone Detection Dataset, with 35,952 annotations at 320 by 256 resolution. The authors introduce an object-relative alignment ratio and an alignment burden curve, and AVID-C simulates seven families of degradation at five severities independently in RGB, infrared or both. A fixed-feature analysis fits bird-drone class overlap.
AI.result: 68.1% of targets have a geometric-mean box side of 8 to 16 pixels, and 32.3% of 300 sampled frame pairs have estimated global translations above 5 pixels. At 12 to 16 pixels, Bhattacharyya error bounds are 0.148 for RGB, 0.198 for infrared and 0.046 for combined features, describing separation in the specified feature and density models rather than detector accuracy.
AI.conclusion: AVID and AVID-C support scale-aware, alignment-aware and sensor-specific studies of tiny aerial targets.

title: FieldGuideRAG: Image-Grounded GraphRAG for Fine-Grained Recognition with Vision-Language Models
summary: We present FieldGuideRAG, a training-free GraphRAG method in which a vision-language model, or VLM, recognizes fine-grained species by comparing the query with real photographs stored on the nodes of a knowledge graph. Multimodal GraphRAG systems describe each entity in text, and text conveys little of the visual detail that separates look-alike species. Our graph stores one photograph on every species node and links each species to its relatives, its geographic range and its ecological facts. A frozen VLM verifies the query against the photograph of each candidate node. FieldGuideRAG fuses the verification scores with the range edge and answers questions about the organism from the fact edges of the verified species. On CUB-200, a Wikidata graph and four iNaturalist domains, the node photograph improves verification over the species name on every graph, while text descriptions add little. Verification of the candidate pool exceeds a SigLIP retriever by up to 16 points, the range edge adds 7 to 19 points on iNaturalist, and answering from fact edges is correct on up to 89.5% of 28,820 ecological questions. The verification scores also detect queries whose species is missing from the graph. Graphs, prompts and code will be released.

AI.tldr: FieldGuideRAG is a training-free GraphRAG method in which a frozen VLM verifies a query against the photograph stored on each candidate species node of a knowledge graph, improving fine-grained species recognition over text-based graph retrieval.
AI.motivation: Multimodal GraphRAG systems describe each entity in text, which conveys little of the visual detail that separates look-alike species.
AI.method: The graph stores one photograph on every species node and links each species to its relatives, geographic range and ecological facts. A frozen VLM verifies the query against each candidate's photograph, the verification scores are fused with the range edge, and answers about the organism are drawn from the fact edges of the verified species.
AI.result: On CUB-200, a Wikidata graph and four iNaturalist domains, node photographs improve verification over species names on every graph while text descriptions add little. Verification exceeds a SigLIP retriever by up to 16 points, the range edge adds 7 to 19 points on iNaturalist, and answering from fact edges is correct on up to 89.5% of 28,820 ecological questions. Verification scores also detect queries whose species is missing from the graph.
AI.conclusion: Image-grounded verification on a knowledge graph is effective for fine-grained recognition, and the verification scores can also flag species absent from the graph.

title: RADI3N: GeometRic ImAge EDiting via ParametrIc 3D CoNtrol
