summary: Recent diffusion-based methods have substantially advanced image editing, yet parametric 3D control at the part level remains challenging. Existing approaches either operate on whole objects with manual rigging, or revert to 2D handles at the part level. They also struggle to model appearance and texture under large transformations, leading to unrealistic outputs in geometry-intensive edits. To address these limitations, we introduce RADI3N, a framework for semantically-grounded part-aware object manipulation with parametric 3D control. Our CS-ARAP deformation module suppresses rotation-field discontinuities at part boundaries via neighborhood covariance smoothing, producing structurally consistent deformations under complex part-level edits. We further introduce an inversion-free selective texture transfer mechanism that suppresses high-frequency positional biases and scales up low-frequency semantic cues within cross-image attention. This eliminates strict spatial bias and supports semantic matching, allowing source appearance to follow the edited part onto its new geometry. Experiments demonstrate that RADI3N achieves state-of-the-art performance in geometric fidelity, viewpoint consistency, and controllability.

AI.tldr: RADI3N is a diffusion-based image editing framework that performs part-level parametric 3D control through a CS-ARAP deformation module and an inversion-free selective texture transfer mechanism, aiming for geometrically faithful edits.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion editing either operates on whole objects with manual rigging or uses 2D handles at the part level, and these methods struggle with appearance and texture under large transformations, producing unrealistic geometry-intensive edits.
AI.method: The CS-ARAP deformation module suppresses rotation-field discontinuities at part boundaries through neighborhood covariance smoothing. An inversion-free selective texture transfer mechanism suppresses high-frequency positional biases and amplifies low-frequency semantic cues within cross-image attention, so source appearance follows the edited part onto its new geometry.
AI.result: The authors report state-of-the-art performance in geometric fidelity, viewpoint consistency and controllability.
AI.conclusion: Semantically grounded, part-aware parametric 3D control can make diffusion-based image editing structurally consistent under complex part-level edits.

title: Prior-Guided Single-Exposure HDR Novel View Synthesis via Base-Gain Representation
summary: Single-exposure high dynamic range (HDR) novel view synthesis (NVS) recovers HDR scenes from low dynamic range (LDR) views captured at a single exposure and estimates camera response function (CRF) for LDR re-exposure. Without HDR ground-truth, using single-exposure LDR views as the sole source of direct supervision underconstrains HDR reconstruction and cannot ensure its faithful recovery, motivating the need for learned LDR-to-HDR reconstruction priors. Moreover, single-exposure LDR views supervise CRF only over a limited range, necessitating a learnable prior for reliable re-exposure beyond it. We propose PriorGS, a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that addresses both challenges by (1) guiding HDR recovery with pseudo-HDR supervision from 2D single-exposure HDR reconstruction methods while anchoring it to input LDR views through a closed reconstruction loop; and (2) regularizing CRF modeling with a learnable prior that guarantees monotonicity and promotes plausible responses. Yet cross-view inconsistencies in independently generated pseudo-HDR targets impair scene reconstruction when HDR is encoded directly as Gaussian's color attribute. We therefore introduce a 3D base-gain HDR representation that factors HDR radiance into an LDR base and an overlaid 3D gain field, promoting robustness to such inconsistencies and enabling 3D HDR appearance editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate PriorGS's substantial superiority over baselines.

AI.tldr: PriorGS is a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that reconstructs HDR novel views from single-exposure LDR inputs and estimates the camera response function (CRF) for re-exposure. It uses pseudo-HDR supervision, a learnable monotonic CRF prior, and a 3D base-gain HDR representation.
AI.motivation: Single-exposure LDR views give weak direct supervision for HDR reconstruction and constrain the CRF only over a limited range, so learned priors are needed; independently generated pseudo-HDR targets are inconsistent across views and corrupt scene reconstruction when HDR is stored as a Gaussian colour attribute.
AI.method: Pseudo-HDR supervision from 2D single-exposure HDR methods is anchored to the input LDR views through a closed reconstruction loop, and the CRF is regularised by a learnable prior that guarantees monotonicity. HDR radiance is factored into an LDR base and an overlaid 3D gain field, which promotes robustness to cross-view inconsistency and enables 3D HDR appearance editing.
AI.result: The abstract reports substantial superiority over baselines in extensive experiments, without specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The base-gain representation makes HDR scene reconstruction robust to inconsistent pseudo-HDR targets and supports 3D HDR editing, extending single-exposure HDR novel view synthesis.

title: Segment Anything Pancreas: A Unified MRI Segmentation Model for Pancreatic Cancer Radiotherapy
summary: Background: Limited tumor annotations and incomplete labels across MRI datasets hinder unified segmentation of pancreatic tumors and organs at risk (OARs) for MRI-guided radiotherapy. Purpose: We propose Pancreas-MedNeXt, a unified model that segments the whole pancreas, its subregions, tumors, and surrounding OARs from one MRI volume. Methods: The model uses a shared MedNeXt encoder-decoder with supervised whole-pancreas and subregion pretraining, followed by multitask fine-tuning. Three output heads predict the pancreatic subregions, tumor, and OARs (stomach, duodenum, kidneys). An annotation-aware loss allows training on partially labeled data without treating unannotated structures as background. Pancreas and tumor were evaluated by three-fold cross-validation on 142 PANTHER patients (92 diagnostic, 50 MR-Linac), subregions and OARs on Cyst-X and AMOS test sets, and pancreas and OARs on 33 external T1-weighted TotalSegmentator scans. Comparisons with nnU-Net, MedNeXt, VISTA3D, and Swin UNETR used the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) with paired bootstrap 95% CIs. Results: Pancreas-MedNeXt achieved the highest mean pancreas and tumor DSC on diagnostic and MR-Linac MRI. Tumor DSC was 58.41% and 42.55%, exceeding task-specific MedNeXt by 4.94 (95% CI: 0.28-9.45) and 5.89 (95% CI: 2.37-9.72) percentage points, respectively. Whole-pancreas DSC was 85.73% and 70.66%. Pretraining improved head, body, and tail DSC by 2.01, 3.00, and 3.78 percentage points over training from scratch. It also achieved the highest DSC for the pancreas, duodenum, and right kidney on AMOS, and for all five organs on external MRI, exceeding the next-best method by 4.92-8.85 percentage this http URL: A single Pancreas-MedNeXt model segments tumors, pancreatic subregions, and OARs on diagnostic and MR-Linac MRI, which could streamline contouring for pancreatic cancer radiotherapy.

AI.tldr: Pancreas-MedNeXt is one MedNeXt-based model that segments the whole pancreas, its subregions, pancreatic tumours and surrounding organs at risk from a single MRI volume. It reports the highest pancreas and tumour Dice on diagnostic and MR-Linac MRI among the compared methods.
AI.motivation: Limited tumour annotations and incomplete labels across MRI datasets hinder unified segmentation of pancreatic tumours and organs at risk for MRI-guided radiotherapy.
AI.method: A shared MedNeXt encoder-decoder is pretrained with supervised whole-pancreas and subregion segmentation, then fine-tuned multitask with three output heads for subregions, tumour and organs at risk. An annotation-aware loss allows training on partially labelled data without treating unannotated structures as background.
AI.result: On 142 PANTHER patients (92 diagnostic, 50 MR-Linac) with three-fold cross-validation, tumour Dice was 58.41% and 42.55%, exceeding task-specific MedNeXt by 4.94 and 5.89 percentage points; whole-pancreas Dice was 85.73% and 70.66%. Pretraining improved head, body and tail Dice by 2.01, 3.00 and 3.78 points. The model also led on AMOS for pancreas, duodenum and right kidney and on external T1-weighted scans for all five organs, beating the next-best method by 4.92 to 8.85 points. Baselines were nnU-Net, MedNeXt, VISTA3D and Swin UNETR.
AI.conclusion: A single model can segment tumours, pancreatic subregions and organs at risk on diagnostic and MR-Linac MRI, which could streamline contouring for pancreatic cancer radiotherapy.

title: Grounding Image Composition with Label-Conditioned Visual Evidence
summary: Image composition labels such as center, diagonal, or rule of thirds describe visual structure rather than object categories. KU-PCP provides image-level labels and class-specific geometric elements, but does not show which visible regions people associate with each of its nine classes. We introduce KU-PCP Elements (KU-PCPE), a label-conditioned region-evidence benchmark for photographic composition. Given an image and a label already judged applicable, the task is to segment the visible regions that explain why the label applies. KU-PCPE contains 4,093 single-annotator training masks and a 1,327-task expert test split with three masks per image-label task. The annotations also include exploratory segment-versus-line ratings that describe whether region or semantic-guideline evidence better explains the label. A held-out expert reaches .867 Dice against the other experts, while the strongest deployable model reaches .664, a proposal oracle .672, and the best vision-language model (VLM) proposal selector .395. KU-PCPE exposes the gap between recognizing a composition label and grounding the human-aligned visual evidence that makes it plausible in a particular image.

AI.tldr: KU-PCP Elements (KU-PCPE) is a benchmark where, given an image and a label already judged applicable, the task is to segment the visible regions that explain the composition label. The strongest deployable model reaches Dice 0.664, well below the 0.867 agreement between experts.
AI.motivation: KU-PCP gives image-level composition labels and class-specific geometric elements but does not show which visible regions people associate with each label, so the gap between recognising a label and grounding its visual evidence is unmeasured.
AI.method: The benchmark provides 4,093 single-annotator training masks and a 1,327-task expert test split with three masks per image-label task. Exploratory segment-versus-line ratings indicate whether region or semantic-guideline evidence better explains each label.
AI.result: A held-out expert reaches 0.867 Dice against the other experts, the strongest deployable model 0.664, a proposal oracle 0.672, and the best vision-language model proposal selector 0.395.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark exposes the gap between recognising a composition label and grounding the human-aligned visual evidence that makes it plausible in a particular image.

title: An Empirical Study on Learning Rooftop Solar Potential from Satellite Imagery Directly Without Explicit Geometry
summary: Rooftop solar potential estimation often relies on LiDAR, digital surface models (DSMs), or pipelines that explicitly reconstruct roof geometry before estimating solar potential. We propose Direct Rooftop Solar Prediction (DRSP), an end-to-end formulation that maps satellite imagery and coarse regional sunlight information directly to application-level solar outputs. DRSP neither requires explicit geometric representations as input nor predicts roof orientation, slope, height, DSMs, or other geometric quantities as intermediate outputs, and therefore requires no geometric intermediate supervision. To enable large-scale study of this formulation, we develop a programmatic data-curation pipeline that converts per-panel information from the Google Solar API into usable-rooftop masks and spatial solar-energy targets, yielding two geographically distinct datasets containing approximately 60K rooftops from the U.S. Midwest and 87K from Texas. We demonstrate the feasibility of DRSP and systematically characterize the effects of geographic training distribution, model depth, image resolution, regional sunlight conditioning, and heatmap regression objectives. Overall, our results suggest that useful rooftop-scale solar information can be learned directly from 2D imagery without explicit geometric intermediate representations, offering a simpler path toward large-scale solar assessment. Our code and dataset are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Direct Rooftop Solar Prediction (DRSP) maps satellite imagery and coarse regional sunlight information directly to rooftop solar outputs, with no geometric inputs or geometric intermediate outputs. The authors argue that useful rooftop-scale solar information can be learned from 2D imagery alone.
AI.motivation: Rooftop solar potential estimation usually relies on LiDAR, digital surface models or pipelines that explicitly reconstruct roof geometry before estimating solar potential.
AI.method: A programmatic pipeline converts per-panel Google Solar API data into usable-rooftop masks and spatial solar-energy targets, yielding about 60K rooftops from the U.S. Midwest and 87K from Texas. The study varies geographic training distribution, model depth, image resolution, regional sunlight conditioning and heatmap regression objectives.
AI.result: The abstract reports the feasibility of DRSP and a systematic characterisation of these factors, without specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Useful rooftop-scale solar information can be learned directly from 2D imagery, offering a simpler path to large-scale solar assessment; code and dataset are released.

title: CompoSET: A Controlled Single-Edit Benchmark for Vision-Language Compositionality
comment: Dataset: this https URL | Code: this https URL | 9 pages main text, 38 pages total
summary: Vision-language compositionality is the ability to identify which properties, relations, quantities, and states bind to which entities in both an image and a caption, and to match those bindings across modalities. Existing benchmarks evaluate this ability through image-text matching: a model ranks candidate image-caption match similarities and succeeds when the correct match comes on top. In such datasets, paired images differ by more than a single binding: scene, layout, and content all differ, with 97% of pixels changing on average. Such pairs do not isolate compositionality: results are confounded by global image differences. We introduce Compositional Single-EdiT (CompoSET), a benchmark dataset in which each base image-caption pair has an edited counterpart, or foil, that preserves the scene but differs by a single controlled edit, such as color, count, spatial relation, or object state. Base and foil images preserve naturalistic scene complexity yet are visually near-identical: only 8% of pixels change on average. Our dataset has many foils per base scene (~22) in order to separate scene difficulty from edit difficulty, a distinction one-foil-per-base benchmarks cannot make. CompoSET contains 1,776 instances across 80 naturalistic scenes, spanning 16 edit types in 4 semantic categories, with captions at 3 verbosity levels. We test 22 dual-encoder VLMs and find that all models perform at or below chance level on CompoSET, despite scoring well on prior benchmarks. This suggests that apparent progress under prior image-text matching protocols may be an artifact arising from confounds in benchmark design, and that compositional understanding in dual-encoder VLMs is far from solved. CompoSET addresses the confounds and offers a better controlled benchmark to measure future progress.

AI.tldr: CompoSET is a benchmark in which each base image-caption pair has a foil that keeps the scene but differs by one controlled edit, isolating vision-language compositionality. All 22 dual-encoder VLMs tested perform at or below chance on it.
AI.motivation: Existing image-text matching benchmarks compare image pairs that differ in scene, layout and content (about 97% of pixels change on average), so results are confounded by global image differences rather than by how properties bind to entities.
AI.method: Each base image has an edited foil differing by one controlled edit in colour, count, spatial relation or object state. Foils are visually near-identical (about 8% of pixels change), and each scene has about 22 foils so that scene difficulty can be separated from edit difficulty. The benchmark has 1,776 instances across 80 naturalistic scenes, 16 edit types in 4 semantic categories, and captions at 3 verbosity levels.
AI.result: All 22 dual-encoder VLMs perform at or below chance on CompoSET, despite scoring well on prior benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Apparent progress under prior image-text matching protocols may be an artifact of benchmark confounds, and compositional understanding in dual-encoder VLMs is far from solved; CompoSET offers a better controlled measure.

title: MotorSense: A Video-EMG Dataset of Motoric Representations for Action Understanding
comment: NeurIPS 2026. 27 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Computer vision models learn hand action only from its visual consequences, without access to the underlying embodied motor signals. We address this absence with MotorSense, the first large-scale paired egocentric video and surface electromyography (EMG) dataset. MotorSense pairs bimanual EMG bands with egocentric video and yields synchronized video, bimanual EMG and IMU, and audio across 100 hours of unscripted manipulation. EMG offers a powerful scalable alternative to manual annotation: it captures finger movement, hand configuration, and the forces exerted between hand and environment as a dense signal free of occlusion and labeler bias, whereas manual annotation is costly, subjective, and unreliable under occlusion. We use MotorSense to learn sensorimotor alignment, producing an organization of action that is shared across the visual and motoric spaces, through cross-modal pre-training between video and EMG. The resultant vision models are then transferred to downstream tasks that benefit from sensorimotor alignment: in this case, action recognition, 3D hand reconstruction, and 3D contact reconstruction. We further demonstrate a generative application in which EMG motor signals are used to condition a video diffusion model, yielding videos of fine-grained hand manipulation. Across four action-centric computer vision tasks and eight popular video datasets, we demonstrate that sensorimotor alignment provides a stronger foundation for visual representation learning than conventional self-supervised learning methods over video, outperforming every baseline across all tasks and datasets evaluated.

AI.tldr: MotorSense is a large paired egocentric video and surface EMG dataset of 100 hours of unscripted bimanual manipulation. Cross-modal video-EMG pretraining yields vision models that outperform conventional self-supervised video baselines on action-centric tasks.
AI.motivation: Vision models learn hand action only from its visual consequences, without the embodied motor signals behind it, and manual annotation of hand actions is costly, subjective and unreliable under occlusion.
AI.method: The dataset pairs bimanual EMG bands with egocentric video, plus synchronised IMU and audio. Cross-modal pretraining between video and EMG learns sensorimotor alignment, a shared organisation of action across visual and motoric spaces. The resulting vision models are transferred to action recognition, 3D hand reconstruction and 3D contact reconstruction, and EMG signals condition a video diffusion model to generate fine-grained hand manipulation.
AI.result: Across four action-centric tasks and eight popular video datasets, sensorimotor alignment outperforms every baseline on all tasks and datasets evaluated, including conventional self-supervised video learning methods.
AI.conclusion: Sensorimotor alignment provides a stronger foundation for visual representation learning of hand action than conventional self-supervised learning over video.

title: MATS: A Multi-Agent Framework for Controllable and Reflective Tumor Synthesis
summary: Synthesizing realistic tumors on medical images helps address data scarcity for clinical AI. Existing diffusion-based methods, however, lack fine-grained attribute-level controllability, closed-loop quality verification, and awareness of which morphological patterns are underrepresented in the target distribution. We present MATS, a multi-agent framework for text-controllable, cross-organ tumor synthesis. Given a target disease, MATS first profiles its morphological distribution over a fine-grained attribute space covering tumor geometry and appearance, and constructs a generation plan that amplifies underrepresented subtypes while keeping common ones dominant. It then localizes the target organ, proposes anatomically valid placement, and executes two-stage diffusion to produce the tumor mask and render texture, each conditioned on the corresponding attributes. A closed-loop reflective mechanism verifies attribute alignment at three checkpoints throughout synthesis and provides targeted feedback to guide re-generation when misalignment is detected. Trained exclusively on a single-source pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor dataset, MATS consistently improves downstream segmentation both in-domain and across LiTS, KiTS, and MSD-Pancreas benchmarks, whereas most prior generative augmentation methods fall below real-only training.

AI.tldr: MATS is a multi-agent framework for text-controllable, cross-organ tumour synthesis on medical images, with closed-loop verification of attribute alignment. Trained on a single pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour dataset, it improves downstream segmentation across several benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based tumour synthesis lacks fine-grained attribute-level controllability, closed-loop quality verification, and awareness of which morphological patterns are underrepresented in the target distribution.
AI.method: MATS profiles the morphological distribution of a disease over a fine-grained attribute space of tumour geometry and appearance, then builds a generation plan that amplifies underrepresented subtypes while keeping common ones dominant. It localises the target organ, proposes anatomically valid placement, and runs two-stage diffusion to produce a tumour mask and render texture, each conditioned on attributes. A reflective mechanism checks attribute alignment at three checkpoints and gives targeted feedback for regeneration.
AI.result: Trained only on a single-source pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour dataset, MATS consistently improves segmentation in-domain and on LiTS, KiTS and MSD-Pancreas, whereas most prior generative augmentation methods fall below real-only training.
AI.conclusion: Controllable, closed-loop tumour synthesis can address data scarcity for clinical AI, giving augmentation that helps where prior generative methods do not.

title: FlowMoDE: Coarse-to-fine Flow Matching for Detail-aware Sim-to-Real Monocular Depth Estimation
summary: Monocular depth estimation is a fundamental capability for 3D spatial perception in robotic and intelligent systems. While data-driven discriminative methods have achieved compelling performance for monocular depth estimation, generative approaches can reconstruct fine structural details with stronger generalization. However, most existing generative diffusion models suffer from low inference efficiency caused by multi-step sampling, whereas single-step diffusion models struggle to recover high-fidelity depth maps. To mitigate these drawbacks, this paper presents FlowMoDE, a coarse-to-fine flow-matching-based framework for efficient, structure-aware monocular depth estimation supporting sim-to-real and cross-scene generalization. The core architecture first conducts coarse-level decoding conditioned on diffused features extracted from a pre-trained semantic encoder, and subsequently restores fine-grained structural patterns via expanded decoding layers. Trained exclusively on a single synthetic indoor dataset, our proposed method outperforms prior methods across five real-world indoor and outdoor datasets, yielding an average 14.1% reduction in relative error against state-of-the-art works as well as 9.9\% reduction in chamfer distance for point cloud reconstruction. We further validate the generalization capability of FlowMoDE on realistic robotic scenes, with qualitative comparisons against state-of-the-art methods. The project page is this https URL

AI.tldr: FlowMoDE is a coarse-to-fine flow-matching framework for monocular depth estimation aimed at efficient, detail-aware sim-to-real generalisation. Trained on one synthetic indoor dataset, it reduces relative error by 14.1% on average across five real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Generative diffusion depth models recover fine structure but need multi-step sampling, which is slow, while single-step diffusion models struggle to recover high-fidelity depth maps.
AI.method: Coarse-level decoding is conditioned on diffused features from a pretrained semantic encoder, and fine-grained structural patterns are then restored by expanded decoding layers.
AI.result: Outperforms prior methods on five real-world indoor and outdoor datasets, with an average 14.1% reduction in relative error versus state-of-the-art works and a 9.9% reduction in chamfer distance for point cloud reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: The coarse-to-fine flow-matching design gives an efficient, structure-aware depth estimator that generalises from synthetic to real scenes, with qualitative validation on robotic scenes.

title: Hawkeye: Reading Illegible Text with Vision Language Models
comment: For datasets, code, models: this https URL
summary: While modern Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have been remarkably successful in general scene text recognition, they consistently struggle with the long-tail distribution of text that is degraded by motion blur or low resolution. These limitations are particularly apparent in egocentric applications like smart glasses, where text is often captured in noisy environments. In this paper, we introduce the \textbf{BSTRB} (Blurry Scene Text Recognition Benchmark), a novel benchmark of 8,398 noisy image samples with high-fidelity annotations derived from 1,699 real-world video sequences. To support this, we present \textbf{Hawkeye}, a VLM fine-tuned on BSTRB to read and reason about illegible text by leveraging contextual priors and pixel-level alignment. Our results show that \name matches much larger VLMs on BSTRB overall and exceeds them on text at or below 20 pixels, in a single pass suited to real-time deployment. We characterize the resolution at which current VLMs begin to fail.

AI.tldr: Hawkeye is a VLM fine-tuned on the new BSTRB benchmark to read motion-blurred or low-resolution scene text. It matches much larger VLMs overall and exceeds them on text at or below 20 pixels, in a single pass.
AI.motivation: Modern VLMs handle general scene text well but struggle with long-tail text degraded by motion blur or low resolution, which matters for egocentric applications such as smart glasses.
AI.method: BSTRB contains 8,398 noisy image samples with high-fidelity annotations from 1,699 real-world video sequences. Hawkeye is fine-tuned on BSTRB to read and reason about illegible text using contextual priors and pixel-level alignment.
AI.result: Hawkeye matches much larger VLMs on BSTRB overall and exceeds them on text at or below 20 pixels; the paper also characterises the resolution at which current VLMs begin to fail.
AI.conclusion: The single-pass design suits real-time deployment, and the benchmark and resolution analysis show where current VLMs fail on illegible text.

title: ReVEAL: Eliciting Role-Aware Latent Visual Evidence from MLLMs for Reasoning Video Object Segmentation
summary: Reasoning video object segmentation (ReVOS) requires segmenting the target specified by an implicit query throughout a video. Existing MLLM-based methods typically require costly cross-model alignment, tying MLLM training to a downstream segmentation model. We present ReVEAL, a decoupled thinking-with-video framework for ReVOS that elicits role-aware latent visual evidence from MLLM reasoning to directly guide segmentation. ReVEAL introduces Visual Evidence Tokens (VETs) into video reasoning to associate necessary visual regions or entities with target, background, or distractor roles, while a Dynamic Attention Layer Router adaptively aggregates VET-to-video attention across layers into role-specific grounding evidence. We train the MLLM to perform VET-augmented reasoning on our constructed ReVEAL-47K dataset, with a Contrastive Attention Grounding Loss as auxiliary supervision to apply role-specific constraints to VET attention and optimize layer routing for reliable latent grounding. At inference, ReVEAL identifies the target through this thinking-with-video process and fuses the resulting role-specific evidence to guide a frozen SAM2 in predicting target masks. Experiments on five benchmarks show that ReVEAL outperforms alignment-free baselines and remains competitive with alignment-based methods.

AI.tldr: ReVEAL is a decoupled thinking-with-video framework for reasoning video object segmentation that elicits role-aware latent visual evidence from an MLLM to guide a frozen SAM2. It outperforms alignment-free baselines and remains competitive with alignment-based methods on five benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM-based ReVOS methods need costly cross-model alignment that ties MLLM training to a downstream segmentation model.
AI.method: Visual Evidence Tokens (VETs) associate necessary regions or entities with target, background or distractor roles. A Dynamic Attention Layer Router aggregates VET-to-video attention across layers into role-specific grounding evidence. The MLLM is trained on the ReVEAL-47K dataset with a Contrastive Attention Grounding Loss as auxiliary supervision, and the fused evidence guides a frozen SAM2 at inference.
AI.result: ReVEAL outperforms alignment-free baselines on five benchmarks and remains competitive with alignment-based methods.
AI.conclusion: Role-specific latent grounding from MLLM reasoning can guide segmentation without cross-model alignment.

title: SketchDirector: Complex Scene Sketching via Agentic Layout Reasoning and Detail Refinement
summary: Existing sketch generation methods often rely on image guidance and are largely limited to individual objects or simplified scenes, leaving text-guided complex scene sketching underexplored. We present SketchDirector, an agentic framework that mimics the human sketching workflow for automatic multi-concept scene sketching. Given a scene-level text prompt, SketchDirector first employs a large language model~(LLM) to decompose the scene into multiple draft assets, where each is represented by a set of Bézier curves. Then, an agentic reasoning loop iteratively plans and executes their spatial arrangement, guided by self-evolving memory. Finally, a detail refinement module leverages diffusion priors to enhance sketch quality while preserving geometric structure. To support future research and applications in multi-concept scene sketch generation, we further introduce the \textit{MCSketch8K} dataset, comprising editable vector assets, compositional layouts, and object-level manipulation annotations. Extensive experiments show that SketchDirector outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in semantic and compositional quality while effectively preserving overall contour organization during refinement. The project page is: \href{this https URL}{this https URL}.

AI.tldr: SketchDirector is an agentic framework for text-guided complex scene sketching that decomposes a scene into Bezier-curve draft assets, arranges them in a reasoning loop, and refines details with diffusion priors. It outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in semantic and compositional quality.
AI.motivation: Existing sketch generation relies on image guidance and is largely limited to individual objects or simplified scenes, leaving text-guided complex scene sketching underexplored.
AI.method: An LLM decomposes the scene prompt into multiple draft assets, each represented by Bezier curves. An agentic reasoning loop iteratively plans and executes their spatial arrangement, guided by self-evolving memory. A detail refinement module uses diffusion priors while preserving geometric structure. The MCSketch8K dataset provides editable vector assets, compositional layouts and object-level manipulation annotations.
AI.result: SketchDirector outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in semantic and compositional quality while preserving overall contour organisation during refinement.
AI.conclusion: The framework and the MCSketch8K dataset support future research and applications in multi-concept scene sketch generation.

title: STAR-FER: Adaptive Selective Restoration for Edge-Based Low-Resolution Facial Expression Recognition
summary: Variable interaction distances continuously degrade facial resolution in edge-based affective interaction, making low-resolution facial expression recognition (FER) difficult under limited computation. Full-face image or feature restoration incurs substantial overhead, whereas lightweight recognition pipelines may miss local cues that remain discriminative after degradation. We propose STAR-FER, a scale-and-task-adaptive selective restoration framework that balances recognition performance and resource constraints. A lightweight image-scale conditioned Gate jointly predicts a pixel-wise spatial ranking and a continuous restoration budget, then applies exact-support projection to obtain an input-dependent free-form mask. The mask-conditioned restorer retains complete facial context while concentrating sparse restoration and residual insertion on the selected support. Across seven degradation scales from x2 to x8 on the complete RAF-DB test set, STAR-FER achieves 80.92% mean accuracy and 71.64% Macro-F1, improving the low-resolution ResNet-18 baseline by 2.25 and 2.71 percentage points, respectively. It surpasses SR-FER by 1.04 accuracy points while requiring 8.84 GFLOPs, a 54.29% reduction, with 28.01% mean mask coverage, and maintains effective recognition at unseen non-integer scales. These results show that spatial-ranking and continuous-budget driven selective restoration reduces spatial modification and computation while maintaining low-resolution FER performance, offering an efficient path to resource-constrained affective interaction.

AI.tldr: STAR-FER is a scale- and task-adaptive selective restoration framework for low-resolution facial expression recognition on edge devices. It reaches 80.92% mean accuracy over seven degradation scales while using 8.84 GFLOPs, a 54.29% reduction relative to SR-FER.
AI.motivation: Variable interaction distance degrades facial resolution in edge-based affective interaction; full-face restoration is costly, while lightweight recognition pipelines may miss local cues that stay discriminative after degradation.
AI.method: A lightweight Gate conditioned on image scale jointly predicts a pixel-wise spatial ranking and a continuous restoration budget, then uses exact-support projection to obtain an input-dependent free-form mask. A mask-conditioned restorer keeps full facial context while concentrating sparse restoration and residual insertion on the selected support.
AI.result: Across seven scales from x2 to x8 on the complete RAF-DB test set, STAR-FER reaches 80.92% mean accuracy and 71.64% Macro-F1, improving the low-resolution ResNet-18 baseline by 2.25 and 2.71 points. It surpasses SR-FER by 1.04 accuracy points, uses 28.01% mean mask coverage, and maintains recognition at unseen non-integer scales.
AI.conclusion: Spatial-ranking and continuous-budget selective restoration reduces spatial modification and computation while maintaining low-resolution recognition performance.

title: Task-Performance Routing for Multi-Teacher Distillation in CT Medical Image Segmentation
comment: Accepted at MICCAI 2026. 11 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Pre-trained models offer complementary strengths in CT organ segmentation, but their relative accuracy varies across organs and spatial regions. Multi-teacher knowledge distillation can combine these strengths in a single student, yet global or instance-level teacher weights overlook variation within a 3D volume. We propose Task-Performance Routing (TPR), which uses region-wise segmentation errors to determine teacher weights during training without learned routing parameters. In hard regions, TPR favors teachers with lower prediction errors; in easy regions, it uses uniform weights to combine their knowledge. A hierarchical spatial partition provides fine-grained routing in shallow encoder stages and coarse-grained routing in deep stages. Experiments on BTCV, MSD-Liver, and MSD-Pancreas with two teacher pairs and two backbone architectures show higher Dice scores than the individual teachers, adaptive ensembles, and evaluated multi-teacher distillation baselines. On MSD-Pancreas, TPR achieves Dice scores of 65.40% with SwinUNETR and 68.25% with U-Net, compared with 64.38% and 67.45% for the corresponding adaptive ensembles. Inference uses the student alone, with no routing or teacher overhead. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Task-Performance Routing (TPR) distils several pretrained CT segmentation teachers into one student, weighting teachers per region by their segmentation errors without learned routing parameters. The student alone performs inference and beats the individual teachers and adaptive ensembles on Dice.
AI.motivation: Teacher accuracy varies across organs and spatial regions, and global or instance-level teacher weights overlook the variation within a 3D volume.
AI.method: Region-wise segmentation errors set teacher weights during training: in hard regions teachers with lower prediction error are favoured, and in easy regions the weights are uniform. A hierarchical spatial partition routes finely in shallow encoder stages and coarsely in deep stages.
AI.result: On BTCV, MSD-Liver and MSD-Pancreas with two teacher pairs and two backbones, TPR gives higher Dice than the individual teachers, adaptive ensembles and evaluated multi-teacher distillation baselines. On MSD-Pancreas it reaches 65.40% with SwinUNETR and 68.25% with U-Net, versus 64.38% and 67.45% for the corresponding adaptive ensembles.
AI.conclusion: Region-level, error-driven teacher routing combines teacher strengths in a single student with no inference overhead.

title: Queryable Gaussian View Index: Text Retrieval and Selective Camera Localization
summary: We present Queryable Gaussian View Index (QGVI) for querying existing Gaussian scene assets and their associated calibrated reference data. Text-view retrieval and selective RGB camera localization return poses in the asset's coordinate frame. QGVI-T turns Gaussian-rendered views into a language-searchable index of scene locations, binding structured captions to known camera poses and place identifiers. Semantic and lexical retrieval select views from distinct places without online rendering, VLM calls, or a scene-specific pose network. The image route, QGVI-I, filters LoGS-based geometric estimates using distinct inlier query keypoints. It omits photometric refinement and preserves accepted pose coordinates. On nine development scenes, QGVI-T achieves 58.3% Top-1 and 78.3% Top-5 joint relevance-and-validity success, compared with 26.1% and 34.6% for our CityLoC reimplementation with refinement. QGVI-I achieves 97.3% scene-mean pose success at 1 m/2 degrees, with pooled false-acceptance and false-rejection rates of 0.707% and 1.142%. A paired cached evaluation retains all 1,775 initializer poses correct at this threshold. Recorded median text query latency is 0.020 s. Matched controls show competitive BM25 retrieval and slightly lower false acceptance for thresholded full LoGS; grid augmentation suggests modest gains on novel-view-derived descriptions. We report model-judged semantic success separately from source-camera recovery, with source-verified or estimated scales for geometric evaluation.

AI.tldr: QGVI indexes Gaussian scene assets for text-view retrieval and selective RGB camera localisation, returning poses in the asset's coordinate frame. QGVI-T reaches 58.3% Top-1 joint relevance-and-validity success on nine development scenes, versus 26.1% for a CityLoC reimplementation with refinement.
AI.motivation: Gaussian scene assets and their calibrated reference data need to be queried by language and by image without online rendering, VLM calls or a scene-specific pose network.
AI.method: QGVI-T turns Gaussian-rendered views into a language-searchable index that binds structured captions to known camera poses and place identifiers, using semantic and lexical retrieval over distinct places. QGVI-I filters LoGS-based geometric estimates using distinct inlier query keypoints, omitting photometric refinement and preserving accepted pose coordinates.
AI.result: QGVI-T achieves 58.3% Top-1 and 78.3% Top-5 joint relevance-and-validity success, versus 26.1% and 34.6% for the CityLoC reimplementation with refinement. QGVI-I reaches 97.3% scene-mean pose success at 1 m and 2 degrees, with pooled false-acceptance and false-rejection rates of 0.707% and 1.142%. Median recorded text query latency is 0.020 s.
AI.conclusion: The index supports fast language-based place retrieval and selective camera localisation; semantic success is reported separately from source-camera recovery, with source-verified or estimated scales for geometric evaluation.

title: Parse Before You Execute: Efficient Spatial Reasoning with Executable Primitives
summary: Spatial reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) has increasingly benefited from tool-integrated pipelines that ground computation in explicit geometry. However, existing systems often compile queries into relatively open-ended artifacts, such as code, task constraints, tool plans, or gathered evidence, leaving what must be resolved before execution under-specified. This can lead to unnecessary tool acquisition and iterative refinement, while still producing plausible reasoning traces from incomplete spatial commitments. We identify this failure mode as under-committed query compilation. To address it, we propose PEPS, a training-free agentic paradigm Parsing Executable Primitives for Spatial reasoning under a typed FESM schema over Frame, Entity, State, and Metric. PEPS follows a parse-before-execute principle: the Parser commits each query to a compact set of executable requirements; the Executor selectively grounds the required primitives through fixed geometric APIs and deterministic computation; and the Verifier checks execution sufficiency, enabling early termination or targeted repair. Extensive experiments across challenging spatial reasoning benchmarks show that PEPS consistently improves reasoning accuracy while substantially reducing refinement rounds, API cost, and end-to-end latency over strong tool-integrated baselines. These results demonstrate that explicit requirement commitment can make tool-integrated spatial reasoning not only more reliable, but also more execution-efficient.

AI.tldr: PEPS is a training-free agentic paradigm for tool-integrated spatial reasoning in VLMs, in which a Parser commits each query to executable requirements before execution. It improves reasoning accuracy while reducing refinement rounds, API cost and end-to-end latency.
AI.motivation: Existing tool-integrated spatial reasoning compiles queries into open-ended artifacts, leaving what must be resolved before execution under-specified; this causes unnecessary tool acquisition and refinement and can yield plausible traces from incomplete spatial commitments.
AI.method: Queries are parsed under a typed FESM schema over Frame, Entity, State and Metric. The Parser commits to a compact set of executable requirements; the Executor grounds the required primitives through fixed geometric APIs and deterministic computation; the Verifier checks execution sufficiency and enables early termination or targeted repair.
AI.result: Across challenging spatial reasoning benchmarks, PEPS consistently improves reasoning accuracy and substantially reduces refinement rounds, API cost and end-to-end latency compared with strong tool-integrated baselines.
AI.conclusion: Explicit requirement commitment before execution makes tool-integrated spatial reasoning more reliable and more execution-efficient.

title: FlexReader: Towards Adaptive Decoding Paths for Efficient Arbitrary-Length Scene Text Recognition
summary: Existing Scene Text Recognition (STR) models are inherently coupled with a specific decoding strategy by their training paradigms, limiting their flexibility in deployment across diverse recognition scenarios. In this paper, we propose FlexReader, an STR model that supports multiple decoding strides, enabling a single model to achieve an optimal accuracy-efficiency trade-off across different datasets. Specifically, we first introduce a Sub-string Perception module to perceive the target sub-string from visual features, followed by multiple parallel decoding blocks that independently decode each character in the sub-string. During inference, FlexReader supports decoding with arbitrary strides within the perceived sub-string range. Furthermore, we propose Adaptive Prefix Decoding, which adaptively selects the decoding stride at each step based on the model's confidence in the decoded characters, thereby identifying the optimal decoding path for each input. Experimental results demonstrate that FlexReader exhibits robust recognition capability across a diverse range of benchmarks, including those featuring long text, curved text, and occlusions. It consistently outperforms existing decoding strategies in recognition accuracy while achieving up to 6-flod decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding.

AI.tldr: FlexReader is a scene text recognition model that supports multiple decoding strides, so one model can trade accuracy against speed across datasets. Its Adaptive Prefix Decoding picks the stride at each step from model confidence, giving up to a 6-fold speedup over autoregressive decoding.
AI.motivation: Existing STR models are coupled to one decoding strategy by their training paradigms, which limits flexibility across diverse recognition scenarios.
AI.method: A Sub-string Perception module perceives the target sub-string from visual features, and multiple parallel decoding blocks decode each character of it independently. Inference supports arbitrary strides within the perceived range, and Adaptive Prefix Decoding selects the stride at each step from the model's confidence in the decoded characters.
AI.result: FlexReader shows robust recognition across benchmarks with long text, curved text and occlusions, consistently outperforming existing decoding strategies in accuracy, with up to 6-fold decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding.
AI.conclusion: A single flexible decoder can find an optimal accuracy-efficiency decoding path for each input.

title: Beyond Trial-and-Error: A Geospatial-Guided Active Reasoning Framework for Robust Aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires UAVs to locate language-specified goals in large-scale urban environments, where objects often appear small and visually ambiguous from high-altitude viewpoints. Existing methods largely follow a reactive paradigm common in indoor VLN, repeatedly updating navigation states from local observations while underutilizing the geospatial structure that remains stable during navigation. As a result, visually similar distractors can cause a reactive goal search to repeatedly reinforce locally plausible goal hypotheses based on passively accumulated evidence, leading to unreliable localization. To address this, we propose GeoReasoner, a robust framework that shifts the paradigm of Aerial VLN from reactive trial-and-error to geospatial-guided active reasoning. Specifically, GeoReasoner first performs pre-search geospatial reasoning to derive region-level priors and constrain the goal hypothesis space. Building on these, it further conducts hypothesis-driven exploration to actively acquire discriminative evidence and refine competing goal hypotheses. Finally, consistency-aware goal verification adversarially assesses complementary evidence sources before stopping, hence reducing premature or erroneous goal confirmations. Experiments on the real-world CityNav benchmark demonstrate that GeoReasoner sets a new SOTA among zero-shot Aerial VLN methods while competing favorably with supervised approaches.

AI.tldr: GeoReasoner is a zero-shot aerial vision-and-language navigation framework that replaces reactive trial-and-error search with geospatial-guided active reasoning. On the real-world CityNav benchmark it sets a new state of the art among zero-shot methods and competes favourably with supervised approaches.
AI.motivation: Aerial VLN methods follow the reactive paradigm of indoor VLN and underuse the stable geospatial structure of the environment, so visually similar distractors can drive repeated, unreliable goal localisation.
AI.method: Pre-search geospatial reasoning derives region-level priors that constrain the goal hypothesis space. Hypothesis-driven exploration actively acquires discriminative evidence to refine competing goal hypotheses. Consistency-aware goal verification adversarially assesses complementary evidence sources before stopping.
AI.result: GeoReasoner sets a new state of the art among zero-shot Aerial VLN methods on CityNav and competes favourably with supervised approaches.
AI.conclusion: Geospatial-guided active reasoning reduces premature or erroneous goal confirmations, giving more robust aerial navigation.

title: BDNet: Fast-slow thinking is all you need
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, this manuscript is an early draft
summary: We present BDNet, a hierarchical image-classification backbone built around fast image features and slow statistical references. Its baseline deformation operator (BDO) transforms the deviation of a feature from a stage-specific reference through a low-rank projection and a learned channel scale. Rather than computing pairwise token similarity, the branch operates directly on baseline-relative residuals with complexity linear in the token count. Each of four reference buffers accumulates detached stage statistics during training and remains frozen at inference. A four-stage pyramid with depths $(2,2,6,2)$ and widths $(96,192,384,768)$ yields a 20.70M-parameter classifier at $224\times224$ resolution. We organize an ImageNet-1K study around clean classification, eight controlled ablations, and Gaussian-noise, contrast, and brightness perturbations. The central hypothesis is that a slow reference can improve the robustness of a compact representation while retaining a simple tensor implementation. We distinguish this training-time statistical mechanism from input-dependent attention and make its linear inference behavior explicit.

AI.tldr: BDNet is a hierarchical image classification backbone that compares fast features against frozen statistical references through a baseline deformation operator, with complexity linear in token count. It is a 20.70M-parameter classifier at 224x224 resolution, evaluated for robustness under noise, contrast and brightness perturbations.
AI.motivation: The paper asks whether a slow statistical reference can improve the robustness of a compact representation without pairwise token similarity computation.
AI.method: The baseline deformation operator (BDO) transforms the deviation of a feature from a stage-specific reference through a low-rank projection and a learned channel scale. Four reference buffers accumulate detached stage statistics during training and stay frozen at inference. A four-stage pyramid with depths 2, 2, 6, 2 and widths 96, 192, 384, 768 gives the 20.70M-parameter classifier.
AI.result: The abstract describes an ImageNet-1K study covering clean classification, eight controlled ablations, and Gaussian-noise, contrast and brightness perturbations, without reporting specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The central hypothesis is that a slow reference can improve the robustness of a compact representation while keeping a simple tensor implementation, distinct from input-dependent attention and with explicitly linear inference behaviour.

title: VariaFlow: Uncertainty-Aware Flow Matching for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
summary: Reconstruction-based anomaly detection no longer fails at reconstruction. Generative models produce high-quality pseudo-healthy reconstructions, and the remaining difficulty is the step of scoring residuals. The residual between a scan and its reconstruction has two indistinguishable sources, genuine pathology and the anatomical variation that separates one healthy brain from another. Scoring against a single reconstruction treats both as anomalous, inflating false positives where healthy anatomy varies most while small or subtle lesions are lost in the surrounding reconstruction error. We identify the missing quantity as the predictive variance, how much a healthy reconstruction can vary at each location. We introduce VariaFlow, which estimates this variance from an ensemble of mask-guided restorations under an unconditional flow matching prior, each started from a different noise initialization, and which normalizes the residual by the resulting standard deviation. Few-step flow matching keeps the ensemble computationally affordable, and restoring at two spatial scales captures lesions of different size. Across three brain MRI datasets spanning stroke and tumor, VariaFlow is trained once on healthy anatomy and generalizes across all three, attaining the highest AUROC (0.94, 0.80, 0.78) on each and the highest AUPRC on both cross-domain datasets, exceeding the strongest baseline by 37% and 50%. Under domain shift, the same baseline drops by up to 52% in AUPRC, whereas VariaFlow stays more stable and achieves the best small-lesion Dice on all three datasets.

AI.tldr: VariaFlow scores brain MRI anomalies by normalising reconstruction residuals with a predictive variance estimated from an ensemble of flow-matching restorations. It attains the highest AUROC on three datasets and is more stable under domain shift.
AI.motivation: A residual between a scan and its reconstruction mixes genuine pathology with normal anatomical variation, so scoring against a single reconstruction inflates false positives where healthy anatomy varies most and loses small or subtle lesions.
AI.method: VariaFlow estimates predictive variance from an ensemble of mask-guided restorations under an unconditional flow-matching prior, each started from a different noise initialisation, and normalises the residual by the resulting standard deviation. Few-step flow matching keeps the ensemble affordable, and restoring at two spatial scales captures lesions of different sizes.
AI.result: Trained once on healthy anatomy, VariaFlow attains the highest AUROC (0.94, 0.80 and 0.78) across three brain MRI datasets spanning stroke and tumour, and the highest AUPRC on both cross-domain datasets, exceeding the strongest baseline by 37% and 50%. Under domain shift the same baseline drops by up to 52% in AUPRC, while VariaFlow stays more stable and achieves the best small-lesion Dice on all three datasets.
AI.conclusion: Modelling predictive variance separates normal anatomical variation from pathology in residual scores, improving small-lesion detection and robustness across domains.

title: VoxLution: Evolving Voxels for High-Fidelity 3D Scene Generation
comment: Project page: this https URL Video: this https URL
summary: High-resolution 3D indoor scene generation is crucial for immersive applications such as virtual reality, spatial computing, and robotics simulation. We introduce VoxLution, a coarse-to-fine transformer-based approach that generates high-fidelity indoor scenes with rich details, overcoming the overly smooth geometry typical of existing generative models. First, we generate a low-resolution spatial layout; then, based on this structural information, we progressively refine the scene geometry locally in chunks. Key to our approach is formulating 3D super-resolution as a sequence modeling problem over multi-resolution sparse voxel grids. To achieve this, we introduce a training-free, resolution-invariant tokenization scheme that compactly encodes the geometric information of eight octants into a single decimal number. We formulate the transformer sequence to include multiple resolutions, allowing the coarse layout to guide the generation of fine local details. To ensure coherence across local chunks, we incorporate adjacent chunk boundary information directly into the transformer sequencing. VoxLution achieves scene generation at a finer voxel resolution than existing baselines, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks with 59.6% lower FPD and 51.1% lower FID on 3D-FRONT, and 70.5% lower FPD and 73.8% lower FID on Scannet++.

AI.tldr: VoxLution is a coarse-to-fine transformer that generates high-fidelity 3D indoor scenes by refining a low-resolution layout locally in chunks over sparse voxel grids. It reports 59.6% lower FPD and 51.1% lower FID on 3D-FRONT, and 70.5% lower FPD and 73.8% lower FID on Scannet++.
AI.motivation: Existing generative models produce overly smooth geometry, which limits the detail needed for immersive applications such as virtual reality, spatial computing and robotics simulation.
AI.method: A low-resolution spatial layout is generated first, then geometry is progressively refined locally in chunks. 3D super-resolution is formulated as sequence modelling over multi-resolution sparse voxel grids, using a training-free, resolution-invariant tokenisation that encodes the eight octants as a single decimal number. Adjacent chunk boundary information is included in the transformer sequence to keep chunks coherent.
AI.result: VoxLution achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks, with 59.6% lower FPD and 51.1% lower FID on 3D-FRONT, and 70.5% lower FPD and 73.8% lower FID on Scannet++, at a finer voxel resolution than existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: Multi-resolution sequence modelling guided by a coarse layout yields finer, less smooth indoor scene geometry than existing generative baselines.

title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Transformer Encoders for Audio-Image-Symbolic Music Retrieval
summary: Score-based multimodal music retrieval requires representations that are both discriminative within each modality and compatible across audio recordings, sheet music images, and symbolic scores. This paper investigates the effectiveness of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) for adapting pretrained music encoders and examines whether modality-specific improvements translate into better multimodal representations. We compare full fine-tuning, LoRA, and QLoRA across nine pretrained audio, image, and symbolic score encoders on TriScore and the Musical Theme Dataset. Encoders are first evaluated and selected through supervised unimodal classification, using frozen-encoder linear probing as a reference. We then introduce a controlled 2x2 design crossing encoder adaptation with task-specific shared projection, comparing frozen and adapted representations before and after projection. LoRA or QLoRA is selected in 14 of 18 modality-target combinations, frequently matching or outperforming full fine-tuning while optimizing substantially fewer parameters. However, these unimodal gains do not transfer uniformly to multimodal classification. Adaptation and projection are complementary for composer classification on TriScore, largely redundant for TriScore instrument and the Musical Theme Dataset instrument and ensemble tasks, and partially interfering for composer classification on the Musical Theme Dataset. The final adapted-and-projected title representation on TriScore supports piece-level retrieval, reaching average Top-5 and Top-10 accuracies of 55.32 and 64.68, respectively. Cross-modal exclusion and neighborhood analyses further reveal strong modality-specific local structure in the projected spaces. Overall, PEFT provides an effective and computationally efficient alternative to full fine-tuning, but improved unimodal discrimination alone does not guarantee better multimodal organization.

AI.tldr: The paper tests parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA and QLoRA) of pretrained audio, image and symbolic music encoders for multimodal score-based retrieval and finds that unimodal gains do not reliably carry over to multimodal organization.
AI.motivation: Score-based multimodal music retrieval needs representations that are discriminative within each modality and also compatible across audio, sheet music images and symbolic scores, and it is unclear whether modality-specific adaptation improves the joint representation.
AI.method: The authors compare full fine-tuning, LoRA and QLoRA across nine pretrained audio, image and symbolic score encoders on TriScore and the Musical Theme Dataset, select encoders with supervised unimodal classification against a frozen linear probe, and use a controlled 2x2 design crossing encoder adaptation with a task-specific shared projection.
AI.result: LoRA or QLoRA is selected in 14 of 18 modality-target combinations, often matching or outperforming full fine-tuning with far fewer trainable parameters. Adaptation and projection are complementary for composer classification on TriScore, largely redundant for the instrument and ensemble tasks, and partially interfering for composer classification on the Musical Theme Dataset. The adapted-and-projected title representation on TriScore reaches average Top-5 and Top-10 retrieval accuracies of 55.32 and 64.68.
AI.conclusion: PEFT is an effective and computationally cheaper alternative to full fine-tuning, but better unimodal discrimination alone does not guarantee better multimodal organization.

title: TACO: Trajectory-Aware Curvature Observation for Memorization Localization and Mitigation in Diffusion Models
summary: Text-to-image diffusion models can reproduce memorized training content within localized image regions, making precise localization essential for targeted mitigation. However, curvature observations at a single denoising state can contain transient responses, while spatially uniform mitigation may disrupt prompt-relevant content. We present Trajectory-Aware Curvature Observation (TACO), a unified framework for local memorization detection and mitigation in diffusion models. Our empirical analysis reveals that memorization-related curvature becomes pronounced during late-stage denoising and persists at consistent spatial locations across neighboring states. Motivated by these observations, TACO aggregates prompt-dependent curvature responses along the late denoising trajectory and applies latent-guided spatial refinement to improve spatial coherence. The resulting memorization map serves both as a localization signal and as a spatial control signal for mitigation. Specifically, TACO uses this map to steer existing inference-time interventions toward memorization-related regions through spatial reweighting and localized guidance correction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TACO consistently outperforms competing localization methods, and improves the Pareto trade-off between memorization suppression, semantic alignment, and perceptual quality. These results establish trajectory-aware spatial analysis as an effective link between memorization localization and targeted mitigation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TACO, a framework that localizes memorized content in text-to-image diffusion models using curvature aggregated along the late denoising trajectory and uses the resulting map to steer mitigation to those regions.
AI.motivation: Single-state curvature observations can be transient, and spatially uniform mitigation can disrupt prompt-relevant content, so precise localization of memorized regions is needed for targeted mitigation.
AI.method: TACO aggregates prompt-dependent curvature responses along the late denoising trajectory, applies latent-guided spatial refinement to improve spatial coherence, and uses the resulting memorization map both as a localization signal and as a spatial control signal that reweights and guides existing inference-time interventions.
AI.result: The authors report that TACO consistently outperforms competing localization methods and improves the Pareto trade-off between memorization suppression, semantic alignment and perceptual quality.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-aware spatial analysis provides an effective link between memorization localization and targeted mitigation in diffusion models.

title: Scout-Refine-Correct: Teaching Flow Models to Refine Their Own Samples
summary: The quality of image generation models trained with diffusion or flow matching is largely fixed by the training budget: at inference, the only available lever is the number of sampling steps, and additional steps improve quality only up to a point. We present a training recipe, Scout-Refine-Correct (SRC), that instead gives a flow-matching generator a genuine inference-time refinement capability. At each sampling step the model takes a scout rollout -- $K$ steps ahead along its own trajectory -- extrapolates a full-sample estimate, and feeds that estimate back to itself as a self-conditioning signal before taking the real step. This can be repeated for $R$ refinement rounds. Two correction losses, applied during training at states the model's own rollouts actually reach rather than only on the ground-truth path, teach the model to use this signal to reach new samples instead of collapsing to a suboptimal one. On ImageNet-256, SRC improves LightningDiT-B from FID~14.5 to FID~7.26 at NFE~550, matching a privileged best-of-$N$ baseline that uses an oracle FID verifier to choose among samples. SRC uses no external verifier, no reward signal, and, after ablation, almost no extra parameters over the base architecture. Combining SRC with best-of-$N$ improves the result further, to FID~3.81 at NFE~4400, showing that the two axes are complementary. We ablate the main design choices -- the architectural pathway for the scout signal, the scout horizon, each correction loss, and the training schedule to demonstrate key working components of training.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Scout-Refine-Correct (SRC), a training recipe that gives flow-matching image generators an inference-time self-refinement capability by conditioning on a scout rollout of their own trajectory, and reports FID improvements on ImageNet-256.
AI.motivation: Image generators trained with diffusion or flow matching are limited mainly by their training budget, and extra sampling steps improve quality only up to a point, so the model has no other inference-time lever.
AI.method: At each sampling step the model takes a scout rollout K steps ahead, extrapolates a full-sample estimate and feeds it back as a self-conditioning signal, repeated for R refinement rounds. Two correction losses applied at states the model's own rollouts reach, not only on the ground-truth path, teach it to use this signal.
AI.result: On ImageNet-256, SRC improves LightningDiT-B from FID 14.5 to FID 7.26 at NFE 550, matching a privileged best-of-N baseline that uses an oracle FID verifier. Combined with best-of-N it reaches FID 3.81 at NFE 4400. SRC uses no external verifier or reward and, after ablation, almost no extra parameters.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time refinement and best-of-N sampling are complementary axes for improving generation quality, and SRC gives a flow model a way to exploit the first.

title: DrawSplat: Atlanta World-Guided Implicit Gaussian SLAM for Indoor Reconstruction
summary: RGB-D SLAM requires accurate online tracking, high-quality rendering, and geometrically consistent reconstruction. Existing Gaussian SLAM methods mainly optimize Gaussian primitives with photometric, depth, or local frame-to-model constraints, which are often insufficient in indoor scenes with weak textures, large planar structures, noisy depth, and long trajectories. The resulting maps may suffer from pose drift, surface thickness artifacts, noisy normals, and blurred structural boundaries. We propose DrawSplat, an Atlanta World-guided implicit Gaussian SLAM framework for indoor reconstruction. DrawSplat follows a drawing-like process: explicit point-line geometry first sketches the structural layout, and implicit neural Gaussians then fill in high-fidelity appearance and continuous geometric details. It estimates camera poses, sparse geometry, and gravity direction through point-line joint tracking, infers structural planes from tracked lines using the shared-gravity component of the Atlanta World prior, and converts them into differentiable regularization terms on Gaussian centers and normals. To improve compactness and efficiency, DrawSplat further combines an anchor-based implicit neural Gaussian representation with adaptive structural sampling, which allocates Gaussian capacity to structurally informative regions. Experiments on multiple datasets show that DrawSplat achieves robust tracking, high-fidelity rendering, and strong geometric reconstruction among Gaussian-based SLAM systems, while maintaining a practical balance among quality, efficiency, and model size.

AI.tldr: The paper presents DrawSplat, an RGB-D Gaussian SLAM system that uses Atlanta World structural priors from point-line tracking to regularize Gaussian geometry for indoor reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Existing Gaussian SLAM methods struggle in indoor scenes with weak texture, large planar structures, noisy depth and long trajectories, producing pose drift, surface thickness artifacts, noisy normals and blurred structural boundaries.
AI.method: DrawSplat tracks camera poses, sparse geometry and gravity direction with point-line joint tracking, infers structural planes from tracked lines using the shared-gravity component of the Atlanta World prior, and turns them into differentiable regularization on Gaussian centers and normals. It also uses an anchor-based implicit neural Gaussian representation with adaptive structural sampling.
AI.result: The authors report robust tracking, high-fidelity rendering and strong geometric reconstruction among Gaussian SLAM systems on multiple datasets, with a practical balance of quality, efficiency and model size.
AI.conclusion: Structural priors from explicit point-line geometry combined with implicit Gaussian appearance modelling give a practical route to accurate indoor Gaussian SLAM.

title: Attention Maps Know When to Think: Training-Free Difficulty-Aware Chain-of-Thought for Reasoning Segmentation
summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has become a standard reasoning strategy in Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), showing strong performance in complex vision-language tasks such as reasoning segmentation. However, our analysis reveals that indiscriminate CoT usage can lead to degraded performance by inducing unnecessary reasoning, a phenomenon we term overthinking. In reasoning segmentation, overthinking often leads to misalignment between the query's intent and visual grounding. To address this, we propose Difficulty-Aware Chain-of-Thought (DA-CoT), a training-free adaptive framework that selectively triggers CoT based on the input's intrinsic difficulty. We find that the entropy of the model's attention maps reliably reflects task difficulty: low entropy indicates confident, localized grounding, while high entropy suggests uncertainty and potential benefit from CoT. DA-CoT uses this entropy signal to determine whether to apply CoT prompting. Additionally, we introduce a Bidirectional Rethinking mechanism that enables the model to automatically flip its reasoning decision when the initial output fails, enhancing robustness by recovering from failures induced by overthinking and underthinking. DA-CoT demonstrates its effectiveness by achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Reasoning Segmentation benchmarks while significantly improving inference efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DA-CoT, a training-free method that triggers chain-of-thought prompting in multimodal LLMs for reasoning segmentation only when the input is difficult, using the entropy of attention maps as the signal.
AI.motivation: Indiscriminate chain-of-thought use in multimodal LLMs can cause overthinking, which misaligns query intent with visual grounding in reasoning segmentation.
AI.method: DA-CoT uses the entropy of the model's attention maps as a difficulty signal, applying CoT only when entropy is high. A Bidirectional Rethinking mechanism lets the model flip its reasoning decision when the initial output fails, to recover from both overthinking and underthinking.
AI.result: The authors report state-of-the-art performance on reasoning segmentation benchmarks together with significantly improved inference efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Attention entropy is a useful, training-free signal for deciding when reasoning helps grounding, so adaptive CoT can improve both accuracy and efficiency.

title: TADP: Dual-Branch Temporally Adaptive Differential Privacy for Expression-Aware Video Anonymization
summary: We present TADP, a temporally adaptive differential privacy (DP) framework for inference-time privacy-preserving video generation under fixed-length clip-replacement adjacency. TADP uses a dual-branch design to extract identity and expression representations, clips and privatizes both branches with temporally adaptive Gaussian mechanisms whose noise scales depend only on preceding privatized releases within the same clip and are bounded below by history-uniform calibrated minima, and accounts for their joint release via adaptive Rényi Differential Privacy (RDP) composition. The clip-level RDP guarantee is converted to $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy, while soft quantization and subsequent temporal processing are applied only after privatization as DP post-processing. Experiments on facial expression datasets show reduced identity leakage under evaluated attacks, usable perceptual quality and temporal stability, and high facial expression recognition utility relative to the evaluated privacy-preserving baselines. TADP formally satisfies clip-level DP and empirically provides a favorable privacy--utility trade-off under the evaluated threat models and datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper presents TADP, a temporally adaptive differential privacy framework for expression-aware video anonymization that privatizes identity and expression representations with adaptive Gaussian noise and reports clip-level DP guarantees.
AI.motivation: Video anonymization must hide identity while preserving expression and temporal quality, and it needs a formal privacy guarantee under clip-replacement adjacency rather than only empirical protection.
AI.method: A dual-branch design extracts identity and expression representations. Each branch is clipped and privatized with temporally adaptive Gaussian mechanisms whose noise scales depend only on preceding privatized releases in the same clip, bounded below by history-uniform calibrated minima. Their joint release is accounted with adaptive Renyi DP composition, converted to (epsilon, delta)-DP, and soft quantization plus temporal processing are applied only after privatization as post-processing.
AI.result: On facial expression datasets the method reduces identity leakage under the evaluated attacks, keeps usable perceptual quality and temporal stability, and retains high facial expression recognition utility relative to the evaluated privacy-preserving baselines.
AI.conclusion: TADP formally satisfies clip-level DP and, under the evaluated threat models and datasets, offers a favorable privacy-utility trade-off.

title: When Depth Lies: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models on Mirror-Induced RGB-D Ambiguity
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have made significant progress in spatial reasoning, particularly by integrating RGB images with depth data, which is often assumed to faithfully reflect physical distances. However, mirrors violate this assumption: they distort depth readings while reproducing object appearances, making reflections difficult to distinguish from real objects. As existing benchmarks rarely consider such reflective scenarios, VLM performance in mirror scenes remains largely unexplored. In this work, we introduce a mirror-centric RGB-D dataset from reflective scenes to evaluate the spatial reasoning capabilities of state-of-the-art VLMs in these scenarios. Specifically, we collect 1,011 RGB-D images from 525 real-world scenes, spanning diverse indoor and outdoor environments, six reflective surface types, and both daytime and nighttime conditions. All images are annotated with reflective surface region masks and mask annotations for both directly observed and mirror-reflected objects. Then, we curate a benchmark named MIRA-Bench (Mirror-Induced Reasoning Ambiguity Benchmark), comprising 14,140 QA pairs across eight sub-tasks organized into three cognitive levels: Reflection-aware Perception, Spatial Reasoning, and Scene-level Decision-making. We evaluate state-of-the-art VLMs on MIRA-Bench and find consistent failures across tasks: models misclassify whether objects are directly observed or reflected, fail to match reflected instances to their real-world counterparts, and produce erroneous spatial inferences. Remarkably, providing depth data actually degrades reasoning performance, implying that VLMs cannot identify incorrect depth in mirror scenes. The code and data are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MIRA-Bench, a benchmark of 14,140 QA pairs over 1,011 RGB-D images with mirrors, and shows that state-of-the-art VLMs fail on mirror-induced depth ambiguity, with depth input even degrading reasoning.
AI.motivation: VLMs are often assumed to use depth faithfully, but mirrors distort depth while reproducing object appearance, and existing benchmarks rarely include reflective scenes, so VLM behaviour there is largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors collect 1,011 RGB-D images from 525 real-world scenes covering six reflective surface types, indoor and outdoor settings, and day and night. They annotate reflective surface masks and masks for directly observed and mirror-reflected objects, and build MIRA-Bench with 14,140 QA pairs across eight sub-tasks in three levels: reflection-aware perception, spatial reasoning and scene-level decision-making.
AI.result: Evaluated VLMs consistently misclassify whether objects are observed directly or reflected, fail to match reflections to real counterparts, and make erroneous spatial inferences. Providing depth data degrades reasoning performance.
