AI.conclusion: VLMs cannot detect incorrect depth in mirror scenes, so reflection-aware evaluation and modelling are needed for reliable spatial reasoning.

title: A Self-Supervised Pose Estimation Approach for Construction Machines
comment: 12 Pages, 12 figures, submitted for the International Symposium on Visual Computing conference
summary: Pose estimation is a computer vision task used to estimate a skeleton of dynamic systems to predict future movements. Most of the research in this direction is based on a supervised learning approach which requires a massive amount of labeled datasets. In this paper, a self-supervised three-stage model based on a contrastive learning approach is introduced for estimating a skeleton of dynamic construction machines; such as excavators without using any labeled images for the first stage. The whole model structure is divided into three stages: the pre-train stage using the SimCLR contrastive approach, and two fine-tuning stages for the transfer learning and the downstream task. The model can leverage the features and learn from a huge unlabeled dataset called ACID to two small datasets generated from NVIDIA Isaac and MATLAB Simscape simulators as well as transfer the knowledge to a smaller dataset with a ratio of 3.5% from the original ACID dataset. The results show that the proposed approach can improve the accuracy of pose estimation for heavy construction machines in real images by 11% and 13% in comparison to the normal self-supervised approach with two backbones ResNet-50 and HRNet-W32, respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a three-stage self-supervised pose estimation model for construction machines that pre-trains with SimCLR on unlabeled data and transfers to small simulated and real datasets.
AI.motivation: Pose estimation for dynamic systems such as excavators usually needs large labelled datasets, which are costly to obtain for heavy construction machines.
AI.method: The model pre-trains with the SimCLR contrastive approach on the unlabeled ACID dataset, then applies two fine-tuning stages for transfer learning and the downstream skeleton estimation task. The small target datasets are generated from NVIDIA Isaac and MATLAB Simscape simulators, and transfer uses 3.5% of the ACID dataset.
AI.result: On real images the approach improves pose estimation accuracy by 11% with a ResNet-50 backbone and by 13% with an HRNet-W32 backbone, compared with the normal self-supervised approach using the same backbones.
AI.conclusion: Contrastive pre-training on unlabeled data followed by simulator-based transfer can improve pose estimation for heavy construction machines without labelled real images.

title: OT-CAL: Optimal-Transport-Guided Adaptive Sample Selection for Efficient Visual Learning
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to the IEEE BigData 2026 Workshop on Efficient AI
summary: Deep neural networks for image recognition are typically trained using mini-batches, with a forward pass to compute predictions and losses followed by a more computationally expensive backward pass to update model parameters. However, not all training samples contribute equally to learning, suggesting that computation can be reduced by performing backward passes only on informative samples. The challenge is that sample informativeness changes throughout training: difficult samples may be valuable early on, improving samples become important later, and class diversity becomes increasingly relevant toward the end. Existing methods often rely on fixed selection rules or computationally expensive per-sample gradient calculations. We propose OT-CAL, an adaptive data selection method that automatically adjusts its sampling preferences during training. OT-CAL represents each sample using five informativeness features, including difficulty, learnability, and uncertainty. A curriculum vector describes the currently preferred sample characteristics, and optimal-transport-based matching assigns selection weights according to how closely samples match this target. The curriculum vector is then updated using the selected samples, forming a feedback loop that adapts without a manually defined schedule. Experiments on three standard visual learning benchmarks show that, when selecting 50% of each mini-batch, OT-CAL improves performance by 1.3--2.1 points over AdaSelection while achieving 1.18--1.24 times faster training than full-data training.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes OT-CAL, an adaptive sample selection method that uses optimal-transport matching against a curriculum vector to choose informative samples in each mini-batch, reducing backward passes while improving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Backward passes on every sample are expensive, and sample informativeness changes during training, while existing selection methods use fixed rules or costly per-sample gradient computation.
AI.method: OT-CAL describes each sample with five informativeness features, including difficulty, learnability and uncertainty. A curriculum vector represents the currently preferred sample characteristics, optimal-transport matching assigns selection weights by closeness to that target, and the curriculum vector is updated from the selected samples in a feedback loop without a manual schedule.
AI.result: Selecting 50% of each mini-batch, OT-CAL improves performance by 1.3 to 2.1 points over AdaSelection on three standard visual learning benchmarks, with 1.18 to 1.24 times faster training than full-data training.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, optimal-transport-guided selection can reduce training cost in visual learning without a hand-designed schedule.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Initialization with Dual-Guided Inversion for Flow-Based Inverse Problem Solvers
summary: Flow models have recently emerged as powerful generative priors for solving inverse problems. Despite their success, most existing flow-based inverse problem solvers initialize the reconstruction process with random Gaussian noise. However, recent studies in image generation have shown that the choice of initial noise can significantly influence generation outcomes. The role of initialization as a distinct design choice in flow-based inverse problem solving remains comparatively underexplored. In this work, we systematically evaluate noise initialization strategies while holding the downstream flow-based inverse solver fixed. We propose Retrieval-Augmented Initialization with Dual-Guided Inversion (RA-DGI), a method that constructs improved initial noise by leveraging retrieved proxy clean images and dual-guided inversion. Extensive experiments across multiple inverse problems demonstrate that the quality of the initial noise substantially affects reconstruction fidelity and perceptual performance. RA-DGI outperforms standard random initialization and achieves superior results compared to inference-time scaling strategies, while requiring less computational overhead. These findings highlight initialization as a critical yet previously overlooked factor in flow-based inverse problem solvers.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RA-DGI, which builds better initial noise for flow-based inverse problem solvers from retrieved proxy clean images and dual-guided inversion, and shows that initialization substantially affects reconstruction quality.
AI.motivation: Flow-based inverse problem solvers almost always start from random Gaussian noise, and the role of initialization as a design choice has been underexplored, even though initial noise strongly affects generation in image synthesis.
AI.method: The authors fix the downstream flow-based solver and systematically compare noise initialization strategies. RA-DGI constructs the initial noise from retrieved proxy clean images using dual-guided inversion.
AI.result: Across multiple inverse problems, RA-DGI outperforms random initialization and beats inference-time scaling strategies while requiring less computation.
AI.conclusion: Initialization is a critical yet overlooked factor in flow-based inverse problem solving.

title: Nereus: A Large-Scale Underwater Dataset for Fine-Grained Attribute Understanding and Grounded Counting Perception
comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track
summary: Underwater imagery records rich ecological information and supports applications such as science communication, fishery monitoring, ecological conservation, and oceanographic research. Beyond general scene understanding, these applications require models to recognize fine-grained biological traits and reason over spatially grounded evidence. However, existing underwater datasets often provide coarse category labels, generic captions, or total-count supervision, which limits their use for organism-level analysis and ecological reasoning. We introduce Nereus, a large-scale dataset for Underwater Fine-grained Perception that jointly supports Fine-Grained Object Attribute Understanding and Grounded Counting Perception. Nereus contains 88K images and 2.68M question-answer pairs, including annotations for 136K marine organism objects across 2,690 species and 1,515 genera, as well as 65K point annotations and 67K grounded counting QA pairs. Experiments with representative multimodal models show that Nereus improves downstream adaptation over existing underwater-domain data and provides a foundation for future research on fine-grained marine perception.

AI.tldr: The paper releases Nereus, a large underwater dataset of 88K images and 2.68M QA pairs with fine-grained organism attributes and grounded counting annotations.
AI.motivation: Existing underwater datasets offer only coarse labels, generic captions or total-count supervision, which limits organism-level analysis and grounded ecological reasoning.
AI.method: Nereus jointly supports fine-grained object attribute understanding and grounded counting perception. It contains 136K marine organism object annotations across 2,690 species and 1,515 genera, 65K point annotations and 67K grounded counting QA pairs.
AI.result: Experiments with representative multimodal models show that Nereus improves downstream adaptation over existing underwater-domain data.
AI.conclusion: The dataset provides a foundation for future research on fine-grained marine perception.

title: SAR-TS-BERT: Physics-Guided Self-Supervised Pre-Training With Polarimetric Features for SAR Time-Series Crop Classification
comment: 18 pages, 13 figures, 18 tables. Jieqiu Wang and Yuhan Zhang contributed equally to this work
summary: Multitemporal synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery provides continuous, cloud-free observations of crop phenology for agricultural monitoring in cloudy and rainy regions, yet high-accuracy classification typically requires extensive labeled samples. Although self-supervised pre-training mitigates label dependency in remote sensing, existing frameworks primarily target optical imagery or generic spatial SAR scenes, underutilizing temporal backscatter dynamics and polarimetric scattering mechanisms. We propose SAR-TS-BERT, a physics-guided BERT-style self-supervised pre-training framework for SAR time-series crop classification. SAR-TS-BERT integrates backscatter intensities and polarimetric ratio features (VV, VH, and VV/VH) with dual-polarimetric Cloude-Pottier decomposition parameters ($H/\alpha/A$) into a six-band input representation through two core designs: 1) a physics-guided span masking strategy (SpanPhysics) that adaptively selects contiguous masked spans based on temporal backscatter change rates to prioritize key phenological transitions; and 2) a dual-branch cross-modal fusion encoder that models backscatter and polarimetric decomposition features through separate Transformer branches followed by bidirectional cross-attention fusion. On independent test sets in Estonia (EuroCropsML) and the USA (California CDL), SAR-TS-BERT achieves overall accuracies (OAs) of 96.78% and 87.29%, respectively, and attains a mean monthly OA of 99.37% on Chongming Island, Shanghai. On the Estonia benchmark, pre-training improves OA and Macro F1 by 1.17 and 1.59 percentage points over training from scratch under full supervision, and by 2.58 and 5.19 percentage points using only 1% labeled data. Incorporating SAR scattering physics into temporal self-supervised pre-training effectively enhances crop classification accuracy, parcel-level mapping consistency, and few-shot transferability.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SAR-TS-BERT, a BERT-style self-supervised pre-training framework for SAR time-series crop classification that incorporates polarimetric decomposition features and a physics-guided span masking strategy.
AI.motivation: Self-supervised pre-training for remote sensing mostly targets optical imagery or generic SAR scenes, and it underuses temporal backscatter dynamics and polarimetric scattering mechanisms in SAR time series.
AI.method: The model combines backscatter intensities and polarimetric ratios (VV, VH, VV/VH) with dual-polarimetric Cloude-Pottier decomposition parameters (H, alpha, A) as a six-band input. It uses SpanPhysics, a masking strategy that picks contiguous spans according to temporal backscatter change rates, and a dual-branch encoder with separate Transformer branches and bidirectional cross-attention fusion.
AI.result: Overall accuracies are 96.78% on the Estonia (EuroCropsML) test set and 87.29% on the California CDL test set, with a mean monthly OA of 99.37% on Chongming Island. On Estonia, pre-training improves OA and Macro F1 by 1.17 and 1.59 points under full supervision, and by 2.58 and 5.19 points with 1% labelled data.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating SAR scattering physics into temporal self-supervised pre-training improves crop classification accuracy, parcel-level consistency and few-shot transfer.

title: Measuring What Matters: A Causal Reliance Score for Histopathology Image Segmentation
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures, accepted into Medical Image Understanding and Analysis (MIUA) 2026 conference
summary: Reliable histopathology segmentation requires models that rely on pathology-relevant structures rather than spurious background correlations. In this work, we argue that improving architectures alone is insufficient if models continue to rely on spurious correlations rather than pathology-relevant features. We introduce a causality-inspired evaluation framework based on controlled interventions that explicitly probes model sensitivity to foreground tissue structure and background/domain variation. Building on this, we propose the Causal Reliance Score (CRS), a metric that quantifies the relative sensitivity of model predictions to foreground perturbation versus background/domain variation under controlled interventions. To support this analysis, we design augmentation strategies that act as implicit counterfactual interventions during training, encouraging invariance to nuisance factors while preserving morphology. We demonstrate how these interventions reveal behavioural differences between models that are not captured by standard metrics such as Dice or IoU. While we instantiate our framework using a self-supervised transformer (CAUSE-ViT), the primary contribution of this work is not a new architecture, but a principled intervention-based methodology and evaluation metric for auditing model behaviour in medical image segmentation. Our results suggest that evaluating model behaviour through counterfactual interventions is essential for developing reliable and clinically robust medical image segmentation systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Causal Reliance Score, a metric that measures how sensitive histopathology segmentation predictions are to foreground tissue perturbations versus background or domain variation under controlled interventions.
AI.motivation: Segmentation models may rely on spurious background correlations, and standard metrics such as Dice and IoU do not reveal this behaviour.
AI.method: The authors build a causality-inspired evaluation framework with controlled interventions and define the Causal Reliance Score as the relative sensitivity of predictions to foreground perturbation versus background or domain variation. Augmentations act as implicit counterfactual interventions during training. The framework is instantiated with a self-supervised transformer, CAUSE-ViT.
AI.result: The interventions reveal behavioural differences between models that Dice and IoU do not capture.
AI.conclusion: Counterfactual intervention-based evaluation is essential for auditing and developing reliable, clinically robust medical image segmentation, and its main contribution is the methodology and metric rather than the architecture.

title: WorkIng: A Real-World and Synthetic Highway Work-Zone Benchmark Dataset for Autonomous Navigation
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. 19 pages including supplementary material. (c) 2027 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted
summary: Highway work zones are critical edge cases for autonomous vehicles (AVs), combining atypical geometries and jurisdiction-specific regulations that existing benchmarks fail to capture: real-world datasets lack 360° multi-modal, full-scene 3D work zone annotation, and no single recorded site can span the layouts and regulatory variants needed for generalizable models. We present WorkIng, a dual-domain benchmark and training resource. WorkIng-Highway provides a 360° multi-modal work zone benchmark with synchronized 128-channel LiDAR, six RGB cameras, and RTK-GPS across 32 km, yielding 12,000+ annotated frames and 227,399 tracked 3D bounding boxes. WorkIng-CARLA complements this with procedural simulation spanning 24 regulation-aware scenarios across six canonical topologies and six international traffic standards, populated by 100+ custom 3D assets. Benchmarking representative 3D detection and end-to-end planning architectures shows that real-world data remains the primary performance driver, and that scenario-stratified synthetic augmentation improves architectures across 2D recognition, 3D detection, and trajectory planning. Resources: this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper introduces WorkIng, a dual-domain benchmark of real and simulated highway work zones for autonomous driving, with a 360-degree multi-modal real dataset and a CARLA-based synthetic set covering regulation-aware scenarios.
AI.motivation: Work zones combine atypical geometry with jurisdiction-specific rules, and existing real-world datasets lack full-scene 360-degree multi-modal 3D work-zone annotation, while no single site covers the needed layouts and regulatory variants.
AI.method: WorkIng-Highway provides synchronized 128-channel LiDAR, six RGB cameras and RTK-GPS over 32 km, with 12,000+ annotated frames and 227,399 tracked 3D bounding boxes. WorkIng-CARLA adds procedural simulation with 24 regulation-aware scenarios across six canonical topologies and six international traffic standards, populated with 100+ custom 3D assets.
AI.result: Benchmarks of representative 3D detection and end-to-end planning architectures show that real-world data remains the main performance driver. Scenario-stratified synthetic augmentation improves architectures across 2D recognition, 3D detection and trajectory planning.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic, scenario-stratified augmentation is a useful complement to real work-zone data for autonomous navigation, though real data remains the primary driver.

title: Hard Sample-Conditioned Decorrelated Attention for Robust Face Recognition
comment: Accepted at the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV 2027)
summary: Multi-head attention in Vision Transformers (ViTs) allows independent attention patterns across heads, but without explicit regularization, heads may learn redundant patterns rather than complementary roles. Correlation-based penalties encourage head disentanglement, yet apply uniform regularization across all training samples. In face recognition (FR), hard samples whose embeddings lie close to competing identities are critical for optimization and generalization. Motivated by this, we propose ViT-HarDis, which conditions attention head disentanglement on sample difficulty: samples with high cosine similarity to negative class centers receive stronger head decorrelation, enforcing specialization where identity ambiguity is highest. Experiments show improvements over both the baseline and uniform disentanglement on most benchmarks. Our analysis shows that ViT-HarDis reduces the similarity of hard samples to competing class centers while decreasing inter-head attention similarity, and that applying disentanglement only to the final transformer layers outperforms regularizing the entire network. Trained on WebFace4M, ViT-HarDis achieves SOTA results among ViT-based methods on IJB-B, IJB-C, and TinyFace Rank-1, while achieving the best IJB-B and TinyFace results when trained on MS1MV3, improving FR without architectural modifications or additional inference cost. Code: this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ViT-HarDis, which makes attention-head decorrelation in Vision Transformers for face recognition depend on sample difficulty, applying stronger regularization to hard samples near competing identity centers.
AI.motivation: Correlation-based penalties encourage Vision Transformer heads to be complementary, but they apply the same regularization to every sample, whereas hard samples close to competing identities matter most in face recognition.
AI.method: Head decorrelation strength is conditioned on sample difficulty, measured by high cosine similarity to negative class centers, so hard samples receive stronger head decorrelation. The authors also apply disentanglement only to the final transformer layers.
AI.result: The method improves over the baseline and uniform disentanglement on most benchmarks. Trained on WebFace4M it reaches state-of-the-art results among ViT-based methods on IJB-B, IJB-C and TinyFace Rank-1, and trained on MS1MV3 it gives the best IJB-B and TinyFace results. It reduces hard-sample similarity to competing centers and lowers inter-head attention similarity without architectural changes or extra inference cost.
AI.conclusion: Difficulty-aware attention disentanglement improves face recognition without modifying the architecture or adding inference cost.

title: Different Models, Shared Failures: Auditing Frozen-Encoder Pools for Medical Segmentation
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets. 47 pages, 8 figures. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Average segmentation accuracy and model count do not reveal whether models fail on the same cases. We present CoFailMed, an audit of correlated failures in pretrained-encoder pools for medical segmentation. Across five 2D tasks, we evaluate 11 public pretrained encoders (a controlled sample, not a census) using frozen features and separately trained $1\times 1$ readouts with four seeds per encoder. Shared-checkpoint pairs have the highest mean per-case Dice correlation. An expanded 17-encoder analysis shows that distinct checkpoints within the same encoder family remain more correlated than cross-family pairs. At the pooled 33rd-percentile Dice threshold, four-member pools drawn from distinct encoders have mean effective sizes of 1.56-2.92, estimated from failure correlations in pools with enough failures and passes per member. In the primary pool, richer readouts and fine-tuning narrow the Dice-correlation gap between pairs sharing a checkpoint (or the DINOv2-B/S release) and all other pairs. Yet dependence between different encoders can increase, and fine-tuning does not consistently increase effective pool size at 33rd-percentile thresholds recomputed for each training recipe. A smaller between-group gap can coexist with greater dependence. Pool evaluation should therefore report absolute dependence and threshold-specific effective size alongside accuracy and nominal pool size. The CoFailMed release provides aligned per-case traces, analysis scripts and study code to reproduce the central audit results.

AI.tldr: The paper audits correlated failures across 11 pretrained frozen encoders for medical segmentation and shows that models sharing a checkpoint or family fail on the same cases, so nominal pool size overstates the independent evidence.
AI.motivation: Average accuracy and model count do not show whether segmentation models fail on the same cases, which matters when pools of models are used for medical segmentation.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 11 public pretrained encoders with frozen features and separately trained 1x1 readouts, four seeds per encoder, on five 2D tasks, and expand the analysis to 17 encoders. They measure per-case Dice correlation between models and compute effective pool sizes at a pooled 33rd-percentile Dice threshold.
AI.result: Pairs sharing a checkpoint have the highest mean per-case Dice correlation, and different checkpoints within a family remain more correlated than cross-family pairs. Four-member pools from distinct encoders have mean effective sizes of 1.56 to 2.92. Richer readouts and fine-tuning narrow the correlation gap in the primary pool, but between-encoder dependence can increase, and fine-tuning does not consistently increase effective pool size.
AI.conclusion: Pool evaluation should report absolute dependence and threshold-specific effective size alongside accuracy and nominal pool size, because a smaller gap between groups can coexist with greater dependence.

title: A Patch is More Than a Token
comment: 54 pages, 16 figures, 12 tables. Code and experimental assets: this https URL
summary: Vision Transformers represent each image patch through a canonical token produced under one observation condition. That token is a powerful interface, but it is still one realized state of the patch. We introduce PMTT, which establishes two foundations: a patch representation object can extend from one canonical state to a canonical-centered Representation State Family, and identity-preserving variation opens Patch-Level Local Feature Space. We develop four parts of this representation program. Patch Information Acquisition and Dense Orbital Views expose lawful same-patch states. Visible-to-Hidden prediction tests whether observed states reveal structure beyond themselves. Intrinsic analysis identifies low-dimensional, energy-concentrated, patch-specific, predictive geometry. Representation Organization separates acquiring more information from organizing that information, with an analytic Manifold as the central structured representation. We realize PMTT on frozen DINOv3 S/B/L/H+ backbones without neural post-training of the representation. Across two independent 4,096-anchor cohorts, Manifold explains 70.8-79.6% of Hidden variation, compared with 55.0-72.3% for directly Observed states, and wins on more than 95% of anchors at every scale. Effective rank falls from about 2.5 to 2.0 while dominant energy concentration rises with backbone scale. Across six visual capabilities and four scales, Observed exceeds the canonical Center in 21 of 24 conditions, Manifold exceeds Center in 23, and Manifold exceeds Observed in 16. The strongest current consequence appears in physical correspondence, where MegaDepth satisfies Center < Observed < Manifold at every scale. These results show that pretrained visual backbones contain richer patch information than the standard single-token interface directly exposes. Code and experimental assets are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PMTT, a representation framework that expands each ViT patch from a single canonical token into a family of states and an analytic manifold, showing that frozen DINOv3 backbones hold more patch information than the standard token exposes.
AI.motivation: Vision Transformers represent each patch with one canonical token produced under a single observation condition, which is only one realized state of the patch and may hide richer local information.
AI.method: PMTT builds a canonical-centred Representation State Family through patch information acquisition and dense orbital views, tests with visible-to-hidden prediction whether observed states reveal structure beyond themselves, analyses intrinsic low-dimensional geometry, and organizes the information with an analytic Manifold. It is applied to frozen DINOv3 S, B, L and H+ backbones without neural post-training.
AI.result: Across two independent cohorts of 4,096 anchors, the Manifold explains 70.8 to 79.6% of Hidden variation, compared with 55.0 to 72.3% for directly Observed states, and wins on more than 95% of anchors at every scale. Across six visual capabilities and four scales, Manifold exceeds the canonical Center in 23 of 24 conditions and Observed exceeds Center in 21, with the strongest gains in MegaDepth physical correspondence.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained visual backbones contain richer patch information than the single-token interface exposes, and the manifold representation can surface it.

title: PGGT-Loc: Primitive-Grounded Geometry Transformer for Feed-Forward Camera Localization
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 24 pages, 14 figures, including appendices. Code and models: this https URL
summary: Camera localization methods are mostly multi-stage pipelines relying on dedicated and complex maps that are costly to construct, store, and maintain over time. Alternatively, well-structured maps that organize scenes with compact yet expressive primitives are often readily available, providing rich structural and semantic cues that humans can interpret. However, their potential for direct camera localization remains largely unexplored due to the significant modality gap between map primitives and visual observations. This motivates a new concept for localization, which estimates camera poses by grounding query observations to map primitives. In this paper, we instantiate the concept in the context of planar primitives with PGGT, the Primitive-Grounded Geometry Transformer network. Given a single query image and a set of planar map primitives, the network is trained to predict multiple localization targets for feed-forward 6-DoF camera localization that generalizes to unseen environments. With this straightforward and scalable architecture, our method pushes the state-of-the-art localization performance on both dense surface maps and minimal layout models. The code and models are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PGGT-Loc, a feed-forward network that estimates 6-DoF camera poses by grounding a query image to planar map primitives, reaching state-of-the-art localization on dense surface maps and minimal layout models.
AI.motivation: Existing camera localization relies on complex multi-stage pipelines and costly dense maps, while compact structured maps with primitives are readily available but unused for direct localization because of the modality gap between primitives and images.
AI.method: Given a single query image and a set of planar map primitives, the Primitive-Grounded Geometry Transformer predicts multiple localization targets in a single feed-forward pass, generalizing to unseen environments.
AI.result: The method pushes state-of-the-art localization performance on both dense surface maps and minimal layout models.
AI.conclusion: Grounding queries to map primitives is a straightforward and scalable route to camera localization.

title: ObjectGuidedMap: An Object-Aware Model for Robust Bird's Eye View Map Prediction in High-Occlusion Scenarios
summary: Accurate BEV map prediction is a critical component of autonomous driving systems, enabling downstream planning and control. Recent approaches such as Mask2Map achieve strong performance by predicting vectorized, instance-level map elements directly from multi-view images. However, existing BEV map prediction models operate largely independently of object-level scene understanding, despite the fact that traffic participants frequently occlude or implicitly encode information about road geometry. In this work, we propose a multitask architecture that jointly predicts BEV maps and 3D objects, explicitly enabling information exchange between the two tasks. Building upon Mask2Map, we introduce an object detection branch and incorporate cross-task feature fusion at both the BEV feature level and the instance-query level via deformable attention and cross-attention mechanisms. This design allows map instances to leverage object context while remaining robust to occlusions caused by traffic participants. Experimental results on the nuScenes and Argoverse 2 datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently improves BEV map prediction accuracy, with particularly significant gains of 21% mAP in scenes containing heavy object occlusion.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ObjectGuidedMap, a multitask model that jointly predicts BEV maps and 3D objects with cross-task fusion, improving map prediction under heavy occlusion from traffic participants.
AI.motivation: Existing BEV map prediction models such as Mask2Map operate largely independently of object-level scene understanding, although traffic participants often occlude road geometry or carry information about it.
AI.method: The authors add an object detection branch to Mask2Map and fuse features across the two tasks at the BEV feature level and at the instance-query level, using deformable attention and cross-attention.
AI.result: On nuScenes and Argoverse 2 the approach consistently improves BEV map prediction accuracy, with gains of 21% mAP in scenes with heavy object occlusion.
AI.conclusion: Information exchange with object-level understanding makes map prediction more robust to occlusion caused by traffic participants.

title: Open-Weight MLLMs Cannot Compare What They Cannot Name
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly capable of understanding images and performing complex visual reasoning, suggesting the possibility of using them to automate biological image analysis. This need is becoming increasingly urgent as advances in technology continue to generate ever larger and more diverse microscopy datasets, already exceeding the scale at which manual visual analysis is feasible. With the final aim to use MLLMs for visual comparison of complex phenotypes, we investigate a very simple baseline: comparison of the size of body parts in synthetic images of ants. We find that state-of-the-art open-weight MLLMs fail for some body parts, but not for others, even though the comparison itself is visually trivial for all of them. We evaluate different in-context learning strategies and analyze performance on the related object recognition task. Our results suggest a recognition-driven grounding failure: structures that the models cannot recognize are instead associated with a recognizable semantic concept, impairing the grounding and comparison of both. Further analysis of the vision encoder is consistent with the hypothesis that fine-grained visual structure may be less well preserved without semantic support. Together, our results reveal a surprising limitation of current MLLMs: semantic recognition can gate simple visual comparisons that do not intrinsically require semantic understanding. Our code and data are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper shows that open-weight MLLMs fail at a trivial body-part size comparison on synthetic ant images for some body parts but not others, and attributes this to recognition-driven grounding failure.
AI.motivation: MLLMs are considered for automating microscopy analysis, but before using them for complex phenotype comparison the authors test whether they can make a simple visual comparison.
AI.method: The authors compare the sizes of body parts in synthetic ant images, evaluate several in-context learning strategies, analyse performance on the related object recognition task, and examine the vision encoder.
AI.result: Current open-weight MLLMs fail for some body parts but not others, even though the comparison is visually trivial for all of them. The failures are associated with the models' inability to recognize the structures, which are instead linked to recognizable semantic concepts, and fine-grained visual structure appears less well preserved without semantic support.
AI.conclusion: Semantic recognition can gate simple visual comparisons that do not intrinsically require semantic understanding, which is a limitation for MLLM-based biological image analysis.

title: TwinPast: Benchmarking Historical Evidence Use in Streaming Video Understanding with Evidence Contrastive Video Pairs
summary: High accuracy on streaming video benchmarks does not establish whether a model uses visual history. Our review of OVO-Bench and StreamingBench finds that recent frames suffice for 32% of sampled historical questions, while models also answer many questions correctly from the question and options alone. We introduce TwinPast to test whether answers correctly follow changes in history, using 350 human-reviewed video pairs spanning five historical tasks. Each pair holds the recent video context, question, and ordered options fixed while changing critical historical evidence and the correct answer. Each video is evaluated independently, and PairAcc requires correct answers for both histories. We evaluate 34 model and input configurations. For Qwen3-VL-8B and DeepSeek-Flash, historical inputs improve performance on TwinPast, reversing the recent-frame advantage on existing benchmarks. The strongest evaluated streaming system reaches 49.14% PairAcc, compared with 66.57-91.43% for the evaluated general-purpose models. This gap persists across all five tasks. Case studies further show that models select states from the wrong time or contradict recorded event order despite retaining the relevant evidence. These findings highlight the need to connect historical memory and retrieval with reasoning that uses evidence according to the question's temporal references and event relations.

AI.tldr: TwinPast is a benchmark that tests whether streaming video models actually use historical visual evidence, by pairing videos that share recent context and question but differ in critical history and correct answer. The strongest evaluated streaming system reaches 49.14% PairAcc, versus 66.57-91.43% for the evaluated general-purpose models.
AI.motivation: High accuracy on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench does not show that models use visual history, since recent frames suffice for 32% of sampled historical questions and models also answer many questions from the question and options alone.
AI.method: 350 human-reviewed video pairs across five historical tasks, with recent context, question and ordered options held fixed while the critical historical evidence and the correct answer change. Each video is evaluated independently, and PairAcc requires correct answers on both histories. 34 model and input configurations are evaluated.
AI.result: For Qwen3-VL-8B and DeepSeek-Flash, historical inputs improve performance on TwinPast, reversing the recent-frame advantage seen on existing benchmarks. The strongest streaming system reaches 49.14% PairAcc, compared with 66.57-91.43% for the evaluated general-purpose models, and the gap persists across all five tasks.
AI.conclusion: Case studies show models select states from the wrong time or contradict recorded event order despite retaining the relevant evidence, so historical memory and retrieval must be connected to reasoning that follows the question's temporal references and event relations.

title: FoAViS: Analyzing Learned Fixation Strategies in a Foveated Active Vision System
comment: 79 pages, 6 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Human vision is foveated and active: resolution is highest at the fovea and falls off towards the periphery, and fixations are actively directed to locations of interest. Building a machine system that processes information in the same way lets us study gaze behavior in a controlled setting where the system's components and objectives are known. The emergence of gaze characteristics can therefore be examined systematically, which may in turn inform our understanding of biological vision. This requires a model that can sample like the fovea, handle various tasks from classification to dense prediction, and be trained concurrently with a fixation policy. In our study, we present such a system and study its capabilities and the fixation policies that emerge from it. Our system, FoAViS, samples visual input by adopting the established log-polar foveation and accumulates information in a 2D spatial memory. Due to its 2D structure, the same memory can be read out globally for classification or densely for semantic segmentation, without any architectural change. Fixations are drawn from a 2D map by a policy trained concurrently with the task. We find that learned fixation policies select more informative, task-specific locations than non-learned heuristics. These policies also shape the task representations in a beneficial way: for both classification and segmentation, models trained concurrently with a policy outperform models trained with random locations, even when the latter are provided with learned scanpaths. Moreover, these scanpaths exhibit similarities to human gaze behavior by capturing aspects of empirical scanpath characteristics. Our work marks an important step away from standard passive, single-pass architectures, towards biologically grounded models of vision. It opens a path for studying goal-directed gaze behavior and information representation in the visual system.

AI.tldr: FoAViS is a foveated active vision system with a 2D spatial memory, trained jointly with a learned fixation policy. The learned policies select more informative, task-specific locations than non-learned heuristics, and their scanpaths partly resemble human gaze.
AI.motivation: Standard passive, single-pass architectures do not capture foveated, active sampling, and fixation heuristics that are not trained with the task do not allow the emergence of gaze behavior to be studied in a controlled setting.
AI.method: The system samples input with log-polar foveation and accumulates information in a 2D spatial memory that can be read out globally for classification or densely for semantic segmentation without architectural change. Fixations are drawn from a 2D map by a policy trained concurrently with the task.
AI.result: Learned fixation policies select more informative, task-specific locations than non-learned heuristics. For both classification and segmentation, models trained with a concurrent policy outperform models trained with random locations, even when the latter are given learned scanpaths. The scanpaths capture aspects of empirical human scanpath characteristics.
AI.conclusion: The work is a step away from passive, single-pass architectures toward biologically grounded models of vision, and opens a path for studying goal-directed gaze and information representation.

title: MoETok: Sparse Expert Routing for 1D Visual Tokenizers
summary: Modern visual tokenizers aim to preserve fine-grained visual details while learning high-level semantic representations for downstream generation and understanding. Query-based 1D visual tokenizers encode images into flexible latent sequences, yet how individual learnable queries gather and encode image information remains poorly understood. We reveal that these queries spontaneously develop complementary roles under semantic supervision: a small set of Content queries captures high-level semantic information, while a larger set of Detail queries preserves fine-grained visual details for reconstruction. To adapt token processing to these heterogeneous roles, we introduce MoETok, a 1D visual tokenizer that routes tokens through sparsely activated experts. Jointly optimized with reconstruction and semantic objectives, the router learns role-specialized processing paths adapted to each token's representation. Across model scales and token budgets, MoETok consistently improves reconstruction, semantic representation, and autoregressive generation over dense tokenizers under matched supervision and active computation. On ImageNet, it combines strong reconstruction and semantic representation with state-of-the-art class-conditional generation within the 1D tokenizer family. We further validate MoETok at scale in a unified autoregressive model jointly trained for understanding and generation with a next-token cross-entropy objective. The resulting model combines competitive visual understanding with state-of-the-art generation among unified discrete models, matching or surpassing diffusion-based models such as BAGEL and Qwen-Image on benchmarks including DPG-Bench (87.61), GenEval2 (40.04 GM), and WISE (0.49).

AI.tldr: MoETok is a 1D visual tokenizer that routes tokens through sparsely activated experts, building on the Content and Detail query roles that emerge under semantic supervision. It improves reconstruction, semantic representation and autoregressive generation over dense tokenizers under matched supervision and active computation.
AI.motivation: Query-based 1D visual tokenizers encode images into flexible latent sequences, but how individual learnable queries gather and encode image information is poorly understood, and dense processing does not adapt to the heterogeneous roles the queries take on.
AI.method: A small set of Content queries captures high-level semantics while a larger set of Detail queries preserves fine-grained detail. MoETok routes tokens through sparsely activated experts, and its router, jointly optimized with reconstruction and semantic objectives, learns role-specialized processing paths.
AI.result: Across model scales and token budgets, MoETok consistently beats dense tokenizers on reconstruction, semantic representation and autoregressive generation under matched supervision and active computation. On ImageNet it combines strong reconstruction and semantic representation with state-of-the-art class-conditional generation within the 1D tokenizer family. In a unified autoregressive model it scores 87.61 on DPG-Bench, 40.04 GM on GenEval2 and 0.49 on WISE, matching or surpassing diffusion models such as BAGEL and Qwen-Image.
AI.conclusion: Specializing token processing to the emergent query roles yields a tokenizer that supports competitive visual understanding and state-of-the-art generation among unified discrete models.

title: GeoFlip: Benchmarking Geometry-Sensitive Physics in Video Generation
summary: Video generation models synthesize realistic motion, but can they respond correctly to changes in initial geometry? We introduce GeoFlip, a video generation benchmark centered on physical outcome flips induced by geometry. With shared physical settings and textual prompts held fixed, GeoFlip applies controlled interventions to support extent, object placement, and mechanism configuration, constructing paired scenes with contrasting reference events, such as remaining stable versus falling or tipping. These pairs test whether models translate geometric differences in the first frame into correct physical evolution. The benchmark comprises 482 scene pairs and 964 reference videos across six physical categories, with reference outcomes established through procedural scene construction, physics simulation, and numerical validation and verification of physical events. We evaluate 16 models for image to video generation along three dimensions: event correctness, structural integrity, and similarity to reference videos. We examine evaluation consistency with independent vision language judges. On the 442 conditions shared by all models, the highest event correctness averaged across tasks is 27.98%, revealing substantial limitations in physical generation conditioned on geometry. Model strengths vary across physical mechanisms, and the three evaluation dimensions capture distinct capabilities. Typical failures include ignoring geometric changes, generating incorrect object motion, bending rigid objects, and introducing additional components. Rank correlations between judges reach 0.906 for event correctness and 0.929 for structural integrity. By combining controlled geometric interventions, verifiable physical references, and multidimensional evaluation, GeoFlip assesses progress from visual realism toward physical consistency conditioned on geometry.

AI.tldr: GeoFlip is a benchmark of 482 scene pairs that tests whether image-to-video models produce the correct physical outcome when only the initial geometry changes. The highest event correctness among the 16 evaluated models is 27.98%.
AI.motivation: Video generation models synthesize realistic motion, but it is unclear whether they respond correctly to changes in initial geometry that flip the physical outcome, such as a scene remaining stable or falling.
AI.method: Paired scenes with shared physical settings and fixed prompts differ by controlled interventions on support extent, object placement and mechanism configuration. Reference outcomes come from procedural scene construction, physics simulation and numerical validation. Models are scored on event correctness, structural integrity and similarity to reference videos, with independent vision-language judges checking consistency.
AI.result: The benchmark has 964 reference videos across six physical categories. On the 442 conditions shared by all models, the highest average event correctness is 27.98%. Typical failures include ignoring geometric changes, generating incorrect object motion, bending rigid objects and introducing additional components. Rank correlations between judges reach 0.906 for event correctness and 0.929 for structural integrity.
AI.conclusion: The three evaluation dimensions capture distinct capabilities, and the benchmark exposes substantial limits in physical generation conditioned on geometry beyond visual realism.

title: Any Forcing: Any-Step Generality and One-Step Stability for Autoregressive Video Generation
summary: Autoregressive video generation enables efficient inference through streaming prediction. However, existing methods are typically restricted to fixed sampling steps, limiting the flexibility to balance generation quality and efficiency, while one-step generation suffers from degraded visual quality and error accumulation over long sequences, leading to content drift and generation collapse. To address these issues, we propose Any Forcing, a unified framework for achieving Any-Step Generality and One-Step Stability. Specifically, we introduce a unified adversarial discriminator that jointly performs real-distribution alignment, inter-step consistency alignment, and first-frame quality enhancement, enabling flexible sampling while preserving one-step generation quality. Furthermore, we propose a training-free adaptive long-term memory selection mechanism that selects historical states based on global semantic relevance and local value contribution, while remapping their temporal positions to preserve temporal relationships within the memory cache, thereby enabling stable one-step long-video generation. Experiments demonstrate that Any Forcing achieves high-quality and stable one-step autoregressive video generation, achieving 20.9 FPS and 24.7 FPS for short and long video generation on a single H100 GPU, respectively.

AI.tldr: Any Forcing is an autoregressive video generation framework that supports any sampling step count while keeping one-step generation stable over long videos. It reaches 20.9 FPS for short and 24.7 FPS for long video generation on a single H100 GPU.
AI.motivation: Existing autoregressive video methods are restricted to fixed sampling steps, and one-step generation degrades in visual quality and accumulates errors over long sequences, leading to content drift and generation collapse.
AI.method: A unified adversarial discriminator jointly performs real-distribution alignment, inter-step consistency alignment and first-frame quality enhancement. A training-free adaptive long-term memory selection picks historical states by global semantic relevance and local value contribution, and remaps their temporal positions to preserve temporal relationships in the memory cache.
AI.result: Any Forcing achieves high-quality, stable one-step autoregressive video generation, with 20.9 FPS for short video and 24.7 FPS for long video generation on a single H100 GPU.
AI.conclusion: The framework combines flexible sampling steps with one-step quality and stability, enabling stable one-step long-video generation.

title: Think in 360°: Benchmarking and Bootstrapping Panoramic Video Reasoning
summary: A panoramic video captures all directions around the camera, but relevant evidence can appear in different directions and at different times. Understanding it requires models to connect observations across the viewing sphere and time. We introduce PanoVideoBench, the first manually annotated benchmark for comprehensive panoramic video understanding. Its 1,000 questions span five categories and 15 question types, with diagnostic annotations for target search and panoramic capabilities. Evaluation of 11 proprietary, open-source, and panoramic-specialized models identifies cross-view tracking and sphere-time evidence integration as their weakest capabilities. To strengthen these capabilities, we construct PanoVideoCoT, the first reasoning dataset grounded in real panoramic video, through sphere-time-grounded synthesis that converts verified panoramic observations and successful agentic explorations into 13,465 QA-CoT pairs. Starting from a general video MLLM, PanoVideoReasoner learns from this corpus through Panoramic CoT SFT and Evidence-Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation, a panoramic instantiation of Vision-OPD's OPSD in which the teacher uses verified perspective views to guide student-generated trajectories. It reaches 55.7% on PanoVideoBench, improving the backbone by 12.5 points and the previous SOTA by 2.6. The gains concentrate on the same spatial, cross-view, and temporal capabilities exposed by the benchmark, showing that grounded sphere-time supervision can equip a general video MLLM with panoramic reasoning.

AI.tldr: PanoVideoBench is a 1,000-question benchmark for panoramic video reasoning, and PanoVideoReasoner, trained on a new corpus of 13,465 QA-CoT pairs, reaches 55.7% on it. The model improves its backbone by 12.5 points and the previous state of the art by 2.6 points.
AI.motivation: Relevant evidence in panoramic video can appear in different directions and at different times, and no manually annotated benchmark existed for comprehensive panoramic video understanding.
AI.method: The benchmark has 1,000 questions across five categories and 15 question types, with diagnostic annotations for target search and panoramic capabilities. PanoVideoCoT is built by sphere-time-grounded synthesis that converts verified panoramic observations and successful agentic explorations into 13,465 QA-CoT pairs. A general video MLLM learns from it through Panoramic CoT SFT and Evidence-Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation, a panoramic instantiation of Vision-OPD's OPSD in which a teacher using verified perspective views guides student-generated trajectories.
AI.result: Evaluating 11 proprietary, open-source and panoramic-specialized models identifies cross-view tracking and sphere-time evidence integration as the weakest capabilities. PanoVideoReasoner reaches 55.7% on PanoVideoBench, 12.5 points above its backbone and 2.6 points above the previous SOTA. The gains concentrate on the spatial, cross-view and temporal capabilities the benchmark exposes.
AI.conclusion: Grounded sphere-time supervision can equip a general video MLLM with panoramic reasoning.

title: Rethinking Asymmetry in Self-Supervised 3D Geometry Learning
summary: Self-supervised learning relies on asymmetry between what a model observes and what it must explain. Recent methods learn 3D geometry from unposed images by predicting cameras and scene structure, then rendering held-out views. To avoid trivial solutions, they impose this asymmetry in the input space, restricting how views interact through separate branches or masked attention. We revisit this design with geometric accuracy, rather than rendering quality, as the main objective. When a held-out view lies between context views, the context already constrains the geometry it observes. We therefore impose the asymmetry in the 3D representation space, excluding held-out views only from the reconstructed scene while a shared backbone uses all views for correspondence. This improves depth and pose estimation over input-space designs. We further exploit view density: sparse and dense observations depict the same scene but provide different amounts of correspondence. Aligning sparse-context features with dense-context features supplies a geometric training signal alongside rendering, without a pretrained geometric teacher. We additionally align features with a frozen vision foundation model, which brings further gains. None of these signals requires geometric annotation, and the resulting model improves geometry estimation over prior self-supervised methods. Controlled experiments isolate the contribution of each component, and self-supervised pretraining also improves subsequent supervised training.

AI.tldr: The paper moves the asymmetry in self-supervised 3D geometry learning from the input space into the 3D representation space, which improves depth and pose estimation over input-space designs. Aligning sparse-context and dense-context features and a frozen vision foundation model add further gains without geometric annotation.
AI.motivation: Recent methods that learn 3D geometry from unposed images impose asymmetry in the input space through separate branches or masked attention, which restricts how views interact, although the goal is geometric accuracy rather than rendering quality.
AI.method: A held-out view is excluded only from the reconstructed scene, while a shared backbone uses all views for correspondence. Sparse-context features are aligned with dense-context features to supply a geometric training signal alongside rendering, without a pretrained geometric teacher. Features are also aligned with a frozen vision foundation model.
AI.result: The approach improves depth and pose estimation over input-space designs and improves geometry estimation over prior self-supervised methods. Controlled experiments isolate the contribution of each component, and self-supervised pretraining also improves subsequent supervised training. The abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Imposing asymmetry in the 3D representation space and exploiting view density gives better geometry without annotations, and the pretraining carries over to supervised training.

title: ReLift: Dense 3D Tracking as Lifted Trajectory Repair
summary: Dense 3D tracking from monocular video requires establishing point correspondences over time, estimating their depth, and inferring their trajectories during occlusion. Existing methods typically learn these tasks jointly, a demanding objective given the scarcity of 4D supervision. We show that strong pretrained 2D trackers and 3D geometry models provide an effective foundation: lifted trajectories, with occluded segments simply interpolated, already rival dedicated 3D trackers using the same geometry. However, lifted trajectories inherit correspondence and depth errors, and under occlusion, their depth comes from the occluder rather than the tracked point. We introduce ReLift, an efficient feed-forward framework that recasts dense 3D tracking as geometric trajectory repair and completion. At its core, a trajectory corrector alternates attention along and across trajectories to preserve reliable observations, repair corrupted positions, and complete missing motion. Using only geometric inputs allows us to train directly on 3D trajectories with simulated lifting errors, decoupling training from images and from any specific tracker or geometry model. Concentrating 4D supervision on trajectory refinement yields a reusable model that consistently improves lifted trajectories across trackers and geometry providers without retraining, so it benefits directly from future advances in either component. On WorldTrack, ReLift achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy, improving on the strongest baselines by 2.1 APD on all points and 3.0 on dynamic points, with faster configurations remaining competitive with leading 3D trackers while running faster than 4RC. Visit our supplementry page for more examples and code.

AI.tldr: ReLift recasts dense 3D tracking from monocular video as geometric trajectory repair and completion, using a feed-forward corrector trained on 3D trajectories with simulated lifting errors. It achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy on WorldTrack.
AI.motivation: Dedicated dense 3D trackers learn correspondence, depth and occluded motion jointly, which is hard given scarce 4D supervision, while lifted trajectories from strong 2D trackers and 3D geometry models inherit correspondence and depth errors, and under occlusion take depth from the occluder.
AI.method: Occluded segments of lifted trajectories are interpolated. A trajectory corrector alternates attention along and across trajectories to preserve reliable observations, repair corrupted positions and complete missing motion. It uses only geometric inputs, so training decouples from images and from any specific tracker or geometry model.
AI.result: On WorldTrack, ReLift achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy, improving on the strongest baselines by 2.1 APD on all points and 3.0 APD on dynamic points. Faster configurations remain competitive with leading 3D trackers while running faster than 4RC. The refiner improves lifted trajectories across trackers and geometry providers without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Concentrating 4D supervision on trajectory refinement yields a reusable model that benefits directly from advances in either the tracker or the geometry component.

title: GazeRIB: Systematic Evaluation of Multi-Reader Gaze-Guided Chest X-ray Learning
comment: 20 pages on main manuscripts (3 tables + 4 figures), 14 pages supplementary (10 tables + 8 figures)
summary: Radiologists' visual attention can supervise medical image learning, but how reader panel composition affects its value remains untested. We evaluated GazeRIB (Gaze-guided Radiologist-Informed Blackout), which masks unviewed regions during training and uses unmasked images at inference. Eight experts repeatedly read the same 80 chest X-rays (CXRs). We compared individual readers with three-, five- and eight-reader panels across seven architectures and 10 seeds, evaluating 910 models on a separate 2,897-CXR cohort for four-class severity prediction. Every panel improved macro F1 over the no-gaze baseline by 5.33-7.47 percentage points (pp; Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.007); no individual reader reached significance on this endpoint. Three readers captured 73-80% of the eight-reader gain in macro F1, the area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) and the area under the precision-recall curve (AU-PRC). On external validation without retraining, all four panels improved ROC-AUC on SIIM-FISABIO-RSNA by +1.93 to +4.24 pp (p <= 0.004); on MIMIC-Eye no panel differed significantly from baseline, whereas the single-reader average declined (-1.40 pp, p = 0.008). Reader composition therefore influenced performance, although transfer depended on the cohort.

AI.tldr: GazeRIB masks regions that radiologists did not view during training and uses unmasked images at inference. Reader panels of three or more readers improve chest X-ray severity prediction, and three readers capture 73-80% of the eight-reader gain in macro F1, ROC-AUC and AU-PRC.
AI.motivation: Radiologists' visual attention can supervise medical image learning, but how the composition of the reader panel affects its value had not been tested.
AI.method: GazeRIB (Gaze-guided Radiologist-Informed Blackout) masks unviewed regions during training and uses unmasked images at inference. Eight experts read the same 80 chest X-rays, and individual readers were compared with three-, five- and eight-reader panels across seven architectures and 10 seeds, yielding 910 models evaluated on a separate 2,897-CXR cohort for four-class severity prediction.
AI.result: Every panel improved macro F1 over the no-gaze baseline by 5.33-7.47 percentage points (Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.007), while no individual reader reached significance on this endpoint. On SIIM-FISABIO-RSNA without retraining, all four panels improved ROC-AUC by 1.93 to 4.24 pp (p <= 0.004). On MIMIC-Eye no panel differed significantly from baseline, whereas the single-reader average declined by 1.40 pp (p = 0.008).
AI.conclusion: Reader composition influences performance, but transfer across cohorts depends on the dataset.

title: Inter-Frame Predictive Contour Coding for Semantic Map Compression
comment: 4 pages, 4 figures, to be presented at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Visual Communications and Image Processing, Singapore, December 2026
summary: Dynamic semantic maps have become an important intermediate representation for many computer vision applications. Efficient lossless compression of such maps is essential for reducing storage and transmission costs. Existing contour-based semantic map compression methods mainly exploit spatial redundancy within individual frames while largely ignoring the strong temporal correlation between adjacent semantic maps. In this paper, we propose an inter-frame predictive contour coding framework for lossless semantic map compression. The proposed framework first predicts blob positions and label indexes from the reference frame and then performs contour prediction using corresponding chain-code units in the reference contours. A mode selection mechanism is further employed to choose between intra and inter coding according to the estimated coding cost. By exploiting temporal contour redundancy while preserving the advantages of contour-based representation, the proposed framework significantly improves coding efficiency. Experimental results on the VSPW dynamic semantic segmentation dataset demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art lossless semantic map compression methods. Compared with the recent context-adaptive extended chain coding framework, the proposed inter-frame coding achieves an average bitrate reduction of 3.0\% without significant increase in the average encoding time, demonstrating an effective trade-off between compression performance and computational complexity. The source code is made publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an inter-frame predictive contour coding framework for lossless semantic map compression that exploits temporal contour redundancy. It reduces average bitrate by 3.0% relative to context-adaptive extended chain coding on the VSPW dataset without a significant increase in encoding time.
AI.motivation: Contour-based semantic map compression exploits spatial redundancy within individual frames but largely ignores the strong temporal correlation between adjacent semantic maps.
AI.method: The framework predicts blob positions and label indexes from the reference frame, then predicts contours from the corresponding chain-code units in the reference contours. A mode selection mechanism chooses between intra and inter coding according to estimated coding cost.
AI.result: On the VSPW dynamic semantic segmentation dataset, the method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art lossless semantic map compression methods. Compared with the recent context-adaptive extended chain coding framework, it achieves an average bitrate reduction of 3.0% without a significant increase in average encoding time.
AI.conclusion: The method offers an effective trade-off between compression performance and computational complexity, and its source code is publicly available.

title: TinyAstral: Transferring Self-Evolving Harnesses to Tiny Generalist Manipulation Agents
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures. Project page: this https URL
summary: Robot agents built on vision-language models depend on both the planner and its harness: the tools, feedback, memory, and recovery logic around it. Can improvements to a large teacher's harness be carried into a compact agent with lower inference compute cost? We present TinyAstral, a two-stage approach. We first freeze an open-weight teacher and improve its harness through recursive self-improvement (RSI): frontier LLM agents read the teacher's trajectories and propose harness edits, and each edit is accepted only if it passes a paired statistical test. We then freeze the final harness, collect teacher trajectories with reasoning and failure recovery, and distill a small student that replaces the teacher in the same harness. On RoboTwin, harness evolution raises the teacher's success from 33.4% to 63.6%; the final 4B student reaches 62.8%. Across four harness versions, distilled 4B students score close to their corresponding teachers, and later versions yield stronger students, showing that harness evolution gains carry into compact models. The harness gains also transfer to other frozen planners without retraining. On identical episodes, the final 4B student outperforms open 4B agents, the open 27B harness-RSI model SenseNova-RoboRSI, and our own teacher model placed in three competitors' harnesses. It stays close to its teacher on all three training benchmarks, and on three benchmarks never used for RSI or training it scores close to a 552B planner running the same harness. On the measured deployment episodes, it uses about one fifth of its teacher's accelerator time.

AI.tldr: TinyAstral transfers a harness improved by recursive self-improvement into a distilled 4B student for robot manipulation agents. The final 4B student reaches 62.8% on RoboTwin, close to the teacher's 63.6%, while using about one fifth of the teacher's accelerator time on measured deployment episodes.
AI.motivation: Robot agents depend on both the planner and its harness, meaning the tools, feedback, memory and recovery logic around it, and the question is whether harness gains for a large teacher can be carried into a compact agent with lower inference cost.
AI.method: The teacher's harness is improved by recursive self-improvement, in which frontier LLM agents read trajectories and propose edits that are accepted only if they pass a paired statistical test. The final harness is frozen, teacher trajectories with reasoning and failure recovery are collected, and a small student is distilled to replace the teacher in the same harness.
AI.result: On RoboTwin, harness evolution raises the teacher's success from 33.4% to 63.6%, and the 4B student reaches 62.8%. Distilled 4B students score close to their teachers across four harness versions, and later versions yield stronger students. The harness gains transfer to other frozen planners. The 4B student outperforms open 4B agents, the open 27B SenseNova-RoboRSI and the teacher placed in three competitors' harnesses, and on three unseen benchmarks it scores close to a 552B planner running the same harness.
AI.conclusion: Harness evolution gains carry into compact models, so harness improvement combined with distillation can yield cheaper robot agents.

title: PBSR: Pseudo-Burst Super-Resolution via Zero-Shot Novel View Synthesis
comment: Accepted for publication in New Generation Computing. 17 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables
summary: Burst super-resolution (BSR) achieves higher reconstruction fidelity than single-image super-resolution (SISR) by aggregating sub-pixel information from multiple frames. However, it requires a burst of frames captured under near-static conditions, and such frames are unavailable for single photographs or archival images. We propose Pseudo-Burst Super-Resolution (PBSR), which brings BSR-style reconstruction to the single-image input setting by synthesizing pseudo-burst frames via zero-shot novel view synthesis (NVS). PBSR first generates pseudo-burst frames with realistic parallax using a viewpoint sampling strategy calibrated to the pixel-shift distribution of real burst datasets. The frames are then processed by a BSR backbone equipped with a geometry-aware alignment module that reuses the NVS camera parameters and estimated depth. While the NVS stage is zero-shot, the backbone is fine-tuned with an artifact-aware adaptation so that it can exploit the synthesized frames despite their generative artifacts. Experiments on the BurstSR dataset show that PBSR consistently improves in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS over the single-frame baseline with the same reconstruction backbone.

AI.tldr: PBSR extends burst super-resolution to single images by synthesizing pseudo-burst frames with zero-shot novel view synthesis. Using the same reconstruction backbone, it improves PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS over the single-frame baseline on the BurstSR dataset.
AI.motivation: Burst super-resolution outperforms single-image super-resolution by aggregating sub-pixel information, but it needs a burst of near-static frames, which is unavailable for single photographs or archival images.
AI.method: Pseudo-burst frames with realistic parallax are generated by novel view synthesis, using a viewpoint sampling strategy calibrated to the pixel-shift distribution of real burst datasets. A BSR backbone with a geometry-aware alignment module reuses the NVS camera parameters and estimated depth, and is fine-tuned with artifact-aware adaptation so it can exploit frames with generative artifacts. The NVS stage is zero-shot.
AI.result: Experiments on the BurstSR dataset show consistent improvements in PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS over the single-frame baseline with the same reconstruction backbone.
AI.conclusion: Synthesized pseudo-bursts can bring burst-style reconstruction to single-image inputs when the backbone is adapted to tolerate generative artifacts.

title: Bayesian PET Reconstruction with Learned Flow Matching Priors via Langevin Sampling
comment: Selected as the Best Student Paper Award for 2026 IVMSP
summary: Image reconstruction for positron emission tomography (PET) is a challenging inverse problem due to its inherent ill-posedness and Poisson counting noise, particularly in low-dose acquisitions. In this work, we introduce a novel Bayesian PET reconstruction framework that leverages a flow-matching generative prior learned from high-quality PET images. By incorporating this prior, we formulate PET reconstruction as a Bayesian inference problem and solve it via latent-space posterior sampling using the unadjusted Langevin algorithm. We evaluate the proposed method through numerical experiments and benchmark it against classical reconstruction methods and state-of-the-art deep learning-based baselines. The proposed method achieves improved reconstruction performance while enabling posterior uncertainty quantification.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a Bayesian PET reconstruction framework that uses a flow-matching prior learned from high-quality PET images and samples the posterior with the unadjusted Langevin algorithm in latent space. It improves reconstruction performance and enables posterior uncertainty quantification.
AI.motivation: PET reconstruction is an ill-posed inverse problem affected by Poisson counting noise, especially in low-dose acquisitions, and classical and deep learning baselines leave room for improvement.
AI.method: A flow-matching generative prior learned from high-quality PET images is incorporated into a Bayesian inference formulation, which is solved by latent-space posterior sampling with the unadjusted Langevin algorithm.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show improved reconstruction performance over classical reconstruction methods and state-of-the-art deep learning baselines, and the framework enables posterior uncertainty quantification. The abstract reports no numbers.
AI.conclusion: Combining learned flow-matching priors with Langevin sampling gives a Bayesian route to PET reconstruction that provides both improved reconstructions and uncertainty estimates.

title: PRIN: A Perceptual-Structural Retinex-Inspired Network for Low-Light Image Enhancement
summary: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) focuses not only on visibility recovery but also on preserving structurally meaningful content and perceptual naturalness. Existing learning-based methods may achieve favorable pixel-wise fidelity while still producing over-smoothed textures, color deviations, or spatially incoherent illumination. Retinex-inspired methods provide interpretable decomposition into reflectance and illumination components, however, the asymmetric restoration roles of these components are rarely encoded through branch-specific frequency-domain refinement. To address this issue, we propose a Perceptual-Structural Retinex-Inspired Network (PRIN), which integrates Retinex priors with restoration-role-aware enhancement. PRIN employs a shared encoder and asymmetric decoders to estimate reflectance and illumination components. The reflectance branch performs attention-guided and edge-aware wavelet refinement to preserve textures and boundaries, whereas the illumination branch promotes spatially coherent brightness adjustment. After the recomposition of reflectance and illumination branches, a curve-based post-composition enhancement head calibrates residual tone and exposure deviations. Experiments on LOL-v1, LOL-v2-Syn, and LOL-v2-Real show that the proposed network ties for the best structural similarity index (SSIM) and obtains the second-lowest learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) on LOL-v1, achieves the best SSIM and LPIPS on LOL-v2-Syn, and obtains the highest peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and the second-lowest LPIPS on LOL-v2-Real.

AI.tldr: PRIN is a Retinex-inspired low-light enhancement network with a shared encoder, asymmetric decoders for reflectance and illumination, and branch-specific refinement. It obtains the best SSIM and LPIPS on LOL-v2-Syn and the highest PSNR on LOL-v2-Real.
AI.motivation: Learning-based low-light methods can achieve good pixel-wise fidelity yet produce over-smoothed textures, color deviations or spatially incoherent illumination, and the asymmetric restoration roles of Retinex reflectance and illumination components are rarely encoded.
AI.method: A shared encoder and asymmetric decoders estimate the reflectance and illumination components. The reflectance branch applies attention-guided, edge-aware wavelet refinement to preserve textures and boundaries, the illumination branch promotes spatially coherent brightness adjustment, and a curve-based post-composition head calibrates residual tone and exposure after recomposition.
AI.result: On LOL-v1 the network ties for the best SSIM and has the second-lowest LPIPS. On LOL-v2-Syn it achieves the best SSIM and LPIPS. On LOL-v2-Real it achieves the highest PSNR and the second-lowest LPIPS.
AI.conclusion: Encoding the distinct restoration roles of Retinex components through branch-specific frequency-domain refinement improves perceptual and structural quality in low-light enhancement.

title: Joint-Health-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Robust Robot Control Under Actuator Degradation
summary: Robots deployed in unstructured environments are susceptible to actuator-authority degradation, which reduces the effective control authority of individual actuators and can cause reinforcement learning policies trained under nominal dynamics to fail.
