Existing robustness approaches rely on discrete fault labels, broad domain randomization, or global latent variables, often without explicitly modeling continuous per-joint residual actuation capability. We propose a joint-health-aware reinforcement learning framework for robust robot control under simulated actuator degradation. Our framework encodes actuator condition in a continuous joint-health vector and models degradation as multiplicative attenuation of executed actions. A dedicated HealthNet estimator infers per-joint health from recent observations and actions, allowing the policy to redistribute control effort across healthy and degraded joints. We evaluate the method on Walker, Go2, Cassie, and Panda-based ManiSkill manipulation tasks under diverse degradation masks and severity levels. The method outperforms nominal and degradation-trained no-health baselines on the main evaluated metrics. Relative to the nominal baseline, task-level locomotion returns improve by up to 250.1\% and manipulation success rates by up to 15.2 percentage points; in the high-degradation Cassie group, return increases from 3.94 to 40.50 (+928.0\%). Ablations support the contribution of per-joint health estimation, action-degradation modeling, and health-conditioned control.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a joint-health-aware reinforcement learning framework that encodes continuous per-joint actuator health and infers it with a HealthNet estimator, so the policy can redistribute control under degradation. It outperforms nominal and degradation-trained baselines on Walker, Go2, Cassie and Panda-based ManiSkill tasks.
AI.motivation: Actuator-authority degradation can make policies trained under nominal dynamics fail, and existing robustness approaches rely on discrete fault labels, broad domain randomization or global latent variables without explicitly modeling continuous per-joint residual actuation capability.
AI.method: Actuator condition is encoded in a continuous joint-health vector, and degradation is modeled as multiplicative attenuation of executed actions. HealthNet infers per-joint health from recent observations and actions, allowing the policy to redistribute control effort across healthy and degraded joints.
AI.result: The method outperforms nominal and degradation-trained no-health baselines on the main evaluated metrics. Relative to the nominal baseline, locomotion returns improve by up to 250.1% and manipulation success rates by up to 15.2 percentage points. In the high-degradation Cassie group, return increases from 3.94 to 40.50 (+928.0%). Ablations support per-joint health estimation, action-degradation modeling and health-conditioned control.
AI.conclusion: Explicit per-joint health modeling gives robust control under simulated actuator degradation across locomotion and manipulation tasks.

title: CalibSwitch: Observation-Driven Camera-LiDAR Extrinsic Recovery and Selective Maintenance for Multimodal Perception
summary: Camera--LiDAR perception on mobile robots and intelligent vehicles depends on reliable sensor geometry throughout deployment. Installation variations create uncertainty in the initial extrinsics, while changing observation quality makes frame-wise estimates fluctuate during operation. This paper presents CalibSwitch, an observation-driven framework that separates absolute extrinsic recovery from selective state maintenance. A cross-modal absolute extrinsic generator (CAEG) combines projection-free bidirectional feature interaction with geometry-regularized learning to recover complete SE(3) candidates from image--point observations and coarse view context, without a supplied numerical initial transform. A selective recurrent calibration policy (SRCP) combines observation quality and temporal history to determine when a candidate should replace the working geometry consumed by a frozen multimodal detector. On nuScenes, CAEG achieves mean translation and rotation errors of 0.248 m and 5.884$^\circ$. Under sustained geometric transitions, SRCP reaches a mean composite error of 1.46 with 9.70\% candidate commitments, outperforming quality-based and temporal-consistency gating at comparable commitment rates. Relative to unconditional per-frame updating, it improves frozen-detector mAP and NDS by 1.43 and 0.92 points. Paired geometry--observation uncertainty tests, two real-vehicle platforms, and 13.5-FPS single-camera Jetson execution demonstrate the system value of selective geometric-state maintenance for continuous perception.

AI.tldr: CalibSwitch recovers full SE(3) camera-LiDAR extrinsics from observations and selectively decides when to replace the working calibration. On nuScenes, the selective policy improves frozen-detector mAP and NDS by 1.43 and 0.92 points over unconditional per-frame updating.
AI.motivation: Camera-LiDAR perception on mobile robots and vehicles depends on reliable sensor geometry, but installation variations make the initial extrinsics uncertain, and frame-wise estimates fluctuate as observation quality changes.
AI.method: A cross-modal absolute extrinsic generator (CAEG) uses projection-free bidirectional feature interaction and geometry-regularized learning to recover complete SE(3) candidates from image-point observations and coarse view context, without a supplied numerical initial transform. A selective recurrent calibration policy (SRCP) combines observation quality and temporal history to decide when a candidate should replace the working geometry used by a frozen multimodal detector.
AI.result: On nuScenes, CAEG achieves mean translation and rotation errors of 0.248 m and 5.884 degrees. Under sustained geometric transitions, SRCP reaches a mean composite error of 1.46 with 9.70% candidate commitments, outperforming quality-based and temporal-consistency gating at comparable commitment rates. Relative to unconditional per-frame updating, it improves frozen-detector mAP and NDS by 1.43 and 0.92 points. Two real-vehicle platforms and 13.5-FPS single-camera Jetson execution are also reported.
AI.conclusion: Selective geometric-state maintenance is valuable for continuous perception, and separating absolute extrinsic recovery from selective state maintenance is the key design.

title: Defining Page-Centric Visual Document Retrieval and Evaluating Existing Benchmarks
summary: In modern information retrieval (IR), documents are increasingly encountered as structured sequences of visually rich, paginated units, rather than as flat text. Example documents encountered in our daily life include Word files, PDFs, and slide decks. Free text-centric retrieval systems either ignore this structure entirely or destroy it through arbitrary passage chunking. In this paper, we formulate page-centric Visual Document Retrieval (VDR) with pages as the fundamental indexing units and document context available for assessing page relevance. The formulation distinguishes two retrieval granularities, page and document, and three retrieval paradigms: independent-item, evidence-set, and iterative retrieval. We then assess 42 benchmarks using eight criteria covering corpus characteristics, query construction, relevance annotation, and ranking support. Our analysis shows two main findings on current VDR research. First, evaluation remains concentrated on page-level independent-item retrieval, with fewer resources supporting document-level, evidence-set, and iterative settings. Second, queries originating from real user information needs independently of target corpus content and graded relevance judgments are uncommon, while the coverage and verification of relevance judgments vary substantially. Both findings reveal gaps between the capabilities applications require and those existing evaluation protocols can establish. We provide benchmark selection guidance and identify priorities for future benchmark design, emphasizing alignment between task requirements, relevance semantics, and evaluation protocols.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes page-centric visual document retrieval, with pages as indexing units, and assesses 42 benchmarks against eight criteria. It finds that evaluation concentrates on page-level independent-item retrieval, while realistic queries and graded relevance judgments are uncommon.
AI.motivation: Documents such as Word files, PDFs and slide decks are paginated and visually rich, yet text-centric retrieval either ignores this structure or destroys it through arbitrary passage chunking, and existing benchmarks may not match application requirements.
AI.method: Page-centric VDR is formulated with pages as the fundamental indexing units and document context available for judging relevance. It distinguishes page and document granularities and three paradigms: independent-item, evidence-set and iterative retrieval. The authors assess 42 benchmarks on eight criteria covering corpus characteristics, query construction, relevance annotation and ranking support.
AI.result: Evaluation remains concentrated on page-level independent-item retrieval, with fewer resources for document-level, evidence-set and iterative settings. Queries originating from real user information needs independently of corpus content, and graded relevance judgments, are uncommon, and the coverage and verification of relevance judgments vary substantially.
AI.conclusion: Gaps remain between the capabilities applications require and what current evaluation protocols can establish, and the paper gives benchmark selection guidance and priorities emphasizing alignment of task requirements, relevance semantics and protocols.

title: TopoHyperClinicalGraph: A Geometry and Topology-Aware Multimodal Framework for Cancer Survival Prediction
summary: We developed TopoHyperClinicalGraph, a multimodal framework combining hyperbolic tissue geometry, persistent topology and clinical graph learning for cancer survival prediction. Pre-extracted UNI2-h features are reduced from 1,536 to 1,024 dimensions using training-fold PCA. A pathology backbone combines hyperbolic neighborhoods with Lorentz-centroid attention pooling. Once frozen, its survival logits are adjusted using persistence descriptors from up to 64 landmarks per slide and sampling controls. A five-node clinical graph then learns a further correction from age, sex, stage, T and N. Five-fold patient-level evaluation covered eight TCGA and CPTAC cohorts with 2,364 patients. Mean validation-selected C-indices for TopoHyperClinicalGraph versus pathology-only spatial PatchGCN were 0.7563 versus 0.7386 in COADREAD, 0.6220 versus 0.5998 in HNSC, 0.6755 versus 0.6535 in BRCA and 0.6409 versus 0.6176 in STAD. CPTAC scores were 0.5984 in HNSC, 0.6060 in PDA, 0.8055 in CCRCC and 0.7192 in LUAD. CPTAC-HNSC used TCGA-initialized adaptation; other CPTAC backbones were trained within their cohorts. Geometry accounted for most pathology-only gains, with smaller persistence effects. Clinical graph fusion exceeded its matched node-wise control in five cohorts, tied in one and scored lower in two; clinical-only prediction exceeded fusion in three CPTAC cohorts. The framework supports separate evaluation of geometric, topological and clinical contributions. All scores were validation-selected; independent testing is needed to establish generalizability.

AI.tldr: TopoHyperClinicalGraph combines hyperbolic tissue geometry, persistent topology and a clinical graph for cancer survival prediction, and reports C-index gains over pathology-only PatchGCN in four TCGA cohorts. Its scores are validation-selected, so independent testing is still needed.
AI.motivation: Survival prediction from pathology benefits from separate geometric, topological and clinical signals, and the goal is a framework that supports separate evaluation of each contribution.
AI.method: Pre-extracted UNI2-h features are reduced from 1,536 to 1,024 dimensions by training-fold PCA. A pathology backbone combines hyperbolic neighborhoods with Lorentz-centroid attention pooling. Once frozen, its survival logits are adjusted using persistence descriptors from up to 64 landmarks per slide and sampling controls. A five-node clinical graph over age, sex, stage, T and N learns a further correction. Five-fold patient-level evaluation covers eight TCGA and CPTAC cohorts with 2,364 patients.
AI.result: Mean validation-selected C-indices for TopoHyperClinicalGraph versus pathology-only spatial PatchGCN were 0.7563 versus 0.7386 in COADREAD, 0.6220 versus 0.5998 in HNSC, 0.6755 versus 0.6535 in BRCA and 0.6409 versus 0.6176 in STAD. CPTAC scores were 0.5984 in HNSC, 0.6060 in PDA, 0.8055 in CCRCC and 0.7192 in LUAD. Geometry accounts for most pathology-only gains, with smaller persistence effects. Clinical graph fusion exceeded its matched node-wise control in five cohorts, tied in one and scored lower in two, and clinical-only prediction exceeded fusion in three CPTAC cohorts.
AI.conclusion: The framework allows separate assessment of geometric, topological and clinical contributions, but its scores are validation-selected and independent testing is needed to establish generalizability.

title: OpenVIO: A Versatile Open-Source Visual-Inertial Odometry System
summary: Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) is a fundamental topic in robotics research. Beyond research, VIO has been adopted in a wide range of products. In this manuscript, we present OpenVIO, an open-source VIO system for research and practical applications. It is released under the MIT license. OpenVIO supports pinhole and fisheye cameras and extends this support to stitched 360° images. We describe each part of the system together with its design considerations. We also report benchmark results with other open-source VIO systems on public datasets. OpenVIO is available as open source at this https URL.

AI.tldr: OpenVIO is an open-source, MIT-licensed visual-inertial odometry system that supports pinhole and fisheye cameras and stitched 360-degree images. The paper describes its design and reports benchmark results against other open-source VIO systems on public datasets.
AI.motivation: Visual-inertial odometry is a fundamental topic in robotics and is used in many products, and the authors aim for a system usable in both research and practical applications.
AI.method: The system is described part by part together with its design considerations. It supports pinhole and fisheye cameras and extends that support to stitched 360-degree images.
AI.result: Benchmark results against other open-source VIO systems on public datasets are reported. The abstract gives no numbers.
AI.conclusion: OpenVIO is released as a versatile open-source VIO system for both research and practical applications.

title: Movens-Zero: Scaling Humanoid Motion Foundation Models with Large-Scale Human Videos
comment: Technical report. 86 pages, 31 figures, 15 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Scaling humanoid motion foundation models is constrained by the scarcity of diverse, robot-executable data and by the difficulty of jointly learning from heterogeneous multimodal inputs while supporting real-time closed-loop control. We present Movens-5M, constructed from raw Internet videos through clip generation, quality filtering, semantic annotation, motion recovery, and physical refinement with humanoid retargeting and execution verification. It contains 15 million human-motion sequences and 5 million physically executable humanoid-motion sequences spanning over 10,000 hours, aligned with text, RGB video, speech, and music. Building on this data, we introduce Movens-Zero, a scalable understanding-generation-execution architecture that supports joint learning across modalities and real-time closed-loop execution. Task-mixed flow-matching training jointly optimizes a single action expert across seven generation tasks, enabling direct motion generation from text, speech, music, and video. Multimodal Real-Time Chunking connects overlapping chunks under continuously updated instructions and robot states for continuous closed-loop execution. We further introduce Movens-Intent, a four-track benchmark with 8,192 expert-verified condition-motion pairs across text, speech, music, and video. Experiments show consistent gains across all four modalities when scaling execution-verified data from 1% to 100% and action-expert capacity from 64M to 911M parameters, while demonstrating that data quality and cross-modal supervision improve generation and execution.

AI.tldr: Movens-Zero is a humanoid motion foundation model trained on Movens-5M, which contains 15 million human-motion sequences and 5 million physically executable humanoid sequences. A single action expert handles seven generation tasks from text, speech, music and video, with real-time closed-loop execution.
AI.motivation: Scaling humanoid motion foundation models is constrained by scarce diverse robot-executable data and by the difficulty of learning jointly from heterogeneous multimodal inputs while supporting real-time closed-loop control.
AI.method: Movens-5M is built from raw Internet videos through clip generation, quality filtering, semantic annotation, motion recovery and physical refinement with humanoid retargeting and execution verification. Task-mixed flow-matching training optimizes one action expert across seven generation tasks, and Multimodal Real-Time Chunking connects overlapping chunks under continuously updated instructions and robot states. Movens-Intent is a four-track benchmark with 8,192 expert-verified condition-motion pairs.
AI.result: Scaling execution-verified data from 1% to 100% and action-expert capacity from 64M to 911M parameters gives consistent gains across all four modalities. The dataset spans over 10,000 hours.
AI.conclusion: Data quality and cross-modal supervision improve both generation and execution in humanoid motion foundation models.

title: IGDA-ICMH: an Importance Guided Feature and Network Dual Adaptation Framework towards Image Compression for Machine and Human Vision
summary: With the surge of machine vision applications, image compression for both machine and human vision (ICMH) has become an important research area. Existing studies mainly focus on task-specific adaptation or multi-task joint optimization, yet they often overlook the unequal contributions of different features and network layers to downstream machine vision tasks. To address this issue, we first quantitatively investigate the impact of different feature and network layers on machine vision performance, providing a principled understanding of their importance. Based on this analysis, an Importance Guided feature and network Dual Adaptation (IGDA) framework is developed for ICMH. It adopts implicit neural representation as the basic architecture and designs an efficient adaptation structure with both feature and network weight adaptation. An Importance-Guided Network Adaptation (IGNA) module is developed with a low-rank adaptation strategy to selectively adjust key network layers according to their importance in different tasks. An Importance-Guided Feature Adaptation (IGFA) module is developed with a low-rank and Kronecker product-based transform to explore the non-local property of the features in order to reduce the number of adaptation parameters. Extensive experiments on representative machine vision tasks, including image classification and object detection, demonstrate that our IGDA-ICMH framework achieves significantly better performance than the existing implicit neural representation-based methods for ICMH.

AI.tldr: Proposes IGDA-ICMH, an importance-guided feature and network dual adaptation framework for image compression serving both machine and human vision, built on implicit neural representation. It significantly outperforms existing INR-based ICMH methods on image classification and object detection.
AI.motivation: Existing ICMH studies focus on task-specific adaptation or multi-task joint optimisation but overlook the unequal contributions of different features and network layers to downstream machine vision tasks.
AI.method: The authors quantitatively analyse how different features and network layers affect machine vision performance, then build an INR-based framework with two modules: IGNA, a low-rank adaptation that selectively adjusts key network layers by importance, and IGFA, a low-rank and Kronecker product-based feature transform that exploits non-local feature structure to reduce adaptation parameters.
AI.result: IGDA-ICMH achieves significantly better performance than existing implicit neural representation-based methods for ICMH on representative machine vision tasks, including image classification and object detection.
AI.conclusion: Importance-aware, parameter-efficient adaptation of INR-based codecs is an effective way to compress images for both machine and human vision.

title: REA: A Routed Embodied Agent Runtime for Asynchronous Brain-Cerebellum Control
summary: Foundation models are becoming remarkably reliable at high-level reasoning, yet they remain too slow and costly to serve as fine-grained controllers. Conversely, fast policies like VLAs and whole-body controllers offer more efficient reflexes, but struggle to generalize. While pairing a deliberative brain (foundation models) with a reactive cerebellum (fast policies) seems natural for embodied systems, two obstacles remain: methods are built and scored on incompatible stacks, and their asynchronous coordination is difficult. For example, an agent that calls the VLA in the agentic loop can stall the fast execution, while a VLA that calls the agent on errors tends to re-trigger fallbacks repeatedly or completely miss silent failures. To address this, we propose REA (Routed Embodied Agent), a unified runtime where a deliberative System 2, an embodied router System 1 and reactive System 0 policies cooperate under a single golden rule - no running policy waits on the brain. Instead of querying the brain at each failure, REA employs a route memory that stores each policy's measured success ahead of time, a boundary-triggered judge gate that consults the brain on policy execution, and a shared-budget escalation ladder for bounded recovery. Evaluated on 3,000 test episodes across 60 LIBERO-Pro tasks, REA reaches 95.9% success and beats the best single-agent baseline in its own policy pool (94.7%) while reducing control steps by 25% and control time by 17%. In a separate 100-episode RoboTwin 2.0 study, REA achieves 84% success with VLA policies and 86% with VLA+code, compared with 80% for the strongest single VLA baseline MEDex. These results demonstrate learned and programmatic policies operating within the same runtime. REA also transfers to BEHAVIOR-1K and a real Unitree G1 humanoid, achieving the highest observed success among the compared methods.

AI.tldr: Presents REA, a unified runtime in which a deliberative foundation-model brain, an embodied router and reactive fast policies cooperate so that no running policy waits on the brain. On 3,000 LIBERO-Pro test episodes REA reaches 95.9% success, above the best single-agent baseline in its policy pool at 94.7%.
AI.motivation: Foundation models are too slow and costly to serve as fine-grained controllers, while fast VLA and whole-body policies generalise poorly, and combining them is hindered by incompatible evaluation stacks and difficult asynchronous coordination.
AI.method: REA combines a System 2 brain, a System 1 embodied router and System 0 reactive policies with three mechanisms: a route memory that stores each policy's measured success in advance, a boundary-triggered judge gate that consults the brain at policy execution boundaries, and a shared-budget escalation ladder for bounded recovery.
AI.result: Across 60 LIBERO-Pro tasks, REA reaches 95.9% success against 94.7% for the best single-agent baseline in its own policy pool, while reducing control steps by 25% and control time by 17%. On a 100-episode RoboTwin 2.0 study it achieves 84% with VLA policies and 86% with VLA+code, against 80% for the strongest single VLA baseline MEDex. It also transfers to BEHAVIOR-1K and a real Unitree G1 humanoid, where it reports the highest observed success among the compared methods.
AI.conclusion: Learned and programmatic policies can operate together in one asynchronous runtime, keeping brain-level reasoning off the critical control path while still improving success.

title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory
summary: Recent work shows that a frozen robot policy performs far better inside an agent harness, where control code decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools, or command the arm directly. Yet today these harnesses are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark. We show that harness design can be automated, offering a strong alternative to finetuning on a novel setup. In RoboArchitect, a coding model observes a robot's rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness around the frozen policy. The harness evolves on a set of episodes for its optimization and is evaluated on held-out scenes and tasks. Without updating any model weights, RoboArchitect raises average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5x) and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2x), across multiple benchmarks and policies. The gains are largest where the benchmark is far from the policy's training data: wrapping a general-purpose policy, the evolved harness yields a specialist that often outperforms even the finetuned version. Intuitive control strategies are automatically designed, such as lifting a jammed arm clear or reaching in horizontally when an obstacle blocks the way from above. The harness also evolves its own persistent memory, carrying learned experience, such as effective grasp depths, into later decisions. These results suggest that substantial headroom in robotic manipulation lies in the agent harness, and its design can be effectively automated and optimized without weight updates.

AI.tldr: RoboArchitect uses a coding model to automatically revise the agent harness around a frozen robot policy, including a persistent memory, without updating any model weights. It raises average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks.
AI.motivation: Agent harnesses that wrap frozen robot policies are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark, and finetuning is the usual alternative for a novel setup.
AI.method: A coding model observes rollouts, diagnoses failures and iteratively revises the harness, which decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools or command the arm directly. The harness is optimised on a set of episodes, evaluated on held-out scenes and tasks, and evolves its own persistent memory.
AI.result: Average success rises from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5x) and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2x) across multiple benchmarks and policies. When wrapping a general-purpose policy, the evolved harness often outperforms the finetuned version of that policy.
AI.conclusion: Substantial headroom in robotic manipulation lies in the agent harness, and that harness can be designed and optimised automatically without weight updates.

title: VLA Policies Do Not Know When Not to Act: Unintended Task Execution and Start Suppression
comment: 17 pages, 3 figures, 13 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: A robot should act only on an instruction from a person or on an intent that the robot explicitly represents and generates. Unintended actions taken without such an instruction can cause risk or inconvenience to people and the environment. We examine how recent vision-language-action (VLA) policies respond when the instruction is missing or meaningless. We apply a paired protocol with empty, neutral, nonsense, infeasible, and wrong-task instructions to six model checkpoints in LIBERO-Goal simulation. Holding the initial state fixed and varying only the instruction, we ask three questions: whether the robot starts to move, which task it completes, and what the instruction determines. Even when the instruction was empty, the robot started moving in every episode with all six checkpoints, and with five of them it often completed a task that the instruction had not specified. On two GR00T checkpoints, the instruction determined which task was executed but not whether the robot started moving; the robot moved even on infeasible instructions. We then tested three methods for suppressing the start: prepending "if no task is given do not move" to the instruction; a gate that holds the robot when the first action chunk for the given instruction nearly equals that for an empty instruction; and fine-tuning the policy to hold still on non-task inputs. The prefix stopped the robot in none of the six checkpoints, and the gate held it on non-task inputs in five of the six checkpoints. The fine-tuned policy never completed a task on non-task inputs, but it did not reliably keep the robot still, and it failed to suppress the start on infeasible instructions.

AI.tldr: Six VLA checkpoints on LIBERO-Goal start moving even when the instruction is empty or meaningless, and five often complete a task the instruction never specified. Of three start-suppression methods, a gate on action-chunk similarity works best, holding the robot on non-task inputs in five of six checkpoints.
AI.motivation: A robot should act only on an instruction from a person or an intent it explicitly represents, yet recent VLA policies may act without one, which can cause risk or inconvenience to people and the environment.
AI.method: Under a paired protocol with empty, neutral, nonsense, infeasible and wrong-task instructions, with the initial state held fixed, the authors test six checkpoints in LIBERO-Goal simulation. They then compare three suppression methods: a prompt prefix, a gate that holds the robot when the first action chunk nearly equals that for an empty instruction, and fine-tuning the policy to hold still on non-task inputs.
AI.result: Every checkpoint started moving on empty instructions, and five of six often completed an unspecified task. On two GR00T checkpoints the instruction determined which task ran but not whether the robot moved, even for infeasible instructions. The prefix stopped the robot in none of six checkpoints, the gate held it on non-task inputs in five of six, and the fine-tuned policy never completed a task on non-task inputs but did not reliably keep still and failed to suppress starts on infeasible instructions.
AI.conclusion: Current VLA policies do not reliably know when not to act, so explicit mechanisms are needed to suppress unintended starts, since the instruction alone does not control whether motion begins.

title: Simple Features Beat Most AI Control Monitors
comment: 19 pages (5-page main body plus appendix), 7 figures, 10 tables. Accepted at the EvoRobust workshop at NeurIPS 2026. Code and data: this https URL
summary: AI control relies on monitors to catch a capable model that sabotages its work. These monitors are evaluated on their ability to differentiate honest from backdoored code. We show that on a standard evaluation dataset, simple features beat most monitors without ever running the code, outranking 20 of 24 open-weight models prompted as monitors. The dataset gives its labels away in two ways. People wrote the honest solutions and older language models the backdoors, so the style of the code reveals the class. Additionally, problems that LLMs can backdoor have different characteristics, so basic facts about the problem reveal it too. Swapping one class at a time for code by Claude Sonnet 5 shows that these features reward a contrast between authors, since human code against Sonnet 5's backdoors is easier to separate than the original pairs, 0.95 against 0.79. One in seven backdoors in the standard test set fails our validity checks, which distorts comparisons between attackers. A Sonnet 5 monitor appears to catch 77% of the older models' backdoors but 37% of Sonnet 5's, and 78% against 61% once both are verified. We do not show that published monitors rely on these shortcuts, but our findings suggest that a high score on such a dataset is not by itself evidence of sabotage detection. We release the rebuilt dataset and checks.

AI.tldr: On a standard backdoor-detection dataset, simple code features outperform most AI control monitors without running the code, because the labels leak through authorship style and problem characteristics. One in seven backdoors in the standard test set also fails validity checks, and the authors release a rebuilt dataset and checks.
AI.motivation: AI control relies on monitors to catch sabotage, and these monitors are judged by how well they separate honest from backdoored code, so the evaluation dataset must not give its labels away.
AI.method: The authors compare simple features that never execute the code against open-weight models prompted as monitors. They swap one class at a time for code written by Claude Sonnet 5 to test whether the features exploit the contrast between authors, and they run validity checks on the backdoors in the standard test set.
AI.result: Simple features outrank 20 of 24 open-weight models prompted as monitors. Human code against Sonnet 5 backdoors is easier to separate than the original pairs (0.95 against 0.79). One in seven backdoors fails validity checks. A Sonnet 5 monitor catches 77% of the older models' backdoors but 37% of Sonnet 5's, and 78% against 61% once both are verified.
AI.conclusion: A high score on such a dataset is not by itself evidence of sabotage detection; the authors do not show that published monitors rely on these shortcuts, but they release the rebuilt dataset and checks.

title: AI evaluators favor job applications written by certain AI models, independent of candidate quality
summary: Job applicants increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to write cover letters, while employers deploy LLMs to screen them. In this all-AI setting, we ask whether the \emph{choice of model} affects hiring outcomes independently of candidate qualifications. We introduce a multi-model auditing framework pairing eleven LLM writer agents with nine API-hosted evaluator agents across ten job descriptions and fifty candidates per job. Four findings emerge. First, we identify a generative preference hierarchy: a consistent global ranking of writer models by evaluator acceptance, in which locally hosted models are systematically disadvantaged regardless of their license, compounded by self-preference bias where evaluators favour their own outputs. Second, evaluator models differ substantially in how much bias they introduce based on applicants' tool choice, offering actionable guidance for fairer screening design. Third, this hierarchy has measurable competitive consequences: in the most adverse pairing, approximately two (1.8) out of twenty-five qualified candidates are filtered out purely due to model mismatch. Fourth, a common mechanism explains the patterns above: writer preference and self-preference trace to a combination of how much each writer leans on specific stylistic cues and how strongly evaluators, often unanimously, reward or penalise those same cues. A further check finds little evidence that an unmeasured "writer fingerprint" remains once these same features are accounted for. We discuss implications for algorithmic fairness in employment, regulation of AI-assisted screening, and the design of auditing frameworks that can be reapplied as the model landscape evolves.

AI.tldr: An all-AI audit of LLM-written cover letters screened by LLM evaluators finds a consistent global ranking of writer models, with locally hosted models systematically disadvantaged and self-preference bias present. In the most adverse pairing, about 1.8 of 25 qualified candidates are filtered out purely by model mismatch.
AI.motivation: Applicants increasingly use LLMs to write cover letters and employers use LLMs to screen them, but it is unclear whether the choice of model affects hiring outcomes independently of candidate qualifications.
AI.method: The authors introduce a multi-model auditing framework that pairs eleven LLM writer agents with nine API-hosted evaluator agents across ten job descriptions and fifty candidates per job, and they analyse the stylistic cues that drive writer preference and self-preference.
AI.result: A consistent global hierarchy of writer models by evaluator acceptance emerges, with self-preference bias among evaluators. Evaluators differ in how much bias they introduce depending on applicants' tool choice. In the most adverse pairing, about two (1.8) of twenty-five qualified candidates are filtered out purely due to model mismatch. A common stylistic-cue mechanism explains the patterns, and little evidence remains for an unmeasured writer fingerprint.
AI.conclusion: Model choice alone can affect hiring outcomes, with implications for algorithmic fairness in employment, regulation of AI-assisted screening, and reusable auditing frameworks as the model landscape evolves.

title: General-purpose foundation models surpass specialized ones on chemical property prediction tasks
summary: Foundation models (FMs) learn reusable representations from large collections of unlabeled data. In chemistry the corresponding data mainly consists of molecular structures, which are abundant, whereas experimental measurements are scarce. Chemical FMs such as ChemBERTa and MoLFormer were therefore trained on diverse molecular structures to enable fine-tuning on small experimental datasets (less than 100 datapoints in most realistic scenarios) and subsequent property prediction. At the same time, general-purpose FMs such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were trained on virtually all publicly available data, including knowledge of the humankind on molecular properties and laws governing them. Here we compare accuracies of chemical and general-purpose FMs on tasks from various areas of chemistry. Strikingly, general-purpose GPT-6 Astra outperforms the currently eligible chemical FMs on five physicochemical and quantum-chemical regression tasks when only 60 experimental datapoints are available. Only when provided 10x datapoints do the best chemical FMs reach performance of GPT-6 Astra: on 1,000 and 10,000 points they show performance on par with Astra on 60 and 1,000 points, respectively. Thus, counterintuitively, frontier general-purpose FMs are better suited for guiding chemical research in data-scarce areas than specialized chemical FMs, suggesting that learning relevant primitives (e.g. chemical structures) does not substitute training on relevant humankind knowledge.

AI.tldr: General-purpose foundation models such as GPT-6 Astra outperform specialised chemical foundation models on five physicochemical and quantum-chemical regression tasks when only 60 experimental datapoints are available. The best chemical models match Astra only after roughly tenfold more data.
AI.motivation: Chemical foundation models such as ChemBERTa and MoLFormer are pretrained on molecular structures, but it was unclear how they compare with general-purpose models that also hold broad knowledge of molecular properties, in the data-scarce regime typical of chemistry.
AI.method: The authors compare the accuracy of chemical and general-purpose foundation models on property prediction tasks from several areas of chemistry, varying the number of experimental training datapoints.
AI.result: With 60 datapoints, GPT-6 Astra beats the eligible chemical models on five physicochemical and quantum-chemical regression tasks. The best chemical models reach Astra's performance only with 10x more data: on 1,000 and 10,000 points they match Astra on 60 and 1,000 points, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Frontier general-purpose models may be better guides for chemical research in data-scarce areas than specialised chemical models, suggesting that learning chemical structures does not substitute for training on human knowledge of molecular properties.

title: SecPO: Principled Adversarial Training for Prompt Injection Security
summary: Recognized as a top threat to AI agents, prompt injection allows instructions from untrusted data (email, documents, websites) to manipulate the agent's operation. The existing best-defended LLM, Meta-SecAlign, is trained with the DPO loss but still suffers from attack success rates (ASRs) approaching 100% under adaptive prompt injections. One reason is that DPO anchors the model around the undefended reference model, which is insecure. We show an idealized reference model---an injection-invariant, utility-preserving oracle---can nevertheless be approximated, as its output distribution in training is interestingly accessible. This new observation motivates a theoretically principled SecPO loss. Another Meta-SecAlign shortcoming is that it trains on weak simulated attacks. We implement an efficient adversarial training (AT) pipeline that synthesizes strong injected inputs (best@240), and train the model on them. Our AT reduces ASRs by 1.5-14.5$\times$ across three SoTA adaptive attacks, compared with Meta-SecAlign; the SecPO loss reduces them by a further 2.4-4.6$\times$ compared with using DPO loss. In agentic workflows, our SecPO + AT Qwen3.6-27B is much more secure than Meta-SecAlign: 8.8% vs. 78.8% AgentDojo ASR@800 under the AttackerMovesSecond attack. Moreover, our defended model shows no noticeable reduction in benign utility in nine benchmarks covering agentic tool calling, instruction following, science, and math. We release our $\href{//github.com/Sizhe-Chen/SecPO}{\text{code}}$, $\href{//huggingface.co/datasets/Sizhe-Chen/Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct-SecPO-trainset}{\text{training data}}$ (with optimized injections from AT), and $\href{//huggingface.co/Sizhe-Chen/Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct-SecPO}{\text{model}}$.

AI.tldr: SecPO combines a principled loss for prompt-injection defence with an adversarial training pipeline that synthesises strong injections. Compared with Meta-SecAlign, it sharply cuts adaptive attack success rates while keeping benign utility, and the SecPO-trained Qwen3.6-27B reaches 8.8% AgentDojo ASR@800 against 78.8% for Meta-SecAlign.
AI.motivation: Meta-SecAlign, the best-defended LLM, is trained with the DPO loss yet still reaches attack success rates approaching 100% under adaptive prompt injections, partly because DPO anchors the model to an insecure undefended reference and partly because it trains on weak simulated attacks.
AI.method: The authors argue that an idealised injection-invariant, utility-preserving reference model can be approximated from its output distribution during training, which motivates the SecPO loss. They also build an efficient adversarial training pipeline that synthesises strong injected inputs (best@240) and trains the model on them.
AI.result: Adversarial training reduces attack success rates by 1.5 to 14.5 times across three state-of-the-art adaptive attacks compared with Meta-SecAlign, and the SecPO loss reduces them by a further 2.4 to 4.6 times relative to the DPO loss. In agentic workflows, SecPO plus AT on Qwen3.6-27B gives 8.8% against 78.8% AgentDojo ASR@800 for Meta-SecAlign under the AttackerMovesSecond attack, with no noticeable reduction in benign utility across nine benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Replacing DPO with a principled loss and training on stronger adversarial examples yields markedly more secure agents without sacrificing utility; code, training data and the model are released.

title: AutoAnalysis: An automated, self-updating meta-analysis of human-AI collaboration
comment: Please visit this http URL to explore the data and view the most recent results
summary: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more capable and widely used, understanding when and how humans should work with these systems is becoming increasingly important. However, the empirical evidence in this space offers conflicting recommendations, which leaves individuals and organizations without clear guidance on when to combine human and AI capabilities. Existing meta-analyses can help reconcile these findings, but they require substantial manual effort and cannot readily incorporate new evidence as it emerges. To address this challenge, we introduce AutoAnalysis: an automated, self-updating meta-analysis of when humans and AI work better together, and when they work better alone. AutoAnalysis' most recent run synthesizes 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers. Across this body of work, we found that, on average, human-AI combinations performed significantly better than humans alone, but they performed significantly worse than the better of humans or AI alone. These findings highlight the important distinction between improving human performance and achieving human-AI synergy and underscore the need to evaluate collaboration against both human and AI performance alone. As new studies emerge, AutoAnalysis will integrate their findings into the meta-analysis, providing cumulative evidence about when humans and AI perform better together and how human-AI performance varies across AI agents, tasks, and processes.

AI.tldr: AutoAnalysis is an automated, self-updating meta-analysis of human-AI collaboration whose latest run synthesises 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers. On average human-AI combinations beat humans working alone but perform worse than the better of humans or AI working alone.
AI.motivation: Empirical evidence on when humans and generative AI should work together is conflicting, and existing meta-analyses require substantial manual effort and cannot readily incorporate new studies as they appear.
AI.method: The authors build AutoAnalysis, an automated meta-analysis that continually integrates new studies, synthesising effect sizes across papers and comparing human-AI, human-only and AI-only performance.
AI.result: The most recent run synthesises 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers. On average, human-AI combinations perform significantly better than humans alone but significantly worse than the better of humans or AI alone.
AI.conclusion: Improving human performance differs from achieving human-AI synergy, so collaboration should be evaluated against both human and AI performance alone; AutoAnalysis will keep integrating new evidence as it emerges.

title: Hierarchical World Models with Implicit Dynamics
summary: Planning with world models enables test-time adaptation for embodied agents, offering superior generalization over direct policy learning. However, long-horizon tasks remain hindered by cumulative errors and search complexity. Existing hierarchical methods often use rigid macro-actions or latent skills, leading to brittle representations and limited fine-grained control. We introduce ID-WM (Implicit Dynamics World Models), a hierarchical world model that decouples state-space reachability from local control. Our framework utilizes a high-level model to sample feasible transitions across the state manifold and a low-level world model as an inverse dynamics solver to ground these transitions into precise actions. This allows the planner to identify reachable subgoals without being constrained by low-level execution details. By prioritizing local physical feasibility over global behavioral patterns, ID-WM synthesizes novel long-horizon plans from short segments, transcending the specific behavioral modes seen during training. We demonstrate its effectiveness across three navigation and manipulation suites, achieving a 38.5% improvement over state-of-the-art policy and diffusion-based planners. Crucially, by leveraging this hierarchical structure to mitigate compounding errors, our approach yields a 135% performance gain over single-level world model MPC, particularly in complex, unseen configurations for long-horizon tasks. Videos can be viewed at this https URL

AI.tldr: ID-WM is a hierarchical world model that decouples state-space reachability from local control, letting a planner find reachable subgoals and synthesise long-horizon plans from short segments. It reports a 38.5% improvement over state-of-the-art policy and diffusion-based planners and a 135% gain over single-level world model MPC.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon planning with world models is hindered by cumulative errors and search complexity, while existing hierarchical methods rely on rigid macro-actions or latent skills that yield brittle representations and limited fine-grained control.
AI.method: A high-level model samples feasible transitions across the state manifold, and a low-level world model acts as an inverse dynamics solver that grounds these transitions into precise actions, prioritising local physical feasibility over global behavioural patterns.
AI.result: Across three navigation and manipulation suites, ID-WM achieves a 38.5% improvement over state-of-the-art policy and diffusion-based planners and a 135% performance gain over single-level world model MPC, particularly in complex, unseen configurations for long-horizon tasks.
